posters.title: Schadenfreude in the Digital Public Sphere: A cross-national and decade-long analysis of Facebook news engagement
posters.authors: Nouar Aldahoul, Hazem Ibrahim, Majid Mahmutoğlu, Hajra Tarar, Fareed Zaffar, Talal Rahwan and Yasir Zaki
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Schadenfreude affective polarization online news engagement political ideology social media reactions
posters.abstract: Schadenfreude, or the pleasure derived from others’ misfortunes, has become a visible and performative feature of online news engagement, yet little is known about its prevalence, dynamics, or social patterning. We examine schadenfreude on Facebook over a ten-year period across nine major news publishers in the United States, the United Kingdom, and India (one left-leaning, one right-leaning, and one centrist per country). Using a combination of human annotation and machine-learning classification, we identify posts describing misfortune and detect schadenfreude in nearly one million associated comments. We find that while sadness and anger dominate reactions to misfortune posts, laughter and amusement form a substantial and patterned minority. Schadenfreude is most frequent in moralized and political contexts, higher among right-leaning audiences, and more pronounced in India than in the United States or United Kingdom. Temporal and regression analyses further reveal that schadenfreude generally increases when groups are politically out of power, but these patterns differ across party-lines. Together, our findings move beyond anecdotal accounts to map schadenfreude as a dynamic, context-dependent feature of digital discourse, revealing how it evolves over time and across ideological and cultural divides.

posters.title: How Washington Frames China: A Bipartisan NLP Analysis of Congressional Discourse and Strategic Signaling
posters.authors: Enyu Li
posters.keywords: U.S.–China Strategic Competition Computational Text Analysis Natural Language Processing (NLP) Strategic Framing TF-IDF
posters.abstract: China has emerged as the central long-term strategic challenge shaping contemporary U.S. foreign policy debates. While a broad bipartisan consensus exists in Washington that China represents a major competitor to American power and influence, important differences remain in how political elites interpret, frame, and communicate the nature of that challenge. These differences are reflected not only in policy proposals but also in the language and narratives used by lawmakers in public discourse. Understanding these rhetorical patterns is critical, as elite framing shapes policy priorities, signals strategic intentions, and influences how allies and adversaries interpret U.S. behavior in the international system. This study analyzes China-related discourse in the 2025 U.S. Congressional Record using computational text analysis and interpretable natural language processing methods. Rather than focusing solely on legislative outcomes or voting behavior, the project treats congressional speeches as a central venue through which strategic narratives are constructed, contested, and communicated. Elite rhetoric serves as a bridge between underlying geopolitical conditions and policy action, making it a valuable empirical source for understanding U.S. strategic thinking. To construct the dataset, I collected official Congressional Record text using the GovInfo system and filtered speeches using a validated keyword dictionary capturing China-related ref- erences (e.g., China, PRC, CCP, Beijing, Xi Jinping, Taiwan). From over one thousand con- gressional documents, I extracted thousands of sentences explicitly referencing China, forming a sentence-level corpus that isolates China-specific discourse while minimizing noise from un- related legislative content. Each sentence was labeled by party affiliation, enabling systematic comparison of Democratic and Republican framing patterns. The analytical framework combines computational and interpretive approaches. A shared TF–IDF model was applied to the full corpus to identify salient terms and compare lexical emphasis across parties within a common feature space. Party-level differences in term impor- tance were then computed to detect systematic divergence in rhetorical framing. This method prioritizes transparency and interpretability, allowing quantitative findings to be directly linked to policy-relevant narratives rather than relying on opaque machine learning models. The results reveal both convergence and divergence in how China is framed across the U.S. political system. Across parties, congressional discourse is strongly dominated by regime- centered and security-oriented language. High-salience terms emphasize the Chinese Commu- nist Party, national security risks, military competition, and long-term strategic rivalry, sug- gesting that China is widely conceptualized as a systemic challenger rather than a conventional economic partner. Despite this shared recognition, important partisan differences emerge in emphasis and interpretation. Democratic discourse tends to frame China in the context of global leader- 1 12th International Conference on Computational Social Science IC2S2 July 28-31, 2026, Burlington, VT, United States ship, institutional engagement, and soft power competition. Language associated with inter- national cooperation, development assistance, and global influence suggests a strategy cen- tered on maintaining U.S. credibility and presence in the international system. Republicans, in contrast, more frequently frame China as an ideological and security threat, emphasizing domestic vulnerability, decoupling, legislative oversight, and confrontation with authoritarian influence. These differences reflect distinct strategic logics: one prioritizing global leadership and coalition-based competition, and the other emphasizing resilience, sovereignty, and con- tainment. Importantly, the analysis shows that bipartisan disagreement is not primarily about whether China is a strategic challenge, but about how power, values, and security should be balanced in responding to that challenge. These framing differences have direct implications for policy signaling, alliance coordination, and the credibility of long-term U.S. strategy. Divergent narra- tives may introduce uncertainty into U.S. commitments, potentially influencing how third-party states position themselves within global alignment dynamics. Beyond descriptive analysis, this framework has practical applications for policymakers, researchers, and institutions. By systematically tracking how China is framed in legislative discourse, the approach enables identification of areas where bipartisan consensus may support durable policy and where ideological divergence may constrain action. The framework also supports longitudinal analysis, allowing future research to monitor how congressional attitudes toward China evolve across electoral cycles and geopolitical shifts. Ultimately, this study demonstrates how computational text analysis can provide empirical insight into elite political communication and strategic signaling. By combining interpretable NLP methods with policy-oriented interpretation, the project offers a scalable and transparent tool for analyzing how domestic political narratives shape foreign policy competition in an era of great-power rivalry.

posters.title: The Geometry of Gridlock: Tracking Congressional Polarization with Graph Attention Networks
posters.authors: Jacob Crainic
posters.keywords: congressional polarization graph attention networks spectral analysis co-voting networks computational social science
posters.abstract: Congressional polarization is widely documented but almost exclusively measured through ideological scaling, which misses the relational structure of legislative cooperation. We construct co-voting networks for every U.S. House Congress from the 100th through the 118th and analyze their spectral properties over 36 years, revealing a 94% collapse in algebraic connectivity that standard measures fail to capture. A Graph Attention Network augmented with temporal attention achieves a mean AUC of 0.908 for defection prediction on held-out Congresses and identifies 12 of 20 McCarthy Speaker crisis holdouts from network position alone. We introduce the Structural Resilience Index, which formalizes a regime change in the network's capacity for self-repair: post-9/11 bipartisan cooperation fully recovered, while post-Tea Party damage proved permanent. These findings reframe polarization as a topological phenomenon concentrated in the elimination of fewer than 10% of House members who maintained cross-partisan bridges.

posters.title: Nationalization with evidence from municipal public participation
posters.authors: Chang Ge, Jenna Bednar, Yanna Krupnikov and Sabina Tomkins
posters.keywords: nationalization of politics local governance public comment political polarization natural language processing
posters.abstract: City council meetings are vital sites for civic participation where the public can speak directly to their local government, but they are also potential sites for the nationalization of politics. As national divides increasingly shape how people interpret political conflict, local public comment periods may become venues where nationally salient issues are raised and reframed as local demands. By addressing city officials and calling on them to take action, public commenters can potentially influence policy decisions spanning a broad range of concerns, from housing, to sustainability, to social justice, even when those concerns originate in broader national debates. Yet studies of these meetings have often been limited by the availability of large-scale, geographically diverse data, making it difficult to systematically assess when and how national issues enter local political spaces. Relying on local governments' increasing use of YouTube and other technologies to archive their public meetings, we propose a framework that characterizes comments along two dimensions: the local concerns where concerns are situated (e.g., housing, election administration), and the societal concerns raised (e.g., functional democracy, anti-racism). Based on a large record of public comments we collect from 15 cities in Michigan, we produce data-driven taxonomies of the local concerns and societal concerns that these comments cover, and employ machine learning methods to scaleably apply our taxonomies across the entire dataset. We then demonstrate how our framework allows us to examine the salient local concerns and societal concerns that arise in our data, as well as how these aspects interact, providing leverage to assess the extent to which local political participation reflects broader processes of nationalization.

posters.title: From Childhood Plans to Adult Lives: Aspiration–Realization Gaps at Age 25 in a 1958 British Cohort
posters.authors: Zerui Tian
posters.keywords: life course aspiration–realization gaps childhood essays large language models longitudinal cohort study
posters.abstract: Children often describe vivid images of adult work and family life long before these outcomes can be observed, yet we know little about how such early plans align with later realized lives. This study benchmarks aspiration–realization gaps by linking age-11 essays from the 1958 National Child Development Study to realized partnership, marriage, employment, and fertility outcomes at age 25 (linked sample size 7,281). Essays were annotated with a large language model to extract whether respondents imagined specific age-25 outcomes. Imagined indicators were compared with observed outcomes using mismatch rates and direction-of-error measures, and heterogeneity was assessed by sex, father’s social class, and cognitive test scores measured by age 11. Early-life narratives substantially overpredicted family transitions by age 25. In comparable samples with both imagined and realized measures observed, mismatch rates were high for partnership (0.639), marriage (0.665), and having children (0.574), while employment mismatch was lower (0.245). Errors were dominated by false positives, indicating that children often described normative milestones that did not occur by age 25. For fertility counts, respondents overpredicted the number of children by 1.07 on average, with a mean absolute error of 1.37. Mismatch patterns were socially patterned, with higher employment mismatch among women and higher mismatch in having children among men. These results quantify aspiration–realization gaps from late childhood to early adulthood and show how historical narratives annotated by LLMs can be used to measure early life plans at scale. The findings suggest that childhood depictions of adulthood reflect shared cultural scripts and timing expectations, offering a new lens on stratified life-course trajectories.

posters.title: The Governability Gap: Structural Limits of Algorithmic Governance
posters.authors: Nadia Urban and Piotr Sochoń
posters.keywords: governability algorithmic governance machine learning social media content moderation
posters.abstract:
Social media platforms increasingly govern public life through algorithmic systems that rank, recommend, and moderate content at scale (Bucher, 2018; Gillespie, 2020; Just & Latzer, 2017). Over the past decade, extensive regulatory and technical effort has been devoted to making these systems accountable: transparency obligations, explainability tools, algorithmic audits, and risk-based frameworks have proliferated (Barredo Arrieta et al., 2020; Hüllermeier & Waegeman, 2021; Seyfert, 2022). Yet persistent governance controversies remain: moderation failures recur, user adaptation proliferates, and algorithmic outcomes resist stabilization. We argue that the central problem is not regulatory lag or inadequate enforcement, but structurally limited governability: a bounded capacity to steer machine learning systems operating in dynamic, open social environments. We term this structural condition the governability gap.

Analytical Framework

Drawing on Kooiman’s (2008) systems-theoretical notion of governability – the capacity of governing arrangements to direct systems toward intended outcomes – we integrate critical platform studies with core properties of machine learning systems. We conceptualize social media algorithms as multi-objective optimization systems operating under partial observability, embedded in feedback-coupled social environments, and subject to non-stationary data distributions. We analyze governability constraints across three stages of the machine learning lifecycle – design, training, and deployment – which correspond to dominant governance approaches. Intentionalist approaches, such as China’s algorithm filing system, address what algorithms are designed to do: embedding values, specifying objectives, or mandating harm-reduction targets. These face a structural limit: social media algorithms are multi-objective optimization systems operating in dynamic, feedback-rich environments where competing logics (regulatory, economic, affective) are compressed into a shared optimization space. Objectives cannot be stabilized in practice even when formally specified, because user behavior, advertiser pressure, and regulatory priorities continuously reshape the optimization landscape through hidden feedback loops (Bottou et al., 2012; Sculley et al., 2015). Intentionality becomes distributed rather than centralized, limiting steerability at the level of system objectives.

Essentialist approaches, such as EU’s General Data Protection Regulation, govern what algorithms are: their structure, training data, and internal logic. Explainable AI (XAI), auditing tools, and transparency obligations fall here. We draw on recent impossibility results (Bilodeau et al., 2024) instability findings (Fisher et al., 2018) to show that even technically sophisticated explainability methods provide backward-looking, model-relative accounts of past behavior. Because supervised learning captures correlations rather than causal structures, interpretability does not imply controllability. Legibility improves without increasing steerability.

Behavioristic approaches, such as EU’s Digital Service Act govern what algorithms produce, regulating outputs, contesting decisions, and deploying abstention mechanisms. These encounter the most acute limits because deployment is where technical indeterminacy meets social openness. Machine learning models are closed with respect to their representational space (Zhou, 2022) but deployed in open social media environments subject to data drift, concept drift, and aleatoric uncertainty that cannot be eliminated through retraining (Pelosi et al., 2025; Veprikov et al., 2025). Under conditions of forced decisiveness at scale, irreducible uncertainty is structural rather than transitional Across these stages, governability constraints accumulate rather than cancel out (fig 1). The result is a systematic gap between governance ambition and achievable system steering.

System-level effects

The governability gap becomes visible not only in technical failures but in emergent behavioral adaptations. Users respond to perceived algorithmic thresholds by restructuring communicative environments: anticipatory self-censorship, strategic linguistic substitution (algospeak), and pre-emptive content modification reflect attempts to navigate uncertain moderation boundaries.These behavioral responses are not anomalies but systemic manifestations of bounded steerability in open machine learning systems.

On Xiaohongshu, female users routinely apply graphic overlays (stickers, blur patches) to images of their own bodies prior to posting, obscuring armpits, stomachs, and belly buttons, to preempt algorithmic demotion under China's co-governance regime (fig 2). Algospeak – the deliberate linguistic substitution of terms to evade automated detection while remaining intelligible to human audiences (Steen et al., 2023) – illustrates a parallel dynamic at the level of language. Users treat the algorithm as the primary audience, modifying expression to achieve machine illegibility. On Polish social media, the neologism "Żymianin" substitutes for "Żyd" ("Jew") through phonetic manipulation (fig 3); while creators frame this as risk-avoidance, the term appears almost exclusively in derogatory discourse.

Contribution

This paper offers following contributions to computational social science. Theoretically, it introduces the governability gap as a structural property of machine learning systems embedded in dynamic social environments, distinguishing it from regulatory lag or implementation failure. It maps governability constraints onto the machine learning lifecycle, demonstrating how the gap emerges from multi-objective optimization, feedback coupling, and non-stationarity. Finally, it connects machine learning theory with platform governance scholarship, offering a unified framework for analyzing algorithmic accountability limits without reducing them to institutional inadequacy or technical deficiency. Rather than treating recurring governance controversies as failures, this framework reframes them as structurally produced outcomes of governing stochastic optimization systems operating within open social worlds.

posters.title: Hedging the Black Box: A Feasibility Study of Financial Risk Transfer for AI Adoption via Generative Agent Simulation
posters.authors: Yixuan Yuan, Dedai Wei, Chudong Qian, Ziyue Lin, Yuheng Zhao and Xinwu Ye
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: AI governance LLM-driven Agent-Based Social Simulation AI Risk Hedging Financial Instruments Human Wellbeing
posters.abstract: The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) tools has demonstrated immense potential to enhance societal well-being and operational efficiency. However, the ``black box'' nature and inherent unreliability of modern AI systems, typified by large language models (LLMs), have created a significant barrier to entry. Many enterprises remain hesitant to integrate these tools deeply into their workflows due to concerns about unpredictable losses and liability. While existing technical solutions strive to enhance model reliability, they often struggle to effectively mitigate the ``long-tail'' risks associated with real-world deployment. In this paper, we introduce a socio-economic framework that allows enterprises to mitigate the stochastic risks of AI adoption by leveraging financial hedging instruments. To validate it, we introduce an LLM-driven Agent-Based Social Simulation (LABSS) system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our simulation by benchmarking it against established economic and sociological baseline theories, as well as comparing it with traditional agent-based modeling (ABM). Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed financial framework effectively mitigates individual risk, thereby significantly accelerating the aggregate adoption rate of AI tools and promoting overall social productivity.

posters.title: Gendered Signals in Adolescents’ Writing: An Embedding-Based Index and Associations with Later-life Outcomes for a UK Cohort
posters.authors: Zerui Tian
posters.keywords: gender atypicality text-as-data cohort studies life course computational sociolinguistics
posters.abstract: Using the 1958 British National Child Development Study, I construct a language-based index of gender atypicality from 10,507 age-11 essays imagining life at 25 and link it to adult trajectories. After masking explicit gender cues with a constrained large language model, essays are embedded with a transformer and used to train a sex classifier; the calibrated probability of the non-true sex defines a continuous atypicality score. Adjusted regression models show that higher atypicality predicts greater likelihood of managerial/technical class at ages 33 and 50, slightly poorer midlife health and wellbeing, lower odds of ever marrying, and higher odds of ever having a same-sex partner, with modest, sex-differentiated effect sizes.

posters.title: Beyond Left vs Right: Profiling User Activity Patterns with Two-Dimensional Political Compass Self-Reports on Reddit
posters.authors: Yukun Yang, Yijing Chen and Lu Xian
posters.keywords: Political Leaning Political Compass Reddit Ideology Measurement User Activity
posters.abstract: This paper addresses the trade-off between scalability and construct validity in measuring political ideology on social media using computational approaches and self-report surveys, and the limitations of one-dimensional ideology measurement (e.g., Left versus Right). Leveraging Reddit users' self-reports from the Political Compass Test, we collect a large-scale dataset of 210k users' ideological labels along both the social axis (Authoritarian or Libertarian) and the economic axis (Left or Right). Based on their submissions across all subreddits from 2013 to 2021, we ask: 1) which ideological axis is more salient in analyzing users' activity patterns, and 2) what nuances in user activity patterns can 2D ideological labels capture but not 1D labels? Analyzing subreddit-level user ideological compositions and network-level ideological communities, our analysis finds greater ideological variation on the subreddit level along the economic axis and lower ideological extremity in larger subreddits. We highlight the added value of using two-dimensional labels by demonstrating that low-prevalence ideological subreddits (e.g., AuthLeft) are more likely to be overshadowed, and that Auth and Right ideological communities outstandingly differ from their 2D subordinates. Together, our study not only showcases a novel approach to ideological mapping using large-scale user self-reports but also underscores the importance of using granular, multidimensional political labels to analyze user activity patterns by highlighting specific ideological groups' representations.

posters.title: Inflation in the Spotlight: Salience and Populist Support
posters.authors: Jeremy Fang
posters.keywords: Issue Salience Google Trends Digital Trace Data Electoral Behavior Populism
posters.abstract: Populism has recently regained political prominence in several democratic countries, yet objective economic conditions alone cannot fully explain this trend. Motivated by this observation, this paper examines whether pre-election public salience of inflation is associated with support for populist candidates in U.S. presidential elections. Using a state–election-year panel from 2004 to 2024, I combine state-level election results, candidate populism scores, and Google Trends data to construct an inflation salience measure, defined as the maximum within-state standardized search intensity for “inflation” during the three months before Election Day. I estimate OLS models with state fixed effects and state-clustered standard errors, controlling for unemployment, nominal GDP, and the annual national inflation rate. The results show that higher inflation salience is positively and significantly associated with populist support: a 1-standard-deviation increase in salience corresponds to roughly a 0.10 increase in the weighted populism score. Overall, the findings suggest that public attention to economic issues is closely related to electoral outcomes.

posters.title: Tracing Dual Strategy by Authoritarian Regime: Evidence from North Korea under Kim Jong-un
posters.authors: Songhyeon Kim and Jaehyuk Park
posters.keywords: Authoritarian regime Dual strategy Policy discourse Network analysis North Korea
posters.abstract: This study examines authoritarian resilience as a dual strategy in North Korea under Kim Jong un by analyzing how official discourse combines durable regime control with selective policy adjustment. Using the Korea Institute for National Unification database of 1,579 titles from Kim Jong un public activity press releases through 2025, we preprocess the text, apply TF IDF, and build a word co occurrence network with 292 nodes and 1,085 edges. We identify the macro structure of discourse with Leiden clustering and modularity, interpret cluster substance with centrality measures, and track continuity and change over time using a Jaccard based river network approach. Results show a stable control and legitimation core anchored in party authority, political organization, and ritualized events that remains central and consistently present across years. In contrast, adaptive domains linked to governance performance, including industry, livelihood, science, youth mobilization, and housing, are selectively reconfigured over time, with sharper fluctuations around 2018 indicating greater flexibility in developmental and welfare oriented emphasis. Military discourse also evolves through strategic layering, shifting from early maritime focus toward rapid strike capacity and later reintroducing maritime power narratives, while organizational and legitimacy themes persist throughout. Overall, North Korean policy discourse under Kim Jong un is best understood as patterned coexistence of stability and adaptation, where major environmental shifts reorganize the salience and structure of adaptive policy domains without displacing the regime’s enduring legitimizing center.

posters.title: #MakeBeefGreatAgain: Politicized Health Lifestyle Discourse and Agenda Melding in Early #MAHA Discourse
posters.authors: Haoning Xue, Yue Li, Andy King and Ben Lyons
posters.keywords: agenda-setting entity-targeted sentiment analysis public health discourse social media analytics structural topic modeling
posters.abstract: This study presents a large-scale cross-platform analysis of the early diffusion of #MakeAmericaHealthyAgain (#MAHA) during the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign. Analyzing N = 41,819 posts from seven platforms, we identify two levels of agenda melding. First, public discourse diverges from the campaign agenda: only 18.4% of posts reference stated campaign priorities, while discussions increasingly center on politicized healthy lifestyle themes. Second, platforms exhibit distinct thematic and evaluative patterns, indicating that agenda construction is further shaped by platform-specific communities. Overall, #MAHA functions less as a unified campaign agenda than as a flexible discursive organizer across fragmented online environments.

posters.title: Selective exposure and platform choice - a cross-platform study
posters.authors: Zoltán Kmetty, Ádám Stefkovics and Michelle Horváth
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Selective exposure news diet polarization multiplatform data data donation
posters.abstract: This study utilizes a data-donation framework to provide a rare multi-layered analysis by integrating digital trace data from three distinct platforms: Google page visits, YouTube watch history, and Facebook interactions (N=758). Using a hybrid classification approach (LLMs, manual labeling, and audience-based slant mapping), we quantify selective exposure across varying technical architectures. Our results demonstrate that while Google browsing remains relatively balanced, Facebook drives significant bimodal polarization. Crucially, the analysis reveals a cross-platform reinforcement effect, indicating that polarized consumption patterns on social media extend into general web browsing and YouTube consumption

posters.title: What counts as ‘educational inequality’ in the UK Parliament: Operationalising Hansard corpora for education policy research
posters.authors: Elena Minina
posters.keywords: educational inequality parliamentary discourse computational text analysis corpus linguistics Hansard critical policy analysis
posters.abstract: This presentation examines how educational inequality is defined and rendered governable within UK parliamentary debate. Drawing on a broader study that developed a computational corpus of Hansard debates between 2000 and 2025, it analyses how inequalities are constructed, stabilised and prioritised in the House of Commons and the House of Lords. The study is grounded in a cultural-sociological understanding of inequality as not merely reflected in measurable outcomes but actively produced through institutional practices of classification, evaluation and comparison, and politically constituted before it becomes governable. Parliamentary debate is treated as a central arena where inequalities are made visible, morally framed and translated into policy concerns. Methodologically, the project combines critical policy analysis with large-scale computational text analysis in R. Computational mapping of patterns of salience, association and recurrence serves as a heuristic for identifying discursive regularities beyond close reading. The analysis identifies nine recurring inequality dimensions and reveals a hierarchy of governability. System-level inequalities—particularly socio-economic disadvantage and attainment gaps—dominate parliamentary discourse because they align with existing data infrastructures and accountability mechanisms characteristic of neoliberal education governance. By contrast, institutional micro-processes, along with cognitive and emotional dimensions of inequality remain marginal, suggesting that parliamentary discourse privileges measurable outputs over generative mechanisms and reflects a governing rationality centred on comparability and performance. The presentation concludes by highlighting the methodological potential of repurposing institutional texts as computational corpora for critical policy analysis.

posters.title: VideoNorms: Benchmarking VideoLLMs for Socio-Cultural Norm Mining and Understanding
posters.authors: Nikhil Reddy Varimalla, Yunfei Xu, Meng Fan Wang, Arkadiy Saakyan and Smaranda Muresan
posters.keywords: social norms cultural norms video analysis LLM multimodal AI
posters.abstract: Video large language models (VideoLLMs) are LLM models with sufficient long-context ingestion ability to enable processing of video inputs. These models have been evaluated on general object/action recognition (Xu et al., 2016), temporal reasoning (Li and et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2021; Jang et al., 2017), or narrative understanding (Tapaswi et al.. 2016), showing promising performance. However, it remains questionable whether such models could be useful beyond surface-level analysis performed by computational social scientists, such as mining and analysis of cultural norms from videos. In addition, it is unclear whether model biases would preclude the usage of the model in less-represented cultural contexts. In the textual modality, frameworks for evaluating cultural competence are largely based on understanding social norms - rules of thumb for human behavior, such as "It is rude to run a blender at 5am" (Forbes et al., 2020; Emelin et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Ziems and et al., 2023) in differing cultural contexts Shi et al. (2024); Huang and Yang (2023); Li et al. (2023); CH-Wang et al. (2023). Expanding on these approaches, we propose to evaluate the competence of VideoLLMs for cultural analysis through benchmarking their understanding of cultural norms: societal rules or standards that "delineate an accepted and appropriate behavior within a culture" (American Psychological Association, 2025). For example, does the video language model understand that when two people introduce themselves and shake hands, they adhere to the greeting norms in US culture? This is particularly challenging in the multimodal context, where understanding whether a cultural norm is present and adhered to requires correct interpretation of implicit meaning expressed through both nonverbal cues (e.g., gaze, gestures) (Pang et al., 2024; Hessels et al., 2025), and verbal features (e.g., sarcasm) (Rakov and Rosen- berg, 2013; Tepperman et al., 2006). Additional challenge stems from the cross-cultural aspect, due to the documented differences in norms and values across cultures (Inglehart, 2018; Hofst- ede, 1984; Gelfand et al., 2011). We create VIDEONORMS, a dataset to benchmark understanding of cultural norms from videos by VideoLLMs in two cultural contexts: US and China. The benchmark was created using a human-AI collaboration pipeline (c.f. Figure 1): (1) select clips from eight US and Chinese television shows spanning both formal and informal contexts; (2) use a teacher VideoLLM (Gemini-2.0-Pro DeepMind (2024)) to extract candidate norm category, adherence/violation, and verbal/non-verbal evidence; (3) refine the model-generated data by obtaining edits from 3 trained annotators with a relevant cultural background on each instance. To construct a comparable cross-cultural benchmark for cultural norm recognition, we selected eight popular television shows, four from the US and four from China, representing both formal (workplace) and informal social settings across drama and comedy genres. For each show, we sample 15-second clips as input for the video language model. The video language model is then prompted to identify relevant cultural norms applicable to the clip and determine if adherence or violation of the norm occurred, as well as other items (see Table 1). Our prompt for cultural norm annotation was inspired by speech act theory (Searle, 1969; Austin, 1 PAGE 212th International Conference on Computational Social Science $IC^{2}S^{2}$ July 28-31, 2026, Burlington, VT, United States 1962) and based on prior work on norm understanding (Li et al., 2023) and the Linguistic Data Consortium taxonomy (Linguistic Data Consortium, 2022). The prompt was also adapted in Mandarin. See full prompts in Table 6 Each candidate annotation generated above was further verified by 3 annotators. We ensured that each annotator's relevant mono-cultural identity by confirming their country of residence, primary language, mono-cultural self-identification, earliest language in life, and other factors. Annotators validated or modified each field in Table by checking whether the selected timestamps isolate the correct behavior, confirming the norm category, and ensuring the verbal and nonverbal evidence supports the adherence or violation label. Each annotator was first trained on initial 20 instances, where their answered were reviewed to ensure high-quality completion and instruction following. All annotators were fairly compensated above the local minimum wage guidelines. See a screenshot of the interface and instructions in Figure 2 Figure 3 compares the teacher model's initial outputs with annotator refinements for both US and Chinese shows. Analysis of rates of changes implemented by annotators revealed a discrepancy between model performance in US and Chinese contexts. The VideoLLM was relatively accurate in the US context, as measured by combined annotator change percentages (total number of fields across all norms and all annotators that have been changed divided by the total number of fields) ranging from 18.28% to 26.04%. In contrast, combined annotator change percentages for Chinese shows were notably higher, ranging from 42.35% to 53.39%, signifying a higher need to change the initial VideoLLM annotation. This extends the previous findings in that LLMs perform more effectively in WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) cultural contexts (Mihalcea et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) to the video modality. Comparing inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss's (Fleiss et al., 1971), c.f. Table 2) across genre (comedy/drama) and setting (workplace/informal), both US and Chinese subsets display higher agreement for workplace drama shows (Suits $k=0.76$ and Best Partner $k=0.45)$, while showing lower agreement on comedy shows. Unlike for US shows, the agreement for Chinese shows in informal settings yielded lower agreement than workplace settings ($\kappa=0.27-0.33$ vs. $k=0.42-0.45$), aligning with findings conform with psychology studies Sino-US workplace flexibility (Lai et al., 2022; Wei and Royle, 2024). Based on the collected data, we create a VIDEONORMS benchmark to evaluate open-soruce VideoLLMs, consisting of two tasks. Task 1 (Adherence/Violation Prediction): given a video segment, transcript, norm category, and a specific norm, the model predicts whether the behavior adheres to or violates that norm (binary classification). Adherence labels were determined by majority vote among annotators sharing identical category-norm pairs. Cases with two annotations and without clear majority agreement are excluded, though these represent a negligible portion of the dataset. Task 2: (i) predict Adherence/Violation and (ii) generate (a) verbal evidence referencing the spoken content (e.g., quoted phrases), and (b) nonverbal evidence referencing visual social cues (e.g., gaze, gesture, distance, facial expression). We benchmark recent commonly used open-weight VideoLLMs: LLAVA-Next-Video (Zhang et al., 2024), LLAVA-OneVision (Li et al., 2024), InternVL-3 (Zhu et al., 2025), InternVL-3.5, (Wang et al., 2025), Qwen2-VL (Wang and et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-VL (Qwen et al., 2025), VideoChatR1 (Li et al., 2025). Our findings reveal that 1) detecting norm violation is more challenging than adherence; 2) models perform worse on Chinese culture compared to US; 3) Non-verbal evidence is harder to extract than verbal evidence, indicating a lack of understanding of non-verbal cues in videos; and 4) Models perform worse in formal cultural contexts (c.f. Table 4 (US) and Table 5 (CN)).

posters.title: Does Explanatory Complexity shape Opinion Dominance? The Role of Online Deliberation and Agent-Based Modeling
posters.authors: Shinichi Honna and Takashi Hashimoto
posters.keywords: discourse structure online persuasion ChangeMyView generative agent-based model Opinion Dynamics
posters.abstract: Online deliberation is often expected to support agreement, yet many discussions end with a few viewpoints becoming dominant. Prior work has mainly explained this through contact patterns and opinion-updating rules, but this leaves open how persuasion works when it depends on whether an explanation that links claims, reasons, and counterarguments is understandable and can be integrated. Using Reddit r/ChangeMyView (Winning Arguments corpus), we represent each comment as an RST-based discourse tree, identify issue-related units via TF–IDF, and examine labeled local interaction sequences. Persuasion is associated with a reorganization of explanation in which issue-related units become more strongly connected to surrounding material than in comparable non-persuasive or unlabeled cases, and outcomes are most likely when both participants tend to produce more complex discourse structures. Guided by these empirical patterns, we build an agent-based model where agents learn by structurally integrating issue-focused parts of others’ explanations and change opinion only when integration increases issue-centered connectivity; simulations show that differences across individuals in discourse-structural complexity amplify opinion dominance beyond what contact patterns alone produce.

posters.title: Counter-Storytelling in Racial Counterpublics: How Community Context Shapes Narrative Strategies on Reddit
posters.authors: Uma Sushmitha Gunturi, Jimin Mun, Maarten Sap, Long Le-Khac and Maria Antoniak
posters.keywords: counter-storytelling racial stereotypes computational narrative analysis online discourse Reddit
posters.abstract: When people challenge racial stereotypes online, their rhetorical and narrative strategies vary systematically by community context, speaker identity, and racial target group. We present a computational analysis of counter-storytelling across Reddit, developing a three-dimensional taxonomy (Narrative Position, Audience, and Identity) grounded in Critical Race Theory and narratology. Across 1,681 counter-stories in 192 communities, our framework reveals striking variation in how, to whom, and from whose perspective counter-stories are told. We also demonstrate that automated toxicity classifiers sometimes may penalize counter-stories over the stereotypical posts they respond to with direct implications for platform moderation.

posters.title: Agency Affiliation as Cultural Infrastructure in the VTuber Economy with Evidence on Exposure Amplification, Monetization Gaps, and Audience-Overlap Networks
posters.authors: Tomohiro Murakami and Mitsuo Yoshida
posters.keywords: VTubers creator economy platform labor cultural infrastructure audience-overlap networks
posters.abstract: We study how organizational intermediaries shape attention and income in the VTuber creator economy, framing agency affiliation as cultural infrastructure in platform labor markets that structures audience flows. We merge a community-edited roster with YouTube traces to build two partially overlapping panels (comments: 500 creators, 7.62M comment lines; live chat: 458 creators, 190.3M chat lines, 790k Super Chats, 7.20M membership events). Standardizing lifecycles into non-overlapping 50-upload bins, we compare gross volumes to per-user intensity and map audience-overlap networks (Simpson coefficients) for commenters and chatters. Agency-affiliated creators show large and persistent advantages in gross engagement and monetization (typically 40–60%), while per-user intensity is much closer, indicating that affiliation primarily amplifies reach rather than uniformly increasing relational intensity. Overlap networks reveal denser local clustering for agency creators, consistent with thicker spillover pathways. Some payment-propensity measures (e.g., Super Chat user ratios) differ more than membership ratios, suggesting limited, modality-specific credibility effects. The results make infrastructural power empirically legible for computational social science and inform governance debates on transparency in recommendation exposure, cross-promotion, and monetization terms.

posters.title: Multimodal Persuasion and the Attention–Action Gap in Digital Fundraising
posters.authors: Jin Ai and Erya Ouyang
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Multimodal Communication Attention–Action Gap Vision–Language Models Digital Fundraising Computational Social Science
posters.abstract: Digital fundraising increasingly relies on multimodal social media content, yet engagement metrics do not reliably translate into real-world contributions. This study examines the attention–action gap in national charitable campaigns by modeling how multimodal persuasion strategies influence donation outcomes. Drawing on rhetorical theory, we operationalize persuasion as configurations of ethos, pathos, logos, and kairos across textual and visual modalities. We analyze a longitudinal dataset of approximately 3.5 million Facebook posts spanning the past decade, linked to campaign-level donation indicators. Methodologically, we combine vision–language models for persuasion classification with Double Machine Learning to estimate causal effects on donation conversion. We also develop a domain-specific generative model to produce outcome-oriented fundraising posts conditioned on empirically effective configurations. By evaluating communication strategies against transaction-level outcomes rather than engagement alone, the study advances an impact-centered multimodal framework for computational social science and platform-mediated collective action.

posters.title: Making Identity Visible: Meme Communication and Intergroup Affect
posters.authors: Kei Ichikawa, Aoi Naito, Jiayu Chen and Kazutoshi Sasahara
posters.keywords: internet memes affective polarization social identity cues identity salience intergroup warmth platform design
posters.abstract:
Collective polarization refers to the division of society into antagonistic groups. Although often discussed in politics, its mechanisms are rooted in intergroup processes. Research shows that in-group bias—favoritism toward one's own group and derogation of out-groups—can increase antagonism, and even minimal or everyday identity distinctions (e.g., place of birth) can generate emotional distancing. In digital environments, such identity-based processes can be amplified on social media. Memes often function as markers of group membership; when they ridicule or stereotype out-groups, they reinforce in-group solidarity while normalizing hostility.

Beyond meme content itself, social media interface designs can also heighten social identity salience. For example, location-disclosure features on X make users' locations more visible, potentially enhancing memes’ identity-signaling function. By increasing the visibility of identity cues, such features can enhance the identity-signaling function of memes and amplify their intergroup effects. To examine this possibility, we conducted a survey experiment in the United States and Japan using regional identity. We tested whether exposure to memes that mock (or are mocked for) place of birth influences warmth toward in-groups and out-groups, and whether these effects are moderated by the visibility of the poster's place of birth.

The findings indicate that visibility of identity cues affected out-group warmth. In general, displaying identity cues decreased warmth. However, when the meme explicitly mocked the out-group, identity visibility increased warmth in the U.S.; no significant effect appeared in Japan. Overall, these results suggest a‘double-edged effect’of cross-cultural UI changes introduced by social media platforms. Such design features can both decrease and increase intergroup warmth in meme communication depending on contextual factors.

posters.title: Course-Skill Atlas: A national longitudinal dataset of skills taught in U.S. higher education curricula
posters.authors: Alireza Javadian Sabet, Sarah Bana, Renzhe Yu and Morgan Frank
posters.keywords: Skill Higher Education Future of Work Labor Economics Complexity
posters.abstract: Higher education plays a critical role in driving an innovative economy by equipping students with knowledge and skills demanded by the workforce. While researchers and practitioners have developed data systems to track detailed occupational skills, such as those established by the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL), much less effort has been made to document which of these skills are being developed in higher education at a similar granularity. Here, we fill this gap by presenting Course-Skill Atlas – a longitudinal dataset of skills inferred from over three million course syllabi taught at nearly three thousand U.S. higher education institutions. To construct Course-Skill Atlas, we apply natural language processing to quantify the alignment between course syllabi and detailed workplace activities (DWAs) used by the DOL to describe occupations. We then aggregate these alignment scores to create skill profiles for institutions and academic majors. Our dataset offers a large-scale representation of college education’s role in preparing students for the labor market. Overall, Course-Skill Atlas can enable new research on the source of skills in the context of workforce development and provide actionable insights for shaping the future of higher education to meet evolving labor demands, especially in the face of new technologies.

posters.title: Voices of the HPV Vaxx: Exploring Online Discourse Surrounding HPV Vaccination in the Philippines
posters.authors: Maria Jeriesa Osorio, Macon Reman and Allena Therese Juguilon
posters.keywords: hpv vaccine network analysis digital health communication cross-platform discourse health misinformation
posters.abstract:
Introduction The Human papillomavirus (HPV) is detected as the “most common sexually transmitted infectious organism” worldwide as of 2025,1 and persistent infection of this virus has been responsible for less than 700,000 new cancer cases per year among men and mostly among women.2–4 Limited access to HPV vaccination programs, inadequate screening services, and social and economic barriers affect LMICs disproportionately, like the Philippines. Besides access to services, the World Health Organization (WHO) insists that elevating public awareness and access to information are critical to cervical cancer prevention,4 especially in a time of massive reliance on the Internet, particularly social media, for health information-seeking.5,6 While the Internet serves as the primary source of HPV-related information, many young Filipino adults have low levels of awareness regarding HPV vaccine availability in the Philippines and think that HPV discussions are limited, thus contributing to low uptake.7,8

Given the indispensable role of social media in facilitating public awareness of health concerns, this study analyzed HPV vaccination discussions within the Philippine health communication landscape amid low vaccine uptake and rising cervical cancer incidence and mortality. By exploring HPV-related discussions on Facebook and TikTok through network analysis and topic modelling, this study particularly aimed to (1) identify key actors driving HPV vaccine-related discussions, (2) identify primary HPV vaccine-related themes using topic keywords, and (3) recommend health communication strategies to address HPV-related concerns. This effort addresses recommendations from previous HPV research on the compelling need for social network analyses to grasp information flow and detect potential agenda-setting9 and on the lack of social media studies on HPV vaccination—the health topic most associated with misinformation leading to vaccine hesitancy. 10,11

Methodology This study analyzes HPV discourse on Facebook and TikTok from January 2020 to July 2024. We scraped data using over 15 keywords (Table 1) on August 2024 using CrowdTangle and Apify for Facebook and TikTok, respectively. TikTok data was supplemented on February 2025. Preprocessing included deduplication, and removal of irrelevant and non-HPV content, resulting in a dataset focused on HPV vaccine discourse.

We conducted a network analysis where content served as the unit of analysis. Social networks were constructed from interactions between public Facebook and TikTok users; hence, a directional network was presumed. On Facebook, we mapped the flow of shared content by identifying source accounts (i.e., users initiating shares) and target accounts (i.e., users receiving the shared content). For TikTok, the sources were accounts using unique HPV-related hashtags, while the targets were other accounts employing the same hashtags. This analysis enabled the examination of information dissemination to identify the key opinion leaders about HPV in each platform.

We employed the BERTopic model, which uses a class-based term frequency-inverse document frequency (c-TF-IDF) algorithm to evaluate the importance of terms within a cluster, reduce the number of topics, and improve word coherence among topics to create term representations.12 We set the BERTopic language to “multilanguage” since the posts are in English and Filipino, and we performed data preprocessing before fitting the model.

Results On Facebook, the HPV network is a fragmented landscape where institutional authorities like the WHO and Department of Health (DOH), commercial entities like WatsonsPH, and advocacy groups like ProjectHPVFree operate in isolated clusters, often missing the synergy needed for a unified public health message (Figure 1). This gap allows for a diverse range of topics, from high-level awareness campaigns and school-based immunization programs to private sector initiatives using hashtags like #VaccineForTheWin; however, it also leaves room for the cross-sharing of vaccine safety concerns and misinformation, such as the #LearnTheRisk and #VaccineInjured trends linked to Gardasil. This environment is further complicated by an "information disorder" 10,11 that has penetrated the Philippine echo chamber, where top keywords regarding vaccine harm and safety, specifically concerning Gardasil 9, pose threats to vaccine confidence and may elevate vaccine hesitancy.

Meanwhile, the HPV network on TikTok is a vibrant, personality-driven ecosystem led by medical influencers and specialists like @dockilimanguru and @dr.aliah_obgyn, whose content naturally overlaps with broader skincare, beauty, and lifestyle clusters (Figure 2). The conversation here is deeply personal and educational, blending clinical advice on vaccination dosages and age requirements with raw, first-person narratives about symptoms like warts or the experience of undergoing smear tests and colposcopies. Moreover, this high level of interconnectivity expands awareness beyond reproductive health topics, however, the platform’s rapid rotation of content can also potentially hinder the permanence and clarity of HPV educational messaging.10,11

Conclusion The analysis of Facebook and TikTok networks reveals an overarching need for greater integration and coordination in HPV messaging in the Philippines. While Facebook displays siloed clusters of health institutions, commercial players, and advocacy groups, TikTok presents partially overlapping communities grounded in varying health and lifestyle interests. In both cases, the presence of influential accounts underscores the critical role of opinion leaders in shaping online discourse. To optimize public health outreach, it is imperative to foster cross-platform and cross-cluster partnerships while standardizing evidence-based content across all digital and community channels.

posters.title: Quantity vs. Quality: How Regulatory Reform Reshaped Risk Disclosure in Japan
posters.authors: Nobuhiro Aikawa and Mitsuo Yoshida
posters.keywords: Natural Language Processing Risk Disclosure Regulatory Intervention Regulatory Reform Information Overload
posters.abstract: This study evaluates Japan's 2019 FSA regulatory reform on corporate risk disclosures using natural language processing on nearly 20,000 firm-year observations (2015–2024). We reveal a distinct quantity-quality trade-off. Positively, the reform prompted structural improvements: firms significantly increased disclosure volume, updated text annually (reduced stickiness), and better aligned risks with management strategies (increased relevance). However, this expansion degraded communicability. Specificity and readability significantly declined, while boilerplate language persisted. These paradoxical outcomes suggest that while the principle-based reform improved what firms disclose, it failed to address how they communicate, risking "information overload" that raises processing costs for investors.

posters.title: Learning Policy Processes from Social Media
posters.authors: Misha Melnyk, Mitchell Dolny, Joshua Elkind, Michael Tjhin, Saisha Chebium, Blake Vanberlo, Annelise Russell, Michelle Buehlmann and Jesse Hoey
posters.keywords: policy transformer social media Twitter US Senate
posters.abstract: This study examines whether machine-learning models can reliably reproduce expert interpretations of political communication at scale. We study a large dataset of US senator postings on Twitter (1.68m tweets in total). Our objective is to develop an automated method to label senatorial posts as either in the problem or solution streams of Kingdon (2003). Two academic policy experts (also co-authors) labeled a subset of 3967 tweets as either problem, solution, or other, achieving a high internal consistency. We split off a subset of 500 tweets into a test set, with the remaining 3467 used for training. During development, this training set was further split by 60/20/20 proportions for fitting, validation, and development test sets. We investigated supervised learning methods for building problem/solution classifiers directly on the training set, evaluating their performance in terms of F1 score on the validation set, allowing us to rapidly iterate through models and hyperparameters, achieving an average weighted F1 score of over 0.8 across the three categories using a BERT model.

posters.title: Dynamic Treatment Effects of a Preventive Health App on Healthcare Utilization and Costs
posters.authors: Magdalena Fuchs, Elgar Fleisch, Florian von Wangenheim, Tobias Kowatsch, Peter J. Mucha and Mia Jovanova
posters.keywords: causal inference observational social data treatment effect heterogeneity preventive health digital trace data
posters.abstract: We evaluate the three-year impact of an insurer-provided preventive digital health intervention (DHI) by linking seven years of Swiss insurance claims data with time-stamped DHI adoption and engagement records. Using a quasi-experimental design (staggered-adoption difference-in-differences), we estimate the intervention's dynamic treatment effects on inpatient and outpatient utilization, as well as healthcare costs, quarterly up to three years post-adoption. DHI adoption is associated with significant reductions in inpatient care frequency and total claims costs per individual, with effects concentrated in the first 15 months and stronger among users with sustained early engagement. The study contributes to computational social science by identifying how individual technology adoption decisions translate into measurable changes in healthcare utilization and costs at population scale in a real-world institutional setting. Ongoing work builds on this foundation by integrating detailed digital trace data from the DHI with insurance records to examine behavioral mechanisms as well as applying causal forest models to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects.

posters.title: A Method and Case Studies for Tracking Emerging Spaces and Venues of Influence
posters.authors: Tasmeer Alam, Daniel Palamarchuk, Danyil Butkovskyi and Cody Buntain
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: emerging spaces cross-platform reconfiguration dynamic network analysis external shocks conflict studies
posters.abstract: Digital ecosystems reorganize when central sources are disrupted, with such disruptions increasingly coming from government shutdowns, kinetic conflict, or deplatforming. Despite these shocks, portable, structural methods for modeling and tracing cross-platform reconfiguration are lacking; while we can identify what sources are becoming more important to the ecosystem, we often lack insight into who is shifting to these sources. We introduce a framework that models temporal user–venue bipartite networks, projects venue–venue graphs, and tracks centrality to measure venue-level prominence over time. We then apply this framework across three major events: government backlash to demonstrations in Hong Kong, conflict-driven volatility around Ukraine, and Parler’s deplatforming in the wake of the January 6 attack on the US Capitol. This work contributes an interpretable, comparative method for identifying emerging spaces of influence across heterogeneous disruption contexts.

posters.title: Occupational Convergence or Divergence? Mapping Structural Shifts Driven by AI Penetration
posters.authors: Rafiazka Hilman and Júlia Koltai
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: occupations structural shifts AI penetration adaptation entry barrier
posters.abstract:
Introduction The increasing penetration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping how indi- viduals perform their professional roles across occupational domains. Although AI is widely celebrated for its substantial contributions to efficiency, productivity, and task automation, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding the requisite technical and procedural know-how (Choi and Leigh, 2024). This gap not only reflects uneven adaptation across the workforce (Zhang, 2025) but also has the potential to induce additional structural shifts in the skill re- quirements and qualification profiles (Chen, Yang and Wu, 2025) in contemporary job listings. Moreover, the demand for AI competencies is positively associated with wage levels. Accord- ing to Alekseeva et al. (2021), job postings that list AI skills earn an 11% salary premium within firms and a 5% premium within identical job titles. Furthermore, companies with stronger AI skill requirements generally provide higher compensation, extending beyond purely AI-focused positions. In this study, we comprehensively assess the transformative impact of automation and AI on labor markets using large-scale job listing data. Vacancy postings from major platforms, including LinkedIn, Indeed, and Glassdoor, are collected globally to capture trends in demand for AI-related skills and roles. Each posting is mapped to the 2018 Standard Occupational Clas- sification (SOC) to standardize occupations and enable cross-occupational comparisons. Our objectives are twofold: (i) to examine the relationship between required work experience and AI-related skills, and (ii) to model structural interdependencies between job categories and AI competencies using a bipartite network. Contributing to existing literature, this study provides a cross-country analysis of how AI adoption reshapes labor market demands in both the Global South and North, highlighting regional, occupational, and experience-driven variations in AI skill demand.

Data and Methods We developed an integrated pipeline that comprises data collection, computation, and visual- ization. At first, a robust web extraction is conducted to scrape structured data including job titles, descriptions, listed qualifications, posting dates, and other metadata from LinkedIn, In- deed and Glassdoor from December 2025 to February 2026. The geographical coverage of this study considers regional representation in both the Global North and the Global South, encom- passing ten countries: Brazil, China, Germany, India, Indonesia, the Netherlands, Singapore, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It is followed by a computational part which preprocess the textual descriptions using Nat- ural Language Processing (NLP) techniques: tokenization, lemmatization, and keyword-based classification to detect the presence of AI-oriented terms such as ‘machine learning’, ‘deep learning’, ‘NLP’, ‘automation’, ‘predictive analytics’, etc. Each job is assigned to a SOC cat- egory through a hybrid approach combining rule-based mapping (using keyword matching of job titles). Experience is extracted from job descriptions by using regular expressions (regex), denoting the seniority level (internship, entry level, mid-senior level, and director). Examina- tion of the distribution of AI related keywords is then performed across SOC categories, high- lighting which occupational groups demand AI-intensive roles more frequently and how these roles correlate with years of experience. An interactive dashboard namely ’The Occupation Observatory’ enables users to explore labor market insights through thematic visualizations. It displays AI skill demand by occupation and country, geographic distributions of job listings, and word clouds of key competencies. A bipartite network maps relationships between occu- pations, skills, and seniority levels, while cluster analysis highlights how experience intersects with AI skill requirements.

Results The results are presented in an online interactive dashboard. Figure 1 shows the distribution of job listings requiring AI-related skills across occupation clusters by country. In all countries, ’STEM & Technical’ occupations dominate, accounting for roughly 75–85% of postings, with particularly high shares in India. ’Management & Business’ roles form the second-largest cat- egory (about 10–20%), with relatively higher shares in Indonesia than in India. The remaining clusters, namely ’Health & Education’, ’Service, Production & Logistics’, and ’Public Service & Care’, each represent less than 5% of AI-related postings. Overall, the figure highlights a strong global concentration of AI demand in technical occupations, with limited diffusion into non-technical sectors and only modest cross-country variation. Moreover, our findings provide empirical evidence of how AI deployment is reshaping labor demand, increasing the need for specialized skills in certain occupations, and potentially contributing to labor market bifurcation. Interestingly, AI is reshaping labor demand, boosting demand for specialized skills and contributing to labor-market bifurcation. Using a skill-rank space (skills ordered by share of listings), Figure 2(a) shows that in United States data skills, especially Python, dominate mentions across ’Management & Business’, ’STEM & Technical’, and ’Service & Logistics’; Figure 2(b) shows the strong Python demand across salary levels, and Figure 2(c) ties these skills to high-paying roles (e.g.: data scientist, software developer). The bipartite network linking job categories to different types of AI-related skill require- ments is constructed to explore the interconnectedness of job categories and AI competen- cies, offering a novel lens for understanding labor market transformations. Figure 3(a) reveals clusters of occupations with similar AI demand profiles: technical fields such as ’Computer & Mathematics’, ’Architecture & Engineering’, and ’Business & Financial Operations’ show strong AI intensity, while managerial and administrative roles exhibit weaker or more special- ized demand (Figure 3(b)). Moreover, AI skill requirements are concentrated at the entry level (Figure 3(c)), suggesting that AI adoption may reinforce labor market inequality and raise bar- riers to entry.

Discussion This study contributes a cross-country, data-driven characterization of AI skill demand by com- bining large-scale vacancy data, standardized occupational mapping, and bipartite network analysis. It advances prior work by: (i) revealing occupation–skill clusters that differentiate technical and managerial demand; (ii) linking skill mentions to wage and experience profiles; and (iii) delivering an interactive dashboard that makes these patterns accessible to policymak- ers and researchers. The dashboard draws on job-platform data from LinkedIn, Indeed, and Glassdoor, and its outputs are grounded in a standardized SOC mapping that facilitates cross- country comparison and reproducibility. Based on these findings, we will refine the search category into a systematic, evidence-based pipeline that begins with a literature-driven seed list of AI and data-skill keywords and expands them via contextual embedding and co-occurrence analysis to reduce selection bias. Technical enhancements will include multilingual parsing, contextual NLP (transformer embeddings and topic models) to detect implicit AI tasks.

posters.title: Gender Disparities in LLM-Based Intimate Partner Violence Detection
posters.authors: Tabia Tanzin Prama, Mikaela Fudolig, Abigail Crocker, Chris Danforth and Peter Dodds
posters.keywords: Algorithmic Bias Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) Gender bias Large Language Models (LLMs) Counterfactual evaluation
posters.abstract: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) is a global crisis affecting individuals across gender and sexual orientations. As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as tools for advice and support, it is critical to examine whether they reproduce gendered biases present in online discourse. We investigate whether LLMs perceive IPV differently depending on victim–perpetrator gender configurations. Using 475 Reddit relationship-advice posts, we generated four controlled gender-swapped variants per post (M/M, M/F, F/M, F/F) and evaluated GPT-5o, Llama 4, Gemini 3, and Grok 3 across ten IPV-related outcomes. Results reveal systematic intra-model and inter-model disparities. In particular, several models show attenuated IPV and intent detection in mixed-gender dyads where the original poster is male, alongside amplification effects in same-sex female dyads. Mixed-effects logistic regression confirms that gender configuration significantly predicts labeling behavior across multiple abuse categories. These findings suggest that LLM interpretative frameworks remain sensitive to gendered priors embedded in training data, potentially embedding a digital double standard in automated IPV detection systems.

posters.title: Collaboration and Conflict in the Redditverse: Longitudinal Network Dynamics in Protest Spaces
posters.authors: Janine Schröder, Yukun Yang, Raji Ghawi and Jürgen Pfeffer
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Network Analysis Reddit Protest Collaboration Conflict
posters.abstract:
Recent findings in social movement studies have highlighted the role of information communication technologies (ICTs) in collective action [15]. A platform that has been used by a broad range of protest campaigns and Social Movement Organizations (SMOs) is Reddit. Studies have analyzed protest coordination and mobilization related to the Arab Spring [20], the Syrian war in 2017 [12], the Hongkong protests in 2019 [1], protest series in Cuba [13], and for global climate activism [8]. Further, campaigns on the platform tied to Occupy Wall Street [11] and the resistance to the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA) [9, 10] have been studied. Conceptually, whereas these case studies contribute to the knowledge about how ICT impacts the emergence and developments of singled-out, stand-alone movements, there is a lack of understanding on how these movements collaborate with each other for joint mobilization [18]. Additionally, large-scale longitudinal analysis of conflict between protest communities on the platform via antagonistic user engagement are lacking, as studies so far have solely focused on single subreddits without addressing changes over longer periods of time [4, 16].

Our study addresses these gaps by analyzing an extensive set of protest communities on Reddit over the span of twelve years to examine 1) dynamics of collaborative and conflictual overlap between them, 2) underlying mechanisms of their formation, and 3) the impact of reactions towards conflicts. By doing so, we contribute to a better understanding of the protest landscape on Reddit by mapping how protest subreddits overlap based on shared active users. Moreover, we clarify whether this dyad-level subreddit overlap is collaborative or conflictual. Ultimately, we illustrate how these dynamics change by proposing the “(anti)-social homes” based on users’ scores and highlight active communities in initiating or receiving anti-social activities. In this context, we use the framework “(anti-)social homes” [4] based on user’s positive or negative reactions towards content. The data collection relied on the Arctic Shift subreddit dataset, retrieved via Academic Torrents. The dataset comprises 22 Million subreddits and their descriptions (words displayed on their subreddit bio on their homepage). From this dataset, we obtained a list of relevant subreddits by matching their public names and descriptions against a keyword list (e.g., protest, activism). We performed further quality control by filtering out gaming subreddits irrelevant to our study, which resulted in a sample of 17,805 remaining subreddits. For this subset, we iterated through the monthly pushshift comment and submission files from June 2005 to December 2024 to collect all comments and submissions for the protest subreddits in the subset. The resulting corpus contains 190,441,324 comments (from March 2008) and 23,892,894 submissions (from February 2008) from 12,560,863 users (combined for comments and submissions). We set the time span of the data starting from January 2011 to include prominent social movements and protest campaigns that were active on Reddit from 2011, as described above. Further, we limited our data to the end of 2022 to exclude the noise introduced by the Reddit API blackout in June 2023 [19]. Additionally, we conducted a regular expression search for false-positive matches and relied on an LLM-based annotation using a zero-shot model1. With a team of two raters, we manually classified subreddits from a random sample (n = 200) into five categories and followed with an LLM-based classification of the entire random sample. Finally, we removed presumptive bots by excluding outliers in user activity across comments and submissions (See Descriptives in Figures 1, 2, and 3).

For every pair of subreddits Si and Sj, we obtain the year, month, and their respective sizes |Si| and |Sj|, which refer to the number of active users (comments only). We obtain the overlap between every subreddit pair |Si ∩ Sj| with the common users of Si and Sj. The overlap rate |Si ∩ Sj|/|Si| of subreddit Si is calculated as the proportion of the overlap to size |Si|. Additionally, we calculate jaccard indices |Si ∩ Sj|/|Si ∪ Sj|, which give the proportions of the overlap to the union of the two subreddits. We classified a user’s collaborative or conflicting affiliation with a subreddit as either social home and anti social home based on the scores of their comments. For each user i, we aggregated their scores for every subreddit in every month, and transform every comment’s score si into a robust score: ri = sgn(si)· log(1 + |si|). Additionally, we calculate the negative ratio ρ by dividing the sum of negative comments by the total number of comments. To examine whether a user i is active in a social home or an anti-social home, we calculate the home score z ∈ [−2.25, 1.0], which we use both as a numeric measure and as a binary classification (social home when ≥ −0.25 for the binary-based): z = tanh (µ(ri))− λ ∗ ρ, where λ ∈ [0.5, 1.5] refers to the weight of the negative ratio and is set to 1.25 to enforce a stricter categorization. Therefore, a subreddit is classified as “social home”, when tanh(µ)− 1.25·ρ ≥ −0.25. Further, we calculate the normalized mean Euclidean distance as sim=1/1+¯d with a range of [0, 1]. A higher value indicates a greater proximity of the users from the ideal (1, 1) point. A “collaboration axis” gives a line at a 45◦ angle starting from the origin and pointing toward (1, 1), with which we can project each user’s vector (xu, yu), where (xu) and (yu) are the numeric home scores in Si and S j, onto the unit vector a, which is displayed in Figure 5. Therefore, we obtain the fractions of users who are in the positive-positive quadrant (collaboration), in the positive-negative or negative-positive quadrant (conflict), and in the negative-negative quadrant (rejection).

Ultimately, we constructed the two graphs, G_collab based on the positive-positive fraction %Collab= 1/(N ∑u 1[xu > 0 ∧ yu > 0]), and G_conflict based on the positive-negative fraction %Conflict= 1/(N ∑u 1 (xu > 0 ∧ yu ≤ 0) ∨ (xu ≤ 0 ∧ yu > 0). For each graph, we obtain monthly slices to capture change in tie formation and dissolution. To analyze collaboration and reactions towards conflict, we apply two frameworks, which are described in Figure 4. For collaboration, we use Separable Temporal Exponential Random Graph Modeling (STERGM) to model the forming and dissolution of collaborative ties over time. These modeling approaches fit, when the exact time of tie changes within a network are unknown and when the ties are expected to be relatively permanent over time, as for example in political or peer-networks [17, 7]. By applying this framework to our collaboration graph, we uncover mechanisms of emergence among protest communities over time. For conflictual connections, we use a novel user migration framework. Here, we analyze the effect of downvoting user comments [14, 6, 3] on longterm engagement in their respective anti-social homes as a form of resilience against antagonistic engagement and trolling [2, 5]. By doing so, we contribute to the understanding of how effective online communities can defend their virtual space against (ideological) opponents.

posters.title: Document-conditioned LLM analysis for measurement of procedural and legal outcomes in eviction cases
posters.authors: Will von Geldern and Curtis Atkisson
posters.keywords: housing evictions access to justice natural language processing large language models
posters.abstract: Despite growing interest in eviction as a measure of housing insecurity, the civil court proceedings where evictions take place remain a largely inaccessible "black box" for researchers. Prior studies have relied either on time-intensive hand coding of case documents or national databases that capture only counts of cases filed and eviction judgments. This paper presents an analytic pipeline that uses document-conditioned LLM analysis to bridge this gap. Working with approximately 195,000 PDF documents from 8,500 unlawful detainer cases filed in a high-volume urban eviction court in Washington state between 2022 and 2024, we classify document types, extract text via computer vision, and prompt an LLM (GPT-4o) to answer targeted questions about procedural and legal outcomes. We validate the pipeline against 300 hand-coded cases, achieving 98.6% overall accuracy across eight boolean variables and a mean absolute percentage error of 0.84% for a measure of the amount owed by tenants at filing. Substantive findings reveal that 39.8% of tenants submitted an appearance, hearings were held in 60.2% of cases, and that tenants attended hearings in 76.3% of cases in which hearings were held. These outcomes are all strongly associated with tenants access to legal representation through Washington’s tenant right to counsel program.
