The relationship between tenants' access to legal representation (45.8% of all cases) and legal outcomes varied throughout the study period – while access to legal counsel was strongly associated with better outcomes in 2022 and 2023, this gap narrowed substantially in 2024 after the lapse of COVID-era rental assistance funds. Notably, the association between representation and record protection orders grew each year, suggesting that legal aid increasingly shields tenants' rental histories in cases where tenants cannot avoid displacement. These results demonstrate that document-conditioned LLM analysis offers a promising alternative to both administrative records and hand coding of case documents for analysis of high-volume legal proceedings.

posters.title: Dynamic Opinion-policy Feedback Model Explains Long-Term Patterns of Public Opinion Change
posters.authors: Rachael Kha, Vicky Chuqiao Yang and Adam Berinsky
posters.keywords: agent based model opinion dynamics public opinion societal change generational turnover
posters.abstract:
Public opinion evolves through a complex interplay of individual belief change, generational turnover, and institutional influence—but not all issues progress equally. While attitudes on gender roles and gay marriage have shifted steadily, others like abortion rights fluctuate or remain stagnant (Figure 1). This paper introduces a dynamic model of long-term opinion dynamics that integrates two often-overlooked forces: the replacement of older generations with younger ones, and the feedback between public opinion and institutional rules. The model captures how young people form beliefs based on inherited views, social context, and perceived behavioral norms, while also accounting for societal pushback against perceived extremes in policy. Through simulations, we show that this framework can reproduce three types of trajectories in public opinion: steady progress, long-term stagnation, and oscillation. These dynamics are driven by issue-specific thresholds for belief change and the strength of societal resistance. Our results help explain why some social changes persist while others stall or reverse, and highlight the importance of institutional context and intergenerational dynamics in shaping public discourse. This work offers a foundation for understanding the conditions under which lasting societal change can occur.

Research in opinion-dynamics modeling has largely focused on equilibrium outcomes arising from interpersonal influence and pairwise interactions. Yet this approach neglects two fundamental pathways of long-term societal change: generational cohort replacement and institutional rules. Empirical studies demonstrate that two primary mechanisms contribute substantially to shifts in public attitudes—such as those regarding gender roles and same-sex marriage—by disentangling the effects of within-cohort adaptation and intergenerational turnover [1], [2], [3]. Despite this evidence, few models quantitatively integrate these processes or account for variation across issues. Furthermore, long-term opinion change is shaped not only by interpersonal interactions but also by institutional rules, which both reflect and constrain public sentiment. This reciprocal feedback between institutions and public opinion remains a critical yet underexplored dimension of opinion-dynamics research.

To address these gaps in modeling long-term societal opinion change, we develop a coarse-grained, cohort-level framework that integrates generational replacement and institutional feedback within a unified model of opinion dynamics. The framework unpacks four core mechanisms of change: (1) individual belief updating over time; (2) opinion formation among new generational cohorts; (3) the emergence of institutional rules; and (4) the influence of those rules on individual attitudes. The model is organized around three interacting state variables—beliefs, behaviors, and the policy environment. Here, beliefs represent attitudes toward a specific issue; behaviors denote observable expressions of support or opposition; and the policy environment corresponds to explicit rules or institutional constraints governing permissible behaviors (Figure 2). We also introduce two parameters: behavior threshold and pushback strength. The former refers to the amount of evidence an individual needs to change or update their beliefs about a given issue. The latter refers to resistance that occurs in response to extremes in policy.

Our model is at the cohort level, wherein we model the opinions and behavior of birth cohorts as our primary unit. In our simulation, the population consists of a set of cohorts that age over time. At each time step, new cohorts are born and old cohorts die, giving us an aging chain for generational replacement. For simplicity, we consider that each cohort “forms a belief” or opinion at age 18, according to what they have learned from others (represented as the average population belief of cohorts aged 18+, B̄_t) but adjust it according to their own experiences, H_t. Here H_t is population-level behavior at time t. Cohorts compare this to H_0, an issue-specific behavior threshold for opinion change [4]. All variables here are normalized to be within 0 to 1, where 0 and 1 each represent an extreme in belief (i.e., disagree/agree, disapprove/approve).

B_{i,t,age=18} = { B̄_t + (k_B(H_t − H_0) − k_1 P_t) B̄_t if B_{t,age=18} < 0 B̄_t + (k_B(H_t − H_0) − k_1 P_t)(1 − B̄_t) if B_{t,age=18} ≥ 0 }

(1)

These newly adult cohorts are also influenced by pushback to the extremity of policy, P(t), which follows Equation 2 in response to current rules/policy, R(t) [4].

P_t = (R_t − 0.5)^2 · sign(R_t − 0.5)

(2)

Rules, or the policy environment, are defined by the opinions of older generations (aged 50–80 in the simulation) and follow the average belief of these generations [5]. At each time step, all cohorts also update their beliefs according to observed changes in behavioral norms and the status of the policy environment.

In addition to understanding long-term trends in opinion, we also use this model to understand the impact of exogenous shocks. These sudden changes have been demonstrated throughout history, such as in times of war when it became necessary for women to join the workforce in traditionally male roles. This we interpret as a behavioral shock. More recently, we also have seen sudden changes in policy such as with the COVID-19 mask mandate, which we identify as a shock to the policy environment. Through simulation, we observe that these shocks can reverse the trajectory of public opinion. This can occur through either a shock to policy or behavior. Whether or not a shock reverses the direction of the dynamics depends on the size of the shock relative to the value at the time of the shock (see Figure 3).

In this paper, we introduce a parsimonious, cohort-based model of long-term opinion dynamics that integrates generational replacement with endogenous feedback between public attitudes, social norms, and institutional rules. This framework reproduces the primary qualitative trajectories observed in empirical public opinion data—steady progress, long-term stagnation, and cyclical reversal—and clarifies the mechanisms underlying these divergent outcomes. By identifying the behavior threshold and pushback strength as key, interpretable parameters, the model provides a unifying explanation for why some social issues become self-reinforcing over time while others remain prone to backlash or stalled change. Moreover, the model demonstrates how exogenous shocks to policy or behavior can alter long-run trajectories, highlighting the critical role of institutional context in shaping durable social change. Together, these results establish a simple and generalizable foundation for studying the coupled evolution of opinion and policy, and offer a principled starting point for future empirical and theoretical work on the dynamics of social change.

posters.title: Asymmetric Flows: How Expressive Style Shapes Political Interaction on Social Media
posters.authors: Yuhang Liu
posters.keywords: language politics ideological asymmetry social networks social media
posters.abstract: Moral and emotional language is linked to engagement on social media, but aggregate metrics do not show whether engagement stays within or crosses ideological camps. We combine post-level language measures with directed interaction links to describe how moral and emotional cues relate to both engagement volume and engagement direction. In preliminary analyses, right-leaning users use more moral language, while left-leaning users show higher anxiety expression, and emotional language factor are associated with different engagement patterns across camps. These results are descriptive and suggest possible ideological asymmetries in how expressive style relates to political interaction online.

posters.title: Detecting Digital Dependence: Inferring Government Use of Hyperscaler Cloud from Internet Infrastructure Data
posters.authors: Jaakko Kilpi, Otto Kässi, Godofredo Ramizo Jr. and Vili Lehdonvirta
posters.keywords: digital sovereignty internet measurement supervised machine learning government digital services cloud hosting
posters.abstract: On whose infrastructure are government digital services hosted? We address this question by assembling a ground-truth dataset through Freedom of Information (FOI) requests to government organisations in the United Kingdom, Finland, and the Philippines, yielding 250 verified hosting records. These were supplemented with 19 cases of Chinese hyperscaler use confirmed through public sources. The FOI data reveal striking cross-national variation: US hyperscalers (AWS, Azure) account for 77% of UK and 64% of Finnish government services, while the Philippines retains 62% self-hosting. No Chinese hyperscaler use was reported in any FOI response. We train supervised classification models to infer these dependence patterns from publicly observable Internet infrastructure features, specifically name server records, mail exchanger records, AS descriptions, and TLS certificate issuers. The best-performing model achieves 81% accuracy distinguishing US hyperscalers, Chinese hyperscalers, and other providers, substantially outperforming single-record heuristics used in prior work. Preliminary cross-country validation suggests the models capture transferable signals of hyperscaler dependence. The methodology offers a scalable complement to institutional transparency mechanisms for studying digital sovereignty.

posters.title: Conformity to popular, not average, opinions: Models, data, and evolution
posters.authors: Kaleda Denton, Marcus Feldman and Jonathan Johannemann
posters.keywords: conformity opinion dynamics networks polarization wisdom of crowd
posters.abstract: In assessing how individuals in a network estimate a quantity, it is often assumed that they take an average or weighted average of the estimates of others they observe, as in the French-DeGroot learning model. However, individuals may actually copy clusters of similar opinions among their peers, a process that we call conformity. For example, if four individuals estimate a quantity to be near 0 and four individuals estimate it to be near 100, then although the average estimate may be near 50, one might conform by choosing a number closer to 0 or 100. Here, we (a) develop a model of conformity to clusters of popular opinions, (b) evaluate this model and two models of French-DeGroot averaging on human decision-making data, and (c) simulate evolutionary dynamics of each model under different kinds of population structure, including static and adaptive networks. In many of the conditions we analyze, the conformity model provides a better fit to the data than either of the French-DeGroot models. In addition, evolutionary simulations reveal considerable differences among the models; for example, compared to the French-DeGroot model, the conformity model can produce faster shifts in populations toward "extreme" opinions (where individuals' estimates of a quantity are either very large or very small) and can reduce individuals' average estimation accuracy. These findings have implications for research on consensus formation, polarization, and wisdom of crowds.

posters.title: The Lasting Psychological Impacts of COVID-19: Evidence from Natural Language
posters.authors: Yun Evelina Bao and Ashwini Ashokkumar
posters.keywords: language emotions identity social media upheavals
posters.abstract:
Summary Paragraph:

The COVID-19 pandemic can be conceptualized as a collective upheaval that caused major disruptions in people’s daily experiences across communities for years. Prior research has observed psychological shifts during the early months of the pandemic, including increased sadness and anxiety, decreased positive emotions, and strengthened familial ties and collective identity. In this study, we examined whether these shifts in emotions and collective identity persisted over time and probed the nature of the associations between changes in emotions and collective identity during collective upheavals. To answer these questions, we analyzed 63.8 million Reddit comments from over 3 million users from over 50 U.S. city communities using LIWC-22, which served as our measure of emotions and identity. We also ran topic modeling using BERTopic on the text data to track the topic prevalence across years. We found that the COVID-19 pandemic led to a decline in emotional well-being and the emergence of a collective identity that lasted for 4 years, demonstrating that the pandemic induced a cultural shift that established new emotional and identity norms. From mixed-effects cross-lag time-series analysis, we also found that people tend to express more collective identity when they feel negative, but this increase in collective identity expression did not predict reduced negative emotion. Together, our study deepened our understanding of the psychological meaning of collective coping with large-scale upheavals.

Extended Abstract:

The COVID-19 pandemic can be conceptualized as a collective upheaval that caused major disruptions in people’s daily experiences across communities for years. Prior research has observed psychological shifts during the early months of the pandemic, including increased sadness and anxiety, decreased positive emotions, and strengthened familial ties and collective identity1–3. Do these findings represent transient psychological responses, or did the pandemic produce lasting psychological shifts? In this study, we documented the long-term psychological impacts of the pandemic on emotion and collective identity. Further, we investigate the psychological function of emergent collective identity. Specifically, we ask whether crisis-induced negativity promotes collective identity and whether this emergent identity, in turn, alleviates that negativity. Past literature on collective upheavals has documented social connections as collective coping behaviors after crises, such as talking about experiences and feelings within communities 4. Studies have suggested that engagement in social connections during crises facilitates the emergence of collective identity, which may yield psychological benefits because the perceived availability of community social support from these group interactions can protect people from potentially adverse effects of stressful events5,6. However, other literature has found support for the opposite view that social sharing of emotions during these social engagements would trigger more emotional turmoil and rumination due to exposure to others’ negative experiences7. While these studies have examined the psychological effects of different collective coping behaviors, no past research has directly investigated the connection between emotional well-being and the emergence of collective identity. Understanding the associations between emotions and collective identity is critical for understanding the psychological meaning of living through large-scale upheavals as a community. To examine the long-term psychological impacts of the pandemic on emotion and identity, and the links between these effects, we analyzed large-scale natural language data from Reddit. Our dataset has 63.8 million comments from over 3 million users across 50 U.S. city communities, across four years before and after the COVID-19 pandemic (2016-2024). We analyzed text data using LIWC-22, which served as the psychological measure for emotions and identity. To assess the long-term shift in emotions and identity during the COVID-19 pandemic, we plotted person-level monthly means in the dataset across 2016 and 2024 and examined the pandemic’s yearly effect using mixed-effects models. We observed a spike in negative emotions and a drop in positive emotions immediately following the pandemic declaration (Fig 1). These shifts showed a slight recovery as the pandemic waned, but negative emotion remained elevated (b = 0.10, p < .001) and positive emotion remained dampened for 4 years (b = –0.13, p < .001). We also observed similar patterns in discrete negative emotions, including anxiety, sadness, and fatigue, which all spiked after the pandemic declaration and remained relatively higher than pre-COVID levels (Fig 2). These findings suggested an overall decline in people’s emotional well-being that lasted at least 4 years since the pandemic’s onset, indicating a new post-pandemic baseline of lower well-being. A similar pattern in collective identity was found, as measured by the use of first-person plural pronouns (we, us, etc). Collective identity spiked immediately after the pandemic declaration and remained higher than the pre-COVID baseline for four years (b = 0.04, p = .015), suggesting an elevated post-pandemic baseline of collective identity (Fig 3). Further, following the collective coping literature, we reasoned that the emergent collective identity might reflect a concern for the current collective crisis. To test this, we examined the prevalence of discussions directly related to the ongoing crisis, relative to the discussions of collective issues unrelated to the crisis. We ran topic modeling with BERTopic on a 1% subset of the dataset and applied KNN clustering to the full dataset to categorize comments into topics. We found an increase in the prevalence of COVID-19-related topics (e.g., vaccines, healthcare) and a parallel decrease in topics on collective issues unrelated to COVID (e.g., immigration, homelessness) during the first 2 years of the pandemic (Fig 4). These results indicate the prioritization of crisis-relevant concerns and suggest that the emergent collective identity is directly related to the crisis. Finally, we examined the psychological function of the emergent collective identity. That is, if the collective identity is beneficial, we would expect that people who experience greater negative emotion would subsequently emphasize collective identity, and that this identity would alleviate their negative emotional states. We performed a mixed-effects cross-lagged time-series analysis at the person level to examine whether negative emotions of the previous day predicted the expression of collective identity the following day. We found that, after the pandemic’s onset, when people expressed more negative emotions the previous day, they tended to express higher levels of collective identity the following day (Fig 5). We then ran similar models examining whether collective identity of the previous day predicted negative emotions the following day, and found that when people expressed greater collective identity the previous day (Fig 6), they expressed more negative emotions the subsequent day, suggesting the expression of collective identity had no emotional benefit. Our research observed that the COVID-19 pandemic led to a decline in emotional well-being and the emergence of a collective identity that lasted for 4 years, demonstrating that the pandemic induced a cultural shift that established new emotional and identity norms. In addition, our study probed the psychological functions of the shifts in negative emotions and collective identity. Specifically, we found that people tend to express more collective identity when they feel negative, but this increase in collective identity expression did not predict reduced negative emotion. Together, our study deepened our understanding of the psychological meaning of collective coping with large-scale upheavals.

posters.title: Modeling Affective Polarization and Conflict Disposition under Divergent Narrative Exposure
posters.authors: Sherwin Brown, Jiaman Li, Vrinda Malhotra, Hanjing Shi and Dominic DiFranzo
posters.keywords: Agent-Based Modeling Cognitive-Affective Polarization Narrative Framing Agent Zero COVID-19
posters.abstract:
This study examines how divergent COVID-19 narratives across government websites, mainstream media, and Reddit shape cognitive-affective polarization and conflict disposition. We combine LLM-assisted narrative and sentiment extraction with a hybrid cognitive-affective agent-based model grounded in Epstein’s Agent Zero framework. Messages are encoded as Narrative-Emotional Imprint Matrices and stored in agents’ episodic memory with ACT-R–inspired decay. A PCA-derived one-dimensional signal updates agents’ affect and conflict thresholds over time.

Simulation results under exclusive-source exposure show systematic divergence: Reddit exposure produces the highest and earliest conflict disposition, mainstream media yields moderate polarization, and government narratives remain comparatively stable and never cross the conflict threshold. By separating text-level sentiment from internal affect dynamics, the model provides a mechanism-focused framework for linking narrative environments to polarization trajectories and for evaluating communication strategies in public health contexts.

posters.title: Can AI Strengthen Democracy? Improving Public Trust in Elections with a Civic Chatbot
posters.authors: Do Won Kim, Cody Buntain, Giovanni Luca Ciampaglia and Riley Lankes
posters.keywords: democracy election integrity AI chatbot civic AI (mis)information
posters.abstract:
Free and fair elections are a cornerstone of modern democracy, but these foundations are at risk: trust in democratic institutions is falling, with confidence in voting as an instrument for change especially in decline. Many Americans are disengaging from the political process, particularly at the state and local level, where elections have the greatest chance to shape their own communities. While state and local election authorities have deep expertise in administering and safeguarding elections, they have limited resources to address constituent concerns at the moment they are most needed. The resulting information voids leave voters without adequate information to understand how their local elections work, inundated instead with national coverage that makes it difficult to evaluate integrity in local processes and to exercise their voice.

Evidence-based civic tech solutions can counter these trends, especially when they take advantage of existing infrastructure to ensure community adoption. Some local governments are already experimenting with AI to improve constituent services. Much of the research in this space, however, has focused on how chatbots can be developed and deployed to relieve administrative burdens, leaving open questions about their impacts on citizens' political engagement, institutional trust, and informed participation in electoral processes. This gap is critical given the resources needed to deploy sophisticated AI agents and research showing AI chatbots "are not necessarily more impactful than traditional Internet search". That is, local officials may be better served using resources to ensure election information is easily accessible online rather than deploying sophisticated AI.

Therefore, we ask: Can an AI-powered election information chatbot (i) improve how citizens access, understand, and trust election information, and (ii) enhance their engagement in democratic processes? To answer this question, we will test the effects of talking with an AI election chatbot we have developed, namely the Voter Information from Official Local Election Trusted Sources (VIOLETS). VIOLETS is an AI-powered election chatbot grounded in official sources from local and state election authorities. It employs a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture with allow-listed sources only, transparent citation of official documentation, and hallucination-prevention protocols that route unanswerable queries to human review. Additionally, VIOLETS engages in extended, evidence-based dialogue to address voter doubts and election-related misconceptions.

We hypothesize that encouraging voters to use VIOLETS will: (H1) increase trust in local election officials and democratic institutions; (H2) increase election-related procedural knowledge; (H3) reduce election conspiracy beliefs and increase confidence in vote counting; and (H4) increase political engagement, including information-seeking from official sources and likelihood of voting.

To test these hypotheses, we will conduct a three-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) with residents of a target county (redacted for anonymity), recruiting registered voters from L2 voter registration records as well as young adults (18--29) via campus partnerships within this region. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the following conditions: (1) a Chat condition, where participants interact with VIOLETS; (2) a Search condition, where participants use a lightweight search engine providing access to the same official resources but requiring self-directed navigation; or (3) a pure Control condition. The Chat and Search conditions both will have access to the same underlying official information from local and state resources, allowing us to isolate the causal effect of AI-facilitated dialogue over and above access to official election resources alone.

In IC2S2, we aim to present findings from a pre-launch pilot study that will be conducted in June 2026 in conjunction with local primary elections in the target county. First, we will assess the performance of VIOLETS by analyzing a sample of its generated responses. Specifically, we plan to examine (a) accuracy (i.e., whether responses are faithfully attributable to official local election authority documents); (b) cite-guard performance (i.e., whether the system reliably blocks citations to non-allowlisted sources); and (c) hallucination prevention performance (i.e., whether the system correctly routes unanswerable or ambiguous queries to human review rather than generating potentially misleading responses).

Second, we will evaluate user experience through both behavioral and self-reported measures collected from pilot participants. Behavioral indicators include session length, number of follow-up queries, and drop-off rates, each serving as a proxy for engagement and perceived utility. Self-reported measures capture the perceived accuracy of chatbot responses, overall satisfaction and open-ended qualitative feedback, as well as confidence in the information received.

Third, where sample size from the pilot study permits, we will report preliminary intent-to-treat estimates of the effects of talking with VIOLETS on key pre-registered outcomes, such as procedural knowledge of local election processes, any conspiratorial beliefs related to the election, trust in election and broader democratic institutions. These estimates from the pilot study will provide effect size priors for powering the November 2026 RCT.

In summary, we expect that the pilot study will inform both the technical refinement and experimental design of the main RCT, while generating early evidence on whether access to official information through local civic AI chatbots can enhance citizens' knowledge, strengthen their relationship with local government, and improve levels of trust and civic engagement. From a scientific standpoint, our findings will contribute to a growing literature on the effects of AI-assisted information delivery in civic contexts, helping to establish when and for whom conversational AI offers advantages over traditional search-based access to official information. From a practical standpoint, our results will offer actionable guidance for election administrators and civic technology developers navigating resource constraints: if VIOLETS demonstrates measurable improvements in procedural knowledge and institutional trust relative to the Search condition, it will provide a compelling case for AI investment in local election communication infrastructure.

posters.title: Structural Contagion: How Narrative Causal Structure Shapes Information Diffusion in Social Networks
posters.authors: Joshua Introne and Qiusi Sun
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: narrative diffusion causal networks social influence information adoption network experiment
posters.abstract: Misinformation spreads not as isolated claims but as causally structured narratives whose components vary in connectivity and importance. We propose a model of narrative diffusion in which adoption of a story item depends on three mechanisms: (1) narrative influence---the structural proximity of a candidate item to items already adopted by an individual, computed over a causal network; (2) social influence---reinforcement from network neighbors who have adopted the item; and (3) individual disposition---stable differences in adoption aggressiveness across participants. Using a controlled network experiment, we show that narrative influence is a persistent and significant predictor of adoption, operating largely independently of individual disposition. Social influence interacts positively with narrative influence, suggesting that social cues are most effective when they align with narrative coherence. Descriptive analyses further suggest that early adopters are primarily driven by narrative structure, while later adopters are more responsive to social pressure.

posters.title: Using LLM-Based Topic Modeling to Design and Test Reframing Interventions for Workplace AI Acceptance
posters.authors: Hanqiu Li and Sherry Wu
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: LLM-based topic modeling Human-AI interaction Workplace AI adoption Computational text analysis Algorithmic aversion
posters.abstract: This paper uses LLM-based topic modeling (TopicGPT) to analyze why employees prefer human over AI assistants across six workplace scenarios (resume screening, promotion, awards, performance review, suggestions, concerns), identifying seven psychological themes that predict preference. Three themes favor AI (impartiality, efficiency, privacy) and three favor humans (contextual nuance, empathy, moral values about technology). We then run two experiments testing whether reframing AI tools to emphasize human-associated strengths increases acceptance. In a description-only study (N = 1,176), AI framed with its own native strengths outperformed AI framed with human strengths. In an interactive chatbot study (N = 581), a chatbot designed to demonstrate empathy and contextual sensitivity shifted mechanism-level perceptions but not overall acceptance. The work contributes a computational social science pipeline from open-ended text to intervention design and finds that anthropomorphic reframing may backfire.

posters.title: Generative AI in Knowledge Work: Digital Trace Evidence of Shifts from Communication to Productivity
posters.authors: Yulin Yu, Yan Chen, Rui Hu, Siddharth Suri and Scott Counts
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: Generative AI Adoption Workplace Productivity Organizational Communication Human-AI-Interaction
posters.abstract: Generative AI is transforming the workplace through its ability to augment and automate cognitive tasks, reshaping not only how organizations innovate but also raising questions about inequality and the future of work. Despite the rapid adoption of AI tools, empirical evidence on how these tools alter work practices remains limited, particularly regarding the kinds of tasks that drive productivity gains and the mechanisms behind them. In this study, we analyze digital trace data from multiple large international companies to examine how the introduction of generative AI tools in knowledge work shifts the balance between two major activities among knowledge workers—communication and productivity-oriented activities (e.g., content creation in Word). Our findings show that AI adoption does more than boost efficiency; it fundamentally changes work habits. Specifically, we observe a shift away from communication and coordination between employees toward individual, documentation-focused tasks such as creating slides using productivity applications (Word, PowerPoint, and Excel). We find that employees who enable and use AI tools significantly increase their use of productivity applications (e.g., reformatting, changing fonts, adding text), far outpacing growth in the use of communication applications (e.g., Teams and email). Further analyses suggest potential mechanisms for this shift: although communication application usage rises slightly, employees send fewer small-group emails, contact fewer recipients, read fewer emails, and devote less effort to managing communications. Moreover, frequent reliance on AI functions such as “suggested reply” and “summary” is linked to a decline in information consumption (reading emails). As AI tools become embedded across workplaces and society, these overlooked changes in work habits may carry profound implications for collaboration, organizational management, and long-term innovation outcomes.

posters.title: From Echo Chambers to Echo Platforms: Fragmentation and Platform Sorting in the Social Media Ecosystem
posters.authors: Edoardo Di Martino, Alessandro Galeazzi, Michele Starnini, Walter Quattrociocchi and Matteo Cinelli
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Echo Chambers Social Media Online Segregation Political Polarization Deplatforming
posters.abstract: Social media platforms are often studied through the lens of echo chambers, where ideological clustering occurs within communities. However, fragmentation may increasingly operate at the level of entire platforms. In this work, we investigate the emergence of "echo platforms", environments that function as ideologically aligned niches within a broader social media ecosystem. Using over 117 million URLs shared by nearly six million users across nine platforms during the 2020 U.S. presidential election, we characterize platform roles along three dimensions: structural centrality, news source reliability, and user ideological composition. Our analysis reveals a fragmented ecosystem in which alt-tech platforms occupy peripheral positions, amplify questionable content, and host ideologically homogeneous audiences. Building on this framework, we explore a longitudinal extension spanning the 2020 and 2024 elections and introduce the concept of platform sorting, whereby users increasingly align with ideologically congruent platforms. Our findings suggest that platform-level ideological asymmetries remain stable over time, indicating that polarization may reflect a structural redistribution of ideological alignment across platforms rather than transient shifts within them.

posters.title: Visual Logic: An Integrated Framework for Understanding Visual Content on Social Media
posters.authors: Fatima Gaw, Yingdan Lu and Erik Nisbet
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: visual content social media influencer computer vision large language model
posters.abstract: Social science theory remains rooted in text-based models or fragmented visual approaches, limiting theorizing in visual-first environments that dominate social media. This study advances “visual logic” as a framework for theorizing patterns of multidimensional visual features that constitute visual norms and then integrates computational visual methods to explicate these norms. We apply our integrated framework to 21,219 TikTok videos from 80 political influencer accounts using computer vision, supervised learning, and vision-language models to identify and measure their visual norms and audience engagement. Political influencers exhibit a distinct visual logic centered on sharp focused shots of emotionally expressive talking heads engaged in education, commentary, and advice. Human-centered, visually dense videos generate higher engagement, but scene and activity features shape engagement in distinct ways. This study offers a comprehensive and scalable framework for theorizing and measuring visual content across contexts, with implications for a wide range of scholarship across disciplines.

posters.title: The collective dynamics of online harassment
posters.authors: Benjamin Emery and Brian Keegan
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: harassment extremism misinformation network analysis rank statistics word embedding
posters.abstract:
I can't find where to add this but I'd like to request to be considered for a lightning talk. Thank you! Now here's my abstract:

Online message boards have been the source of many well-known harassment campaigns in recent years, such as Gamergate in 2014. Much of this activity takes place within individual channels of broader, general interest message board platform such as 4chan and, at one point, Reddit. This is, however, not the case for Kiwi Farms: a message board designed and operated specifically for crowdsourcing targeted harassment of minorities, women, LGBTQ people, neurodivergent people, feminists, journalists, internet celebrities, and video game hobbyists \cite{vuNoEasyWay2024}. Alongside general discussion of their disdain for expanding equality or progressive social movements, the platform targets specific individuals for abuse, referring to such targets as ``lolcows''. The Wikipedia page for Kiwi Farms lists eight harassment campaigns waged on different targets, three of which have lead to the deaths by suicide of the harassment victim. Strategies deployed by users of Kiwi Farms include the publication of private information about the target (doxing), sending false reports of imminent danger to police to have them deployed at the location of the target (swatting), and the mass-reporting of their social media accounts to shut down channels through which the victim would seek peer support. Using network analysis, rank-based statistics, and natural language processing, we conduct mesoscale analyses to demonstrate how changes in behavior and intended targets of this message board could be detected and responded to in real time.

When studying anti-social behavior online, it can be challenging to separate and reliably identify harmful behavior from more innocuous activity. In light of these challenges, Kiwi Farms is a useful platform to study. This is in part due the clear labeling of its threads with the person they're targeting, keeping different harassment targets in separate threads, and hosting them on a specific board separate from threads about other topics. The entire historical archive of Kiwi Farms is included in the ExtremeBB dataset, collected by the Cybercrime Center at Cambridge University \cite{vuExtremeBBDatabaseLargeScale2023}. Posts are collected as rows in a PostgreSQL database, which include the textual content of the post, the date, and unique identifiers for the post, creator, and thread. For thread-level analysis, we collapse posts with the same thread ID into single long-form strings.

It's common for these posts to include hyperlinks either to other websites or to other threads on Kiwi Farms. For internal links, the URL contains the unique identifier for the thread to which it links. We use this feature to aggregate a temporal link network where hyperlinks constitute edges that each originate from a thread and terminate at another thread. Users may link either to a thread or a post in a thread, and in both cases it is considered a link to the thread. This internal link netwok and its degree distribution are shown in Figure \ref{fig:internal-network}. The nodes are colored according to the board in which they reside.

The global assortativity coefficient of this network for board ID is 0.278, indicating a greater-than-chance likelihood that any given link connects threads from the same board \cite{newmanMixingPatternsNetworks2003}. We notice especially strong assortative mixing in certain regions of the largest connected component (LCC). The dense clump of lavender nodes on the outer left of the network consists of threads on the ``Prime Cuts'' board, which houses multiple threads centering on three people, whose online presence has drawn too much attention to be contained to a single thread. Toward the top, the salmon-colored region is made up of threads targeting trans people. Other boards exhibit disassortativity, such as the general discussion board, whose threads are shown as magenta nodes that are scattered around the network.

Turning to the temporal dynamics of this platform, the heavy-tailed nature the activity distribution across threads makes rank-based statistics an effective method of analysis. We therefore apply rank-turbulence divergence, defined as $$ D^\text{R}_{\alpha}(R_1||R_2)=\sum_{\tau \in 1,2;\alpha}\delta D^\text{R}_{\alpha,\tau}(R_1||R_2) = \frac{1}{N_{1,2;\alpha}}\frac{\alpha+1}{\alpha}\sum_{\tau \in 1,2;\alpha}\bigl|\frac{1}{[r_{\tau,1}]^{\alpha}}-\frac{1}{[r_{\tau,2}]^{\alpha}}\bigr|^{\frac{1}{\alpha+1}}, $$ to the rankings of threads by number of unique users posting to each \cite{doddsAllotaxonometryRankturbulenceDivergence2023}. In this case we'll use the set of ranks from the degree Zipf distribution for the aggregate network as $R_1$ and each individual day as $R_2$. Because this metric is a simple sum of contributions, observe changes in the turbulence of the thread-activity distribution.

To use this metric for temporal analysis, we slice the network into weekly and monthly subgraphs, iterating by day on a sliding scale. For each day, we compare the thread ranks for from the month prior to the week ahead. The rank-turbulence divergence ($\alpha=0.25$) at each timestep is shown in Figure \ref{fig:temp-rtd}. We include an allotaxonograph demonstrating which threads contribute to the value of this divergence over the axis of December 01, 2020. These divergences each compare ranked lists of around between one- and ten-thousand threads, and high values indicate larger turnover of threads in this ranking, which can be helpfully analogized as a sort of topical turbulence on the platform.

Finally, we fit a word embedding model, with platform-specific slang decomposed into temporal components \cite{mikolovEfficientEstimationWord2013}. We do this by tagging each occurrence of the unigram ``lolcow'', slang for the targets of this community's harassment, with the year and month of the post containing the occurrence. We then fit the model to this corpus with these labeled unigrams, and note the relative positions of them over time. We show this temporal behavior decomposed to one and two dimensions in Figure \ref{fig:temp-embedding}. We observe five noteable spikes in the first principal component of the embedding position for ``lolcow'', each of which reveal are accompanied by proximal vocabulary that may reveal novel targets around that time.

In doing this work, we add to a body of knowledge that can inform policy or be implemented by watchdog groups in the case that the government does not prioritize the safety of vulnerable people. While we primarily aim to understand how these spaces operate at a systems level, this knowledge of digital traces that can identify an ongoing attack could prove useful to groups trying to mitigate these harassment campaigns in real time. In addition to policymakers and human rights groups, these insights and methods may be useful to social media safety teams. We know that some platforms have user-bases that are more susceptible to being maliciously exposed to hostile audiences on other platforms. For instance, the account LibsOfTikTok on X exists exclusively to provoke the anger of X users toward some users of TikTok. Likewise, many of the victims of Kiwi Farms harassment are targeted due to their activitiy on Tumblr. Knowing the patterns of behavior on Kiwi Farms and what signals to watch for could help safety teams protect the minoritized among their users.

posters.title: An Archetypometric Analysis of Friends
posters.authors: Shun Zhang, Tabia Tanzin Prama, Peter Dodds and Chris Danforth
posters.keywords: Archetypometrics Ensemble Narrative Structure Essential Dimensions Character Similarity Friends
posters.abstract: Long-running ensemble television series must balance character stability with narrative variation. This study examines structural differentiation among the six main characters in using the archetypometric framework developed by the Computational Story Lab. By projecting characters into a six-dimensional archetypal space derived from a large-scale trait–character dataset and computing pairwise inner products, we analyze the geometric relations among ensemble members. The results reveal three structural configurations within the ensemble: strong similarity (e.g., Joey–Phoebe), strong divergence (e.g., Phoebe–Ross), and near-orthogonality (e.g., Ross–Rachel). Together, these patterns suggest that relational diversity in long-running sitcom ensembles can emerge from a distributed archetypal geometry in which resonance, contrast, and independence coexist.

posters.title: Dynamics of Collective Emotion
posters.authors: Rachael Kha, Vicky Chuqiao Yang and Amit Goldenberg
posters.keywords: agent-based model collective emotion emergence collective dynamics dynamical systems model
posters.abstract:
Traditional approaches to studying behavior and decision-making often underestimate the role of emotions, which shape how individuals perceive, evaluate, and respond to their environment. While individual emotional experiences have received increasing attention, collective emotion—the aggregate emotional valence and intensity of a group—remains comparatively understudied. As an emergent property of interacting individuals, collective emotion cannot be reduced to individual states alone. Instead, it arises from feedback, amplification, and social interdependence, and can become a powerful driver of collective behavior, institutional response, and broader societal change.

Empirical studies, particularly those using social media data, document sustained or even amplified collective emotional intensity following events such as police brutality, natural disasters, and terrorist attacks. Notably, collective emotional intensity can persist even as individual-level emotion declines due to habituation and memory effects. These patterns motivate the need for a formal framework capable of explaining how such dynamics emerge.

To address this gap, we develop a mathematical model of collective emotion that formalizes the interaction between individual emotional updating and perceived collective emotion. Individual emotional intensity evolves according to two mechanisms: decay due to habituation and adjustment toward perceived collective emotion. Emotional updating is defined as:

ei(t+1) = (1 − lambda) * ei(t) + (1 / tau_e) * (Pi(t) − ei(t)).

Here lambda represents the rate of emotional decay and tau_e determines how quickly individuals adjust their emotional state toward their perception of collective emotion.

Perceived collective emotion Pi(t) is formed from the observed emotional expressions of individuals in a local social network. For an individual i, perceived collective emotion is estimated as the average emotional display of neighbors:

P_tilde_i(t) = (1 / |Vi(t)|) * sum over j in Vi(t) of bj(t).

Public emotional expression bj(t) is modeled as a stochastic behavioral display. For simplicity, we assume that bj(t) is binary and equals 1 with probability proportional to the individual’s internal emotional state at that time. This distinction reflects the difference between private emotional states and observable emotional expression.

Individuals may also exhibit systematic bias when evaluating the emotional intensity of others. Empirical evidence suggests that people tend to perceive others as more emotionally intense than they perceive themselves. To capture this effect, perceived collective emotion is transformed through a nonlinear bias function controlled by the parameter gamma:

Pi(t) = P_tilde_i(t)^gamma / (P_tilde_i(t)^gamma + (1 − P_tilde_i(t))^gamma), where gamma is greater than or equal to 1.

Using a small-world network, we examine how exogenous shocks—representing emotionally activating events such as terrorist attacks, shootings, or natural disasters—affect the emotional dynamics of a population. Simulation results show that larger shocks generate higher emotional intensity and greater visible emotional expression, which further amplifies collective emotion through feedback processes. When shocks occur repeatedly and in close temporal proximity, they can produce escalating emotional responses. However, habituation moderates these dynamics over time. The model also produces non-zero equilibrium emotional states, suggesting that collective emotional intensity may persist even after individual emotional responses decline.

Although preliminary, this framework provides a tractable and mechanistic account of how collective emotion emerges, amplifies, and stabilizes in social systems. The process of formalizing these dynamics also highlights conceptual challenges in modeling emergent social phenomena, particularly regarding the time scales over which collective emotional processes operate. The model raises new empirical questions about the persistence of collective emotion, including how long emotional states endure and how emotionally charged artifacts such as social media posts may sustain or reactivate emotional responses over time. Together, this work represents an initial step toward a dynamical systems framework for understanding collective emotion and its role in shaping social processes.

posters.title: Dream rural courtyards, precarious land rights: counter-urbanization imaginaries on Chinese social media
posters.authors: Tao Ren
posters.keywords: Counter-urbanization Social media discourse BERTopic LLM-based sentiment analysis Rural land institutions
posters.abstract: This study analyzes 6,360 Xiaohongshu (RedNote) posts about rural courtyards to examine counter-urbanization discourse in China. Using BERTopic topic modeling and LLM-based multi-target sentiment analysis, we identify seven topics spanning practical, affective, and institutional registers, and show that aspirational content dominates while legal-institutional discussion remains marginal. Two qualitative case analyses reveal how creators negotiate tenure precarity through strategies of risk domestication and platform-mediated governance appeals. The study contributes to computational social science methodology for non-English corpora and to substantive understanding of how platform discourse mediates the tension between rural lifestyle aspiration and China’s restrictive land institutions.

posters.title: When LLM Enters the Commons: The Integration of WikiVault in Korean Wikipedia
posters.authors: Inhwa Song and Manoel Horta Ribeiro
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Wikipedia Large Language Models Machine Translation Knowledge Commons
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly incorporated into collaborative knowledge platforms, raising questions about their effects on governance and the future of common knowledge. Yet we lack ecosystem-level accounts of how such tools reshape live knowledge commons. We study the deployment of WikiVault, a community-developed LLM-assisted translation tool introduced to Korean Wikipedia in May 2025. Combining interviews with large-scale analysis of edit logs and pageviews, we examine how WikiVault reshapes content production, social dynamics, and downstream consumption. Despite adoption by only 0.1% of editors, WikiVault-assisted edits account for 27% of total byte growth over nine months. Our findings highlight how LLM tools can simultaneously accelerate knowledge production while redistributing editorial labor, raising new questions about sustainable governance of knowledge commons.

posters.title: Estimating Support for US Presidential Candidates Using X Polls
posters.authors: Chhandak Bagchi, Gayathri Sunil, Arash Khojaste, Vishal Kalakonnavar, Niko Lorantos, Mattia Samory, Junghwan Yang and Przemyslaw Grabowicz
posters.keywords: Polling US elections Social media Demographic bias Machine learning
posters.abstract: Polls posted on social media have emerged in recent years as an important tool for gauging public support for business decisions and political candidates before elections, as well as for political campaigning. On platforms such as X (formerly Twitter), election-related polls can generate massive engagement. For instance, a 2024 US presidential election poll posted by Elon Musk received 5.8 million votes and 153 million views. In 2024, Donald Trump posted multiple times on Truth Social screenshots of X polls during his presidential election campaign. Such polls are considered unscientifc, primarily because users voting in X polls are not demographically representative of the US population, leading to distorted estimates of US presidential candidate. However, such polls may contain unique signals about public opinion not captured by mainstream polls, which face an accuracy crisis and in the US overestimate support for Democrats. Here, to extract valuable public opinion estimates, we de-bias X poll outcomes by correcting respective demographic biases. Specifically, we apply a regression and poststratification methodology to adjust for demographic differences between X users interacting with polls and the US voting population. In this way, we yield estimates of candidate support for the 2016, 2020, and 2024 US presidential candidates that are more accurate than those based on mainstream polls.

posters.title: From Affection to Illusion: Detecting Parasocial Interactions on Livestreaming Platforms
posters.authors: Smriti Janaswamy, Claire Dekker and Kai-Cheng Yang
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Twitch parasocial livestream relationship one-sided large language models LivestreamFail
posters.abstract: Parasocial interactions (PSIs), one-sided emotional connections between audiences and media personalities, have taken on new forms in the context of livestreaming platforms like Twitch. While prior research on PSIs has largely relied on survey methods and focused on traditional media, the fast-paced, chat-driven environment of livestreaming presents both new manifestations of PSIs and new challenges for studying them at scale. This paper introduces a theoretically grounded, rubric-based framework that operationalizes PSIs across three dimensions: affective connection, engagement and perceived reciprocity, and cognitive or relational closeness. We apply this framework to a dataset of 4,241 Twitch clips and over 570,000 chat messages, first using human annotators to establish ground-truth labels and then evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) including GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and the GPT-5 family to automatically detect PSIs. Our experiments follow a factorial design varying prompting strategy (zero-shot vs. one-shot) and contextual information provided to the model. Results show that model performance ranges from 0.48 to 0.69 macro F1, with no consistent advantage for larger or reasoning-enhanced models. These findings highlight the complexity of PSI detection and motivate future work incorporating multimodal signals to improve automated identification of parasocial dynamics in streaming contexts.

posters.title: A Large-Scale Study of Audience Evaluations of TV Characters in Reddit Communities
posters.authors: Souha Ben Hassine and Steven Wilson
posters.keywords: Narrative Analysis Social Norms LLMs Media Reception Reddit
posters.abstract: Introduction: Across digital platforms, millions of viewers debate fictional characters as if they were real moral agents. They defend them, condemn them, forgive them, cancel them, mourn them, and sometimes mobilize entire communities around them. These reactions are not trivial fandom chatter; they are large-scale, publicly observable expressions of collective judgment [Jenkins and Deuze, 2008, Zillman and Cantor, 1977]. Because audiences often evaluate characters in explicitly moral terms, debating whether actions are justified, fair, or redeemable, these discussions also reveal the norms, values, and moral expectations that communities bring to narrative interpretation. Unlike survey-based measures of media reception, online discourse provides naturalistic, time-stamped records of how audiences evaluate characters in real time. Prior work has shown that narratives encode culturally embedded norms and moral structures at scale Rai et al. [2025], Mitran et al. [2025]. Parallel research examines audience reception in digital environments. Mire et al. [2025], Bouzoubaa and Rezapour [2024], Rezapour and Diesner [2017]. Recent work in computational narratology further emphasizes that narrative understanding involves not only events and characters but also the recipient, the audience interpreting the narrative [Piper et al., 2021]. Computational character modeling, meanwhile, has focused primarily on structural properties within texts [Mian et al., 2026, Chang et al., 2025], rather than how audiences evaluate fictional characters in the wild. In this work, we ask: What drives audience sentiment toward fictional characters in large-scale online discourse? Why do some morally flawed characters remain beloved while others provoke backlash? Why do audiences suddenly turn on characters following particular narrative events? And what kinds of reasons do audiences cite when praising or condemning characters? Our work addresses these questions by modeling audience evaluations of fictional characters as structured, theory-grounded expressions of collective judgment in large-scale online discourse [Fish, 2004]. Rather than focusing solely on sentiment or narrative structure, we analyze the reasons audiences provide when evaluating characters, allowing us to study how online communities assign approval, blame, and legitimacy to fictional figures over time. To enable this analysis, we curate a large-scale dataset of Reddit discussions across 24 television series, develop a theory-informed taxonomy of evaluative reasons grounded in communication and media studies, and collect human annotations linking character mentions to sentiment and the reasons underlying those evaluations. Together, these resources provide a computational framework for studying character evaluations at scale and, more broadly, for examining how online communities articulate norms, moral expectations, and interpretive frameworks through discussions of fictional narratives. Dataset: To construct a large-scale corpus of character-centered audience discourse, we began with subreddits categorized under Reddit’s “Movies & TV” topic and filtered to communities dedicated to serial television formats shows. We retained the largest communities while restricting to series that premiered after Reddit’s launch (mid-2005) to ensure contemporaneous discussion. To capture live audience reactions, we required subreddit creation to occur before or within a few days after the show premiere and removed duplicate or overlapping communities (retaining the largest subreddit per series). December 2025 serves as the cutoff for ongoing shows. The final dataset comprises 24 television series spanning multiple genres and networks, with subreddit sizes ranging from approximately 124K to 3.6M members. Using the Reddit Historical Posts dataset1, we extracted the complete history of posts and comments from these communities, yielding over 30M posts and 50M comments. Table 1 summarizes the dataset statistics. To focus on discussions occurring during active viewing periods, we retain only posts created during the airing of a season, as well as a short amount of time after the season ends. To identify character-centered discourse, we use gpt-5-mini to extract character mentions from all posts in the filtered dataset. Extracted names are mapped to canonical character identities using series-specific alias normalization derived from fandom wiki sources. Evaluation on a human-validated subset shows strong performance (precision 0.95, recall 0.91, F1 0.93). We therefore apply the model to the full dataset and exclude posts without identifiable character mentions from downstream analysis. Annotation and Preliminary Findings: For each character-centered post, we label two components: the sentiment expressed by the author toward the character (positive, negative, or neutral) and the reasons mentioned when the sentiment is positive, negative, or both. To capture recurring patterns in how audiences justify their evaluations, we develop a theory-informed taxonomy of twelve evaluative dimensions grounded in prior work in communication, social psychology, and media studies. The taxonomy was constructed through an iterative process involving literature review, refinement and consolidation in collaboration with communication scholars, and multiple rounds of pilot annotations to ensure that the dimensions were both theoretically grounded and observable in real-world discourse. Table 2 summarizes the final set of dimensions and their theoretical foundations. To construct labeled data, we developed an annotation interface in which annotators evaluate sentiment toward a target character and select all relevant reasons from the taxonomy, marking up to two primary reasons. Annotators were recruited via Prolific. Only participants who reported having watched all episodes of a given series in a pre-screening study were invited to annotate posts from that show. Each post was labeled by three independent annotators, and attention checks were included to ensure quality. In a preliminary study across five series, sentiment-level agreement reached moderate levels (Krippendorff’s α between 0.6 and 0.7). A key challenge was class imbalance, as a substantial proportion of posts were neutral, limiting reliable analysis of reason-level agreement. To address this, we introduced an active learning loop in which model predictions are compared against majority human labels to selectively sample posts more likely to contain positive or negative evaluations. Our current best-performing model gpt-5 achieves approximately 0.81 accuracy against human majority sentiment labels. Additional annotation rounds are ongoing to increase coverage of non-neutral cases and strengthen agreement on reason categories. Ongoing Work and Expected Contributions This project is ongoing. Current efforts focus on expanding annotated coverage through additional active-learning rounds and stabilizing agreement on reason-level labels. Once sufficient annotation depth is achieved, we will benchmark LLMs on both sentiment classification and multi-label reason prediction against human judgments, enabling scalable analysis across our full Reddit corpus. At scale, this framework will allow us to examine temporal shifts in character evaluations, identify narrative events associated with changes in audience sentiment, and compare evaluative patterns across series. More broadly, this enables the study of how online communities collectively interpret narrative developments and articulate moral expectations about fictional characters over time.

posters.title: Global Landscape of AI Policy
posters.authors: Munjung Kim, Jaehyuk Park and Jisung Yoon
posters.keywords: AI policy policy discourse global governance cross-national comparison document embedding
posters.abstract:
Governments worldwide are rapidly developing policy frameworks to address the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence. Yet comparative research on AI policy has largely focused on a small number of technologically advanced countries, leaving open the question of whether nations at different levels of development engage with AI in fundamentally different ways. We address this question through a large-scale computational analysis of 111,375 English-language AI policy documents from 138 countries (2000--2025), drawn from the Overton database. Using text embeddings (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B), BERTopic for topic modeling, and SemAxis~[1] for semantic axis analysis, we examine cross-national variation in both the topical structure and discursive framing of AI policy.

We begin by asking whether cross-national variation in document volume reflects meaningful differences in AI policy capacity. Per-country document counts correlate strongly with the Government AI Readiness Index~[2] (Spearman $\rho$ = 0.730; Fig.~1a), an AI-specific measure of national governance, infrastructure, skills, and public services, substantially exceeding correlations with GDP per capita ($\rho$ = 0.518) and the Human Development Index ($\rho$ = 0.553). This suggests that the distribution of documents in our corpus corresponds to national differences in AI governance capacity, infrastructure, and skills---the dimensions measured by the AI Readiness Index.

We then map the thematic landscape of global AI policy. Topic modeling identifies 26 policy topics that organize into five clusters via hierarchical clustering (Fig.~1b): Legislative and Administrative Processes, Socioeconomic Development Policy, Digital Regulation and Governance, Security and External Affairs, and Social Values and International Cooperation. These clusters capture qualitatively distinct modes of policy engagement, from parliamentary and budgetary processes to digital governance and social welfare. Comparing cluster distributions across developed and developing countries reveals where these groups direct their policy attention (Fig.~1c). Developed countries distribute discourse broadly across all five clusters, with notably higher shares of legislative and administrative activity (13.6\% vs.\ 3.8\%) and digital regulation (20.1\% vs.\ 14.1\%), reflecting deeper institutional infrastructure for AI governance. Developing countries concentrate on socioeconomic development (44.0\% vs.\ 37.3\%) and security and external affairs (21.0\% vs.\ 12.3\%), the latter driven largely by trade and international development cooperation. While both groups devote similar overall shares to social values ($\sim$17\%), the composition differs: developing countries emphasize human rights and health, whereas developed countries focus on justice and law enforcement.

Beyond topical differences, semantic axis analysis reveals a divergence in how these groups frame AI policy (Fig.~1d). We construct a semantic axis by computing the vector difference between the centroids of developed and developing countries' document embeddings. We then extract the top 5,000 corpus-wide TF-IDF keywords, project each onto this axis, and select the 30 keywords nearest each pole. Keywords nearest the developed pole characterize developed-country discourse; those nearest the developing pole characterize developing-country discourse. The results show a clear pattern: developed countries cluster around risk and impact assessment (risk assessment, reduce risk, impact society), ethics and transparency (explainability, transparency, human centric), and environmental governance (climate neutrality, environmental impact), positioning AI primarily as a risk to be assessed and governed. Developing countries cluster around education (school, educator, prepare student), government administration (civil servant, minister, prime minister, fiscal), and national development (sector development, regional development), positioning AI within broader agendas of state capacity and human capital building. Together with the topic-level differences above, these results suggest that developed and developing countries diverge not only in which policy areas they prioritize but also in how they orient toward AI: as a risk to be governed versus an instrument for national development.

As the international community moves toward shared AI governance norms, prominent frameworks such as the EU AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, and UNESCO's Recommendation on AI Ethics have largely emerged from the risk governance paradigm characteristic of developed nations. Our results suggest that this paradigm captures only one side of a broader global discourse, and that efforts to build inclusive governance frameworks should attend to the divergent priorities of countries at different stages of development.

posters.title: State Regulation of AI Content in Political Campaigns
posters.authors: Anna-Maria Gueorguieva and Nicholas Weber
posters.keywords: generative AI political campaigns AI disclosure AI detection election regulation
posters.abstract: Concern over AI usage in political campaigns has led 26 U.S. states to enact legislation requiring disclosure of AI-generated content (or prohibiting its use entirely). However, without systematic monitoring tools, disclosure laws rely entirely on self-reporting or litigation from harmed parties. We address this gap by developing a measurement framework for estimating AI use in election campaigns along two dimensions, magnitude (proportion of content detected as AI-generated) and modality (distribution across communication channels). To support this analysis, we compile a comprehensive database of 27,512 candidates spanning federal, state, and municipal levels across 2023–2026 election cycles. In our preliminary analysis applying Pangram, a machine learning-based text detection tool to campaign websites, we find 6.5% of mayoral candidates (N=59) and 5.1% of state house candidates (N=93) have substantial AI involvement in campaign text. Additionally, we show that detection rates vary by content type, with policy pages showing the highest detection signals. We will extend our analysis to all 27,512 candidate-election pairs across 2023–2026 cycle and across text and non-text modalities found in campaign emails, sites, and social media. Our presentation will include updated results from 2025 analysis and preliminary evidence on policy effectiveness in 2026 races.

posters.title: Networks of AI Narratives and Beliefs
posters.authors: Carl Illustrisimo and Kaiona Martinson
posters.keywords: Artificial Intelligence Discussions Computational Folklore Network Analysis Online Communities Topic Modeling
posters.abstract: This work investigates the structure and overlap of AI narratives on Reddit using a computational folklore approach adapted from Tangherlini et al. We construct a generative network model from Reddit posts and comments, extracting syntactic relations (SVO constructions), clustering entities into semantically coherent supernodes, and detecting narrative communities via Louvain community detection. Crucially, we extend this framework with user-level tracking, enabling us to examine patterns of co-occurrence across narrative clusters and identify which components of AI discussions are shared across different users—and, ultimately, which beliefs circulate across narrative and community boundaries. Preliminary findings suggest that boundaries between AI narrative communities are far less discrete than prior work implies. User-level analysis further reveals that individuals may hold seemingly contradictory stances across different narrative contexts, motivating a more relational and less prescriptive approach to stance detection in AI discourse.

posters.title: Modelling Overton-window breakdown with social group pressures and dynamic social identity
posters.authors: Leon Klingborg
posters.keywords: Overton window simulation modelling social media moderation polarization belief dynamics
posters.abstract: To investigate how to prevent Overton window breakdown -- the state where disagreements in a population perpetually deepen -- we simulate plausible interventions in a model of attitude change. Our modelling approach relies on social group pressures and dynamic social identity and is inspired by social identity theory. We find that promoting the attitudes of influential moderate voices consistently prevents Overton window breakdown. Penalizing extreme attitudes is partially effective but also sometimes counterproductive. Diverting attention away from sensitive issues has the opposite of intended effect.

posters.title: Modeling Group Socialization in Online Communities
posters.authors: Iris Zhong, Vinay Koshy, Karrie Karahalios, Benjamin Hill and Amy Zhang
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Online Communities Socialization Norms Text Modeling Social Network Analysis
posters.abstract: Norms, which are the explicit and implicit rules that govern behavior within a social group, define the culture and character of most online communities. Prior work demonstrates that online community norms are dynamic and change over a community's lifespan, but the underlying reasons for this remain unclear. One hypothesis, surfaced in prior qualitative work, is that community norms may shift when newcomer's with different backgrounds and expectations join a group. This is consistent with foundational work in group socialization, which frames socialization as a bidirectional process: newcomers adapt their behaviors to the groups they join, and groups adapt their norms to better suit newcomers. In this extended abstract, we propose a novel, Bayesian model of group socialization in online, text-based communities. We model users' contributions to the community they join as a mixture of in-group language and language from communities they previously participated in, and allow the balance of this mixture to vary by community. We conduct a preliminary qualitative validation of our model. To do this, we fit our model to data from several Reddit communities (subreddits), and examine whether the learned balances of in-group and out-group language align with our prior expectations around the socialization processes of these communities. In the future, we plan to test the whether our model of socialization is able to explain community language patterns better than baseline models which do not include model socialization bidirectionally.

posters.title: How Public Commenters Use Evidence to Persuade Federal Regulators
posters.authors: Sarah Tran and Nicholas Weber
posters.keywords: Federal Rulemaking AI Regulation Computational Text Analysis
posters.abstract: This paper examines how public commenters use evidence to engage with the federal rulemaking process. Drawing on a database of nearly 10.5 million comments across 588 economically significant regulations, we develop a pipeline for extracting and classifying evidential claims from long-form PDF submissions. We apply this pipeline to 13,672 comments on 37 AI rulemakings, and find that evidence use is heavily concentrated among a minority of commenters and that different commenter types, including foundation model companies, exhibit distinctive citation patterns across evidence types. These findings provide a substantive characterization of public participation in nascent, critical regulatory processes and offer new tools for large-scale analysis of notice-and-comment rulemaking.

posters.title: After the Last Brushstroke: How the Death of an Artistic Movement Changes What Gets Remembered
posters.authors: Helena Miton and Joseph Young
posters.keywords: Art CNN Embeddings Cultural Success Optimal Distinctiveness Collective Memory
posters.abstract:
Introduction

What determines which artists achieve lasting recognition? We associate Pablo Picasso and Vincent Van Gogh with very unique, distinctive visual movements, and think of them as trend- setters, ahead of their time. But are these two characteristics—distinctiveness and early entry into a movement—a sure recipe for success and longevity? Were they already strong predictors of success during these artists' lifetimes, when the art movements to which they belonged were still active, producing new artworks and attracting new members? Across diverse cultural markets, successful cultural products tend to be “typical” of the category they are in, or moderately (optimally) distinctive from other products (Askin, N. & Mauskapf, M. 2017; Hsu, G. 2006; Kovacs, B. & Johnson, R. 2014). However, it is unclear whether these effects hold in the same way when a category (such as an art movement) is still active and expanding, as when it is mostly static (e.g., after an art movement “died”). We argue that, as artistic movements are dynamic, what counts as “typical” in a movement's formative years differs from what is typical after its canon is established, and that this, in turn, changes what factors drive cultural success. We investigate the impact of a movement’s state on drivers of cultural success: whether a movement is still actively receiving new contributions (alive) or has effectively ceased to produce new artworks (dead). While these questions typically used to be difficult -if not impossible- to answer, recent advances have made them tractable at scale. Computational studies of success in the arts have linked career position to recognition (Fraiberger, Sinatra, Barabási et al., 2018), while advances in CNN-based art analysis have shown that deep image embeddings can capture stylistic features relevant to evaluation and recognition (Banerjee, Cole, & Ingram, 2023). Using large naturalistic data, studies of collective memory have demonstrated that cultural attention decays along predictable trajectories (Candia et. al, 2019). Computational approaches to measuring conformity and distinctiveness have also shown that a product’s position in a high-dimensional feature space predicts its reception (Berger & Packard, 2019, Askin & Mauskapf, 2017). Here, we combine these approaches to test whether artists are evaluated differently when the art movement they belong to is still active or has died out. We test three hypotheses, all based on the idea that some cues (timing, visual conformity) are more informative when an art movement is lively than once it no longer receives new contributions. First, being an early contributor to a movement helps an artist achieve cultural success more when the movement is still alive than when it is dead. Second, visual conformity to a movement has a greater impact on cultural success while that movement is still alive than when it is dead and its canon is established. Third, visual distinctiveness from the broader (“global”) artistic landscape matters more in alive movements, where evaluators face greater uncertainty.

Methods
