We construct a comprehensive dataset linking artworks from the WikiArt digital encyclopedia of fine art with several measures of cultural success, including counts of mentions of an artist on the Wikipedia pages of styles they produce in (public visibility), museum holdings documented in the Oxford Benezit Dictionary of Artists (institutional recognition), and counts of citations in canonical art history textbooks (scholarly canonization). Our sample includes 46,617 artworks spanning multiple centuries, classified into 71 recognized artistic movements (e.g., Impressionism, Abstract Expressionism, Pop Art). We classify stylistic movements as “alive” if they continue to receive new contributions in recent decades (based on whether the minimum time between creation and auction is less than ten years), and “dead” otherwise. To measure an artwork's visual distinctiveness, we use high-dimensional image embeddings from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Srinivasa Desikan, Shimao, & Miton, 2022). Specifically, for each painting, we extract activation vectors from the penultimate layer of a pre-trained deep CNN, yielding a high-dimensional representation of the artwork's visual content. We compute cosine distance from each artwork to two reference points: (1) its movement centroid (the average embedding of all works in the same movement) capturing within-movement conformity, and (2) the global centroid (the average embedding across all artworks) capturing overall distinctiveness from the broader artistic landscape. For both measures, larger distances reflect higher visual distinctiveness, and smaller distances, more conformity. We test whether the relationship between an artwork’s position within its stylistic movement and its cultural success varies with the movement's state. Specifically, we examine how the timing of production within a movement’s history, visual distinctiveness from its movement, and visual distinctiveness from the global artistic landscape predict cultural recognition, and whether their effects differ between dead and alive movements. We estimate logistic and OLS regressions for several measures of cultural success, with movement-level fixed effects and standard errors clustered at the level of the artist.

Preliminary Findings

Our results (See Table 1) clearly support the first prediction: being an early contributor matters more in alive movements, with the association between relative timing and cultural success substantially stronger when a movement is still active. The evidence for the second prediction is more mixed: within-movement distinctiveness interacts with movement state for some measures of cultural success (Wikipedia mentions, textbook citations) but not others, suggesting that the role of visual conformity may depend on the dimension of recognition considered. Alive and dead movements further seem to differ in the functional form of this relationship. Alive movements exhibit an inverted-U relationship between within-movement distinctiveness and cultural success, consistent with optimal distinctiveness, while dead movements exhibit a U-shape, suggesting that collective memory favors either prototypical or exceptional works (See Figure 1). The impact of global distinctiveness does not seem to differ significantly between alive and dead movements. Together, these patterns suggest that when a movement is still expanding, its boundaries and prototypes are unstable, and timing and conformity to the movement may serve as stronger signals of which artists will achieve lasting recognition. In dead movements where the identity has settled, these same cues matter less.

posters.title: Block Me from Myself: Adversarial Self-Use in Digital Overuse Recovery Narratives from r/nosurf
posters.authors: Sally Ahmed, Manasa Kudumu and Pattie Maes
posters.keywords: Digital Ethnography Digital Wellbeing Social Media Platforms Online communities Problematic Internet Use
posters.abstract: Digital self-control tools—app blockers, screen time limits, focus modes—are widely adopted yet show weak statistical evidence of effectiveness. We analyze 4,552 posts from r/nosurf, a Reddit community dedicated to reducing compulsive internet use, to understand why these interventions fail from the user perspective. Using sentence embeddings, HDBSCAN, and KMeans clustering followed by qualitative analysis, we identify three cross-cutting themes: users frame their phone use through the language of addiction; they systematically circumvent self-imposed digital constraints through what we term \textit{adversarial self-regulation}; and they struggle to find restrictions compatible with daily life. Our findings suggest that current tools fail not because they lack features, but because they do not account for users' anticipation of their own future non-compliance. We discuss future work involving data analysis and design implications.

posters.title: Beyond Aggregates: A Longitudinal Network Approach to Detecting Candidate Viability with Campaign Contributions
posters.authors: Marcelina Przespolewska and Erik Nisbet
posters.keywords: network analysis political networks donor networks campaign finance candidate viability
posters.abstract: Campaign contributions are among the major factors influencing the viability of a presidential candidate before the primaries, yet their role is typically analyzed using aggregate measures, ignoring the relational structure embedded in donor behavior. Moreover, as donor networks remain comparatively understudied, little is known about whether their structure captures information about candidate viability that aggregate metrics overlook. This paper fills this gap by introducing a new method for estimating candidate viability with relational donor data over time during presidential primaries. We construct a donor-donor network representation of campaign finance that captures similarities in donor support patterns across candidates and derive the properties of candidate-level subnetworks to improve predictions of candidate viability compared to conventional aggregate indicators. Our study reveals how network representation of donor data can be used to estimate candidate viability and helps advance methodological approaches to predicting campaign performance.

posters.title: The Unexpectedness Gap: Decomposing the Socioeconomic Inequality in the Quality of Employment Self-predictions
posters.authors: Hanzhang Ren
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: forecasting precarious labor predictability longitudinal survey overoptimistic bias
posters.abstract: Who experiences more unexpectedness in life than others? My work studies how and why socioeconomically disadvantaged people have less success in foreseeing a key life outcome: whether one will be employed in four months. Economists observe that people predicting an x-percent employment probability usually have a less-than-x-percent chance of employment, especially among the less well-off. However, such calculations of systematic bias cancel out positive and negative prediction errors and do not compare the importance of systematic bias to that of other factors determining unexpectedness. Verifying American household heads’ self-predictions in public longitudinal data from the Survey of Consumer Expectations, I show that higher-earning respondents better foresee both employment and nonemployment. I then decompose the mean squared error produced by this national sample with a technique thus far reserved for predictions by machine learning algorithms and expert forecasters. The decomposition shows that in expectation, differences in systematic bias explain at most 15% of the unexpectedness gap between the top and bottom earning groups. Disadvantaged people have unexpected outcomes mainly because they lack the employment stability and effective advance notice necessary for foreseeing nonemployment.

posters.title: Strategy Space: A unified corporate strategy space for managerial decision support
posters.authors: Sanggoo Kang, Doeun Kim, Oh-Hyun Kwon, Woo-Sung Jung and Jaehyuk Park
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: Corporate strategy Strategic positioning Sentence embedding Competitive dynamics Earnings Calls
posters.abstract:
Understanding corporate strategic positioning is fundamental to explaining competitive dynamics, yet traditional financial metrics often fail to capture real-time, multidimensional strategic intent. We propose "Strategy Space," a unified framework that projects Earnings Call transcripts into a continuous semantic landscape using Transformer-based SBERT embeddings. By mapping firms onto four specific strategic axes, including Exploitation-Exploration, Domestic-International, Short-term-Long-term, and Specialization-Diversification, we quantify latent strategic orientations and trace their dynamic trajectories.

This methodology allows for a comprehensive analysis of strategic adaptations driven by both external environment shocks, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, and internal firm-specific factors, such as size and growth. An empirical analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic identifies a strategic synchronization toward a "COVID-19 anchor" in 2020, reflecting institutional isomorphism under extreme uncertainty. However, by 2022, strategic discourse rapidly recovered to pre-pandemic baselines, suggesting the crisis acted as a transient attractor. Furthermore, multivariate regression analysis reveals that these strategic orientations are systematically affected by internal resource constraints, such as firm size and growth rates. This research bridges the longstanding gap between qualitative managerial discourse and quantitative strategic modeling by demonstrating that narrative expressions are systematic responses to both competitive landscapes and internal resource constraints.

posters.title: Reconstructing Gender Values from Film: Digital Twins of Fictional Characters as Surveyable Agents
posters.authors: Vivienne Bihe Chi, Reyhan Jamalova, Lyle Ungar and Sharath Chandra Guntuku
posters.keywords: Digital Twins Generative Agents Survey Emulation Gender Norms Cultural Measurement
posters.abstract: We present a proof-of-concept study that explores whether fictional characters can be used to reconstruct historical cultural values at scale. We adapt a digital-twin architecture to transform movie script characters into surveyable LLM agents, enabling measurement of gender attitudes portrayed in film. Using 160 U.S. movie scripts from 1990–2019, we reconstruct lead-character personas from dialogue and scene descriptions, condense these into structured reflections, and simulate responses to three gender-norm items from the World Values Survey. Results show systematic gender differentiation among agents: female characters express stronger disagreement with male-privileging norms even without explicit gender prompting. However, agent responses diverge from real survey data, producing more egalitarian attitudes and larger gender gaps. These findings suggest that narrative media encode coherent value systems but may amplify or stylize gender distinctions relative to population attitudes.

posters.title: Social risk in the longitudinal health trajectories of 8 million patients
posters.authors: Katie Spoon and David Rehkopf
posters.keywords: social determinants of health clinical NLP health trajectories health equity electronic health records
posters.abstract: This paper introduces a computational framework for studying how social inequalities in health accumulate and diverge over the life course, using longitudinal primary care records from 8.5 million U.S. patients linked to individual-level Census and American Community Survey data. We address two fundamental limitations in population health research: the invisibility of upstream social risk factors in structured clinical data, and the dominance of cross-sectional, prediction-oriented modeling approaches that obscure where and why health trajectories diverge. We recover social determinants of health from unstructured clinical notes at population scale using a two-stage NLP pipeline, and integrate these measures into interpretable longitudinal health trajectories represented as paths on a state-transition network. This representation makes divergence itself the object of study, enabling identification of where similar trajectories separate into pathways of deterioration, stable management, or recovery, and how transition probabilities vary across demographic and neighborhood groups. Descriptive analysis reveals that social risks appear in clinical notes at rates three to five times higher than in structured fields, with gaps that vary systematically by patient race and ethnicity. This work offers computational social science a scalable, interpretable framework for studying how social disadvantage accumulates into health risk.

posters.title: The multi-dimensional role of trust and peer influence in vaccination opinion
posters.authors: Duilio Balsamo, Chiara Chiavenna, Vittoria Offeddu, Lorenzo Lucchini and Alessia Melegaro
posters.keywords: Vaccine Attitudes Trust Peer Influence Institutions Social Media
posters.abstract: Vaccination attitudes emerge from a complex interplay of individual characteristics, social influence, and differentiated trust across distinct social spheres. Most empirical studies, though, model these phenomena as unidimensional, despite their dynamic and multidimensional nature. Using survey data from 22,228 individuals in six European countries, in this work we examine how peer influence, trust in close contacts, institutions, and media sources jointly shapes vaccine opinions. We implement an XGBoost classifier and interpret results through SHAP values to identify nonlinear and asymmetric effects. Findings show that overall trust and household norms are among the strongest predictors of vaccination attitudes. Trust in institutional actors is generally associated with positive views, while trust in certain social media sources contributes negatively, particularly among individuals with lower health literacy. Importantly, trust amplifies prevailing local norms, reinforcing both supportive and skeptical positions. These results highlight vaccination opinion as the outcome of nested social influence processes and suggest that effective vaccination policies should combine institutional trust-building with interventions targeting household dynamics and information environments.

posters.title: Edit Storms on Wikipedia: Temporal Dynamics of Article Editorship
posters.authors: Lawrence Swaminathan Xavier Prince
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: Wikipedia Temporal analysis Online social systems Collective attention
posters.abstract:
Wikipedia is the largest collaborative knowledge repository in the world and is maintained largely by decentralized communities of volunteers who create, revise and maintain articles. Since articles are continuously edited to maintain and incorporate new relevant elements, they serve as a useful resource to study as large-scale records of collaborative knowledge production and community behavior. Prior research has examined Wikipedia’s collaborative structures, particularly among editors, conflict dynamics, polarization, and content quality (Keegan & Tan, 2020; Shi et al., 2019). Since Wikipedia articles are influenced by real world sociopolitical events and changing cultural perceptions, they are not immune to change over time. Various works studying human social dynamics have shown ‘bursts’ or spikes of intensive activity across online social datasets including editorship on Wikipedia (Choi et al., 2021). However, these studies largely treat burst periods as endpoints rather than as phases within longer temporal ranges. As a result, we know little about what happens after heightened edit activity subsides.

Researchers have characterized media storms as rapid, high-intensity bursts of attention that disrupt routine coverage patterns and then decay (Litterer et al., 2023). These events are marked not only by peaks but also by post-peak trajectories. While this framework has been widely applied to news production, an analogous analysis of ‘editorship storms’ has not been systematically applied to collaborative knowledge production on platforms like Wikipedia. We are interested in studying the temporal dynamics of article editorship after they have reached their peak in popularity, particularly looking for signs of an eventual reaching of editorial stability. We analyze whether editorial activity following peak salience converges to stable low-variance states or exhibits persistent elevated engagement. Further, we seek to understand the underlying relationship between editorship and popularity of articles. We conceptualize editorship and viewership of articles as two distinct but meaningful forms of attention. Our goal is to use editorship as a new way to analyze and better understand the attention dynamics of online social systems.

We start by constructing a dataset of Wikipedia articles that ranked among the top 1,000 by peak pageviews every month between July 2015 and December 2019. Because articles may enter the top 1,000 in multiple months, aggregating unique entries yields 12,956 distinct articles. This window ensures sufficient post-peak observation and prevents the inclusion of articles whose long-term editorship is uncertain. Each article’s editorship is represented as a monthly time series of edit intensity from its creation through December 1, 2025. Edit intensity is defined as the number of revisions per month. Since different articles will have varying levels of editorship and popularity, we focus on the patterns within each article rather than absolute edit volumes across the whole dataset. We detect editorship storms using Facebook Prophet, an unsupervised anomaly detection model previously used to detect media storms (Markus et al., 2025). We illustrate this through the example of the ‘Brexit’ article as seen in Figure 1. Periods of intensive editing coincide with major political events and increases in unique editor participation, followed by gradual stabilization toward a persistent baseline.

If edit activities reflect collective attention, we would expect page views and edit activity of articles to closely track one another. To assess this, we examine the relationship between peak viewership and peak editorship across prominent articles. Figure 2 shows the scatter plot comparing the peak page views and editorship activity of 907 highly popular articles within our original dataset of 12,956 articles. We arrived at this subset by restricting the sample to articles that remained in the top 1,000 for at least six months and exhibited a minimum of 100 edits in their peak month. Peak page views account for approximately 25% of the variance in editorial activity (R² = 0.251), indicating a moderate association between public attention and editorial attention. Still, we find that the majority of variation remains unexplained by viewership alone, suggesting that additional social or institutional dynamics shape editorship intensity. This finding suggests that internal editorial dynamics extend beyond visibility-driven attention.

We perform a preliminary case analysis using our subset of prominent articles. We find clear bursts of editorial attention to articles during periods of social, political, or cultural relevance. Articles about political figures and events, particularly elections, go through recurring temporal motifs, including sharp burst and decay patterns, prolonged elevated plateaus, and cyclical resurgence tied to recurring events. Articles rarely converge to complete inactivity. Instead, they stabilize at a persistent baseline level of engagement. In several instances as seen in Figure 3, secondary spikes emerge years after the original event, often corresponding to renewed relevance or structurally similar contemporary events. This suggests that politically significant topics exhibit path-dependent reactivation, remaining structurally embedded in cycles of public discourse rather than decaying into static historical records.

In contrast, entertainment-related articles exhibit more cyclical and release-driven patterns of engagement. Rather than a single crisis-induced spike followed by decay, film and television articles often show multiple peaks corresponding to premieres, sequels, streaming releases, or renewed cultural relevance. Decay is less abrupt, and baseline engagement remains comparatively elevated. This suggests that editorial storms in cultural domains are embedded within recurring consumption cycles, whereas political events more often produce punctuated bursts tied to discrete historical moments. These domain-specific motifs indicate that post-peak trajectories are shaped not only by attention intensity but by the structural rhythms of the underlying social system.

By extending the media storm framework to collaborative knowledge production, this work highlights the unique dynamics of editorship as a complementary signal of online attention. Future research will examine whether these post-storm dynamics correspond to structural shifts in editor interaction networks along with the influence of institutional and editor-editor dynamics.

posters.title: Defending Digital Democracy: Mitigating Adversarial Redundancy in Voting Advice Applications using Clone-Robust Weighting
posters.authors: Liv Weiss, Frédéric Berdoz, Damien Berriaud and Roger Wattenhofer
posters.keywords: Voting Advice Applications Adversarial Robustness Cloning Attack Recommender Systems Natural Language Processing Computational Political Science
posters.abstract: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are widely used tools that match voters with candidates based on policy preferences, but their standard recommendation mechanism is vulnerable to manipulation. By injecting redundant or paraphrased survey questions, malicious actors can give specific policy topics disproportionate influence over voter-candidate recommendations. This extended abstract applies Clone-Robust Weighting (CRW), a framework that downweights questions based on their semantic similarity to others in the survey, as a defense against this attack. We evaluate CRW across 10 transformer-based sentence embedding models using real data from the 2023 Swiss National Council elections, testing five types of adversarial clones of increasing difficulty. Results show that CRW consistently reduces recommendation distortion across all models and clone types, with the best-performing model achieving a 31.5% relative improvement in recommendation preservation. A targeted election manipulation simulation further demonstrates that CRW meaningfully reduces artificial boosts to party visibility, neutralizing 38 to 69% of the distortion under realistic attack conditions. The method requires no labeled data and is directly applicable to existing VAA platforms.

posters.title: PoliSpace: Political Opinion Prediction using Shared Latent Space
posters.authors: Johanna D'Ciofalo, Frédéric Berdoz and Roger Wattenhofer
posters.keywords: Opinion Prediction Contrastive Learning Voting Advice Applications Representation Learning Digital Democracy
posters.abstract: Accurately modeling and predicting political opinions remains a significant challenge for AI. While recent LLM-based approaches encode human beliefs into latent spaces, they often lack robustness to question rephrasing. To address these limitations, we propose PoliSpace, an interpretable framework that embeds voters as learnable vectors and questions as text-encoded representations in a shared latent space where alignment directly reflects agreement. The text-encoder has been fine-tuned to account for rephrased and negated versions of questions using contrastive learning. We evaluate our proposed model using real-world data from the Swiss voting advice application SmartVote across four increasingly difficult scenarios. PoliSpace achieves an F1 score of 89.81% on seen opinion prediction for indirectly seen questions, competitive with current state-of-the-art and achieving performance comparable to GPT-4 prompting. Furthermore, by integrating retrieval and confidence-aware thresholding, our model reaches up to 100% accuracy while maintaining interpretable. While prediction on entirely new questions remains challenging, we see PoliSpace as a foundation for building more robust and interpretable models of political opinion.

posters.title: State Housing Policy Environments and Suicide Risk among Households Experiencing Eviction in the US from 2011 to 2021
posters.authors: Aparna Ananthasubramaniam, Sarah Burgard, Daniel Romero, David Jurgens and Briana Mezuk
posters.keywords: natural language processing suicide deaths eviction foreclosure state housing policy
posters.abstract:
Objective. To assess whether state housing policy environments moderate risk of suicide death following the initiation of formal eviction or foreclosure proceedings.

Methods. We use techniques from natural language processing to identify suicide decedents who received an eviction or foreclosure filing from narrative texts in the National Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS) from 2011 to 2021. We then combine the NVDRS with multiple external data sources to create a county-level population-scale dataset examining the joint distribution of suicide, eviction, foreclosure, and state policy over an 11-year period. Finally, we test whether three sets of policies are associated with changes in suicide risk following eviction and foreclosure: (1) the state-level eviction and foreclosure policies from 2011-2018, (2) each state’s time-varying enforcement of the federal COVID-19 eviction moratoria from 2020-2021, and (3) the time-varying state-level COVID-19 eviction protections from 2020-2021. We explored county- and individual-level correlates of suicide risk following eviction and foreclosure.

Results. Between 2011-2018, we find that people in households experiencing eviction are less likely to die by suicide when they live in a state with strong resident protections than in a state with weak protections; there are no differences in suicide rates among households experiencing foreclosure. Decedents in states with strong resident protections tend to have more contributing circumstances preceding the eviction and report lower levels of emotional distress and displacement from housing. Suicide risk following eviction is particularly attenuated by strong state-level resident protections in counties where more residents have risk factors for eviction, civic engagement is weaker, and social safety nets are stronger. During the COVID-19 pandemic, states that enforced the federal eviction moratoria or introduced additional state eviction protections had higher suicide risk following eviction.

Conclusion. Following a Health in All Policies approach, this work identifies opportunities for suicide prevent through policies protecting residents against housing loss.

posters.title: Repair Motivations in Digital Discourse: A Social Listening and Machine Learning Approach
posters.authors: Barna Lipics, Pálma Mogyorósi, Zoltán Kmetty and Ágnes Buvár
posters.theme: Social Media Platforms and Online Communities
posters.keywords: repair behavior circular economy social listening large language models vector embeddings
posters.abstract: Extending product lifecycles is critical for sustainability, yet a significant gap persists between positive consumer attitudes and actual repair behavior. The literature on repair motivations commonly distinguishes between rational appeals, which emphasize benefits such as economic utility or functional value, and emotional appeals for example framing objects as part of the "extended self" or carriers of memories. Recent experimental evidence suggests that persuasive repair messages employing rational appeals directly increase repair choices, without generating more positive attitudes toward repair behavior. To investigate these drivers without the bias inherent in self-assessment, we employed a social listening approach, analyzing 30,000 comments and 7,000 articles from a multi-platform aggregator from the last 3 years. We customized our text analysis tools for Hungarian. We then trained a machine learning model using examples we checked by hand, to automatically filter out irrelevant content. The analysis utilized UMAP for dimensionality reduction and HDBSCAN to identify latent thematic clusters within the discourse. A hybrid framework of local and proprietary Large Language Models (LLMs) then extracted specific user motivations. We used a novel approach, GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) prompt optimization technique to assess scientifically trustworthy LLM extraction. We anticipate establishing a foundational taxonomy of repair motivations and to evaluate the extent to which existing classifications are reflected in organic discourse. Furthermore, we aim to quantify the frequency and distribution of these drivers. The results can be applied to design more relevant and effective communication interventions to promote repair behavior. This research demonstrates the efficacy of modern NLP techniques in extracting psychological insights from unstructured social data, offering a more ecologically valid perspective on circular economy behaviors.

posters.title: AI Labeling Reduces Perceived Accuracy but Has Limited Spillovers: A Nationally Representative Digital Experiment
posters.authors: Chuyao Wang, Patrick Sturgis and Daniel de Kadt
posters.keywords: AI Disclosure Labels Algorithm Aversion Digital Survey Experiment AI Accountability AI Trust
posters.abstract:
AI-generated content (AIGC) is increasingly difficult to distinguish from human-written text, raising concerns about transparency, trust, and misinformation. Disclosure labels that indicate AI involvement are widely proposed as a governance response. However, prior experiments suggest an unintended consequence: holding content constant, AI labels can reduce perceived accuracy. What remains less clear is the scope of this credibility penalty. Does AI labeling primarily affect evaluations of the labeled item, or does it spill over to broader judgments such as policy engagement, policy support, and generalized misinformation concern?

We address this question using a 3-factor survey experiment embedded in a nationally representative probability-based sample of UK adults (n = 3,861). Respondents read a realistic news-style policy article about Universal Basic Income (UBI). We manipulate three features of the information environment: (1) AI salience (a brief neutral description of generative AI and its use in news production prior to the article), (2) AI disclosure labeling (no label vs. an explicit “generated by ChatGPT” label), and (3) policy framing (one-sided advocacy vs. two-sided balanced framing). This design estimates the population-average causal effect of labeling and tests whether labeling effects depend on contextual cues that may shape attention, skepticism, or normalization of AI-assisted authorship.

The experiment proceeds in four steps: salience prime (when assigned), exposure to the UBI article formatted to resemble a BBC News webpage, presence/absence of the AI label, and post-exposure measurement of four outcomes on Likert scales: perceived accuracy, interest in learning more about UBI, policy support, and general concern about misinformation in online news. Treatment effects are estimated via weighted least squares with robust standard errors, using survey weights provided by the panel vendor (design, nonresponse, and post-stratification). Results are robust to unweighted OLS and weighted ordinal logistic specifications.

Three findings emerge. First, AI labeling reduces perceived accuracy of the article. On a five-point scale, the label yields a statistically significant negative effect (β = −0.163; p < .001), replicating the “AI label credibility penalty” documented in previous studies and extending external validity to a large probability-based sample. This pattern is consistent with an algorithm-aversion mechanism, whereby disclosure cues skepticism toward algorithmic authorship even when content is unchanged.

Second, spillover effects are limited. AI labeling reduces expressed policy interest (β = −0.096 on a four-point scale; p < .01), suggesting that disclosure can dampen engagement. Yet labeling has no meaningful effect on policy support (β = −0.022; p = 0.616) and does not increase general concern about misinformation (β = −0.014; p = 0.742). The overall pattern indicates that labeling primarily affects proximal judgments tied to the presented message (credibility and immediate engagement), rather than more stable attitudes (policy support) or broader environmental perceptions (misinformation concern), at least under single-exposure conditions.

Third, contextual cues do not systematically amplify labeling effects. AI salience enhancement has no significant main effects on any outcome and does not strengthen labeling effects on interest, support, or misinformation concern. The principal exception is perceived accuracy: salience attenuates the labeling penalty (Label × Salience β ≈ 0.160; p < .05), implying that neutral information about generative AI may partially normalize the technology and reduce subsequent trust costs of disclosure. One-sided versus two-sided framing does not reliably moderate labeling effects, and higher-order interactions are not statistically significant.

Taken together, AI labeling exhibits a robust but narrow footprint in this policy-information setting. It reliably reduces perceived accuracy and modestly reduces policy interest, but does not shift policy support or generalized misinformation concern. For computational social science and policy design, the results clarify the causal locus of disclosure effects: labels reshape credibility assessments and engagement more than downstream preferences, at least in a realistic news exposure context. Future work should examine whether these patterns generalize across policy issues, content formats, repeated exposures, and interactive human–AI settings, particularly as public familiarity with generative AI increases and labeling becomes routine.

posters.title: Large Language Models are often politically extreme, usually ideologically inconsistent, and persuasive even in informational contexts
posters.authors: Nouar Aldahoul, Hazem Ibrahim, Aaron Kaufman, Talal Rahwan and Yasir Zaki
posters.keywords: Large language models Political ideology Ideological measurement Survey experiments Political persuasion
posters.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are a transformational technology, fundamentally changing how people obtain information and interact with the world. As people become increasingly reliant on them for an enormous variety of tasks, a body of academic research has developed to examine these models for inherent biases, especially political biases, often finding them small. We challenge this prevailing wisdom. First, by comparing 31 LLMs to legislators, judges, and a nationally representative sample of U.S.\ voters, we show that LLMs' apparently small overall partisan preference is the net result of offsetting extreme views on specific topics, much like moderate voters. Second, in a randomized experiment, we show that LLMs can promulgate their preferences into political persuasiveness even in information-seeking contexts: voters randomized to discuss political issues with an LLM chatbot are as much as 5 percentage points more likely to express the same preferences as that chatbot. Contrary to expectations, these persuasive effects are not moderated by familiarity with LLMs, news consumption, or interest in politics. LLMs, especially those controlled by private companies or governments, may become a powerful and targeted vector for political influence.

posters.title: Diagnosing Heuristic Distortions in AI-Assisted Studies of Online Discourse
posters.authors: Shaunette Ferguson
posters.keywords: computational social science temporal networks natural language processing algorithmic bias digital discourse
posters.abstract:
Summary We introduce a diagnostic framework for identifying heuristic distortions in AI-assisted analyses of online discourse. In large-scale digital environments, users and researchers rely on cognitive shortcuts (or fast judgment rules used under uncertainty). Such shortcuts treat visible commenters as representative (representativeness), equate visibility with prevalence (availability), and rely on early information to interpret what follows (anchoring). People rely on cognitive shortcuts because they are efficient responses to scale but, when combined with platform ranking systems and automated text analysis, they can systematically distort visible emotional and thematic patterns. We integrate temporal network analysis with lexicon-based natural language processing to show that visually similar discourse trajectories can arise from fundamentally different mechanisms: (i) genuine temporal constraint versus (ii) participation heterogeneity and visibility effects. We demonstrate how temporal null models distinguish these mechanisms by using two high-visibility YouTube discussions. Our framework improves inference in computational social science and informs responsible AI by reducing misinterpretation of online discourse as consensus, polarization, or collective sentiment.

Extended Abstract Across the social sciences and humanities, researchers are relying increasingly on sentiment analysis, topic modeling, engagement-based metrics, and large-scale text classification to interpret public discourse online, at a scale and ubiquity unmatched in earlier periods of scholarship. These methods promise unprecedented access to collective expression, yet they often rest on a critical assumption, that the most visible online discourse is broadly representative of underlying public attitudes. A growing body of work suggests that this assumption is fragile, particularly in platform-mediated environments where participation is sparse, visibility is algorithmically structured, and interaction unfolds over time (Lazer et al. 2009; Lazer et al. 2014).

We argue that classic cognitive heuristics (i.e., representativeness, availability, and anchoring) operate as structural forces in online communication systems and are systematically reproduced by AI-assisted analytic pipelines. Originally formalized by Tversky and Kahneman (1974), these heuristics describe how humans rely on cognitive shortcuts when making judgments under uncertainty. However, in digital environments, these shortcuts do more than shape individual perception; they interact with platform design and analytic practice to distort the visible record of discourse itself.

Representativeness distortions arise because participation in online discussions is highly selective. A small and atypical subset of viewers produces the majority of visible content, yet computational analyses often implicitly treat commenters as indicative of a broader audience (Nonnecke and Preece 2000). Availability distortions emerge because platform ranking systems amplify content that is emotionally salient or engagement-rich, leading researchers and users alike to mistake visibility for prevalence (Lerman et al. 2010). Anchoring distortions occur when early contributions appear to shape subsequent interpretation and thematic structure, even when their prominence reflects timing, exposure, or cumulative advantage rather than genuine causal influence.

These heuristics are analytically distinct but they often operate simultaneously and produce overlapping empirical signatures rather than one-to-one effects. Common descriptive patterns include emotionally intense early phases, apparent thematic stability, and strong early–late contrasts. In the absence of explicit diagnostics, these patterns can be easily misinterpreted as evidence of collective emotional shifts or emerging consensus. This creates a central challenge for computational social science, that is, distinguishing genuine social dynamics from cognitive and platform-mediated illusion. The present work addresses this challenge by introducing diagnostic tools that allow researchers to empirically test whether visible patterns depend on temporal ordering instead of platform-mediated visibility artifacts.

We address this challenge by introducing a computational diagnostic framework that integrates temporal network analysis with natural language processing to identify when AI-assisted interpretations overstate representativeness, prevalence, or temporal influence. We apply this framework to two high-visibility YouTube comment threads, where users respond to Greta Thunberg’s United Nations climate speech and to Nike’s Dream Crazy advertisement featuring Colin Kaepernick. These cases are well suited for comparison because they exhibit similar early emotional intensity but differ in participation structure and audience composition.

From each comment, we extract LIWC-derived measures of Affect and Social orientation (Pennebaker et al. 2015). Affect captures the proportion of emotionally expressive language, while Social is operationalized as net prosocial minus conflict-oriented language. Figure 1 shows descriptive temporal trajectories for both discussions. In each case, early participation exhibits elevated emotional and social intensity relative to later periods, creating a skewed initial interpretive environment that, on visual inspection, appears consistent with anchoring.

However, descriptive trajectories alone cannot establish whether early expressions exert genuine temporal influence or instead reflect uneven early participation and platform-mediated visibility. To distinguish these mechanisms, we follow established practice in temporal network analysis (Rocha et al. 2010; Karsai et al. 2011; Holme 2015) and employ shuffled timestamp null models. These models preserve comment content, linguistic scores, authorship, and topical structure while randomizing timestamps to isolate the causal role of event ordering. For each dataset, we generate 10,000 shuffled realizations.

We quantify anchoring by measuring the difference in linguistic scores between the first thirty original (top-level) comments and all later comments in the thread. We then compare this empirical early–late difference to the null distribution generated by randomizing timestamps on comments. Empirical gaps consistent with the null distribution indicate that the observed early–late differences do not depend on temporal ordering and therefore do not reflect anchoring. Instead, they are consistent with heterogeneity in early participation and platform-mediated visibility, which can produce similar patterns without temporal constraint. Figure 2 shows that, despite similar descriptive patterns, the two discussions exhibit fundamentally different temporal dynamics. In the Greta Thunberg discussion, early–late gaps for both Affect and net Social fall in the extreme tails of the null distributions, indicating genuine temporal constraint. However, for the Colin Kaepernick discussion, comparable gaps arise frequently under shuffled orderings, which is consistent with early prominence reflecting uneven participation and engagement-based visibility rather than temporal influence.

Our other results indicate a similar pattern in thematic structure, where topics that appear early on persist across later windows, while temporally localized or late-emerging themes fail to reorganize the discourse. This produces the appearance of thematic stability even when alternative frames are present, consistent with thematic anchoring driven by early temporal structure rather than semantic consensus.

These findings demonstrate that visually similar patterns of emotional intensity or thematic stability can arise from distinct mechanisms with different inferential consequences. Temporal null models provide a general diagnostic for separating causal temporal structure from cognitive and platform-mediated illusion. As AI-assisted analyses increasingly inform research, media narratives, and policy, responsible practice requires explicit attention to how participation, visibility, and temporal ordering shape what becomes visible as public discourse.

posters.title: Replicating Motivated Reasoning Studies with LLMs
posters.authors: Neeley Pate, Adiba Proma, Hangfeng He, James Druckman, Daniel Molden, Gourab Ghoshal and M Ehsan Hoque
posters.keywords: Large language models (LLMs) Motivated reasoning Opinion formation Argument assessment Political science
posters.abstract: Motivated reasoning, a concept that describes how individuals process information, is often portrayed as pursuing a directional (predetermined) conclusion or an accurate (non-directional) conclusion. A particular motivation can ultimately affect individuals’ opinions and actions. We explore whether base LLMs - with no personality prompts given - can mimic motivated reasoning by replicating 4 prior political motivated reasoning studies. We find LLM behavior does not align with expected human behavior for neither opinion formation nor argument assessment. These findings have implications for using base LLMs to forecast reactions to political arguments and formation of political opinions, as well as argument assessment, where motivations may play a role in human response.

posters.title: Advancing AI Negotiations: A Large-Scale Autonomous Negotiation Competition
posters.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Michael Caosun, Harang Ju, Sinan Aral and Jared Curhan
posters.keywords: Agentic AI Negotiation Competition
posters.abstract: We conducted an International AI Negotiation Competition in which participants designed and refined prompts for AI negotiation agents. We then facilitated over 180,000 negotiations between these agents across multiple scenarios with diverse characteristics and objectives. Our findings revealed that principles from human negotiation theory remain crucial even in AI-AI contexts. Surprisingly, warmth—a traditionally human relationship-building trait—was consistently associated with superior outcomes across all key performance metrics. Dominant agents, meanwhile, were especially effective at claiming value. Our analysis also revealed unique dynamics in AI-AI negotiations not fully explained by existing theory, including AI-specific technical strategies like chain-of-thought reasoning and prompt injection. When we applied natural language processing (NLP) methods to the full transcripts of all negotiations, we found positivity, gratitude and question-asking (associated with warmth) were strongly associated with reaching deals as well as objective and subjective value, whereas conversation lengths (associated with dominance) were strongly associated with impasses. The results suggest the need to establish a new theory of AI negotiation, which integrates classic negotiation theory with AI-specific negotiation theories to better understand autonomous negotiations and optimize agent performance.

posters.title: Effects of News Delivery Formats on the Article Diversity
posters.authors: Kaho Suzuki, Masaki Chujyo, Fujio Toriumi, Shotaro Ishihara and Ryo Namiki
posters.keywords: Information diversity Online news News Delivery Formats User Behavior Generalist–Specialist Score
posters.abstract:
Information diversity in online media consumption has become a central concern in computational social science, as exposure imbalance is linked to societal polarization[1, 2, 3, 4]. Prior studies have primarily examined the role of recommender systems in shaping users’ information diversity[5, 6, 7]. However, online news platforms also employ editorially curated Bundled formats alongside continuously updated Streaming formats, and the impact of such content organization formats on user-level diversity remains largely understudied. In this study, we compare two contrasting content organization formats on a large online newspaper platform: editorially curated Bundled articles and continuously updated Streaming articles. Bundled articles are human-curated and released as fixed packages at scheduled times, whereas Streaming articles are incrementally added to a dynamic feed without bundle-level editorial curation. We examine how these contrasting formats are associated with information diversity. Using one year of behavioral logs from a large online newspaper platform where Bundled and Streaming formats coexist within the same user environment, we analyze differences in the diversity of articles consumed across formats. We find that Bundled articles are consistently associated with higher information diversity than Streaming articles across multiple analyses, including matched-user comparisons and within-user evaluations. These findings suggest that the structural characteristics of content organization may play an important role in shaping information diversity.

This study uses behavioral log data from the digital edition of Nikkei, one of Japan’s major national newspapers. On the Nikkei digital platform, articles are delivered through two structurally distinct organizational formats. The first is the Bundled format (Morning and Evening Editions), in which a fixed set of articles is editorially curated and released at scheduled times in a stable, newspaper-like layout. Users typically browse these articles as a finite package. The second is the Streaming format (news articles), in which newly published articles are continuously added to an ongoing feed and displayed in a dynamically updating list. Users typically encounter these articles through incremental, feed-based browsing. To compare the effects of article formats on information diversity, we identify user groups with distinct exposure patterns to Bundled and Streaming articles. Based on the distribution of the share of Bundled articles in each user’s reading history (Figure 1), we select the top 2,000 users with the highest proportion of Bundled-article consumption as Bundled users and the bottom 2,000 users with the lowest proportion as Streaming users. These groups enable comparisons between users with substantially different format exposure. We measure semantic diversity using the Generalist–Specialist (GS) score based on text embeddings [8, 9]. The GS score is computed by first obtaining the mean embedding vector of the articles and then calculating the average cosine similarity between each article embedding and the mean vector, where lower average similarity indicates greater semantic dispersion (i.e., higher diversity). For user-level analyses, GS scores are computed separately for each user based on the set of articles they consumed. Article titles are embedded into 1,536dimensional vectors using the OpenAI text-embedding-3-small model. We focus on article titles rather than full text because, in the Nikkei digital interface, articles are predominantly presented in headline-centric list layouts where users typically make click decisions at the preclick stage. Under this interface structure, title embeddings provide a behaviorally grounded proxy for the exposure space available to users. To control for observable user characteristics, we apply propensity score matching (PSM) to compare users predominantly exposed to Bundled or Streaming articles. In addition, we conduct within-user comparisons using users who consume both formats to test robustness.

Table 1 Table 1 shows that Bundled articles exhibit lower GS scores than Streaming articles (Bundled: 0.459, Streaming: 0.462), indicating greater topical diversity in editorially curated bundles. Although the absolute difference is modest, the pattern is consistent. Table 2 and Figure 2 show the differences between Bundled users and Streaming users. After controlling for observable user characteristics using PSM, users predominantly exposed to Bundled articles consume more diverse content than users exposed to Streaming articles. Table 3 and Figure 3 show Bundled users exhibit consistently lower GS scores (mean: 0.460) than Streaming users (mean: 0.474), indicating higher semantic diversity in their reading behavior. Distributional comparisons further show that high-concentration reading patterns (higher GS scores) are substantially more common among Streaming users, suggesting that Bundled articles are linked to lower topical concentration and broader information exposure. To test whether the observed diversity differences are driven by individual characteristics, we conduct within-user comparisons using users who consume both Bundled and Streaming articles. Among these users, Table 4 and Figure 4 show that article consumption under Bundled exposure exhibits consistently lower GS scores than consumption under Streaming exposure (Bundled: 0.530, Streaming: 0.537 on average), indicating higher semantic diversity within the same individuals. Statistical tests confirm that this difference is significant, and because this comparison is conducted within the same individuals, the pattern is less likely to be driven solely by stable user preferences, suggesting that content organization formats are associated with information diversity at the individual level. Across all analyses, Bundled articles are associated with higher information diversity than Streaming articles. Article-level analyses show that Bundled articles exhibit greater semantic diversity, and matched-user comparisons indicate that users predominantly exposed to Bundled articles consume significantly more diverse content even after controlling for observable user characteristics. Within-user comparisons further confirm that the same individuals exhibit higher diversity when consuming Bundled articles than when consuming Streaming articles. Together, these findings suggest that the structural characteristics of content organization may play an important role in shaping information diversity, with editorially curated bundles potentially facilitating broader incidental exposure to heterogeneous topics.

posters.title: A Computational Analysis of Media Framing Effects in Online Comments
posters.authors: Matteo Guida, Yulia Otmakhova, Eduard Hovy and Lea Frermann
posters.keywords: framing theory framing effects discourse quality
posters.abstract:
When a news article describes immigration as an "economic burden" versus a "humanitarian crisis," it selectively emphasizes certain aspects of the issue. These choices—known as framing—shape how audiences interpret and respond to information (Entman, 1993). Framing effects refer to the measurable impact these presentational choices have on audience understanding and behavior. While framing theory has long recognized that audiences actively reconstruct frames rather than passively absorbing them (Neuman et al., 1992; Scheufele, 1999)—a perspective known as the constructionist approach—computational and empirical work has ignored this interrelationship.

The Gap Between Theory and Methods. Online news landscapes offer a unique opportunity to study this interrelationship by examining both article framing and audience responses in reader comments. However, computational framing research has focused exclusively on automated frame detection in source documents (news articles, political speeches, social media posts) without examining how audiences respond, treating framing as an isolated classification task. Meanwhile, small-scale communication studies manually analyzing reader comments produce contradictory findings, with some showing that article frames influence comment frames, others finding no relationship. These inconsistencies stem from limited data (often single articles), single-topic analyses, and varying frame definitions that prevent generalization. We present the first large-scale computational framework that bridges this gap, operationalizing framing as an interactive process between media content and audience reception, and demonstrating how framing dynamics systematically influence online discourse quality.

A Framework for Analyzing Framing Effects. We developed an automated framework to analyze framing effects at scale (Figure 1). The framework has three components: (1) Topic identification using BERTopic and manual clustering to categorize articles and comments by subject matter (e.g., climate change, immigration, healthcare); (2) Frame classification using transformer-based models to label sentences with generic frames—building on the Media Frames Corpus (e.g., Economic, Morality, Health and Safety, Fairness and Equality, Cultural Identity; as in Card et al., 2015); and (3) Primary frame detection to identify the dominant frame in each article and comment, enabling comparison of frame retention versus reframing (see Figure 1 for examples and definitions). We created sentence-level classifiers that work across both formal news articles and informal reader comments, as previous work assumed frames could only be detected in professionally written content. To validate this cross-genre approach, we built the Frames in Articles and Comments (FrAC) corpus with 556 sentences annotated by six trained coders, achieving substantial agreement. We analyze frame retention and reframing patterns using linear mixed-effects models controlling for topic and article-level clustering.

How Readers Reconstruct Media Frames. Analyzing 2,748 news articles and 386,090 reader comments from The New York Times (US) and The Globe and Mail (Canada) across eleven topics (climate change, immigration, Trump & elections, healthcare, gun control, abortion, LGBT+ rights, Israel-Palestine, Russia-Ukraine, Syria & ISIS, education), we find that readers reframe content at least as often as they retain original frames (50% retention in NYT, 37% in SOCC). Crucially, reframing follows systematic patterns. When readers depart from the primary article frame, they predominantly engage in selective reframing—adopting secondary frames already present in the article (49-63% of cases)—rather than complete reframing that introduces entirely novel frames (only 5-12% of cases), as exemplified in Figure 2. This provides large-scale empirical evidence for constructionist theory: readers work within the frame repertoire established by articles, selectively emphasizing different aspects rather than wholesale acceptance or rejection. Frame retention varies by frame type in remarkably consistent ways across both outlets. Objective, factual frames (Health and Safety, Economic, Political) show high retention (82-89%), while value-laden frames requiring alignment with personal beliefs (Morality, Fairness and Equality, Cultural Identity) show substantially lower retention (72-80%). This pattern holds across outlets with strong correlation, suggesting general principles of audience frame reconstruction rather than outlet-specific quirks. Topic effects are more outlet-specific: Trump coverage shows highest retention in NYT; international conflicts show consistently low retention across both outlets, suggesting these topics particularly invite alternative framings.

Framing Effects on Discourse Quality. Building on these patterns, we examine how framing influences discourse health, defined as constructive, good-faith engagement that invites productive discussion (Price et al., 2020). Using transformer-based classifiers to predict health in comments, we find that both article frame choice and comment-level frame alignment significantly predict discourse quality, again applying linear mixed effects models that control for topic and article-level clustering. Articles using value-laden frames (Morality, Fairness, Political) generate substantially less healthy discussions than those using objective frames (Health, Economic). Moreover, frame alignment matters: comments matching article frames are healthiest (81-82% healthy), selective reframing shows moderate health (79%), and complete reframing shows lowest health (75-76%). This clear gradient holds across all eleven topics. Thread-level analysis reveals cascade effects: unhealthy top-level comments generate unhealthy replies uniformly across all frame types, while healthy comments generate healthy replies. This suggests a two-stage model where article framing sets baseline discourse environments, while individual comment health governs propagation through reply chains independent of frame type. These findings establish that frame reconstruction patterns predict not just what audiences say but how they engage.

Implications and Future Directions. This work opens new research and application directions. First, it validates constructionist framing theory at scale, enabling study of frame reconstruction across contexts where manual analysis was infeasible. Cross-outlet frame consistency versus topic-specific variation suggests both universal and context-dependent mechanisms. Second, linking framing to discourse quality enables proactive moderation: platforms could flag high-risk discussions based on frame dynamics rather than reactively detecting toxicity. We demonstrate this potential through a prototype LLM-based system that analyzes article and comment frames to stratify risk levels and provide real-time reformulation suggestions, helping users express their core message more constructively. Third, these patterns could inform persuasion models, argumentation mining, and misinformation detection. Future work should explore causal mechanisms, deeper thread propagation, linguistic drivers, and cross-cultural generalization.

References

Card, D., Boydstun, A. E., Gross, J. H., Resnik, P., & Smith, N. A. (2015). The media frames corpus: Annotations of frames across issues. ACL.

Chong, D., & Druckman, J. N. (2007). Framing theory. Annual Review of Political Science, 10, 103-126.

Entman, R. M. (1993). Framing: Toward clarification of a fractured paradigm. Journal of Communication, 43(4), 51-58.

Neuman, W. R., Just, M. R., & Crigler, A. N. (1992). Common knowledge: News and the construction of political meaning. University of Chicago Press.

Price, I., et al. (2020). Six attributes of unhealthy conversations. Workshop on Online Abuse and Harms, ACL.

Scheufele, D. A. (1999). Framing as a theory of media effects. Journal of Communication, 49(1), 103-122.

posters.title: Exposure to news and political content on TikTok: A Case Study Around the 2024 US Election
posters.authors: Chang Ge, Nilay Gautam, Shreyas Vajjhala, Christina Ng, Ariel Hasell and Sabina Tomkins
posters.keywords: TikTok social media recommender system news recommendation US 2024 election
posters.abstract: TikTok is a major social media platform with a distinctive centralized recommendation system used by 56% of adults under 34 years of age in the U.S. In this study, we deploy approximately 200 sock puppet accounts during the 2024 U.S. election to examine how TikTok’s recommendation algorithm might respond to users' interests in news and political content. Drawing on over 217,064 unique videos viewed by these accounts, we provide a data-driven analysis of the extent to which accounts with different interests are exposed to news media and political discourse. We find that TikTok rarely shows news or political content to accounts. Even the accounts that only engage with news and political content are recommended less than 0.30 total news videos per browsing session on average, though they are recommended slightly more non-news political content (1.60 total political videos on average). We find that users are recommended far more political content posted by everyday users than by news organizations. The lack of news content on TikTok, especially for users who have demonstrated an interest in news, has implications for political knowledge amongst social media users.

posters.title: Deep Value Benchmark: Measuring Whether Models Generalize Deep Values or Shallow Preferences
posters.authors: Joshua Ashkinaze, Hua Shen, Saipranav Avula, Eric Gilbert and Ceren Budak
posters.keywords: AI alignment large language models human values preference learning benchmarking
posters.abstract: We introduce the Deep Value Benchmark (DVB), an evaluation framework that directly tests whether large language models (LLMs) learn fundamental human values or merely surface-level preferences. This distinction is critical for AI alignment: Systems that capture deeper values are likely to generalize human intentions robustly, while those that capture only superficial patterns in preference data risk producing misaligned behavior. The DVB uses a novel experimental design with controlled confounding between deep values (e.g., moral principles) and shallow features (e.g., superficial attributes). In the training phase, we expose LLMs to human preference data with deliberately correlated deep and shallow features—for instance, where a user consistently prefers (non-maleficence, formal language) options over (justice, informal language) alternatives. The testing phase then breaks these correlations, presenting choices between (justice, formal language) and (non-maleficence, informal language) options. This design allows us to precisely measure a model’s Deep Value Generalization Rate (DVGR)—the probability of generalizing based on the underlying value rather than the shallow feature. Across 9 different models, the average DVGR is just 0.30. All models generalize deep values less than chance. Larger models have a (slightly) lower DVGR than smaller models. We are releasing our dataset, which was subject to three separate human validation experiments. DVB provides an interpretable measure of a core feature of alignment.

posters.title: A Search Changer: Auditing Google’s AI Overviews Interface in Political and News Search
posters.authors: Shir Weinbrand
posters.keywords: Google AI Overviews search user interface political information query characteristics
posters.abstract: Search engines have become a key gateway to political and news-related information, shaping how individuals access, interpret, and engage with public affairs (Nielsen & Ganter, 2018; Toff & Nielsen, 2018). While prior research has demonstrated that search engines influence issue salience, exposure diversity, and political learning (Granka, 2010; Wojcieszak et al., 2022), these effects have largely been examined in the context of ranked lists of hyperlinks. The recent introduction of Google’s AI Overviews (AIOs) - AI-generated summaries prominently displayed at the top of the search engine results page (SERP) - marks a substantial shift from information retrieval toward AI-driven curation. By replacing ranked results with a single synthesised response, AIOs reshape patterns of political and news exposure. Despite their rapid rollout, AIOs remain largely unexamined in political communication and computational social science research. This study presents the first systematic mapping of Google’s AIOs for political and news-related search queries. It addresses 3 interrelated research questions: (RQ1a) how AIOs manifest on desktop search, (RQ1b) how they manifest on mobile search, and (RQ2a–b) how the structure and presence of AIOs relate to query characteristics across platforms. Methodologically, the study combines interface auditing and algorithm auditing approaches (Sandvig et al. 2014). A dataset of 160 predefined political and news-related search queries was constructed based on established query typologies in prior research (Menchen-Trevino et al., 2023; Van Hoof et al., 2024; Haak & Schaer, 2023). Using automated data collection, Google Search result pages were gathered daily for desktop (N = 10,720 SERPs) and mobile (N = 6,300 SERPs) interfaces. For each observation, a custom Python-based pipeline captured the full HTML DOM, screenshots of the SERP, and the extracted plain text of the AIO when present. Overall, I found that AIOs appear in nearly half of all observations: 47% on desktop and 49% on mobile, despite Google’s claims of not showing AIOs for news queries (Reid, 2024). Importantly, availability changes over time. During the observation period, the share of searches with an available AIO rose sharply - from below 40% to around 50% - while the number of results without an AIO declined substantially (see Figure 1). This shift occurs for both desktop and mobile versions, and might indicate a coordinated expansion of Google’s AIOs. To further systematically map the ecosystem of Google’s AIOs, I also developed a dedicated taxonomy that captures all interface subcomponents and elements emerging from the AIO data and defines their purpose, function, and interpretation. Hierarchical cluster analysis is then applied to identify distinct structural types of AIOs across queries and platforms. Finally, regression models examine how query characteristics - such as topical focus and leaning versus neutrality intent - predict the likelihood and type of AIO generated. The findings demonstrate that AIOs are neither uniform nor neutral across political and news domains. Political issue queries are significantly more likely to trigger comprehensive and information-dense AIOs, while news-politics queries tend to elicit more constrained summaries. These results suggest that AIOs introduce differentiated forms of algorithmic curation that may shape political information exposure. Beyond its empirical findings, the study makes several broader contributions. First, it offers a transferable taxonomy for analysing AI-powered search interfaces across platforms and contexts. Second, it provides a methodological blueprint for auditing AI-generated components embedded within large-scale information infrastructures. Third, by documenting AIOs at an early stage of deployment, the study preserves a critical moment in the evolution of search engines and highlights the growing role of AI systems in reshaping news and political exposure. As AI-powered search continues to expand, these insights provide a foundation for future accountability, transparency, and democratic impact research.

posters.title: Chinese Debates Become More Homogeneous: Experimental Evidence from Paired English-Chinese LLM Debates
posters.authors: Huiqian Lai and Jiaman Li
posters.keywords: multi-agent debate language conditioning randomized controlled trial output homogeneity AI alignment
posters.abstract: Multi-agent debate, in which multiple large language models argue opposing positions, is increasingly used to improve AI reasoning and support alignment-oriented judgments. A critical but underexplored risk is that these systems may collapse into homogeneous arguments, and that the degree of this collapse may vary systematically across languages. We conduct a pre-registered, paired randomized controlled trial to causally isolate the effects of topic-selection policy and language conditioning on debate homogeneity. Our two-stage design first randomizes policy domains and motions from a bilingual WUDC 2023–2025 pool, then runs paired English and Chinese debate sessions on each motion with yoked model-to-role assignments, randomized language order, and strict context resets. We measure homogeneity using a composite index combining lexical similarity (generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence) and semantic similarity (embedding-based cosine aggregation), with anchored standardization for cross-lingual comparability. Across 99 paired draws, switching to Chinese causes a large increase in homogeneity (ATE = 0.499, 95% CI [0.442, 0.556], Fisher p < 0.001), substantially exceeding domain-level differences. This effect operates on both lexical and semantic dimensions and cannot be attributed to task misunderstanding. These findings reveal a previously unquantified form of linguistic inequality in AI systems, consistent with English-centric alignment training imposing a disproportionate diversity cost in non-English contexts, and motivate alignment strategies that decouple safety from consensus.

posters.title: Epistemic divergence in AI-mediated search across countries and systems
posters.authors: Matthew R. DeVerna, Ronald E. Robertson and Jeffrey T. Hancock
posters.keywords: AI-mediated search algorithmic gatekeeping large language models information ecosystems information integrity
posters.abstract:
Google Search now serves AI Overviews and chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini are common entry points for information seeking. However, we know little about how often these summaries appear or the types of sources they cite. For one month, across seven countries, we collected queries each day related to the top 25 country-specific Google Trends and issued them to three systems: Google Search and two web-search-enabled LLMs, Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4o. We find AI Overviews appear significantly more often in the United States, while overall prevalence remains low because many trending queries are sports-related and Google favors providing scorecards instead of AI Overviews in these cases. We also compare---for identical queries---the web sources returned in Google's organic results, AI Overviews, and LLM responses to assess their similarity. We find that source similarity is low: overlapping sources are scarce, and correlations in source quality are modest at best. This cross-national audit shows that LLM-powered search systems can surface distinct slices of the web, offering early evidence of an AI-driven fracturing of information search systems.
