posters.title: LLM-assistance is associated with faster, but not better, academic writing
posters.authors: Fengyuan Liu, Molly Crockett and Talal Rahwan
posters.keywords: peer review large language models acceptance delay AI4Science science of science
posters.abstract: Using a dataset of 7 million Open Access papers published between 1997 and 2025, we examine whether large language model (LLM) assistance reduces linguistic barriers in academic publishing. Leveraging a text-based LLM-detection algorithm, we document three main findings. First, LLM adoption is geographically uneven, with higher adoption rate among authors based in the Global South. Second, beginning in 2023, papers classified as LLM-assisted are accepted significantly faster than non-assisted papers, with the acceptance gap peaking in early 2024 and subsequently narrowing. This acceleration coincides with a reduction in longstanding Global South–Global North disparities in paper acceptance delay. Third, analyses of approximately 50,000 PLOS papers with public peer-review reports show no differences in reviewers’ language-quality ratings between LLM-assisted and non-assisted manuscripts. Instead, faster acceptance is driven by shorter author revision times. These findings are supported by multiple robustness checks and placebo analyses to address key validity concerns. Together, the evidence indicates that LLMs streamline the revision process for the authors, yet they do not improve reviewers’ judgments of textual quality.

posters.title: The Democratic Paradox in Large Language Models’ Underestimation of Press Freedom
posters.authors: Isabella Loaiza, Roberto Vestrelli, Andrea Fronzetti Colladon and Roberto Rigobon
posters.keywords: Press Freedom Large Language Models LLM alignment Democratic Institutions
posters.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming central intermediaries in the global information ecosystem. As millions rely on them for political and institutional information, their representations of democratic institutions may shape public perception \cite{briggs2024generative}, trust, and geopolitical narratives at scale, much like social media \cite{aral2021hype}. Yet while substantial research has examined demographic and political bias in LLMs \cite{feng2023pretraining, manvi2024geographically, motoki2024more, rozado2023political,tao2024cultural, yang2025unpacking}, far less attention has been devoted to how these models portray core democratic institutions themselves. In this paper, we investigate how six widely used LLMs evaluate press freedom across 180 countries and compare their assessments to expert benchmarks from the 2024 World Press Freedom Index (WPFI) \cite{RSF2024}.

Using a computational pipeline that adapts the full 117-question WPFI survey into country-specific prompts, we generate over 21,000 evaluations per model and construct LLM-based press freedom scores following the original scoring methodology. We study GPT-4, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and Falcon, representing firms headquartered in the United States, China, France, and the United Arab Emirates. We then quantify misalignment between LLM and expert evaluations using country-level and pooled regression frameworks.

Our analysis reveals three systematic distortions. First, we document a generalized negative misalignment. All six LLMs systematically underestimate press freedom relative to expert assessments. Even the least misaligned model underrates press freedom in 71\% of countries, while others do so in over 90\% of cases. Across models, score distributions are consistently shifted leftward relative to the WPFI benchmark, indicating a pervasive tendency toward more critical assessments.

Second, we uncover a paradoxical pattern we term differential misalignment. LLM deviations from expert scores are not random; instead, they depend systematically on a country’s level of press freedom. Specifically, LLMs are more negatively misaligned in countries that are rated as freer by experts. Regression estimates show that misalignment becomes more negative as WPFI scores increase. In effect, LLMs disproportionately penalize freer societies while showing comparatively smaller deviations in more restrictive regimes. This pattern suggests that misalignment is structurally linked to the distribution of training data and information availability rather than idiosyncratic model error.

Third, we identify a positive home bias in five of the six models. After accounting for both generalized and differential misalignment, most LLMs rate press freedom in their home country more favorably than expected. Chinese models display strong positive bias toward China; Western models exhibit similar bias toward the United States; and Falcon exhibits bias toward the UAE. This pattern is consistent with previously documented in-group biases in generative models and suggests that geopolitical alignment may be embedded in model outputs.

We hypothesize that these distortions arise in part from asymmetries in the informational environment. In freer societies, journalists and citizens can openly criticize government institutions, generating large volumes of negative coverage that become overrepresented in training corpora. In more restrictive regimes, critical reporting is suppressed, limiting the availability of negative information. This “democratic dilemma”, previously observed in mass media \cite{heinze2010public}, may induce LLMs to associate freer countries with greater negativity while underrepresenting censorship in authoritarian contexts. Reinforcement learning and alignment processes may further amplify national in-group tendencies.

These findings carry important implications for computational social science. First, they highlight the need to treat LLMs not merely as tools but as sociotechnical actors that encode structural biases from the information ecosystem. Second, they raise concerns about the downstream effects of LLM-mediated institutional representations on public trust. Independent validation shows that WPFI scores correlate positively with survey-based measures of media trust, suggesting that systematic LLM misalignment could influence perceptions of democratic legitimacy. Third, the presence of home bias raises questions about the geopolitical consequences of globally deployed AI systems and the potential for soft power projection through algorithmic mediation.

Our work shows how to design a scalable framework for benchmarking LLM representations of complex social institutions using structured survey instruments and expert indices. Beyond press freedom, we aim to extend this framework to examine how LLMs represent other democratic institutions and human rights domains. These questions are especially urgent in a context of rising geopolitical tensions and accelerating democratic backsliding worldwide.

posters.title: Computational frame analysis revisited: on LLMs for studying news coverage
posters.authors: Sharaj Kunjar, Alyssa Smith, Tyler Mckenzie, Rushali Mohbe, Samuel Scarpino and Brooke Foucault Welles
posters.keywords: content analysis language modeling mixed methods news framing mass communication AI evaluation
posters.abstract: Computational approaches have previously shown various promises and pitfalls when it comes to the reliable identification of media frames. Generative LLMs like GPT and Claude are increasingly being used as content analytical tools, but how effective are they for frame analysis? We address this question by systematically evaluating them against their computational predecessors: bag-of-words models and encoder-only transformers; and traditional manual coding procedures. Our analysis rests on a novel gold standard dataset that we inductively and iteratively developed through the study, investigating six months of news coverage of the US Mpox epidemic of 2022. While we discover some potential applications for generative LLMs, we demonstrate that they were consistently outperformed by manual coders, and in some instances, by smaller language models. Some form of human validation was always necessary to determine appropriate model choice. Additionally, by examining how the suitability of various approaches depended on the nature of different tasks that were part of our frame analytical workflow, we provide insights as to how researchers may leverage the complementarity of these approaches to use them in tandem. We conclude by endorsing a methodologically pluralistic approach and put forth a roadmap for computational frame analysis for researchers going forward.

posters.title: Can LLMs Emulate Human Belief Dynamics?
posters.authors: Adiba Proma, Neeley Pate, James Druckman, Gourab Ghoshal and Ehsan Hoque
posters.keywords: Agent-based Modeling Large Language Models Belief Dynamics Misinformation Social Networks
posters.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human attitudes, opinions, and behaviors. In this research, we explore whether LLMs can simulate human belief dynamics within network settings by replicating an existing study on belief dynamics. Evaluating LLM capabilities across models and parameters, we show that while LLMs could potentially approximate initial belief distributions, LLM behavior systematically diverges from humans when it comes to belief changes and network restructuring. LLMs tend to be more easily influenced by others' opinions and prefer more diverse opinions compared to humans when selecting opinions to include in their networks. As there is a broader push toward using LLM-based agents to simulate large-scale social systems, our findings highlight potential pitfalls and can, therefore, inform future research on where LLMs can and cannot be used as human proxies. Our research directly contributes to the topics ``Empirically calibrated simulation models" and ``Agent-based or other simulation of social phenomena".

posters.title: Detecting and Mitigating Demographic Bias in LLM-Based Resume Evaluation
posters.authors: Oluwadayo Bamgbelu, Maria Teleki, Xiangjue Dong and James Caverlee
posters.keywords: Algorithmic bias automated resume screening LLM-as-a-Judge design fairness hiring
posters.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen job applicants, understanding whether they exhibit racial or gender bias is critical. We test four LLMs (GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, Phi) by taking real resumes, swapping names associated with different demographic groups, and asking models to evaluate them. We compare two evaluation formats: comparative ranking (pick the best of four candidates) and independent scoring (rate each candidate 0-100). Ranking produces measurable bias. For example, White female names are ranked first 40% of the time versus the expected 25%. Independent scoring, however, shows no significant bias across any model (Cohen's d < 0.02, all p > 0.8). This divergence shows that how a model is asked to evaluate matters as much as which model is used. Building on these findings, we outline ongoing work on bias mitigation strategies, including prompt-level interventions, counterfactual calibration, and chain-of-thought auditing.

posters.title: The effect of elections and external events on political news diets
posters.authors: Zoltán Kmetty, Adam Stefkovics, Bendegúz Váradi, Emese Bata and Petra Parragi
posters.keywords: news diet political news polarization event analysis data donation
posters.abstract: This study utilizes a longitudinal data-donation framework (N=758) to provide a unique analysis of political news diets in Hungary over a continuous five-year period (2018–2023). By processing 4.9 million Google page visits through a classification pipeline involving Sentence Transformers, h-NNE clustering, and a BERT-based NLP model, we track how external events—such as elections and the COVID-19 pandemic—affect individual-level news slant. Our results indicate that while news interest peaks during major events, consumption patterns remain remarkably stable and balanced at both the aggregate and individual levels. This research distinguishes itself within computational social science by moving beyond short-term event analysis to explore the long-term temporal dynamics of digital trace trajectories.

posters.title: Augmenting Expert Judgment in Multimedia Science Education via Eye tracking and Machine Learning
posters.authors: Jason Coronel, Matthew Sweitzer, James Bonus, Rebecca Dore and Blue Lerner
posters.keywords: Expert Judgment Eye Tracking Machine Learning Educational Technology Multimedia Learning
posters.abstract: Experts (academics, disciplinary specialists, and educational consultants) help design real-world educational media by deciding which visual elements to emphasize, label, or simplify. These decisions assume that experts can identify which on-screen elements best support learning. We test this assumption using eye tracking and machine learning. In a study of 197 children watching a camouflage video, experts predicted that the focal animal and its label would be most important for predicting comprehension. However, a neural network trained on moment-to-moment gaze data revealed that attention to the environmental background -- an element experts did not select -- was most predictive of learning. That omission is striking because camouflage is fundamentally about how an animal relates to its surroundings. In the context of growing collaborations between researchers and media developers, tools that help expand what experts consider can be valuable. These findings show how experts can use eye tracking and machine learning to surface visual features that might otherwise be missed. Bringing those features into consideration can lead to more complete instructional design decisions and reduce reliance on potentially narrow assumptions about learning.

posters.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
posters.authors: Emőke-Ágnes Horvát, Dmitry Kobak, Rita González Márquez and Jan Lause
posters.keywords: Artificial Intelligence Linguistic Style Academic Writing LLM Adoption PubMed
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT can generate and revise text with human-level performance. These models come with clear limitations, can produce inaccurate information, and reinforce existing biases. Yet, many scientists use them for their scholarly writing. But how wide-spread is such LLM usage in the academic literature? To answer this question for the field of biomedical research, we present an unbiased, large-scale approach: we study vocabulary changes in over 15 million biomedical abstracts from 2010--2024 indexed by PubMed, and show how the appearance of LLMs led to an abrupt increase in the frequency of certain style words. This excess word analysis suggests that at least 13.5\% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs. The lower bound differed across disciplines, countries, and journals, reaching 40\% for some subcorpora. We show that LLMs have had an unprecedented impact on scientific writing in biomedical research, surpassing the effect of major world events such as the Covid pandemic.

posters.title: A Marketplace for AI-Generated Adult Content and Deepfakes
posters.authors: Shalmoli Ghosh, Matthew DeVerna and Filippo Menczer
posters.keywords: Marketplace Generative AI Safety Deepfakes Adult content
posters.abstract:
Generative AI systems increasingly enable the production of highly realistic synthetic media. Civitai, a popular community-driven platform for AI-generated content, operates a monetized feature called "Bounties", which allows users to commission the generation of content in exchange for payment. To examine how this mechanism is used and what content it incentivizes, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of all publicly available bounty requests collected over a 14-month period following the platform's launch. We find that the bounty marketplace is dominated by tools that let users steer AI models toward content they were not trained to generate. At the same time, requests for content that is "Not Safe For Work" are widespread and have increased steadily over time, now comprising a majority of all bounties. Participation in bounty creation is uneven, with 20% of requesters accounting for roughly half of requests. Requests for "deepfake"- media depicting identifiable real individuals - exhibit a higher concentration than other types of bounties. A nontrivial subset of these requests involves explicit deepfakes despite platform policies prohibiting such content. These bounties disproportionately target female celebrities, revealing a pronounced gender asymmetry in social harm. Together, these findings show how monetized, community-driven generative AI platforms can produce gendered harms, raising questions about consent, governance, and enforcement.

posters.title: How women's empowerment combats national brain drain
posters.authors: Alireza Javadian Sabet, Junghyun Lim, Yixiao Li, Lisa Simon and Morgan Frank
posters.theme: Labor, Work, and the Future of AI Employment
posters.keywords: Gender equality Return migration Brain drain Skilled migration Scientific productivity
posters.abstract: The rapidly growing knowledge economy has intensified the global competition for talent with women comprising a growing share of the skilled workforce and of migrants seeking education and training. However, as origin countries attempt to repatriate high-skilled emigrants, women's societal participation may influence their decisions to return. Here, we analyze millions of LinkedIn profiles to trace the education, career trajectories, and migration patterns of immigrants to the U.S. On average, women are less likely than compatriot men to return with larger discrepancies in return migration for countries with lower women's empowerment. Female immigrants are more likely to return when their home country exhibits greater female representation in government, higher female labor-force participation, and higher rates of women's educational attainment. Those who do not return tend to publish more peer-reviewed articles than both compatriots who return and otherwise similar non-migrants in their countries of origin. Taken together, these findings suggest that domestic social structures contribute to local ``brain drain'' and highlight a potential incentive for developing economies to prioritize women's empowerment.

posters.title: Collaboration at Scale: How LLMs Reshape the Global Distribution of Coding Styles
posters.authors: Yuto Tamura and Sho Tsugawa
posters.keywords: Large Language Models Social Conventions Coding Style Software Development GitHub
posters.abstract: Social conventions emerge through repeated local coordination and diffuse across social networks, with their global distributions shaped by network topology. Changes in network structure can therefore transform how conventions spread and stabilize. As the performance of large language models (LLMs) improves, they are increasingly applied across diverse domains. A small number of foundation models now interact with massive user populations and function as centralized super-hubs within collaboration networks. How such super-hubs reshape the distribution of social conventions remains unclear. We examine software development, one of the domains where LLM adoption has accelerated, to assess how LLM integration alters global coding conventions. Using large-scale GitHub data, we analyze changes in naming practices for functions, variables, and arguments. First, comparing repositories created in September 2025, we find substantial stylistic divergence between projects with LLM-referenced commits and those without. Second, in longitudinal data from 2015 to 2025, we document a sharp decline in coding-style diversity beginning in late 2024, coinciding with rapid LLM adoption. These findings suggest that LLM super-hubs may drive global convergence of social conventions and motivate further investigation.

posters.title: Language Style and Emotion Matching in Chatbot Conversations
posters.authors: Shalmoli Ghosh, Ozgur Can Seckin, Filippo Menczer and Kristina Lerman
posters.keywords: language style emotion convergence LLM chatbots
posters.abstract:
Language style matching (LSM) refers to the phenomenon where conversation partners unconsciously mirror each other's use of function words (pronouns, prepositions, articles, conjunctions, negations), which in humans signals growing closeness, trust, and approval. To complement the limited research in this context, we examine LSM and emotional convergence in conversations between LLM-based chatbots. Using simulated conversations, we measure convergence across three aspects: reply length, language style, and emotional expression of chatbot conversations. Our results show that chatbots exhibit significant convergence across all measures. The relative difference in reply length decreases over the conversation turns. All nine LIWC function word categories demonstrate positive convergence. For emotions, we find that positive emotions (joy, optimism, love) show higher convergence than negative emotions (fear, anger, disgust). Notably, sadness also shows convergence, suggesting some level of empathy among chatbots. Our findings raise important concerns about vulnerability towards manipulation. Since LSM and emotional mirroring signal trust and intimacy in human relationships, chatbots' ability to naturally exhibit these behaviors, combined with their capacity to impersonate people online, creates potential risks for psychological manipulation through seemingly benign conversations.

posters.title: Violence Depiction in Media Coverage of Gaza
posters.authors: Timothy Dörr and Baird Howland
posters.keywords: Violence Descriptions News LLMs Israel-Palestine Structured Extraction
posters.abstract: Since October 7, 2023, the Israel-Palestine conflict has generated intense debate about whether US and UK news media cover Israeli and Palestinian victims fairly. We address this question empirically using a corpus of 16,156 articles from ten major anglophone outlets, leveraging GPT-5 to extract over 121,000 structured descriptions of violence and applying Best-Worst Scaling to measure the emotional intensity of that language. Across all three dimensions we examine (volume of coverage, emotional weight of violence descriptions, and naming of perpetrators) we find consistent evidence of a pro-Israel bias: most outlets published more articles on Israeli victims despite Palestinian casualties being more than 30 times higher, described violence against Israelis with more anger-evoking language, and omitted the perpetrator in articles about Palestinian victims at more than twice the rate they did for Israeli victims. These patterns hold across outlets that span the ideological spectrum, from Breitbart to The Guardian, suggesting the bias is not reducible to individual editorial slant. Our findings offer systematic, large-scale evidence that US and UK media coverage constructs a hierarchy of victimhood that may shape public empathy and political accountability in ways consequential for US foreign policy toward the conflict.

posters.title: The Illusion of Abstract Semantic Geometry in LLMs: Evidence from Cross-Domain Conceptual Mapping
posters.authors: Xuanlong Qin and Yuxuan Zheng
posters.keywords: large language models abstract semantics cross-domain mapping human-AI alignment conceptual representation
posters.abstract: As computational social science increasingly utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) as “silicon samples”, distinguishing between surface-level behavioral alignment and genuine mechanistic isomorphism is critical. Research shows that when humans map concepts across domains (e.g., “if a nurse were an animal...”), they rely on abstract semantic dimensions such as Evaluation, Potency, and Activity (EPA). This study investigates whether LLMs develop similar grounded semantic geometry. We evaluated six LLMs (across GPT, Llama, and Qwen families) using a three-condition “cognitive stress test” that manipulates the required level of abstraction. Employing mixed-effects regressions, we pitted human cognitive predictors directly against distributional text statistics. Results reveal that while LLMs exhibit striking behavioral alignment with human response distributions and entropy, including their projections in EPA space, their underlying mechanisms diverge significantly. LLM choices are overwhelmingly driven by baseline probability (frequency/typicality) and word association. However, abstract semantic similarity (EPA) never positively predicted LLM selections across any condition. We conclude that LLMs create an “illusion” of abstract semantic geometry, achieving human-like outputs through fundamentally different computational routes based on statistical regularities rather than structural isomorphism. This highlights the risk of building social simulation theories on distributional mirages rather than grounded human cognition.

posters.title: Agency and Valence - Disecting the Portrayal of Key Stakeholders in News Reporting of the 2025 US Government Shutdown
posters.authors: Timothy Dörr
posters.keywords: News Media Government Shut Down Stakeholder Portrayal Stereotype Content Model LLMs Automated Content Analysis
posters.abstract: Political conflicts unfold across partisan media ecosystems that frame the same actors in systematically different ways. This study develops and applies an LLM-assisted content analysis pipeline to examine how 11 major anglophone outlets portrayed key political stakeholders during the 2025 U.S. government shutdown, which was the longest shutdown in US history at 43 days. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and related work on agency and communion, we operationalize stakeholder portrayal across eight theoretically grounded sub-dimensions: four capturing agency (competence, power, autonomy, strategic capacity) and four capturing valence (morality, warmth, societal benefit, legitimacy). Applied to 913 articles and over 20,000 extracted entities, the pipeline scores each actor-article pair on all dimensions using GPT-5.1 with chain-of-thought reasoning, while attributing portrayals to journalist framing or quoted speech. Three findings emerge. First, partisan divergence concentrates in valence, not agency: outlets across the ideological spectrum portray political opponents as highly capable while morally delegitimizing them. Second, warmth and sociability ratings are uniformly low across all actors and outlets, reflecting the adversarial context of shutdown coverage. Third, over 80% of negative ingroup portrayals in partisan outlets derive from quoted speech, suggesting that outlets strategically deploy oppositional voices to generate outrage while maintaining a veneer of balance. These findings advance understanding of partisan media framing, affective polarization, and the methodological challenge of actor-attributed dimensional coding in multi-stakeholder news texts.

posters.title: LLMs Reproduce Human Purchase Intent via Semantic Similarity Elicitation of Likert Ratings
posters.authors: Ben Maier, Ulf Aslak, Luca Fiaschi, Christian Luhmann, Kli Pappas and Thomas Wiecki
posters.keywords: Purchase Intent Synthetic Consumers Synthetic Focus Groups NLP LLMs
posters.abstract: Consumer research costs companies billions annually yet suffers from panel biases and limited scale. Large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative by simulating synthetic consumers, but produce unrealistic response distributions when asked directly for numerical ratings. We present semantic similarity rating (SSR), a method that elicits textual responses from LLMs and maps these to Likert distributions using embedding similarity to reference statements. Testing on an extensive dataset comprising 57 personal care product surveys conducted by a leading corporation in that market (9,300 human responses), SSR achieves 90% of human test--retest reliability while maintaining realistic response distributions (KS similarity > 0.85). Additionally, these synthetic respondents provide rich qualitative feedback explaining their ratings. This framework enables scalable consumer research simulations while preserving traditional survey metrics and interpretability.

posters.title: Logical Fallacies in Cross-Border News Debates: A Case Study of Bangladesh–India Discourse
posters.authors: Tabia Tanzin Prama, Chris Danforth and Peter Dodds
posters.keywords: Logical Fallacies Cross-Border News Debates YouTube Discussion Intensity Polarization
posters.abstract: User comment sections increasingly shape public perception in cross-border political debates, yet their rhetorical structure remains underexplored. We introduce BIFaD (Bangladesh–India Fallacy Discourse Dataset), a seven-year (2019–2026) corpus of 1,849 Bangladesh-origin news videos about India and approximately 2.5 million YouTube comments. Using Large Language Model (LLM)-based annotation, we categorize comments into a 16-class fallacy taxonomy to analyze their distribution across fifteen news topics and varying levels of geopolitical tension. We find that fallacious discourse is strongly event-driven, peaking during major geopolitical crises (e.g. May 2025 India–Pakistan escalation and the late-2025 Bangladesh–India diplomatic rupture). These periods are dominated by Appeal to Emotion, Tu Quoque, and Appeal to Fear. Fallacy prevalence is nearly perfectly correlated with total commenting activity ($r = 0.98$), highlighting the strong link between flawed reasoning and conversation density. We show that geopolitically sensitive topics like International Affairs, Politics, and Military exhibit higher discussion intensity, and that fallacies such as Circular Reasoning and Bandwagon are positively associated with increased within-thread “social heat” beyond topic and engagement effects.

posters.title: Exploring the Consequences of Unbalanced Online News Consumption with LLM Simulations
posters.authors: Josh Nguyen, Upasana Dutta, Samar Haider, Bryan Li, Neil Fasching and Duncan Watts
posters.keywords: Media Bias News Consumption Political Communication LLMs Simulation
posters.abstract: In the online information ecosystem, there are increasingly divergent patterns of news consumption. This is partly driven by a proliferation of partisan media outlets and the freedom with which individuals can consume whichever source of information matches their preferences. Many believe this is closely related to the growth of undesirable social outcomes, such as polarization. The challenge to studying selective exposure empirically, however, is that real-world field experiments are extremely costly. In this work, we present a study of how political attitudes elicited by large language models (LLMs)—instead of humans—vary as a function of the partisan content they are systematically exposed to. We show that a host of attitudinal outcomes are robustly sensitive to the source of information that is selected for consumption by GPT-4.1. However, a balanced news diet does not guarantee a neutral stance toward several politically salient topics. The behavior of LLMs studied in this work has the potential to inform our understanding of that of humans, because the former may be treated as a silicon pilot for a real-world experiment, or because humans are increasingly influenced by LLMs when learning about the world via the news.

posters.title: Who Gets Which Message? Auditing Demographic Bias in LLM-Generated Targeted Text
posters.authors: Tunazzina Islam
posters.keywords: Large language models microtargeting demographic bias bias audit climate communication persuasion bias
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of generating personalized, persuasive text at scale, raising new questions about bias and fairness in automated communication. This paper presents the first systematic analysis of how LLMs behave when tasked with demographic-conditioned targeted messaging. We introduce a controlled evaluation framework using three leading models—GPT-4o, Llama-3.3, and Mistral-Large 2.1—across two generation settings: Standalone Generation, which isolates intrinsic demographic effects, and Context-Rich Generation, which incorporates thematic and regional context to emulate realistic targeting. We evaluate generated messages along three dimensions: lexical content, language style, and persuasive framing. We instantiate this framework on climate communication and find consistent age- and gender-based asymmetries across models: male- and youth-targeted messages emphasize agency, innovation, and assertiveness, while female- and senior-targeted messages stress warmth, care, and tradition. Contextual prompts systematically amplify these disparities, with persuasion scores significantly higher for messages tailored to younger or male audiences. Our findings demonstrate how demographic stereotypes can surface and intensify in LLM-generated targeted communication, underscoring the need for bias-aware generation pipelines and transparent auditing frameworks that explicitly account for demographic conditioning in socially sensitive applications.

posters.title: XChoice: Explainable Evaluation of AI–Human Alignment in LLM-based Constrained Choice Decision Making
posters.authors: Weihong Qi, Fan Huang, Rasika Muralidharan, Jisun An and Haewoon Kwak
posters.keywords: AI-Human Alignment Evaluation Large Language Models Explainability Decision Making
posters.abstract: We present XChoice, an explainable framework for evaluating AI-human alignment in constrained decision making. Moving beyond outcome agreement such as accuracy and F1 score, XChoice fits a mechanism-based decision model to human data and LLM-generated decisions, recovering interpretable parameters that capture the relative importance of decision factors, constraint sensitivity, and implied trade-offs. Alignment is assessed by comparing these parameter vectors across models, options, and subgroups. We demonstrate XChoice on Americans’ daily time allocation using the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) as human ground truth, revealing heterogeneous alignment across models and activities and salient misalignment concentrated in Black and married groups. We further validate robustness of XChoice via an invariance analysis and evaluate targeted mitigation with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) intervention. Overall, XChoice provides mechanism-based metrics that diagnose misalignment and support informed improvements beyond surface outcome matching.

posters.title: Measuring the impact of Google AI Overview on administrative burdens
posters.authors: Allison Wan
posters.keywords: Google AI Overview administrative burdens web-browsing data online behavior LLM based URL classification
posters.abstract:
Administrative burdens can be characterized as the frictions individuals face when participating in various government processes, services, and programs (Herd & Moynihan, 2019). For instance, applying for social assistance often requires time, effort, mental energy, and money to learn about a program, comply with demands such as filling out complex forms, scheduling interviews, and gathering documents, as well as the psychological costs of stress and stigma. Aside from being an inconvenience, administrative burdens often raise the barrier to accessing government services, benefits, and tax credits in a way that disproportionately affects those with lower socioeconomic status (Chudnovsky & Peeters, 2021; Herd & Moynihan, 2025).

While governments have increasingly moved towards digital first means of providing public services, often as a way to increase efficiency and lower burdens, scholars have pointed out various ways in which online self service portals exacerbate rather than alleviate burden (Peeters,2023). Individuals become their own case workers, often navigating their own idiosyncratic situations without domain specific knowledge (Madsen et al., 2022). While individuals may turn to informational websites, search engines, or online forums, they often lack knowledge of the specific keywords to even articulate the problem at hand. This is especially true for more complex cases.

As generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become more ubiquitous, we ask whether the technological affordances of this new advancement can help individuals overcome some of these challenges. On the one hand, generative AI may be able to quickly serve up personalized assistance, saving individuals time and energy sifting through informational resources or contacting a caseworker (Jo et al., 2025). On the other hand, generative AI is prone to errors, hallucinations (Huang et al., 2025), and may suffer from similar shortcomings to traditional search engines more broadly. This includes the surfacing of low quality information (Aslett et al., 2024), and a dependence on whether individuals can correctly articulate the problem they are facing.

To begin to address this question, we use observational web-browsing data to examine the effect of Google AI overview, an AI generated summary presented in some of Google’s search results, on the amount of time individuals spend on online tax-related activities. We focus on Google AI Overview due to the fact that during the time of data collection, individuals are automatically presented with AI overview without selecting in to using it unlike many other commercial generative AI products. We focus on taxes because it is a relatively common administrative process compared to other services. Specifically, we filter web-browsing data from the National Internet Observatory (Feal et al., 2024) to users who have visited a seed set of tax websites, and collect all websites they have visited one hour before and four hours after the target tax website (See the data processing pipeline in Figure 1). Through a combination of matching lists, keyword flagging, and large language model (LLM) based classifications, we label each website (by the URL only) as tax related or not. For each user, browsing history is broken down into discrete tax-related activity sessions. A session is a period of tax-related browsing by a user where each visit happens within 5 hours of the previous one. A new session begins after a break of more than 5 hours between visits to tax-related sites. We filter to sessions where users used Google search for a tax related query at least once. This results in 554 individuals, and 1,356 total activity sessions(123 sessions with AI overview).

Looking descriptively, by regressing the log of total session time on AI overview exposure we find that sessions where users were presented with an AI overview spend on average 50% more time on tax related sites after controlling for the number of Google searches in that session (a simplified proxy for task complexity; β = 0.405, SE = 0.185, p = 0.028). As this can be easily driven by confounders of task complexity or individual motivation, we test this effect causally by using an instrumental variables design. We first filter the data to the first session of every user and use the proportion of other individuals who were exposed to an AI Overview on the same day as an instrument for exposure to AI Overview. Due to small sample sizes, our preliminary results show a weak instrument (F = 4.24 for the first stage) and noisy results. We are currently collecting more data that includes the 2026 tax season as well as expanding to other government services such as Federal Student Aid and Medicare enrollment. Finally, we plan on considering the effect of more granular time outcomes (e.g. time specifically spent on informational websites as opposed to time with online tax form), different measures of burden (e.g. number of different websites visited), and the extent to which this effect is mediated by potential errors present in the AI overviews.

posters.title: PROMPTHELPER: A Prompt Recommender System for Encouraging Creativity in AI Chatbot Interactions
posters.authors: Jason Kim, Maria Teleki and James Caverlee
posters.keywords: LLM Recommender System Prompting Creativity Personalization
posters.abstract: Prompting is central to interaction with AI systems, yet many users struggle to explore alternative directions, articulate creative intent, or understand how variations in prompts shape model outputs. We introduce prompt recommender systems (PRS) as an interaction approach that supports exploration, suggesting contextually relevant follow-up prompts. We present PromptHelper, a PRS prototype integrated into an AI chatbot that surfaces semantically diverse prompt suggestions while users work on real writing tasks. We evaluate PromptHelper in a 2x2 fully within-subjects study (N=32) across creative and academic writing tasks. Results show that PromptHelper significantly increases users' perceived exploration and expressiveness without increasing cognitive workload. We argue that PRS introduce a new layer of algorithmic mediation in human–AI knowledge production, structuring semantic search trajectories and shaping how ideas diverge or converge—opening a computational social science agenda around prompt-space navigation, personalization, and epistemic diversity.

posters.title: Beyond Creativity Outcome: Comparing Human and AI Search Trajectories
posters.authors: Yulin Yu, Anthony Shen, Dawei Wang and Brian Uzzi
posters.keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence Human–AI Creativity Divergent Thinking
posters.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence has the potential to expand the frontiers of innovation by introducing forms of creativity that differ fundamentally from human cognition—both independently and in collaboration with people (\cite{wang2025divergent}). While recent work shows that large language models can match or even exceed average human performance on standardized creativity benchmarks (\cite{wang2025divergent,bellemare2026divergent}), such comparisons typically rely on aggregate outcome metrics. These scalar evaluations obscure the generative processes through which ideas unfold (\cite{kenett2019creativity}). Creativity is not merely a static endpoint but a dynamic search process shaped by resource access, path dependence, and structured exploration across conceptual domains (\cite{mednick1962associative,simonton1999origins,uzzi2013atypical}). Understanding whether human and machine creativity arise from shared mechanisms or fundamentally distinct search regimes requires a process-level perspective.

In this study, we adopt a dynamic, sequence-based approach to compare human and machine creativity using the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a validated measure of creative potential that requires participants to produce ten semantically distant words (\cite{olson2021dat}). The DAT provides a uniquely tractable setting for analyzing creative search because it is sequential and increasingly constrained: each newly generated word must remain distinct not only from the first word but from all previously generated words. As the sequence unfolds, combinatorial constraints accumulate, increasing strategic complexity (\cite{ward1994structured,kenett2018flexibility}). This structure enables direct observation of how humans and LLMs navigate expanding semantic constraints over time.

Our dataset consists of 5,000 human responses drawn from a globally diverse sample and 5,000 matched responses generated by 20 recent large language models (\cite{wang2025divergent}). We focus on the top 10\% of responses ranked by DAT score because our analysis and prior evidence shows that, although average human and machine creativity may appear comparable, the highest-performing human responses substantially outperform machine outputs. Restricting attention to the upper tail allows us to compare peak creative performance and isolate differences in generative dynamics rather than differences driven by mean-level variation. Rather than focusing solely on overall DAT scores, we analyze ordered word sequences to examine three core dimensions of creative search: (1) access to creative resources, (2) path dependence and semantic diffusion, and (3) categorical structure and cross-domain exploration.

First, we examine the “raw materials” of creativity—lexical diversity, word frequency, and concreteness. Vocabulary breadth is measured as the number of unique word types produced within the analyzed sample. Word frequency is estimated using the \texttt{wordfreq} package, which aggregates frequency statistics across multiple large-scale corpora (\cite{speer2022wordfreq}); we use the inverse of frequency to represent lexical rarity. Concreteness is measured using established human ratings of how concrete versus abstract a word is (\cite{brysbaert2014concreteness}), with higher values indicating greater concreteness. We find that highly creative humans deploy substantially broader vocabularies than machines. Among the top 10\% of responses, humans use 1,860 unique words compared to 315 used by the average top-performing model. Humans also select significantly rarer words while simultaneously drawing on more concrete concepts, consistent with theories linking semantic network structure and creative ability (\cite{beaty2017semantic,kenett2018flexibility}). In contrast, LLMs show a stronger tendency toward abstract and phenomenon-related terms.

Second, we analyze how word choice evolves across sequence positions to capture path dependence and diffusion dynamics. We operationalize these dynamics using two complementary metrics: (1) local semantic distance, defined as the cosine distance between consecutive words in the sequence, and (2) global semantic diffusion, defined as the cosine distance between each word and the initial word using the embedding space introduced in (\cite{olson2021dat}). Humans exhibit gradual semantic expansion away from initial anchors, sustaining increasing local and global semantic distances across the sequence. This aligns with cognitive accounts of structured imagination and anchor-based constraint accumulation (\cite{ward1994structured}). In contrast, LLMs tend to exhibit maximal divergence early in the sequence—reflected in larger early global distances—followed by convergence as subsequent words become increasingly similar within the embedding space. Although both systems experience convergence as combinatorial space fills—measured by declining mean semantic distance to all previously generated words—humans maintain more stable optimization under constraint accumulation.

Third, we investigate categorical structure using the WordNet hypernym hierarchy to quantify conceptual jumps across semantic categories (\cite{miller1995wordnet,fellbaum1998wordnet}). WordNet organizes nouns into synsets connected through hypernym relations, forming a tree-structured semantic network. For each adjacent pair of words in a response, we identify their corresponding synsets and compute the shortest-path length to their lowest common hypernym within the hierarchy. This shortest-path distance serves as a measure of categorical distance, capturing the magnitude of conceptual transitions between consecutive words. From this structure, we derive multiple metrics: (1) average categorical distance, reflecting the typical size of conceptual shifts; (2) variance of categorical distance, capturing volatility in the search trajectory; (3) maximum categorical distance, identifying the largest conceptual leap within a sequence; and (4) depth of categorical representation, measured as the average distance of each word’s synset from the WordNet root node, indicating the specificity of concepts used. To assess categorical breadth, we additionally count the number of unique semantic categories represented at a fixed hypernym depth level across each response and in the aggregate dataset.Using these measures, we find that humans demonstrate substantially higher variance in categorical transitions and achieve larger maximum conceptual jumps, consistent with L\'evy-flight–like exploration patterns observed in creative cognition (\cite{abe2011levy,kenett2018flexibility}). At the collective level, humans cover more semantic categories across hierarchical depths than machines, suggesting distributed exploratory advantages. Finally, we assess how these strategic dimensions predict creative outcomes using regression and feature-importance analyses. While many machine strategies correlate positively with higher DAT scores, similar aggregate performance emerges from structurally distinct generative regimes.

Our findings show that when approaching creativity, humans engage in grounded, high-variance exploration with sustained semantic diffusion, whereas LLMs follow corpus-optimized but narrower trajectories characterized by early divergence and stronger convergence (\cite{brown2020gpt}). By uncovering these process-level differences, we provide a foundation for designing hybrid human–AI systems that combine complementary search strategies to expand innovation capacity.

posters.title: Into the Unknown: Accounting for Missing Demographic Data when Mitigating Ad Delivery Skew
posters.authors: Isabel Corpus and Allison Koenecke
posters.keywords: platform audit paid search advertising algorithmic fairness ad delivery skew
posters.abstract: Online advertising platforms use algorithmic systems to power the process of matching ads to users, termed ad delivery. Prior audits have demonstrated that ad delivery can be skewed by demographic attributes, such that ads are systematically under-delivered to certain groups despite advertiser intent to reach groups proportionally. In the context of employment, housing, and credit, ad delivery skew by legally protected attributes can amount to discrimination. While not covered by anti-discrimination law, skew in the delivery of ads promoting public services and benefits poses similar concerns. In particular, the under-delivery of ads about public services can prevent individuals from accessing information about opportunities and resources on the basis of their demographic identity. In the absence of platform-provided solutions to skewed ad delivery, advertisers can counteract skew by targeting demographic groups directly. However, direct targeting excludes users whose demographics the platform cannot infer ("unknown users") on advertising platforms such as Google Ads, which do not provide a way to target such users. We collaborate with a state-level government agency to reduce gender-based skew in ad delivery with an advertising intervention that accounts for unknown users while incorporating gender-based targeting. We find that this intervention serves as a middle ground in the trade-off between higher costs (from more granular demographic targeting) and skew (from ignoring demographics entirely). This approach is responsive to the needs of real-world, resource-constrained advertisers who are committed to the equitable distribution of public service outreach via online advertising. We conclude with recommendations for government advertisers, online advertising platforms, and researchers.

posters.title: From Searchable to Non-Searchable: Generative AI and Information Diversity in Online Information Seeking
posters.authors: Yulin Yu, Yizhou Li, Siddharth Suri and Scott Counts
posters.keywords: generative AI ChatGPT search engines information diversity knowledge diversity human AI interaction
posters.abstract:
The rapid emergence of conversational generative AI systems such as ChatGPT is fundamentally transforming how people search for and engage with information. Unlike traditional search engines, which require users to translate information needs into keyword-based queries and navigate ranked lists of documents, generative AI supports conversational, iterative, and open-ended inquiry (\cite{pang2025understanding}). This shift changes not only the volume and form of information seeking, but also the underlying mechanisms of knowledge access. As a result, these systems may reshape how people formulate questions, interpret answers, and reflect on decisions—core processes of learning and knowledge work that ultimately underpin intelligent behavior and innovation (\cite{horvitz1999principles,liu2023conversational,shneiderman2022human,suri2024use,buccinca2021trust,sharma2024generative,yen2024search,brachman2025current}).

In this paper, we examine how generative AI reshapes both input diversity (the diversity of user queries) and output diversity (the diversity of information returned), through the lens of \textit{searchability}—whether a query could plausibly be answered by a traditional search engine. Using over 200,000 real-world human–ChatGPT interactions collected between 2023 and 2025, we ask three core questions: (1) To what extent do users engage in non-searchable forms of inquiry when interacting with ChatGPT? (2) How does the diversity of ChatGPT responses compare with traditional Google Search results for equivalent searchable queries? (3) How does AI output diversity shape subsequent user inquiry?

\subsubsection*{Methods and Data}

Our analysis is based on a corpus of 234,839 real-world conversations between humans and ChatGPT collected from 2023 to 2025, drawn from the \textsc{WildChat-4.8M} dataset (\cite{zhao2024wildchat}\footnote{\url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/WildChat-4.8M}}) To mitigate temporal imbalance, we construct a weekly balanced subset, sampling up to 2,000 conversations per calendar week. Conversations consist of multi-turn user–assistant exchanges within a session. Then, we train a \textit{searchability classification} model to classify which human inputs are searchable. To operationalize whether a query is searchable, we combine LLM-assisted pre-labeling, human verification, and supervised learning. We manually validate a sample of 3,000 queries and train a classifier to distinguish searchable from non-searchable inputs. The final model achieves 91\% with human validation.

We then measure the diversity of user inputs and the outputs generated by ChatGPT and Google Search for the anaysis. \textbf{ Information Diversity-input:} We operationalize the \emph{information diversity of inputs} as dispersion in a semantic embedding space, following prior work that uses a similar approach to define knowledge space in science~(\cite{hao2026artificial}). For a set of user inputs in group \(g\) (searchable vs.\ non-searchable), we encode each input into a unit-normalized embedding vector \(\mathbf{x}_i\) (SentenceTransformer; \texttt{all-MiniLM-L6-v2}). We compute the group centroid \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_g = \frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i \in g}\mathbf{x}_i\), and define each input’s deviation as the Euclidean distance \(d_i^{\text{in}}=\lVert \mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_g\rVert_2\). When quantifying the knowledge space of each group (e.g., searchable versus non-searchable inputs), we define the group-level input information diversity as the maximum deviation within the group, \(\text{ID}_{g}^{\text{in}} = \max_{i \in g} d_i^{\text{in}}\)~(\cite{hao2026artificial}).

\textbf{ Information Diversity-output:} We operationalize the \emph{information diversity of outputs} following a similar method used to define input information diversity; instead, we use responses from ChatGPT or Google Search for seachable queries. We retrieve Google Search results using the Google Custom Search API and collect the top 10 results per query. For each group \(g\), we embed every AI response into a unit-normalized vector \(\mathbf{y}_i\), compute the centroid \(\bar{\mathbf{y}}_g = \frac{1}{n_g}\sum_{i \in g}\mathbf{y}_i\), and define distances \(d_i^{\text{out}}=\lVert \mathbf{y}_i-\bar{\mathbf{y}}_g\rVert_2\). The size of the knowledge space is defined as (\cite{hao2026artificial}), \(\text{ID}_{g}^{\text{out}} = \max_{i \in g} d_i^{\text{out}}\).

\subsubsection*{Results}

\textbf{Input Diversity} We find that 79\% of ChatGPT user queries are classified as non-searchable, while only 21\% resemble traditional search-engine queries. As shown in Figure 1C, the proportion of searchable user inputs decreases over time. Non-searchable queries span a significantly broader semantic space than searchable ones, indicating expanded modes of inquiry beyond keyword-based search. Figures 1A–B present the diversity metrics. In Figure 1A, we observe that user inputs in non-searchable chats display a broader distribution, with a maxium diversity score of 1.0826, whereas searchable chats show a more concentrated distribution with a maxium of 1.0421. Figure 1B shows that only 4 of the 24 topics have more searchable inputs than non-searchable inputs.

\textbf{Output Diversity} We next examine the diversity of information feedback following user queries, specifically comparing potential ChatGPT outputs with Google Search outputs given the same user input. We observe that, on average, Google Search—whether using the top 1, 3, 5, or 10 results—has significantly higher information diversity than ChatGPT (1.052 vs. 1.027, p $<$ 0.001 for Google Top-5 vs. ChatGPT; results for Top-1/Top-3/Top-10 are qualitatively similar. Figures 2A–B illustrate this difference. We conduct the same analysis across topics. Most topics exhibit the same overall pattern, with one notable exception: in creative topics, ChatGPT outputs display substantially higher diversity than Google Search results (1.190 vs. 1.114, p $<$ 0.001)

\textbf{Impact of input on Users} Figure 3A shows input diversity declines over the course of multi-turn conversations: on average, user inquiry diversity decreases by approximately 4.6\% from the first to the 70th turn. We next ask whether the diversity of AI outputs is associated with the diversity of user inputs in the subsequent turn. Regression Analysis shows that a one standard deviation increase in AI output diversity is associated with a 0.5\% increase in next-turn user input diversity (Figure 3B), controlling for prior user diversity.

\subsubsection*{Conclusion and Future Work}

Our study highlights both expansion and contraction dynamics in generative-AI–mediated search. While generative AI enables broader and more exploratory forms of questioning, its responses may narrow the diversity of information exposure relative to traditional search engines. These dynamics have important implications for knowledge production, learning, and innovation.

Future research should examine hybrid systems that integrate generative AI and traditional search, as many platforms increasingly combine both paradigms. Longitudinal studies could further assess how sustained interaction with generative AI reshapes users’ information-seeking habits, curiosity, and downstream decision-making. By quantifying diversity at the level of inputs, outputs, and conversational feedback, this study provides an empirical foundation for understanding how generative AI restructures online knowledge exploration.

posters.title: LLMs in social services: How does chatbot accuracy affect human accuracy?
posters.authors: Jennah Gosciak, Eric Giannella, Zhaowen Guo, Michael Chen and Allison Koenecke
posters.keywords: language models chatbots social services experimental design benchmark data
posters.abstract: As governments increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) to improve social service delivery, robust and reliable AI evaluations are critical. Social service programs such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, or food stamps) have eligibility rules that can be challenging to understand, even for caseworkers who do outreach and regularly help individuals access these programs. Given that caseworkers may support clients in navigating a dozen or more complex programs, LLM-based chatbots may offer a means to provide better, faster help to clients whose situations may be less common. In this paper, we measure the potential effects of LLM-based chatbot suggestions on caseworkers' ability to provide accurate guidance. We first created a 770-question multiple choice benchmark dataset of difficult, but realistic questions that a caseworker might receive from a SNAP client. Next, using these benchmark questions and corresponding expert-verified answers, we conduct a randomized experiment with real caseworkers recruited from nonprofit outreach organizations in Los Angeles. Caseworkers in the control condition did not see any chatbot suggestions and had a mean accuracy of 49%. Caseworkers in the treatment condition saw chatbot suggestions that we artificially varied to range in aggregate accuracy from low (53%) to high (100%). We find that caseworker performance significantly improves as chatbot quality improves: low-quality chatbots (53-73% accurate) improved caseworker accuracy by 8 percentage points on average, while high-quality chatbots (96-100\% accurate) improved caseworker accuracy by 27 percentage points. At the question-level, incorrect chatbot suggestions substantially reduce caseworker accuracy, with a two-thirds reduction on easy questions where the control group performed best (without chatbot suggestions). Finally, we observe that improvements in caseworker accuracy level off as chatbot accuracy increases, a phenomenon that we call the "AI underreliance plateau," which is a key point of concern for real-world deployment and highlights the importance of evaluating human-in-the-loop tools with their users.

posters.title: Belief Alignment Amplifies Susceptibility of Large Language Models to Manipulation
posters.authors: Ozgur Can Seckin, Shalmoli Ghosh, Alessandro Flammini, Maria Elizabeth Grabe, Kristina Lerman and Filippo Menczer
posters.keywords: LLM chatbots Belief Resonance Persuasion Manipulation
posters.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) can manipulate people, yet little is known about how and whether they can manipulate each other. To investigate this, we simulate dialogues between two agents: a target LLM that role-plays a human persona based on demographic and psychological attributes, and an influencer LLM that attempts to amplify the target's beliefs. We examine two manipulation mechanisms: resonance, where the influencer reinforces a belief the target already holds, and persuasion, where the influencer promotes a belief the target initially considers unimportant. Across affective and behavioral measures, we find that both mechanisms increase the belief strength of the target. However, resonance produces consistently stronger amplification than persuasion. We further show that belief reinforcement propagates to related beliefs, suggesting interconnected belief structures within LLM agents. These findings indicate that LLMs are susceptible to belief amplification, particularly when messages align with their existing beliefs, raising implications for personalized AI agents and multi-agent AI ecosystems.
