posters.title: The Visibility–Verification Gap in Agentic AI Discourse: Evidence from Reddit Discussions
posters.authors: Hanjing Shi and Dominic DiFranzo
posters.keywords: Agentic AI discourse Verification timing Platform visibility Online discourse dynamics Computational social science
posters.abstract: Public discussions of agentic AI increasingly shape expectations before most users directly interact with these systems. In such environments, credibility often emerges from platform-visible engagement signals rather than explicit verification of claims. Using Reddit discussions from two communities focused on agentic AI, we analyze how thread visibility relates to the timing of verification behaviors, operationalized as requests for sources, citations, or other forms of evidence. We identify a consistent visibility–verification gap: highly visible threads are more likely to eventually contain verification cues, yet these cues appear significantly later in the discussion. This temporal asymmetry creates a window in which early claims can circulate and accumulate engagement prior to substantiation, highlighting how the ordering of engagement and verification signals shapes collective interpretation in emerging technology discourse.

posters.title: AI Search Engines and U.S. Political Echo Chambers: An Audit of News Citations Patterns Across Ideological Queries
posters.authors: Claire Dekker, Rui Wang, Shengchun Huang and Kai-Cheng Yang
posters.keywords: AI LLMs Search Engines U.S. Politics News
posters.abstract: As AI-powered search engines that summarize results and directly answer users’ questions begin to rival traditional search engines, we evaluate how these systems cite information in their responses. We focus specifically on U.S. political search queries and the news domains cited in AI responses. Our findings reveal that: 1. AI search systems tend to draw information from a narrow pool of mainstream news outlets; 2. Left-leaning news domains are significantly overrepresented in the cited sources; and 3. Politically-framed search queries significantly influence which sources the models cite, i.e., right-leaning queries yield more right-leaning citations. These findings are consistent across all tested models from different providers.

posters.title: Towards a Human-in-the-Loop Classification of Police Violence Using Small Language Models
posters.authors: Maria Gabriela Ayala and Andrew D Zaharia
posters.keywords: large language models fine-tuning text classification natural language processing human-in-the-loop
posters.abstract: Mapping Police Violence (MPV) is a public database tracking fatal police violence in the United States, relying on manual human review of news articles to identify relevant incidents. This process is slow, costly, and exposes researchers to graphic content. With no federal requirement for agencies to report use-of-force deaths, accurate open-source tracking is critical. We fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini, a small language model (SLM), to classify news articles as relevant or irrelevant to MPV's definition of police violence. Recall was prioritized as the primary objective, as failing to capture a case of police violence is more consequential than flagging a false positive for a database where comprehensive coverage is the core mission. The model achieves 96% recall, 95% precision, and 94% accuracy on a 10,000-article test set, compared to an estimated 27% accuracy for the existing keyword heuristic, with an AUC of 0.98. In practical terms, this represents an approximately 3.5x reduction in researcher workload. Full automation, however, is neither the goal nor ethically appropriate: accountability databases require human judgment to handle nuanced cases, monitor for bias, and preserve public trust. We therefore propose a human-in-the-loop architecture in which researcher decisions continuously retrain the model, combining the efficiency of a SLM classification with the oversight that this work demands.

posters.title: Cross-Cultural Evaluation of LLMs: A Mixed-Method Study of Chinese-to-English Movie Title Translation
posters.authors: Xiaoxuan Jacqui Wang, Jialing Wu and Yingyu Cheng
posters.keywords: large language models cultural adaptation machine translation film title translation computational social science
posters.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for machine translation, yet their ability to adapt culture specific items(CSIs) remains unclear in domains with short and highly condensed text such as film titles. We study Chinese to English movie title translation using a dataset of 81 films whose titles contain cultural elements, with official English titles treated as references and Chinese synopses used as optional context. We evaluate three prompting conditions, Title only, Title + Synopsis, and Culture aware, across three models, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 flash, and Llama 3.1. Quantitatively, we compare outputs using BLEURT, BERTScore, sentence embedding cosine similarity, and CSI-Match, and test effects of model and prompt using a two-way ANOVA. Results show significant differences across models and prompting conditions. GPT-5 with Title + Synopsis achieves the best overall performance across all metrics, indicating that narrative context substantially improves semantic alignment and CSI translation. A qualitative analysis of this best setting finds that the model most often preserves or transforms cultural elements, while omission and mistranslation are less frequent but reveal failures on implicit cultural references. These findings highlight the importance of CSI-focused evaluation for cross cultural title translation.

posters.title: When AI Is Allowed to Lie: Testing the Impact of Honest versus Dishonest LLM Persuasion
posters.authors: David Rand
posters.keywords: AI persuasion large language models misinformation deception experiment
posters.abstract:
Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated striking persuasive capabilities when engaging in dialogue with humans (Costello et al. 2024; Argyle et al. 2025; Lin et al. 2025; Hackenburg et al. 2025; Salvi et al. 2025). A primary concern raised by this persuasiveness is the possibility that the models persuade by misinforming – that is, by providing false information. Consistent with this concern, Hackenburg et al. (2025) found that LLMs that were optimized for persuasion generated more inaccurate claims. This association could imply that false claims are more persuasion, but does not provide clear causal evidence. Lin et al. (2025), on the other hand, found that message-level accuracy did not predict persuasion differences across LLM-generated arguments. Thus, the causal effect of model deceptiveness on persuasion remains unclear. We address this gap with a preregistered experiment that directly randomizes whether or not an LLM tasked with persuading may lie. We do so across factually contestable topics (firefighter budgets, recess length) and topics where one side demands fabrication (pro-homeopathy, pro-Myers-Briggs employment screening).

Methods We recruited N = 851 U.S. adults from the Lucid Marketplace online panel. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 14 conditions in a 2 × 2 × 4 design: AI honesty (honest vs. lying) crossed with the four policy issues crossed with persuasion direction. (Due to a coding error, one of the topic-direction pairs was implemented incorrectly and dropped from analysis). All participants completed a chat-based conversation with an LLM (GPT-4 class) that argued for the assigned issue position-direction. In the lying condition, the AI was instructed to use whatever claims would be most persuasive, regardless of accuracy; in the honest condition, it was instructed to only make accurate claims. Attitudes toward all four topics were measured on 0–100 scales before and after the conversation. In the lying conditions only, participants were then debriefed, with the AI explicitly correcting all false claims, and then attitudes were re-measured a third time. Analyses use OLS regression with HC1-robust standard errors, controlling for pre-treatment attitudes and condition fixed effects (z-scored), with all liar × covariate interactions. Cross-topic heterogeneity is assessed via random-effects meta-analysis. As a manipulation check, we used a Perplexity AI model to fact-check the models’ claims (an approach which has been validated in Lin et al., 2025) and found that the lying AI was significantly less accurate than the honest AI (t(660)=5.7, p<.0001).

Results Across conditions, AI conversations produced large attitude change in the intended direction on the target outcome (+17.0 points on a 0–100 scale; t(850) = 18.41, p < .001; Figure 1), while not significantly changing attitudes towards the non-target outcomes (-2.0 points; t(850) = −1.02, p = .307). As a result, the treatment moved the target outcome significantly more than the non-strategy outcomes (+18.95 points (t(850) = 8.53, p < .001). Thus, we demonstrate strong baseline persuasive effects, with effect sizes on the higher end of prior work. Critically, however, there was no significant difference in persuasiveness of the lying AI relative to the honest AI (+1.93 points, 95% CI: −1.33 to 5.19, p = .25; Figure 1). An imputation analysis carrying forward baseline attitudes for the 8.2% of participants who did not complete the post-survey yields identical conclusions (b = 1.76, p = .28). Furthermore, meta-analysis found no evidence of heterogeneity in lying effect across the seven topic-direction combinations: I² = 0%, Q(6) = 3.59, p = .73. Thus, we find no evidence that instructing the LLM to lie improved its persuasiveness (or that instructing the LLM to be honest reduced its persuasiveness). Moreover, correcting the AI’s false claims in the lying condition significantly reduced persuasion (mean reversal: −5.8 points, p < .001) – such that when comparing final attitudes (honest AI post-conversation vs. lying AI post-debrief), lying+correction left participants significantly less persuaded than honest AI alone (b = −4.59, p = .007). This penalty was particularly driven by the Myers-Briggs and homeopathy conditions, where the correction most sharply reversed the initial persuasion. Examining participants’ evaluations of the AI, we found that while the lying AI and honest AI was rated as similarly informative (p = .25), the lying AI was rated as significantly less accurate (b = −0.55 on a 1–10 scale, p = .003), and trust in generative AI increased significantly less after conversing with the lying AI compared to the honest AI (b = −0.15, p = .04; although genAI trust still significantly increased pre-to-post in both conditions, p<.001). Discussion Contrary to common intuition, allowing an AI to lie did not increase its persuasive impact. Moreover, when corrections followed dishonest persuasion, final attitudes were move less than in the honest baseline, implying that lying is actively counterproductive in contexts where disclosure is likely. These results suggest that the association between persuasiveness and inaccuracy documented by Hackenburg et al. (2025) does not reflect a causal effect. Instead, it seems likely that pushing the model to produce more factual claims (which Hackenburg found was the key driver of persuasiveness) leads it to produce inaccurate claims as it runs out of accurate claims. More broadly, beyond AI persuasion these results bear on debates around the nature of misinformation (e.g. Allen et al. 2025). While the literature on misinformation and fake news has largely focused on outright falsehoods (e.g. Pennycook & Rand, 2021), it has been argued that claims that are factually true but misleading (e.g. “Healthy doctor dies two weeks after receiving COVID vaccine”) are a larger problem because they receive much wider circulation (Allen et al. 2024). Our findings support this conclusion, demonstrating that even when striving to be factually accurate, it is possible to produce large persuasive effects in either direction on a given issue.

posters.title: AI and The Digital Divide
posters.authors: Isabelle Langrock and Jen Schradie
posters.keywords: Inequality Generative AI Digital Trace Data Text Analysis Comparative
posters.abstract: Generative AI chatbots like OpenAI’s chatGPT have transformed the internet, changing the ways people seek information and recording hundreds of millions of active users. Yet ubiquity does not entail equality. In this paper, we show that ChatGPT use, and generative AI use more broadly, is highly socially stratified by income, education, gender, and race, as well as by digital knowledge and social media use. Triangulating across three data types -- a two wave survey fielded in the United States and France about AI use and online habits, digital trace data from nearly quarter of survey respondents, and open ended text questions about the harms and benefits of AI -- we find that AI use is socially dependent in both France and the United States. While time spent online and digital skills leads to more AI use in both countries, there is a larger gender gap in the United States than in France. In France, education level is much more salient. Users in both countries are apprehensive about AI use, despite also appreciating that it provides information more quickly than alternatives. This work sheds light on the social groups who are most left out of the AI transformation and who might be least resilient to the digital and social upheavals continually promised by generative AI companies.

posters.title: #God Save the Children: Examining Religious Identities and Polarization in Predator Vigilantism Discourse
posters.authors: Maylee Sexton, Kimberly Ingold, Pekka Santtila and Brian Hall
posters.keywords: moral foundations theory religiosity polarization child sexual abuse sentiment analysis
posters.abstract: This study uses computational text analysis of 1.2 million social media comments to investigate whether conservative Christian identity drives the escalating sanctity/purity rhetoric observed in predator vigilante discourse and subsequently moral rhetorics surrounding child sexual abuse online on ideologically homogeneous platforms. Building on Moral Foundations Theory and Perry's (2022) framework of religious polarization, we develop an automated religiosity classification pipeline and test whether religious identity mediates the relationship between platform environment and moral rhetoric intensification using mixed-effects temporal models and random forest prediction.

posters.title: Cross-National Evidence of Disproportionate Media Visibility for the Radical Right in the 2024 European Elections
posters.authors: Íris Damião, João Franco and Joana Gonçalves-Sá
posters.keywords: Media salience political visibility computational text analysis European Parliament elections media bias
posters.abstract: This study provides a systematic comparative analysis of media visibility of different political families during the 2024 European Parliament elections. We analyzed close to 21,500 unique news from leading national outlets in Austria, Germany, Ireland, Poland, and Portugal - countries with diverse political contexts and levels of media trust. Combining computational and human classification, we identified parties, political leaders, and groups from the article's URLs and titles, and clustered them according to European Parliament political families and broad political leanings. Cross-country comparison shows that the Mainstream and the Radical Right were mentioned more often than the other political groups. Moreover, the Radical Right received disproportionate attention relative to electoral results (from 2019 or 2024) and electoral projections, particularly in Austria, Germany, and Ireland. This imbalance increased in the final weeks of the campaign, when media influence on undecided voters is greatest. Outlet-level analysis shows that coverage of right-leaning entities dominated across news sources, especially those generating the highest traffic, suggesting a structural rather than outlet-specific pattern. Media visibility is a central resource, and this systematic mapping of online coverage highlights how traditional media can contribute to structural asymmetries in democratic competition.

posters.title: Hostile Tone Overrides Partisan Endorsement in Science Communication
posters.authors: Miriam Schirmer, Nicholas Ornstein, William Brady and Ágnes Horvát
posters.keywords: science communication hostility partisan identity political endorsement social media engagement
posters.abstract: Hostile science communication on social media, i.e., posts that attack researchers, is widespread online, yet its effects on audiences are poorly understood. We report two experiments in which participants evaluated simulated science posts crossing tone (hostile vs. neutral) with political endorsement (none / Dr. Anthony Fauci / RFK Jr.) across three science topics. Hostile framing produced large reductions in perceived accuracy, liking, sharing intention, and relevance. These findings were consistent across both studies, all topics, and both endorsers. Partisan alignment with the endorser shaped accuracy and engagement ratings under neutral tone, but this effect collapsed entirely under hostile tone. Taken together, results suggest that hostile anti-science messaging is largely self-limiting, and that identity-congruence effects in science communication are present but fragile.

posters.title: AI-assisted hidden profile decision-making
posters.authors: Jose Cordova, Chun-Wei Chiang, Miriam Schirmer, Ming Yin and Agnes Horvat
posters.keywords: Human-AI Decision Group Decisions Collective Intelligence AI Assistance
posters.abstract: Groups often fail to aggregate distributed information effectively. In hidden-profile tasks, members must share privately held information to reach the correct decision, yet groups tend to focus on shared evidence and overlook unique information. We study whether large language models (LLMs) can support group decision-making without knowing the correct answer. In an online experiment (N = 114), triads completed a hidden-profile hiring task under three conditions: no LLM, individual-level LLM, and a group-level LLM. Both LLM conditions achieved higher decision accuracy than control groups, suggesting that LLMs may act as coordination scaffolds in group decision making.

posters.title: Evaluating 21st-Century Competencies in Postsecondary Curricula with Large Language Models: Performance Benchmarking and Reasoning-Based Prompting Strategies
posters.authors: Zhen Xu, Xin Guan, Chenxi Shi, Qinhao Chen and Renzhe Yu
posters.keywords: Curricular analytics 21st-century competency large language models (LLMs) prompt engineering chain of thought (CoT)
posters.abstract: The growing emphasis on 21st-century competencies in postsecondary education, intensified by the transformative impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the economy and society, underscores the urgent need to evaluate how they are embedded in curricula and how effectively academic programs align with evolving workforce and societal demands. Curricular analytics, particularly recent advancements powered by GenAI, offer a promising data-driven approach to this challenge. However, the analysis of 21st-century competencies requires pedagogical reasoning beyond surface-level information retrieval, and the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in this context remain underexplored. In this study, we extend prior research on curricular analytics of 21st-century competencies across a broader range of curriculum documents, competency frameworks, and models. Using 7,600 manually annotated curriculum-competency alignment scores (38 competencies and 200 courses across five curriculum document types), we evaluate the informativeness of different curriculum document sources, benchmark the performance of general-purpose LLMs on mapping curricula to competencies, and analyze error patterns. We further introduce a reasoning-based prompting strategy, curricular chain-of-thought (CoT), to strengthen LLMs’ pedagogical reasoning. Our results show that detailed instructional activity descriptions are the most informative type of curriculum document for competency analytics. Open-weight LLMs achieve accuracy comparable to proprietary models on coarse-grained tasks, demonstrating their scalability and cost-effectiveness for institutional use. However, no model reaches human-level precision in fine-grained pedagogical reasoning. Our proposed curricular CoT yields modest improvements by reducing bias in instructional keyword inference and improving the detection of nuanced pedagogical evidence in long text. Together, these findings highlight the untapped potential of institutional curriculum documents and provide an empirical foundation for advancing AI-driven curricular analytics.

posters.title: From Strategy Recognition to Strategic Adaptation: Validating LLM Agents in Spatial Voting Models
posters.authors: Aojie Ju and Yulu Pi
posters.keywords: computational social science large language models agent-based modeling agent validation party competition
posters.abstract:
Political parties’ strategic positioning is a central mechanism of electoral competition, and spatial models have provided a tractable way to study how behavioral rules generate collective political dynamics. In the classic work of Downs (1957), parties are modeled as vote-seeking competitors who choose policy positions in an ideological space to maximize voter support, while voters select the party closest to their own positions. Laver (2005) extended the classic framework of spatial models in an agent-based model where parties in a two-dimensional policy space, each representing economic and social dimensions, follow one of five adaptive strategies: Sticker (never moves), Predator (chases the largest party), Aggregator (moves toward the supporter centroid), Hunter (repeats moves that gain votes), and Random (moves randomly). Laver’s model allows the observation of how different strategies in political competitions produce distinct movement patterns and vote trajectories, and more importantly, it enables the evaluation of simulated agents on whether they can recover and enact known mechanisms of strategic interactions.

As computational social science increasingly experiments with LLM-based agents to simulate social and political actors Park et al.(2023); Argyle et al.(2023); Horton (2023), a fundamental question arises: can LLMs accurately recognize the strategic behaviors of political parties from observational data, and can they themselves act as effective strategic agents in competitive electoral settings? Answering these questions is critical because LLMs that cannot recognize mechanisms are unlikely to implement strategic adaptation.

To tackle our research questions, we present two complementary studies that address these questions within Laver’s simulation framework. Study 1 tests whether LLMs can infer party strategies from time-series data alone. Study 2 tests whether an LLM can adopt effective strategies as a competing party agent embedded in the simulation.

Study 1—Mechanism Recognition: We generated 50 simulations of the Laver model, each running 100 time steps with 3–7 parties and 500–1,000 voters, producing 254 individual party–strategy instances distributed across the five strategies. We evaluated six LLMs: GPT-4o, MiniMax, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-0.6B. Each model received sampled time-series data on party positions and vote counts and was asked to classify every party’s strategy without access to labels. To manage context length, we provided a 30-step summary of positions and votes from evenly spaced windows across each simulation.

The performance across models is largely varied, as GPT-4o achieves the highest overall accuracy at 39.0%, nearly double the random baseline of 20% and substantially above the second-best model, MiniMax (25.2%). A clear strategy difficulty hierarchy emerges: Sticker is near-trivially detectable (100% for GPT-4o) due to zero positional variance, while Predator is hardest (≤12.1% for all models) because it requires cross-party relational reasoning through tracking which party is largest and whether movement targets it. The GPT-4o confusion matrix reveals systematic error patterns: Predator, Aggregator, and Hunter instances are predominantly misclassified as Hunter, suggesting models default to a “movement-toward-something” heuristic without distinguishing the target.

Plus, model scale alone does not predict performance. In our implementation, Qwen3-30B, the largest open-source model tested, scores lowest at 9.4%, indicating that architecture and training regime matter more than parameter count for this task.

Study 2—Strategic Adaptation: We then deployed GPT-4o as an active party agent within the same simulation framework, competing against four rule-based opponents. Every three time steps, the LLM agent received its current position, vote share, and opponents’ positions, then selected from the five Laver strategies for its next moves. We tested six matchup conditions: LLM versus four identical-strategy opponents (Sticker, Predator, Aggregator, Hunter, or Random) and a mixed-strategy condition, with 3 replications per matchup over 50 time steps with 500 voters.

The LLM agent performs best against disorganized opponents: it exceeds the 20% equal-share baseline against Random (31.0%) and Predator (33.6%) opponents, performs near baseline against Sticker (20.5%) and Hunter (24.9%), but falls below baseline against Aggregator (18.2%) and in the mixed condition (15.1%). Critically, the LLM overwhelmingly converges on the Aggregator strategy regardless of opponent type, selecting it in 83–98% of decisions across all matchups. This rigid preference is effective against opponents that leave the voter center uncontested, but it fails against Aggregator opponents competing for the same centrist voters and in mixed environments requiring adaptive responses. The LLM’s poor performance in the mixed condition (15.1%, well below the 20% baseline) is particularly revealing, as real political competition involves heterogeneous opponents, and the inability to adapt strategy to a diverse competitive landscape represents a significant limitation for simulation applications.

Cross-Study Implications: Comparing GPT-4o’s inference accuracy (Study 1) with its strategy usage frequency (Study 2) across the five strategies reveals a disconnect: the LLM’s strategic repertoire is narrow regardless of its recognition ability. It gravitates toward Aggregator even though it can identify Sticker successfully and struggles to recognize the very strategy it overwhelmingly adopts. These findings suggest that while LLMs can partially identify strategic patterns from observational data, they lack the adaptive, opponent-contingent reasoning required for robust political agency. For the growing use of LLM agents in computational social science simulations, our results indicate that passing an inference test is necessary but insufficient, as effective agency demands flexible strategic adaptation that current models do not yet exhibit. We argue that validation benchmarks for LLM-based social simulation agents should test both recognition and behavioral competence in adversarial settings, rather than relying only on survey-style alignment with human responses.

References Downs, A. (1957). An Economic Theory of Democracy. Harper & Row.

Laver, M. (2005). Policy and the Dynamics of Political Competition. American Political Science Review, 99(2):263–281.

Park, J. S., O’Brien, J. C., Cai, C. J., Morris, M. R., Liang, P., & Bernstein, M. S. (2023). Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior. In Proceedings of the 36th ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST).

Argyle, L. P., Busby, E. C., Fulda, N., Gubler, J. R., Rytting, C., & Wingate, D. (2023). Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples. Political Analysis, 31(3):337–351.

Horton, J. J. (2023). Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus? NBER Working Paper 31122.

posters.title: Characterizing How LLMs Respond Differently to Venting and Advice-seeking
posters.authors: Vivienne Bihe Chi, Adithya V Ganesan, Ryan L Boyd, Lyle Ungar and Sharath Chandra Guntuku
posters.keywords: Interpersonal Emotion Regulation Online Help-Seeking and Social Support Human-AI Interaction AI Emotional Support LLM Evaluation
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners for emotional support, yet little is known about how they respond to different help-seeking styles. Drawing on interpersonal emotion regulation theory, we examine a key distinction in online support discourse: venting (emotion-focused coping) versus advice-seeking (problem-focused coping). Using a large Reddit corpus (≈178k posts from 14,040 users), we first show that these discourse modes are linguistically and psychologically distinct. We then introduce a scalable annotation framework that distinguishes regulatory responses (e.g., validation, containment) from escalatory alignment (e.g., emotional amplification, appraisal endorsement) in LLM outputs. Prompting GPT-5 with 1,602 posts, we find that venting elicits stronger emotional validation but also greater escalation-adjacent responses than advice-seeking. The results suggest LLMs mirror users’ communicative style, potentially shaping emotional trajectories in human–AI interaction.

posters.title: What Stays and What Goes: Auditing the Discursive Impact of LLM Summarization on Political News
posters.authors: Pavel Savgira, Elisa Kreiss, Amir Ghasemian and Homa Hosseinmardi
posters.keywords: Large Language Models Text Summarization Political Bias Algorithmic Auditing
posters.abstract: As reading Large Language Model (LLM)-produced summaries becomes an inescapable part of information consumption, it is crucial to understand how they change our political discourse. While prior work focuses on perceived utility, we examine whether LLM-generated summaries preserve the political lean of original news articles. We find that LLM-based summarization, at aggregate, neutralizes the lean of both Republican and Democratic sources, though with stronger moderation for Republican-leaning articles. However, this pattern obfuscates two key systematic effects. Firstly, news topics significantly shape this moderation. Secondly, summaries do not uniformly neutralize political lean, most strongly impacting moderately partisan content while retaining the extreme stances of strongly partisan articles. These findings complicate the narrative of a general leftward bias, showing moderation primarily affects moderate perspectives rather than tempering extremes. Finally, our automated framework demonstrates the need to evaluate not just perceived quality, but the active role summaries play in shaping contemporary political discourse.

posters.title: AI Persuasion in Negotiation: Personality, Fairness, and Human Resistance to LLM Agents
posters.authors: Sean Noh and Ho-Chun Herbert Chang
posters.keywords: LLM agents negotiation personality AI persuasion AI disclosure
posters.abstract: AI negotiation agents are reshaping digital commerce. Online marketplaces now deploy automated bargaining systems to handle supplier negotiations and enable customer price haggling. As platforms increasingly endow these agents with distinct personality traits, understanding how personality shapes negotiation fairness, exploitation dynamics, and linguistic toxicity becomes critical for platform governance and consumer protection. Recent work has shown that LLMs can shift political beliefs through strategic argument and reduce conspiracy beliefs through sustained dialogue, while studies on persuasion-based jailbreaking raise concerns about manipulation in consumer-facing applications. Yet two fundamental questions remain open: how do personality-initialized LLM agents behave in structured bargaining games, and can humans effectively resist AI persuasion when negotiating with these agents? This paper investigates this in two parts. First, we simulate 3,500 AI–AI negotiation games using personality-prompted GPT-4 agents within the alternating-offers framework, establishing how OCEAN personality traits propagate to canonical measures of rationality, fairness, and exploitation. Second, we extend this framework to human–AI interaction through a survey experiment in which participants negotiate moral and political issues with LLM agents they believe to be human, testing whether negotiation framing and AI disclosure moderate persuasion and concession behavior. Together, this investigation bridges computational and behavioral accounts of negotiation, providing an empirical foundation for the design and regulation of AI agents in adversarial social contexts.

posters.title: Do Large Language Models Exhibit Cognitive Dissonance? Distributional Evidence from Moral Decision Making
posters.authors: Baihui Wang, Bernard Koch and Shiyang Lai
posters.keywords: large language models cognitive dissonance moral cognition probability distributions coalition dynamics
posters.abstract: This paper investigates whether large language models exhibit behavior analogous to cognitive dissonance when updating moral judgments. We examine the full probability distributions over moral positions, enabling a distributional perspective on belief change. Using GPT-4o and 78 moral dilemmas, we conduct three experiments to measure how probability mass shifts under different cognitive and social pressures. Study 1 reveals confirmation bias: opposing cues weaken the model’s prior belief but redistribute probability locally rather than toward distant alternatives. Study 2 demonstrates irrational commitment, where fabricated memories of prior decisions lead the model to justify and persist in previously rejected choices, even after corrective information. Study 3 simulates multi-agent deliberation and shows that belief stability depends on coalition structure: when the agent forms an in-group alignment and faces inter-group disagreement, resistance to belief change becomes strongest. Together, these findings suggest that LLM reasoning can exhibit structured belief-maintenance dynamics resembling human cognitive dissonance.

posters.title: Will Language Models Lie for Their Home Countries? Asymmetric Propagation of Positive Misinformation
posters.authors: Ho-Chun Herbert Chang, Tracy Weener, Yung-Chun Chen, Sean Noh, Mingyue Zha and Hsuan Lo
posters.keywords: language models misinformation foreign influence AI auditing favorability bias
posters.abstract: As language models (LMs) continue to develop, concerns over foreign misinformation through models developed in authoritarian countries have emerged. Do LMs favor their home countries? This study audits four frontier LMs by evaluating their favoritism toward world leaders, then measuring how favoritism propagates into misinformation belief. We found that although DeepSeek favors China, it also rates some Western leaders highly. We discuss the conflict between data bias and guardrails, how language shapes favoritism, the “positive” future of LM-based soft propaganda, and how an AI’s own internal thoughts can unwillingly reveal explicit directives.

posters.title: Would Artificial Leaders Launch the Nuke? Inclination of LLMs' Nuclear Weapon Usage in Civilization V
posters.authors: John Chen and Lexie Zhao
posters.keywords: large language models for social research artificial decision-making agents complex social systems simulation
posters.abstract: This paper examines agentic LLM decision-making behavior through Civilization V, a generative, longitudinal, competitive environment that serves as an open-ended complex systems simulation. Across 228 games and ~1,200 LLM player trajectories spanning six large language models (LLMs), we study their inclination toward nuclear weapon usage under two agentic configurations. We find that models generally favor nuclear escalation; that passive information-framing by subordinate agents seems to implicitly shift leader inclination; and that reframing decisions as real-world governance causes models to moderate extreme positions but does not fundamentally alter their strategic reasoning. We plan to extend the work into human-AI decision-making. As it stands, this work contributes to computational social science at the intersection of artificial decision-making agents, complex social systems simulation, and large language models for social research.

posters.title: From Job Titles to Jawlines: Using Context Voids for Probing Generative AI Systems
posters.authors: Shahan Ali Memon, Soham De, Sungha Kang, Riyan Mujtaba Memon, Bedoor Alshebli, Katie Davis, Jaime Snyder and Jevin West
posters.keywords: Red teaming LLMs AI Ethics Evaluations Speculative Design
posters.abstract: In this work, we present a methodological framework for probing socio-technical AI systems under conditions of missing context, revealing algorithmic bias and representational assumptions in multimodal generative models. We present a speculative design methodology for studying the behavior of generative AI systems, framing design as a mode of inquiry. We propose bridging seemingly unrelated domains to generate intentional context voids, using these tasks as probes to elicit AI model behavior. We demonstrate this through a case study: probing the ChatGPT system (GPT-4 and DALL-E) to generate headshots from professional Curricula Vitae (CVs). In contrast to traditional ways, our approach assesses system behavior under conditions of radical uncertainty—when forced to invent entire swaths of missing context—revealing subtle stereotypes and value-laden assumptions. We analyze how the system interprets identity and competence markers from CVs, translating them into visual portraits despite the missing context (i.e., physical descriptors). We show that within this context void, the AI system generates biased representations, potentially relying on stereotypical associations or blatant hallucinations.

posters.title: Limits of Literature-Conditioned Large Language Models for Predicting Behavioral Experiments
posters.authors: Robin Na, Duncan Watts and Abdullah Almaatouq
posters.keywords: large language models prediction meta-science research synthesis experimental design
posters.abstract:
Predicting the outcome of behavioral experiments before running them can be a powerful driver for scientific progress. It can complement human-subject experiments by guiding researchers toward more efficient study design (Balietti et al. 2021), informing valid statistical inference with fewer data (Angelopoulos et al. 2023; Broska et al. 2025), and generating hypotheses that may not be immediately apparent to human researchers (Ludwig and Mullainathan 2024). Prediction can also serve as a way to reflect on the state of cumulative knowledge in a particular domain (Almaatouq et al. 2024). If models exposed to decades of research can anticipate outcomes in novel situations, this would suggest that the accumulated literature encodes meaningful regularities about when particular behavioral effects emerge.

Researchers have often been collecting such predictions of social science experiments from human judgment—either domain experts drawing on their experience with the literature, or laypeople drawing on everyday intuitions about social behavior (DellaVigna et al. 2019; DellaVigna and Pope 2018; DellaVigna et al. 2020). Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown potential in contributing to this forecasting exercise. These models, trained on the vast scale of human language data including the scientific literature and everyday language, were able to predict experimental outcomes often competitively with domain experts and laypeople across several domains (Hewitt et al., 2024; Lippert et al. 2024; Schoenegger et al. 2025; Santtila et al. 2025). The LLMs in these studies are typically off-the-shelf models that have not been further exposed to specific documents or data. The authors therefore encouraged further investigation on how specialized versions of these can further boost the predictive utility (Hewitt et al., 2024), including giving access to relevant external information (Santtila et al. 2025) such as data from scientific publications (Lippert et al. 2024).

Recent work has also shown LLM’s capability in literature-grounded question answering and synthesis, with many of the advancements relying on giving LLMs access to scientific articles through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). RAG conditions the model’s response on documents retrieved from a corpus without requiring computationally expensive training processes from the off-the-shelf LLMs. RAG-based systems have improved LLM performance on scientific question-answering (Lála et al. 2023), literature synthesis (Asai et al. 2024), and recommendation tasks (Li et al. 2024). These evaluations, however, often assess whether outputs faithfully represent what papers say, judged in terms of alignment with annotations and opinions from human experts. Whether probing the model’s response this way improves its predictive accuracy remains untested. Here, we ask whether grounding LLM’s predictions on published research articles improves its ability to predict the outcome of behavioral experiments in settings whose outcomes were not publicly available at the time of prediction. We test this by comparing predictions from GPT-4.1 (baseline condition) against predictions from the same model augmented with a corpus of 1,398 peer-reviewed articles collected from Web of Science (augmented condition; Figure 1). Within the augmented condition, we varied the papers provided to the LLM since papers may differ in reliability and relevance to the target prediction settings (Ioannidis 2005; Button et al. 2013; Holzmeister et al. 2024). This variation includes conditions providing a single article, repeated over all 1,398 papers in our corpus, as well as 620 curated collections of articles constructed using different selection criteria (discipline, journal impact factor, citation count, publication year). As a robustness check, we also varied the format used to provide paper content (full text, abstract only, LLM-generated summary). If the literature contains extractable signals that improves predictions, we would expect some augmentation strategy to outperform the baseline. If augmentation consistently fails to help, or degrades the performance overall, it points to limitations on either the information that these papers provide or the LLM’s ability to utilize it for forecasting.

We test this using 20 new experiments on peer punishment in cooperation dilemmas, where the prediction task is to determine how much punishment mechanisms increase or decrease group welfare across different settings (Alsobay et al. 2025). Consistent with prior findings, the baseline off-the-shelf GPT-4.1 model performance matches or exceeds every human (laypeople and experts) forecaster we tested (Figure 2). We then condition the model on the individual papers and their collections. To our surprise, conditioning on these papers–individual or collections–rarely reduces prediction error, and in many cases it makes predictions worse (Figure 3). Nonetheless, this strategy substantially increases the model’s internal confidence measured through the perplexity of predicted tokens (Figure 4). This trend is robust across language models, augmented format, and filtering criteria, with no single LLM outperforming the out-of-sample prediction of statistical model (elastic-net) trained on systematically sampled experiments (Alsobay et al. 2025).

Furthermore, we identify two potential mechanisms for such limitation. First, we find little evidence that LLMs are capable of improving their prediction even when given various versions of documents that are based on the experimental dataset that shows superior performance when using simple statistical models. Second, our LLM-assisted extraction of experimental papers from the literature shows striking underspecification and biases in the parameter values relevant for the prediction task, with most papers being focused on specific regimes (e.g., 4 player game with 10 rounds, 1:3 punishment ratio) instead of being systematically explored (Figures 5-6). These results suggest that more informative systems for LLM-based experimental design require direct evaluation of their predictive utility, foundation models that are specifically designed to make accurate predictions based on available experiments, and an experimental paradigm that systematically explores design spaces such as integrative experiments (Almaatouq et al. 2024).

posters.title: Alignment as Social Choice: Welfare Effects of Five Major AI Developers’ Alignment Frameworks in Large-Scale Human Preference Data
posters.authors: Carina I Hausladen
posters.keywords: AI alignment Social welfare Welfare trade-offs Company alignment strategies Empirical alignment evaluation
posters.abstract:
Extended Abstract

This paper interprets the stated alignment principles of five major technology companies—Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, Meta, and Microsoft—through the lens of welfare economics and social choice theory, and maps them to explicit social welfare functions (SWFs). We then apply these SWFs to a large-scale empirical alignment preference dataset (PRISM) to study their practical consequences.

Related Work

This paper sits at the intersection of three strands of literature: the normative foundations of AI alignment, pluralistic and heterogeneous preference modeling, and the formal application of social choice theory to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

Our contribution differs from each of these strands. First, we move beyond axiomatic analysis and operationalize company-implied SWFs on real data. Second, rather than designing a new algorithm for a single model, we work with established welfare-economic archetypes of social welfare functions. Third, we ground the analysis in a large-scale, cross-company human preference dataset, enabling a comparative empirical evaluation of alignment philosophies.

Formalizing Company Alignment Philosophies

For each company, we construct a qualitative value profile based on flagship alignment and safety documents. We interpret these materials through a social choice framework and identify four shared structural commitments: monotonic improvement, interpersonal comparability, cardinal aggregation of welfare signals, and an explicit concern for harm avoidance.

Normative divergence arises along four central dimensions: (i) how constraints are traded off against aggregate welfare, (ii) whether fairness is defined at the level of individuals or groups, (iii) the degree of inequality aversion embedded in the objective, and (iv) the treatment of catastrophic or worst-case outcomes.

We then systematically code each company along a common set of normative lenses derived from welfare economics and social choice theory. This yields value profiles that can be mapped to stylized classes of social welfare functions. At a high level, OpenAI and DeepMind display predominantly utilitarian orientations. Anthropic aligns with a lexicographically catastrophe-averse prioritarian stance. Meta emphasizes group-level fairness and maximin reasoning. Microsoft adopts a robustness-oriented, configuration-based framework consistent with constitutional and mechanism-design traditions.

Consequences of Company Alignment Philosophies

We operationalize the identified SWFs on the PRISM dataset to quantify their downstream welfare implications. PRISM contains human evaluations from 1,396 unique participants who engage in open-ended conversations with different large language models and subsequently rate model responses on a 0–100 scale.

We implement five aggregation rules corresponding to the formalized company philosophies, rank models under each rule, and select the top-performing model. Across these five rules, three distinct winners emerge. Command ranks first under the Microsoft-, DeepMind-, and OpenAI-style objectives and achieves the highest median welfare. Chat-Bison wins under a group-maximin objective (corresponding to Meta’s approach), maximizing the mean welfare of the worst-off demographic group in the sample. In contrast, GPT-4 performs best under a threshold-based objective (corresponding to Anthropic’s stance) that minimizes the share of users falling below a welfare floor.

These results demonstrate that model selection is highly sensitive to the underlying normative criterion. Different alignment philosophies systematically select different “best” models and privilege different users.

Empirical Properties of Human Alignment Preferences

The alignment frameworks we examine do not explicitly incorporate the empirical distribution of large-scale user preferences. We therefore ask what changes once this distribution is taken seriously.

First, a single-model solution appears insufficient. The top-performing model covers only about half of users’ top-three rankings. To achieve roughly 80 percent Pareto-style coverage of users’ top preferences, six models would need to be deployed. Companies increasingly employ mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures with learned routing mechanisms to dynamically select specialized sub-models per input. Yet such architectures are not discussed in the alignment documents we analyze. From a social choice perspective, this is closely related to multi-winner election problems: instead of selecting one optimal model, one selects an optimal set. Multi-winner theory could therefore guide both the number of models to deploy and the composition of such a set.

Second, model performance varies systematically across substantive domains. While Command ranks as the top model in most topic clusters, it falls outside the top three in several political and civic domains, such as debates about abortion and the death penalty. Conversely, models such as Zephyr perform comparatively better in politically sensitive domains and may be preferable if domain-specific coverage is prioritized.

Importantly, the alignment documents reviewed do not specify concrete substantive domains for which performance should be optimized or guaranteed. A more explicitly democratic approach—such as PRISM, where users reveal what matters to them by selecting discussion topics—provides an empirical signal about which domains warrant additional attention and fine-tuning.

Discussion

We show that major AI developers differ systematically in their normative choices about alignment. We formalize these choices within a social choice framework and demonstrate that they induce distinct welfare consequences. Alignment is therefore not merely a technical optimization problem but a normative aggregation problem under structural constraints.

Making these normative commitments explicit, and empirically evaluating their distributive implications, is a core task for alignment research. Welfare economics and social choice theory provide the appropriate conceptual and formal tools for this analysis.

Our findings also underscore the importance of democratic input. The pluralistic structure of observed preferences reveals that some value conflicts are not fully reconcilable within a single-model paradigm, which has implications for multi-model and MoE-based deployment strategies. Moreover, participatory and democratic mechanisms can help determine which domains and topics alignment efforts should prioritize, since such decisions inherently involve distributive and value-laden trade-offs.

This study has several limitations. Company-authored alignment documents may not fully reflect internal practices or operational decision-making, though they function as public commitments that shape research and policy discourse. Our mapping from textual frameworks to formal aggregation rules is necessarily interpretive, and alternative formalizations are plausible. Finally, our empirical analysis relies on a single large-scale preference dataset. Although PRISM is diverse and pluralistic, questions of external validity remain. Extending the analysis to additional datasets is an important direction for future research.

posters.title: Behavioral Archetypes as Transferable Individual Representations: Archetype-Augmented LLM Simulation Beyond the Experimental Design Space
posters.authors: Robin Na, Kehang Zhu, Logan Cross and Michiel Bakker
posters.keywords: large language models behavioral heterogeneity public goods games agent-based simulation out-of-distribution generalization
posters.abstract:
Behavioral experiments are essential for institutional and policy design, but they are expensive to run and inevitably sparse relative to the space of plausible interventions. The practical question is therefore predictive: how will people behave in institutional settings that have not been experimentally tested? This is an out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization problem for social science, where both the inputs (institutional design) and the targets (human strategies) shift.

Public goods games (PGGs) offer a canonical setting for this challenge. Micro-level decisions (contribute, punish/reward, communicate) aggregate to macro-level outcomes (cooperation and welfare), yet behavior is highly heterogeneous. Many players are imperfect conditional cooperators (Fischbacher et al., 2001), and sanctioning can sustain cooperation while also reducing welfare depending on context (Fehr and Gachter, 2000; Chaudhuri, 2011). For mechanism design, matching average outcomes is not enough: simulators must preserve the distribution of strategies that generate those averages.

Recent work proposes large language models (LLMs) as components of generative agent-based models for social science, capable of reproducing qualitative patterns and exploring counterfactuals (Aher et al., 2023; Argyle et al., 2023; Horton et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Vezhnevets et al., 2023). A key limitation is that prompt-only agents are typically conditioned on demographics and game rules but lack an explicit representation of latent, multi-dimensional strategy (e.g., norm enforcement, retaliation, communication style, end-game behavior). As a result, they can underperform on action prediction and drift toward over-homogeneous behavior when rolled out autoregressively.

We address this by extracting \emph{behavioral archetypes}: structured natural-language profiles that summarize how an individual tends to behave along the behavioral dimensions enabled by the institutional setting. From training games, an LLM reads each participant's transcript and produces an \emph{oracle archetype} using a mechanism-aware tag schema. Tags include active mechanisms such as contribution, communication, punishment/reward, respond to end game, respond to punishers, keeping the representation aligned with the environment. The resulting archetypes make heterogeneous strategies explicit (e.g., stable high cooperation, conditional cooperation with norm reinforcement, strategic end-game unraveling, selective punishment, and distinct communication styles).

To apply archetypes in new environments and for unseen individuals, we introduce an \emph{Archetype Retrieval Model} (ARM) that maps observable demographics $D$ and game environment parameters $E$ to an archetype $A$ drawn from the training corpus. ARM learns to predict an embedding of the oracle archetype and retrieves the nearest-neighbor archetype text. Retrieval keeps the prompt augmentation grounded in empirically observed behavior while allowing $(D,E)$ to shift which archetype is selected.

We then condition an LLM-based decision model on $(D,E)$ and the retrieved archetype. We evaluate micro-level predictive accuracy on held-out games (i.e., given the history up to Round $t\!\-\!1$, predict each player's action in Round $t$) and macro-level rollouts that generate full game trajectories. Figure~1 summarizes the four-stage pipeline. The key comparison is between (i) no archetype, (ii) random archetype, (iii) retrieved archetype (ARM), and (iv) oracle archetype (available only when full transcripts are observed).

Across both contribution prediction and punishment prediction, archetype conditioning improves accuracy and provides a clear upper bound via oracle archetypes. Figure~2 shows that retrieved archetypes reduce contribution mean absolute error relative to both the no-archetype baseline and a random-archetype control, and are statistically comparable to oracle archetypes. Figure~3 shows an analogous pattern for punishment prediction, where retrieved archetypes substantially improve F1 compared to baselines and remain close to oracle performance. In macro-level rollouts, archetype augmentation improves predicting not only mean outcomes (e.g., average contribution rate, average payoff) but also preserves heterogeneity in individual trajectories, supporting distributional predictions relevant for policy evaluation.

Beyond predictive gains, the learned mapping $(D,E)\rightarrow A$ provides interpretable structure about how institutional settings and demographics relate to behavioral strategies---information that is hard to recover solely from game-level summaries. In our data, enabling chat is the strongest design predictor of the within-game distribution of strategy types: it shifts groups toward more stable high cooperation (fewer end-game collapses) while reducing reliance on punishment/reward mechanisms. Availability of punishment further stabilizes cooperation and reshapes response patterns; other design parameters are substantially less predictive. On the demographic side, older participants communicate less and punish less while exhibiting more dynamic cooperation strategies; education robustly differentiates communication style (high school participants are more playful/sociable, college participants more norm-reinforcing, and graduate-degree participants more likely to stay silent); and gender shows no reliable association with archetype.

Taken together, behavioral archetypes offer a practical bridge between micro-level heterogeneity and macro-level outcomes for OOD generalization. Our approach complements recent validation work on generative agent-based models in social dilemmas by making heterogeneity explicit and learnable from data (Cross et al., 2025), and by leveraging grounded retrieval to avoid unconstrained persona generation (Vezhnevets et al., 2023). This provides a data-driven, interpretable route to archetype-augmented simulation that can forecast untested institutional designs while remaining anchored to observed human behavior.

posters.title: A Text-Augmented Audit of Police Search Legality
posters.authors: Madison Coots, Hans Gaebler, Josh Grossman, Alex Chohlas-Wood, Julian Nyarko and Sharad Goel
posters.keywords: policing large language models auditing
posters.abstract: A growing body of research has used empirical methods for examining the constitutionality of police stop-and-search practices. However, a significant limitation of past work is that researchers have largely been restricted to using only structured features in administrative police data and have lacked scalable methods for incorporating potentially important contextual information from officer-written narratives that often accompany structured data. Our work develops a scalable and easily replicable method for extracting contextual information using large language models. We use this extracted narrative information to improve contraband risk prediction and enable a more comprehensive assessment of the information plausibly available to officers at the time of a search. Applying this approach to over 2 million stops across major California agencies reveals that many searches occur among individuals with relatively low predicted contraband risk. More broadly, our results demonstrate how language models can enable large-scale empirical audits of police search practices by systematically incorporating narrative records into administrative data analyses.

posters.title: Verify the Unverifiable: A Platform for AI in Unverifiable Decision Scenarios
posters.authors: Zheng Jiang, Wei Wang, Gaowei Zhang and Yi Wang
posters.keywords: Large Language Models Social Decision-Making Unverifiable Scenarios Computational Social Science
posters.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in social decision-making, yet many real-world decisions do not have an objective ground truth for evaluating correctness. Research on these unverifiable settings is still fragmented across domains, creating a gap between rapid deployment and the shared infrastructure needed to assess utility, risk, and accountability. To address this gap, we present \emph{Verify the Unverifiable}, an open platform designed as research infrastructure for AI in unverifiable decision scenarios. The platform organizes and links scenarios, papers, datasets, models, and evaluation methods through a unified metadata schema, and supports structured community submission and review workflows with contributor attribution. It also provides interactive visualization tools for discovery and gap identification, enabling cumulative and interdisciplinary research across previously isolated domains. By establishing this platform, we aim to enable more rigorous, comparable, and socially responsible research on AI in unverifiable decision contexts.

posters.title: The Geometry of Ideology in Large Language Models: Decomposing Political Dimensions with Sparse Autoencoders
posters.authors: Y. Emre Tapan
posters.keywords: large language models political ideology sparse autoencoders mechanistic interpretability multidimensional ideology
posters.abstract: We use sparse autoencoders to examine whether large language models organize political ideology along separable dimensions rather than a single left–right axis. Analyzing Gemma-2-2B and Qwen-3 with pre-trained SAEs from Neuronpedia, we find that economic and social ideological content activates orthogonal feature sets, producing a block-diagonal similarity structure across six political sub-domains. Social features emerge in earlier layers than economic ones, and a cross-model comparison reveals that model provenance shapes the internal geometry of ideology—not just model outputs. SAE features function as domain markers rather than stance identifiers, complicating unidimensional characterizations of LLM political bias.

posters.title: Figures as Interfaces: Toward LLM-Native Artifacts for Scientific Discovery
posters.authors: Yifang Wang, Nan Cao and Dashun Wang
posters.keywords: Large Language Model AI Agent Data Visualization Scientific Discovery Science of Science
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming scientific workflows, not only through their generative capabilities but also through their emerging ability to use tools, reason about data, and coordinate complex analytical tasks. Yet in most human-AI collaborations, the primary outputs–figures–are still treated as static visual summaries: once rendered, they are handled by both humans and multimodal LLMs as images to be re-interpreted from pixels or captions. The emergent capabilities of LLMs open an opportunity to fundamentally rethink this paradigm. In this paper, we introduce the concept of LLM-native figures: data-driven artifacts that are simultaneously human-legible and machine-addressable. Unlike traditional plots, each artifact embeds complete provenance: the data subset, analytical operations and code, and visualization specification used to generate it. As a result, an LLM can “see through” the figure–tracing selections back to their sources, generating code to extend analyses, and orchestrating new visualizations through natural-language instructions or direct manipulation. We implement this concept through a hybrid language–visual interface that integrates LLM agents with a bidirectional mapping between figures and underlying data. Using the science-of-science domain as a testbed, we demonstrate that LLM-native figures can accelerate discovery, improve reproducibility, and make reasoning transparent across agents and users. More broadly, this work establishes a general framework for embedding provenance, interactivity, and explainability into the artifacts of modern research, redefining the figure not as an end product, but as an interface for discovery.

posters.title: AnnotateThis: Analyzing a human-LLM system for annotating social media data with the concept of climate change mitigation pessimism
posters.authors: Zexuan Li, Ariel Hasell, Derek Van Berkel, John Ryan, Grant Schoenebeck and Sabina Tomkins
posters.keywords: large language models prompt refinement social media climate communication human-in-the-loop
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into research workflows. However, LLMs have been shown to struggle with difficult and nuanced concepts such as those found in computational social science (CSS) research. Within the CSS community, there has been a call for new systems to be developed which center humans in LLM-supported scientific workflows. We develop ANNOTATETHIS, a human- centered system for inspecting and improving LLM annotations, a process we refer to as LLM grounding for a target concept. ANNOTATETHIS is developed with both computational and social scientists to reflect existing workflows for data annotation. It includes a range of information features for users to interrogate the quality and reliability of LLM annotations. We evaluate our system in two settings. In the first, we assume a researcher may not have access to ground truth data and that users of ANNOTATETHIS have limited prior knowledge of the concept they would like an LLM to annotate. That is, they may be conducting concept specification and LLM grounding simultaneously. In the second setting, we assume access to ground truth labels and that the concept is specified for a given annotation task, here the task of LLM grounding is more straightforward. We find that in both settings users can improve the quality of LLM annotations with ANNOTATETHIS and that their final annotations far surpass those created without human intervention. For example when we evaluate with ground truth labels we see an absolute improvement of 0.15 in F-Measure and 0.23 in accuracy over a fully automated state-of-the-art method for prompt refinement.

posters.title: Beyond Network Metrics: Graph Neural Networks for Sociological Network Analysis
posters.authors: Hana Shepherd and Brent Hoagland
posters.keywords: graph neural networks hierarchical linear models connectivity school belonging
posters.abstract: Social network analysis operationalizes "structure" with network metrics, assuming that the right summaries capture how connectivity shapes experience. Yet metric–outcome links vary across settings. Using friendship networks from 24,191 students in 56 middle schools (Paluck, Shepherd, and Aronow 2016), we find that centrality predicts belonging unevenly across schools, and reciprocity explains only part of this heterogeneity. The remaining variation may reflect context dependence, but it may also reflect information loss when connectivity is compressed into metrics. Graphs carry node attributes, edge attributes, global context, and connectivity (Sanchez-Lengling et al. 2021), whereas standard multilevel models retain the first three and replace the fourth with metric summaries (Raudenbush and Bryk 2002). Here we show how graph neural networks (GNNs) can serve as a diagnostic in network analysis. GNNs learn from adjacency via neighborhood aggregation (Kipf and Welling 2017; Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec 2017), enabling comparisons between metric-based and connectivity-preserving predictions. We quantify prediction divergence between a multilevel baseline and a regularized graph convolutional model (Li, Han, and Wu 2018) to identify contexts where adjacency carries predictive information about belonging. This study clarifies when cross-school variation tracks differences in the social meaning of network position, when it tracks information loss from metric compression, and when both operate together.

posters.title: Modeling Simultaneous Collective Human Dynamics via Autoregressive Diffusion
posters.authors: Takayuki Mizuno, Shouji Fujimoto, Atushi Ishikawa, Takuma Narizuka and Hiroshi Iyetomi
posters.keywords: Multi-Agent Trajectory Generation Spatiotemporal Dynamics Autoregressive Diffusion Collective Behavior Causal Inference
posters.abstract: Modeling simultaneous multi-agent interactions is a fundamental challenge in social system science. Conventional autoregressive models typically process multiple agents as a strictly ordered sequence, imposing an "artificial sequential bias" that distorts the true causal structure of collective behavior. We propose an Autoregressive Diffusion framework that treats the collective state of agents at each time step as a single "Time Block," utilizing bidirectional denoising to resolve simultaneous dependencies. Using association football as a high-resolution microcosm, we demonstrate that our model preserves the tactical causality inherent in human behavior, which is typically reversed or contaminated in standard sequential architectures. Quantitative validation via the Causal Asymmetry Index (CAI) confirms that our framework successfully neutralizes these architectural artifacts. This approach provides a scalable paradigm for simulating various high-density social environments, such as crowd dynamics and urban mobility, where preserving mutual dependencies is paramount.

posters.title: Which Research Becomes Patents? Within-Researcher Evidence on Knowledge Selection
posters.authors: Fei Wang and Takayuki Mizuno
posters.keywords: Knowledge selection Science of science Patent–science linkages Text embeddings Within-researcher analysis
posters.abstract: This study focuses on researchers with prior patenting experience and examines the within-researcher structure of patenting decisions at the paper level. While prior studies have primarily compared differences between patenting and non-patenting researchers, little attention has been paid to why researchers who have patented before choose not to patent some of their research outputs. Rather than attributing these differences to researcher ability or disciplinary characteristics, this study emphasizes heterogeneity in decision-making. It aims to quantitatively identify research outputs that were potentially patentable but remained unpatented. Using PATSTAT, this study extract patents citing non-patent literature (NPL) to identify inventors and link them with publication data from OpenAlex to establish paper–patent correspondences. Each publication is labeled by whether it was patented. Employing researcher fixed effects, the analysis examines how factors such as industry proximity, corporate co-authorship, and career stage influence patenting choices, thereby revealing decision-making gaps in the research commercialization process.

posters.title: City Structure Shapes Experienced Segregation
posters.authors: Arianna Salazar Miranda, Paolo Santi and Carlo Ratti
posters.keywords: experienced segregation spatial structure exposure to diversity 15-minute city urban mobility
posters.abstract: Everyday mobility allows urban residents to encounter diversity beyond their neighborhoods, potentially reducing segregation. The extent of these interactions, however, depends on two components. First, the city’s social hardware: the spatial distribution of racial and socioeconomic groups across urban space. Second, the social software: how people move through that spatial distribution. Here, we quantify the outsized contribution of the former to urban segregation. We analyze 380 U.S. metropolitan areas to examine how this social hardware---measured by the spatial structure of cities---shapes potential exposure to racial and income diversity through travel. Using a stylized model, we show that when demographically similar neighborhoods are clustered together, travel offers limited exposure gains. Empirically, residents in less clustered cities can access nearly 80% of their citywide diversity within 50 minutes of travel, compared to 60% in more clustered cities---a 20 percentage-point gap. Spatial structure alone explains up to 35% of the variation in exposure across cities. We then examine the trade-offs of promoting local living by estimating how much exposure would be lost if travel were limited to 15 minutes. Most cities experience only modest reductions, but those in the South and Midwest face steeper trade-offs. Our findings show that spatial organization of cities---their social hardware---imposes significant structural limits on their ability to support both proximity and exposure to diversity.

posters.title: The Genealogy of Ideas: Detecting Schools of Thought and Predicting Impact in the Economics Academic Network
posters.authors: Xinke Li
posters.keywords: Academic Genealogy Heterogeneous Graph Transformer Innovation Premium Economic Network Community Detection
posters.abstract: This study investigates whether an economist's career is shaped more by their advisor's social network ("invisible college") or their autonomous research interests ("invisible syllabus"). By combining genealogy and bibliometric data, I construct a massive Heterogeneous Information Network (HIN) yielding a comprehensive dataset of 21,227 economists and 17,829 validated advisor-student pairs. To untangle these dynamics, I employ Louvain community detection, Node2Vec embeddings, and a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT). Results reveal that despite high structural rigidity and US-centric geographic enclosure in the discipline, there is a significant "Innovation Premium." Career success (H-index) is negatively correlated with advisor-student structural similarity. Furthermore, an ablation study demonstrates that a student's intrinsic research choices vastly outperform social ties in predicting academic trajectories. Ultimately, intellectual divergence, not structural conformity, drives career impact, suggesting successful mentorships structurally permit students to cultivate divergent interests. These dynamics illustrate how academic networks actively shape the evolution of the scientific frontier by mediating the interplay between institutional inheritance and intellectual innovation.

posters.title: Changes in Urban Crime Risk Due to COVID-19: Spatial Machine Learning Analysis of Residential Burglary in Tokyo’s 23 Wards
posters.authors: Naoki Ohashi, Masanori Ajito, Shintaro Terabe, Hideki Yaginuma and Kazuya Inagaki
posters.keywords: Residential Burglary COVID-19 Spatial Machine Learning GGPR Geoshapley
posters.abstract: This extended abstract examines how COVID-19 reshaped neighborhood-level determinants of residential burglary in Tokyo’s 23 wards, focusing on iaki—burglaries committed while residents are present. The authors compile a chome-level dataset by integrating open data from the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department and Japanese national ministries for 2014–2024. To isolate pandemic-related shifts, they estimate separate models for three periods: pre-pandemic (2014–2019), pandemic (2020–2021), and post-pandemic (2022–2024). The outcome is the iaki incidence rate (incidents per household), and candidate predictors (35 variables) capture local accessibility and built-environment characteristics such as distance to rail stations, housing attributes, and land use. Modeling uses Geographical Gaussian Process Regression (GGPR) to handle spatial dependence and nonlinearity in a low-frequency crime, achieving high predictive performance (R² = 0.74, 0.83, and 0.78 across the three periods). For interpretability, GeoShapley decomposes—by chome—how each predictor contributes to predicted risk. Variable importance changes markedly over time: before COVID-19, the share of children (population aged ≤14) is the leading contributor; during COVID-19, one- to two-story apartment households dominate with positive effects concentrated in central areas; after COVID-19, three- to five-story apartment households become most influential with broader positive contributions. The findings suggest crime prevention should be adjusted by period and area as demographic and housing structures evolve.

posters.title: Evacuation Dynamics under Liquefaction-Induced Network Disruptions: An Agent-BasedSimulation Study
posters.authors: Ritsuki Goro, Masanori Ajito, Shintaro Terabe, Hideki Yaginuma and Kazuya Inagaki
posters.keywords: Agent-Based Simulation Liquefaction Evacuation Behavior Disaster Evacuation Road Networks
posters.abstract: This study examines how liquefaction-induced disruptions in road networks affect collective evacuation dynamics using an agent-based simulation model. During large earthquakes, liquefaction and building collapse can reduce road functionality by lowering travel speeds and causing link closures, leading to detours and congestion. However, the effects of liquefaction on network-based evacuation processes have not been sufficiently quantified. An evacuation model was developed on a road network environment using the GAMA platform. Liquefaction was modeled probabilistically at the road-link level as speed reductions and road closures, while building collapse was represented as additional blockages. The model includes heterogeneous agents with different behavioral characteristics, including shortest-path navigation, risk-averse route selection, reduced mobility, and social following behavior. Multiple scenarios were simulated to evaluate the impact of infrastructure damage on evacuation dynamics. Results indicate that evacuation completion time increases under network disruptions, particularly when liquefaction and building collapse occur simultaneously. Mean detour distance increases with liquefaction probability, and inter-trial variability peaks at intermediate damage levels, indicating nonlinear responses of collective evacuation behavior to network degradation. These findings highlight the importance of modeling infrastructure damage as network-level performance decline in computational social science studies of disaster evacuation.

posters.title: Optimization of Distributed Energy Resources and Market Procurement Strategies under Renewable Integration Society
posters.authors: Taiki Onitsuka, Kiyofumi Sato and Yoshikuni Yoshida
posters.keywords: Distributed Energy Resources Electricity Market Optimization SARIMA Forecasting Imbalance Risk Management Renewable Integration
posters.abstract: In recent years, distributed energy resources including solar photovoltaic systems, storage batteries, and on-site power generators have become increasingly important in Japan. This development has been driven by the need to enhance power system resilience following natural disasters and by the deregulation of the electricity retail market. At the same time, the transition from the Feed-in Tariff scheme to the Feed-in Premium scheme is accelerating renewable energy integration [1][2]. Under these structural changes, electricity retailers face substantial operational risks due to the intrinsic variability of photovoltaic generation and the extreme volatility of spot prices in the Japan Electric Power Exchange market [3].
