Forecasting errors directly translate into imbalance settlements under the Japanese market design, significantly increasing procurement costs [4]. This study develops an integrated optimization framework that models the entire operational process of an electricity retailer, from day-ahead electricity procurement to real-time operational control. The objective is to identify economically optimal operational strategies under volatile market environments and increasing renewable penetration. By integrating photovoltaic systems, storage batteries, and on-site generators into a unified decision-making framework, the study evaluates their role as algorithmic hedging instruments against price and volume uncertainty. As the foundation of the optimization framework, a time-series forecasting model based on the Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average methodology is constructed. Forecasting of photovoltaic generation has been extensively studied in the literature [5], and electricity price forecasting remains a central research topic in competitive power markets [6][7]. The model forecasts next-day photovoltaic generation, electricity demand, and Japan Electric Power Exchange spot prices. Accurate forecasting is critical because even small deviations between contracted and actual supply volumes result in financial penalties. To enhance predictive performance, the Akaike Information Criterion is employed to dynamically determine the optimal parameter set for each forecasting period. The results confirm that the model effectively captures seasonal structures as well as sudden fluctuations in both photovoltaic output and market prices. Figure 1 presents a representative example of the forecasting performance for market prices, comparing observed and predicted values. These forecasts serve as high-resolution inputs for subsequent optimization and materially reduce exposure to imbalance risk. Based on the forecasted values, a two-stage optimization model is formulated. The first stage corresponds to day-ahead planning, executed at 10:00 a.m. on the day preceding delivery, which coincides with the bidding deadline for the spot market. The model optimizes operations over the subsequent 24 hours in 30-minute intervals using linear programming. Under the strict constraint that forecasted demand must be satisfied, procurement decisions are determined across multiple sources, including the spot market, continuous backup contracts, and on-site generation. To hedge against forecasting uncertainty, buffer margins are incorporated into storage battery capacity constraints, thereby embedding risk tolerance into the optimization structure. The second stage addresses real-time operations on the day of delivery. Demand and photovoltaic generation are reforecast for the next three hours at 30-minute intervals. The model optimizes battery charging and discharging while accounting for depth-of-discharge constraints and conversion losses, and simultaneously determines the dispatch level of the on-site generator. In the event of surplus electricity, excess energy is stored in the battery. In the case of shortages, a cost-based priority hierarchy selects the most economical adjustment measure among battery discharge, on-site generation, and purchasing imbalance power. The coordinated operation of storage and controllable generation has been discussed in previous studies [8][9], but its strategic viability under different volatility regimes remains insufficiently clarified. Empirical validation is conducted using actual operational data from an electricity retailer in the Kyushu region covering the period from January 2019 to December 2022. To examine structural robustness, simulations are performed under three distinct market environments characterized by low and stable prices, high and volatile prices, and moderately stable prices. The analysis focuses on an integrated configuration consisting of a 7,500kWh storage battery and a 600kW city gas-fired on-site generator. The simulation results reveal that, in the absence of distributed energy resources, forecasting errors directly translate into physical imbalances and substantial financial penalties. This effect is particularly pronounced during periods of high price volatility, when imbalance payments escalate rapidly. The introduction of an on-site generator provides a controllable supply resource that significantly mitigates shortage exposure and produces stronger cost reduction effects than battery-only configurations. To further clarify the structural conditions of strategic selection, Figure 2 visualizes the results in a two-dimensional volatility space defined by average market price and the standard deviation of market price. The analysis reveals a clear region-partitioning structure. In the low-price and low-volatility region, market procurement alone is economically optimal and Distributed Energy Resource investment cannot be justified. When average prices exceed a threshold while volatility remains moderate, on-site generation alone becomes the optimal strategy. As both price levels and volatility intensify, a new regime emerges in which the coordinated operation of storage batteries and on-site generation becomes the dominant cost-minimizing strategy. The boundary lines separating these regions function as viability thresholds governing technology adoption. These findings demonstrate that the economic value of distributed energy resources is not static but emerges endogenously from market volatility structures. The proposed framework contributes to computational social science by revealing how algorithmic decision systems interact with stochastic market environments and by identifying structural phase boundaries that condition strategic technology deployment in liberalized electricity markets.

posters.title: Use public disclosure to govern conflict of interests of research-active editors
posters.authors: Fengyuan Liu, Bedoor Alshebli and Talal Rahwan
posters.keywords: peer review editor conflict of interest policy online survey
posters.abstract: Public trust in science may be undermined by conflicts of interest (COIs), including those arising from relationships between editors and authors. Current policies typically rely on recusal, yet blanket restrictions can limit the availability of qualified editors and have shown limited effectiveness. We propose public disclosure of editor-related COIs, together with a clear description of the steps taken to ensure impartiality, as an alternative governance mechanism. To evaluate this approach, we conducted a preregistered survey experiment with 910 participants who rated their trust in hypothetical scientific findings and their authors. When a COI was mentioned but not publicly disclosed, trust in the associated finding declined significantly, while trust in the author remained unchanged. When the COI was openly disclosed and accompanied by information about mitigation measures, trust in the finding returned to baseline levels and trust in the author increased. These effects were confined to the affected article. The results indicate that transparent disclosure can govern editor COIs without reducing trust in science.

posters.title: Reconciling Bilateral Migration Flows and Net Migration via Information Projection
posters.authors: Boris Barron, Maciej Danko and Emilio Zagheni
posters.keywords: International Migration Information Projection Bilateral Flows Net Migration Demographic Estimation
posters.abstract: International migration estimates depend on two complementary but formally inconsistent sources: bilateral flow data recording directional counts between country pairs, and national records providing country-level net migration values. Since net migration is mathematically determined by bilateral flows, the inconsistency is not merely inconvenient—it means two mutually constraining sources of information are used in isolation. This paper develops a principled framework for reconciling them using information projection (I-projection), which finds the minimum Kullback–Leibler divergence adjustment to a prior flow distribution subject to net migration constraints. The approach carries a formal improvement guarantee: the reconciled estimates are strictly closer, in a well-defined statistical sense, to any values consistent with the net migration constraints than the original estimates are — regardless of which net-consistent bilateral flow values are realized. The framework is fully general with respect to the form of the prior, accommodates uncertainty in net migration values, and reduces to existing estimators as special cases. It is implemented as a post-processing pipeline for the Human Migration Database (HMigD), handling on the order of a thousand European bilateral corridors jointly.

posters.title: Using LLMs to classify digital traces: A case study on measuring parental digital behavior with web tracking data
posters.authors: Joshua Claassen and Melanie Revilla
posters.keywords: Large Language Models Digital Trace Data Web Tracking Automated Classification Digital Behavior
posters.abstract: As survey self-reports on digital behavior are often inaccurate, social and behavioral researchers increasingly utilize digital traces. Existing methodological research has mostly focused on collecting these traces, leaving open the question of how to classify traces to draw robust conclusions about digital behavior. Since the high volume of traces renders the application of manual, human-based coding approaches inefficient, a promising alternative is represented by the utilization of Large Language Models (LLMs). The present study utilizes traces obtained through web tracking to measure parental digital behavior, focusing on the following research question: What is the agreement between LLM-based classifications and manual, human-based coding of traces in the form of website visits, search terms, and app usage, respectively? We obtained up to 24 weeks of web tracking data and self-reports on (expectant) parenthood (N = 800) through the Netquest online panel in Spain in 2023 and 2024. An external ethics advisor approved the study and we followed the “data minimization” principle by specifying lists of websites, URL keywords, search terms, and apps related to (expectant) parenthood a priori. Based on these lists, Netquest extracted about 184,000 traces, including 56,822 unique websites, 11,309 unique search terms, and 115 unique apps. Drawing on our classification scheme consisting of seven substantial categories (e.g., PDB related to health) and an eighth category for unrelated traces, we evaluated the agreement between two LLMs (Llama 3.2 3B and Mistral 7B) and manual, human-based coding conducted by a Spanish native speaker. To this end, we employed few-shot prompting as well as two different temperatures (0.8 and 0.2), and we calculated macro precision, recall, and F1 scores to assess agreement. Our preliminary findings show marked differences between the three types of traces, LLMs, and temperatures. Specifically, across both LLMs and temperatures, macro F1 scores are highest for apps, second-highest for search terms, and lowest for websites. Both LLMs perform better if employed with a temperature of 0.2 and achieve similar F1 scores regarding websites and search terms. However, Mistral shows a higher macro F1 score than Llama 3.2 when applied to apps. Our study goes beyond previous studies that often focused on only one type of trace. By examining three types of traces simultaneously, our study draws a more holistic picture of LLM-based classifications in the context of digital trace data. Importantly, by illuminating the impact different types of traces and LLMs have on research outcomes, our study also contributes to discussions on reproducibility in computational social science.

posters.title: Peer-Conditioning in Survey Response Simulation
posters.authors: Fabrizzio Pezzolla, Andrés Abeliuk, Mitchell Bosley and Sergio Toro
posters.keywords: survey simulation large language models retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) cultural alignment Peer-conditioning
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human survey responses, offering a scalable complement to traditional polling. We introduce peer-conditioning, a framework that distills attitudinal knowledge from qualitative interviews and injects it into survey simulation through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of grounding predictions in an individual’s own transcript, peer-conditioning retrieves testimony from demographically similar others to model respondents who were never interviewed. We evaluate this approach on four public opinion items from the 2024–2025 CEP survey in Chile’s La Araucanía region, using transcript data from the VOCES study. Across three open-weight instruction-tuned models and multiple prompting variants, results show that RAG improves individual-level prediction only when models effectively integrate retrieved evidence with persona priors. While some configurations increase the correlation coefficient, gains are model- and question-dependent, and high distributional similarity does not imply strong individual alignment. These findings highlight both the promise and limits of distilling qualitative peer information into quantitative survey simulation.

posters.title: Money does not buy time: Time-richness predicts ability to access and allocate time across urban life
posters.authors: Joshua Rosen, Erik Weis, Hamish Gibbs, Sarah Sanchez, Takahiro Yabe, Daniel O'Brien, Brennan Klein and Esteban Moro
posters.keywords: temporal inequality urban inequality human mobility experienced segregation urban science
posters.abstract:
Urban residents inhabit the same physical city yet experience vastly different opportunity structures. Traditional social science theory attributes these disparities to income-based access to resources and amenities [1]. However, we uncover an important empirical puzzle: individuals with comparable incomes utilize the same amenities at systematically different times of day. These temporal divergences are poorly explained by socioeconomic status alone. We argue that this reflects a deeper, unmeasured dimension of inequality—time-richness—capturing individuals' capacity to flexibly structure and allocate their time across the day.

While social scientists have long recognized that the unequal distribution of time generates downstream forms of inequality [2], prevailing approaches operationalize time through coarse aggregates such as discretionary hours after work. Such measures cannot explain why some individuals can reconfigure their daily rhythms (e.g., visiting parks in the early afternoon) while others cannot. Traditional measures of discretionary time also fail to capture this variation. To address this gap, we introduce a mobility-derived measure of time-richness based on three independent components extracted from large-scale smartphone geolocation data: exploration, capturing the ratio of unique visitations to total visits; predictability, capturing how regular and routine an individual's daily movement patterns are; and opportunity, capturing the degree to which an individual's temporal patterns differ from their peers.

Using smartphone geolocation data across 11 U.S. metropolitan areas, we show that these dimensions of time-richness are statistically independent to income. Further, incorporating time-richness into behavioral models substantially improves our ability to predict when and where individuals engage in discretionary activities. Most critically, we demonstrate that time-richness explains variation in experienced segregation far better than income or traditional measures of discretionary time. Our findings reveal that time constitutes an independent axis of inequality, shaping how individuals access the social and spatial dimensions of the city.

References

[1] Chetty, R., Hendren, N., Kline, P., & Saez, E. (2014). Where is the land of Opportunity? The Geography of Intergenerational Mobility in the United States. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 129(4), 1553–1623. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qju022

[2] Vickery, C. (1977). The Time-Poor: A New Look at Poverty. The Journal of Human Resources, 12(1), 27–48. https://doi.org/10.2307/145597

posters.title: Beyond Proximity: Rethinking Urban Accessibility Through Human Mobility Patterns in United States
posters.authors: Saumitra Kulkarni and Esteban Moro
posters.keywords: Human Mobility 15-Minute City Accessibility Urban Science
posters.abstract: Urban accessibility is typically measured by proximity to home, but this overlooks how people navigate cities and use their time. Using mobility data from 1.86 million individuals across 11 U.S. metro areas, we show that access to daily necessities is structured around a small set of key locations—containers—such as home, work, and other routine destinations. We introduce the offer-meets-demand ratio to measure alignment between available POIs to visit and actual visited POIs. Most individuals rely on multiple containers, with the second container often linked to job locations. Our findings highlight a dual nature of accessibility and call for urban policies grounded in human behavior.

posters.title: Ten simple rules for linguistically-responsible NLP: A linguistics primer to enrich NLP methods
posters.authors: Julia Witte Zimmerman, Ashley M. A. Fehr, Katie Ekstrom, Brennan Dell and Juniper L. Lovato
posters.keywords: NLP linguistics primer CSS text
posters.abstract: Many people from diverse fields want to use text as data. While tutorials, textbooks, and documentation for natural language processing (NLP) are abundant, they often either require a significant amount of time and effort to work through, or presuppose relevant background knowledge in linguistics and computer science. We present a brief primer and ten simple rules as conceptual and practical guidelines for extracting signal from text, aimed at providing an overview of prominent theories underlying common NLP methods for researchers with limited background in computational linguistics. Diverse topics include reading and writing in the brain, morphology and syntax, and sociolinguistics. We also cover recent approaches from network analysis to allotaxonometry and large language models (LLMs). Finally, our simple rules synthesize abstract conceptual patterns in linguistic theory and describe common pitfalls in textual analysis. This work supports a holistic approach to extracting signal -- e.g. semantic, pragmatic; structural, statistical -- from text, empowering readers of any background to engage critically with NLP applications in the wild and to deploy NLP methods responsibly.

posters.title: Enhancing LLM-Based Data Annotation with Error Decomposition
posters.authors: Zhen Xu, Vedant Khatri, Yijun Dai, Xiner Liu, Siyan Li, Xuanming Zhang and Renzhe Yu
posters.keywords: Data Annotation Qualitative Coding Large Language Models Human-AI Collaboration Error Decomposition
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable alternative to human coding for data annotation tasks, enabling the scale-up of research across data-intensive domains such as learning analytics. While LLMs are already achieving near-human accuracy on objective annotation tasks, their performance on subjective annotation tasks, such as those involving psychological constructs, is less consistent and more prone to errors. Standard evaluation practices typically collapse all annotation errors into a single alignment metric, but this simplified approach may obscure different kinds of errors that affect final analytical conclusions in different ways. Here, we propose a diagnostic evaluation paradigm that incorporates a human-in-the-loop step to separate task-inherent ambiguity from model-driven inaccuracies and assess annotation quality in terms of their potential downstream impacts. We refine this paradigm on ordinal annotation tasks, which are common in subjective annotation. The refined paradigm includes: (1) a diagnostic taxonomy that categorizes LLM annotation errors along two dimensions: source (model-specific vs. task-inherent) and type (boundary ambiguity vs. conceptual misidentification); (2) a lightweight human annotation test to estimate task-inherent ambiguity from LLM annotations; and (3) a computational method to decompose observed LLM annotation errors following our taxonomy. We validate this paradigm on four educational annotation tasks, demonstrating both its conceptual validity and practical utility. Theoretically, our work provides empirical evidence for why excessively high alignment is unrealistic in specific annotation tasks and why single alignment metrics inadequately reflect the quality of LLM annotations. In practice, our paradigm can be a low-cost diagnostic tool that assesses the suitability of a given task for LLM annotation and provides actionable insights for further technical optimization.

posters.title: Exploring Cognitive Boundaries in Urban Commercial Streets: Insights from Wearable Eye-Tracking in Seoul
posters.authors: Kwangyeong Seo and Jina Park
posters.keywords: Cognitive boundaries Event segmentation theory Spatial behavior Wearable sensing Computational urban science
posters.abstract: Understanding how pedestrians perceive transitions in urban commercial streets is essential for characterizing human spatial behavior, yet conventional definitions rely on static administrative boundaries. This study introduces a computational social science approach to operationalize "cognitive boundaries" (CBs)—micro-moments when individuals unconsciously segment urban space due to visual and semantic shifts. Drawing on Event Segmentation Theory (EST), we conducted an in-the-wild experiment utilizing wearable eye-tracking and open-vocabulary computer vision. By analyzing a high-resolution, synchronized dataset of 14,721 frames from pedestrian trajectories, we demonstrate that semantic shifts and storefront salience significantly predict event-like perceptual boundaries, characterized by distinct gaze and motion patterns. This work provides a scalable, data-driven framework to measure subjective urban experience, bridging cognitive psychology, spatial analysis, and pervasive computing to reveal how commercial districts are behaviorally "lived" rather than merely mapped.

posters.title: Does Political Rhetoric Pay Off? Estimating the Causal Returns to Policy-Aligned Academic Publication in Chinese Social Sciences
posters.authors: Songxuan Luo
posters.keywords: text as treatment causal representation learning double machine learning academic incentives sociology of knowledge
posters.abstract: In China, state political priorities are signaled through institutionalized events such as Five-Year Plans and National Party Congresses. Prior research documents increasing alignment between Chinese social science publications and state policy language, yet the evidence remains descriptive. This study shifts focus to the micro-level incentive structure sustaining such alignment and asks whether adopting state political rhetoric causally increases the probability of obtaining research grants, sustaining publication output, or achieving upward institutional mobility. Using 1.36 million CSSCI-indexed articles published between 2010 and 2024, this study applies the GenAI-Powered Inference (GPI) framework to address the central identification challenge: writing quality, analytical rigor, and topical novelty are embedded in unstructured text and not directly observable as covariates. The GPI framework leverages LLM internal representations to disentangle the treatment feature (rhetorical framing) from confounding features (substantive content). Specifically, hidden states from the final transformer layer of a Chinese-native LLM (DeepSeek-V3) serve as a high-dimensional text representation. A TarNet architecture then learns a low-dimensional deconfounder that captures confounding variation while remaining separable from the treatment indicator, and simultaneously estimates conditional outcome functions under treatment and control. Double machine learning (DML) with K-fold cross-fitting yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the average treatment effect. Preliminary results indicate that political rhetoric adoption increases three-year grant acquisition probability by 4.2 percentage points and sustained publication output by 2.8 percentage points. Heterogeneity analyses reveal a U-shaped institutional gradient, with the largest effects among Project 985 and non-211 scholars. These findings contribute to the sociology of knowledge by providing causal evidence that political rhetoric functions as a rational career strategy embedded in institutional incentive structures, rather than reflecting ideological conformity alone.

posters.title: Competing risks reveal the hidden fragility of states
posters.authors: Vaishnavi Jayakumar, Matthew Wilson and Karoline Wiesner
posters.keywords: Competing risks Survival Democratization Fragility Sovereignty loss
posters.abstract: Understanding and quantifying the stability and longevity of governments is a central concern in computational political science; however, non-democratic states often evade systematic analysis, because they are diverse in nature and particularly susceptible to destabilizing events such as conflict. This study provides new perspectives on the stability and transitions of non-democratic states by introducing a competing risks survival framework, which models democratization and sovereignty loss as mutually exclusive outcomes. Building on prior work that analyzed democratic survival using parametric mixture models, we update the analysis with continuous measures of democracy from the V-Dem Electoral Democracy Index (EDI) and extend it to non-democratic spells between 1900 and 2021. Traditional survival models overestimate democratization probabilities, whereas competing risks models provide a more accurate assessment of spell trajectories. Our results show that roughly half of non-democratic spells democratize, while a significant fraction end through loss of international autonomy. Covariates such as GDP per capita, population size, political crises, colonial history, and regime power structures significantly influence the likelihood and timing of transitions. By thus capturing the complex interplay of competing regime-terminating mechanisms, this work offers novel insights into the hidden fragility of non-democratic states, demonstrating that democratization is neither inevitable nor uniform, and providing a more precise, conceptually grounded understanding of state survival at large.

posters.title: Masking Unfairness: Hiding Causality within Zero ATE
posters.authors: Zou Yang, Sophia Xiao and Bijan Mazaheri
posters.keywords: Causal fairness Algorithmic Bias Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Policy Learning Conditional Independence
posters.abstract:
While modern methods for AI and machine learning are fantastic optimizers, they exhibit concerning potential for bias and unfair inference\citep{ferrara_fairness_2024,angwin_machine_2022}. Numerous works have attempted to formalize fairness over the past decade \citep{dwork2012fairness}. One emerging thread of interest is the use of causal principles to distinguish systematically biased decisions from ``confounded'' imbalances driven by population and demographic differences. For example, hiring primarily male luggage handlers may still be considered ``fair'' so long as the decisions are based on the physical strength of job applicants and not a direct bias against women. However, explicitly denying employment to strong women is evidence of direct unfair bias \citet{nabi_fair_2018}.

A causal notion of fairness is advantageous because it enables the application of causal inference methods to distinguish systematic bias from confounded disparities \citep{imbens_causal_2015, pearl2009causality}. Although individual treatment effects are more informative, most practical methods focus on average treatment effects (ATEs), which can be estimated under weaker assumptions. Building fairness on causal inference inherits its limitations. In particular, the emphasis on average treatment effects allows unequal treatment across subgroups through "subset targeting" \citep{dwork2012fairness, kim_fair_2023}. Because regulators often evaluate decision outcomes rather than internal mechanisms, statistical detectability becomes critical.

Current fairness detection methods, both causal and non-causal, primarily evaluate population level parity. We study how such criteria can be satisfied while unfair treatment persists by optimizing an auxiliary objective. Our results highlight the importance of heterogeneous treatment effects, mixtures of treatment effects, and conditional independence testing in fairness analysis \citep{wager_estimation_2018, mazaheri_synthetic_2025, zhang_kernel-based_2011, de2014bayesian, canonne_testing_2018, runge_conditional_2018}. Because conditional independence testing is information-theoretically difficult and often data-intensive, causally masked policies may evade statistical detection when regulation relies solely on observed decisions \citep{canonne_testing_2018, shah_hardness_2020, he_hardness_2025}. We therefore advocate fairness regulation based on model outputs and enforced through in-process mechanisms.

We introduce the causal masking problem: optimizing an auxiliary reward while enforcing a zero ATE between a protected attribute and a decision. For example, a parole policy may minimize recidivism while maintaining zero racial ATE. We show that globally regulated optimization can produce substantial violations of stratified fairness while appearing fair under average-based metrics. Under simplifying assumptions, causal masking can be formulated as a linear program, providing a theoretical framework for studying disparities between “true” and “masked” fairness. The resulting solutions reveal that masking arises from statistical dependence between protected attributes, observable information, and optimized outcomes. Importantly, causal masking may arise unintentionally as a generic consequence of optimization. Mitigating masking requires fairness criteria based on conditional independence; however, such tests are data-intensive and may fail to detect unfairness for extended periods. This motivates proactive, model-level regulation, rather than reactive approaches based on decision outcomes.

Motivated by this setting, consider a participation decision $D \in \{0,1\}$ (e.g., granting parole, admission). The objective is to maximize expected reward when participation occurs, equivalently maximizing $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid d_1]\Pr(d_1)$ subject to a fixed participation rate, where $d_1$ indicates $D=1$. Decisions are based on observed features divided into protected attributes $P$ and unprotected covariates $X$. For simplicity, let $P\in\{0,1\}$ and $X\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$; continuous covariates can be coarsened into strata without changing qualitative behavior, with larger k providing finer resolution. A decision policy $\alpha(x,p)\in[0,1]$ specifies participation rates for each context, inducing $D\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\alpha(x,p))$. Let $\gamma(x,p)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x,p]$ denote the expected reward and $\pi_{x,p}=\Pr(X=x,P=p)$. The expected reward of a policy is \vspace{-2mm} \[ W(D)=\sum_{x,p}\gamma(x,p)\alpha(x,p)\pi_{x,p}, \vspace{-2mm} \] subject to the participation constraint $\sum_{x,p}\alpha(x,p)\pi_{x,p}=\rho,\quad 0\le\alpha(x,p)\le1.$

This framework distinguishes three policy regimes. The \textbf{Exploit policy} allocates participation to contexts with the highest expected reward until the participation budget is exhausted. A \textbf{Fair policy} enforces decision parity within each stratum, $\alpha(x,1)=\alpha(x,0)\quad \forall x$, ensuring $P \perp D \mid X$ so that decisions depend only on stratum-level rewards $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x]$. In contrast, a \textbf{Masking policy} constrains only the population-level ATE, $\sum_x(\pi_{x,0}+\pi_{x,1})(\alpha(x,1)-\alpha(x,0))=0$, achieving global fairness while permitting disparities within strata. Because stratified fairness implies the masking constraint, masking can achieve higher reward while masking subgroup inequities when $P$ and $X$ are statistically dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:causal diagrams}).

We illustrate this phenomenon using a parole policy derived from the COMPAS dataset, optimizing for minimal two-year recidivism while enforcing zero ATE fairness with respect to minority status. The objective remains $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid d_1]\Pr(d_1)$ with a minimum release-rate constraint $\sum_{x,p}\pi_{x,p}\alpha(x,p)\ge\rho (\rho=0.1)$. Covariates include age category, prior criminal history, charge degree, and sex, discretized into strata to vary resolution $k$. Then, we evaluate each policy using two nested hypotheses. Global fairness tests whether the average treatment effect of P on D is zero across the population, $H_{\text{ATE}}:\sum_x\Pr(X=x)(\alpha_{x,1}-\alpha_{x,0})=0$, ensuring the policy appears fair on average. Stratified fairness requires parity within each stratum, $H_{\text{CATE}}:\alpha_{x,1}-\alpha_{x,0}=0\ \forall x$, which implies global fairness. Accepting global fairness while rejecting stratified fairness is the signature of a successfully masked policy.

We apply these tests to policies evaluated on progressively larger datasets, recording the first sample size at which either hypothesis is rejected. Increasing the number of strata k raises the resolution of both masking and detection. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:rightmost_plot}, exploit policies are rejected quickly, while masked policies persist substantially longer. Even under multiple testing strategies, masking survives over five times longer than exploit policies, with the detectability gap widening as k increases. These results show that ATE-based regulation can drive optimizers toward policies that appear fair while masking subgroup inequities. Although such unfairness is nearly inevitable, demonstrating it is information-theoretically difficult, allowing masked policies to persist for years. Richer covariate information both increases opportunities for masking and widens the detectability gap. Because these limitations stem from the difficulty of detecting conditional independence, they extend beyond causal fairness to any conditional parity framework. This has implications for domains such as college admissions, criminal justice, affirmative action, and wage disparity analysis, where adjusted averages are commonly used. We therefore argue that fairness regulation should operate at the model level, where decision mechanisms are accessible, rather than relying solely on observed outcomes.

posters.title: Public Recognition and Scientists’ Choice of Research Topics
posters.authors: Yuan Tian, Brayden King and Yang Yang
posters.keywords: Research problem choice Public recognition Scientific reward systems Media and social media attention Scientific knowledge production
posters.abstract: We examine whether public recognition—attention from mainstream media and social media—causally shapes scientists' subsequent topic choices. Using 14.8 million journal articles (2012–2019) linked across OpenAlex, MAG, Altmetric, and Dimensions, we exploit exogenous crowd-out in coverage from coincident news events and publication surges as an instrument for attention. We find that greater public recognition increases later commitment to the focal paper's topics, with stronger effects for scientists with lower peer recognition, suggesting public audiences constitute a consequential additional currency of scientific reward.

posters.title: Interdisciplinary Scientists Are More Innovative Than Interdisciplinary Teams
posters.authors: Yiling Lin, Zak Risha, Erin Leahey and Lingfei Wu
posters.keywords: Specialization Team Research Diversity Novelty Innovation
posters.abstract: Using a large-scale dataset of 46 million articles authored by 3 million scientists across 292 fields (1950–2019), we examine how generalists contribute to science, how they collaborate, and how their presence is changing. First, we find that generalists are vanishing: the share of scientists whose work spans multiple fields declined from 52% in 1950 to 29% in 2019. This trend reflects structural forces—career incentives, the growing burden of knowledge, and the rise of large-scale collaborations—that increasingly reward specialization. Second, generalists prefer smaller teams and are less likely to join large, specialized research groups. Third, generalists show strong assortative teaming: when they collaborate, they tend to find one another, forming a distinctive and relatively rare type of all-generalist team. Fourth, and most importantly, all-generalist teams are significantly more innovative. Compared to teams covering the same number of research fields, all-generalist teams are 21% more likely to produce highly disruptive work and 67% more likely to generate highly novel research. These innovation advantages remain robust after adjusting for team size, publication year, and team career age. Together, our findings suggest that not all forms of research diversity are equivalent: diversity within individuals yields higher innovative returns than diversity assembled across team members. This pattern highlights a central paradox of modern science—organizational structures that dominate contemporary research may be crowding out the researchers most capable of advancing knowledge—raising important implications for how scientific training, funding, and collaboration are organized.

posters.title: Using Large Language Models to Understand Open-Ended Survey Response Quality
posters.authors: Masha Krupenkin, Andrew Gordon and David Rothschild
posters.keywords: Large Language Models Machine Learning Text as Data Surveys Data Quality
posters.abstract:
Open-ended survey responses are increasingly used as measures of public opinion in computational social science. Advances in topic modeling, embeddings, and large language models (LLMs) have made it easy to summarize and analyze open-ended text at scale. Yet open-ended responses vary widely in quality, ranging from one-word answers to detailed, reflective paragraphs. While prior research has examined determinants of response length and engagement, much less attention has been paid to how variation in response quality affects downstream automated analyses. If automated text models are sensitive to differences in coherence, elaboration, and lexical diversity, then heterogeneity in response quality may translate into substantively different conclusions about public opinion.

We introduce an LLM-based procedure for measuring the quality of open-ended survey responses and demonstrate that response quality meaningfully shapes the structure of topics inferred from survey text. Using an original survey experiment and three topic modeling approaches, we show that (1) topics derived from lower- and higher-quality responses differ substantially, and (2) experimentally induced improvements in response quality produce systematic, though smaller, shifts in inferred topic structure. These findings suggest that response quality is an underappreciated source of measurement error in text-as-data research.

We analyze responses from an original survey (N = 1,517) asking respondents whether social media is a good or bad thing for society. Respondents were recruited across two survey vendors and randomly assigned to answer either in text or by voice. This design generates both naturally occurring and experimentally induced variation in response quality.

To measure quality, we use an LLM-based pairwise comparison framework. The model is shown two responses and asked to select the higher-quality answer based on clarity, coherence, and elaboration. Aggregating these comparisons using a Bradley–Terry model yields a continuous quality score for each response. Higher-scoring responses tend to be longer, more lexically diverse, and more substantively elaborated, often linking social media to broader issues such as polarization or mental health. Lower-scoring responses are shorter, more repetitive, and less detailed.

Importantly, demographic characteristics explain only a small fraction of the variation in quality scores, indicating that the measure is not simply capturing observable respondent traits. While response length is correlated with quality, it does not fully account for it, suggesting that the LLM-based measure captures richer features of answer quality than verbosity alone.

To assess how response quality shapes substantive conclusions, we divide responses into quality quintiles and estimate topic models separately within each group. We apply three approaches: an LLM-based topic model, BERTopic, and vanilla LDA. For each model, we estimate multiple runs and align topics across runs using cosine similarity and one-to-one matching, allowing us to compare topic structures both within and across quality groups.

Topics are highly stable when models are rerun on the same quality group, especially for BERTopic. However, when we compare topics derived from very low- and very high-quality responses, similarity drops sharply across all three modeling approaches. Depending on the model, only about 30–45 percent of topics derived from very high-quality responses have a closely matching counterpart in very low-quality data. In contrast, rerunning the same model on the same data typically reproduces most topics. In other words, the structure of inferred topics changes meaningfully as response quality changes. These differences are not simply artifacts of stochastic variation in topic modeling; they exceed the level of noise observed across repeated runs on identical data.

Differences across quality quintiles could reflect underlying differences between respondents. To isolate causal effects, we leverage random assignment to response modality. Respondents assigned to answer by voice provide higher-quality responses on average than those assigned to text.

Topic models estimated separately on voice and text responses reveal systematic differences. Cross-modality topic similarity is significantly lower than within-modality stability across all three models. Although the magnitude of these differences is smaller than those observed across extreme quality quintiles, the direction is consistent: exogenous increases in response quality shift the inferred topic structure. Substantively, this implies that two researchers applying identical analytic pipelines to the same survey question could arrive at different topic-based conclusions solely because one collected responses by voice and the other by text.

Our findings demonstrate that open-ended response quality interacts with automated text analysis in consequential ways. Topic models do not merely summarize content; they are sensitive to variation in document quality. As a result, routine research decisions (such as survey vendor choice or response modality) can produce substantively different representations of public opinion when open-ended responses are analyzed using automated methods. As open-ended survey data become more common and LLM-based tools more widely adopted, understanding how upstream response behavior shapes downstream model outputs is essential. Our study provides both a scalable approach to measuring response quality and experimental evidence that even modest quality shifts can alter automated interpretations of public opinion.

posters.title: Systematic Churn in Application-Based Mobile Tracking
posters.authors: Zoltán Kmetty, Julia Koltai and Bence Ságvári
posters.keywords: mobile tracking systematic churn digital trace data selection bias socio-technical factors
posters.abstract: This study analyzes systematic churn in application-based mobile tracking using a multi-stage participation funnel of 2,905 Hungarian Android users. With an overall attrition rate of 83%, the results reveal a non-random "socio-technical filter" that skews the representativeness of digital trace data during the 14-day passive telemetry phase. Logistic regression models indicate that while initial demographics have low explanatory power, the data transmission stage is significantly biased against female participants, individuals with lower education, and users of specific brands like Google, Huawei, or Xiaomi compared to Samsung. Furthermore, psychometric variables—including trust in science, privacy concerns, and extroversion—significantly impact long-term retention. These findings highlight that selection bias is driven by the interaction between user characteristics and the mobile technical environment, necessitating brand-aware methodological corrections to ensure data generalizability.

posters.title: Quantifying Ageing Effect in Scientific and Innovative Careers
posters.authors: Yangfanyu Yang, Alex J. Yang and Yian Yin
posters.keywords: Career ageing Preferential attachment Network densification Innovation dynamics Recognition inequality
posters.abstract: Recent advances in science and innovation have accumulated growing empirical evidence that old innovators continue to exert a lasting impact on science and technology. Citations, funding and awards are increasingly directed towards senior innovators, resulting in newcomers experiencing greater delays before achieving recognition. Despite the broad implications of this ageing phenomenon for scientific production, communication, and evaluation, our quantitative understanding of the underlying mechanisms remains limited. Here, we systematically quantify the ageing phenomenon across multiple innovative domains, covering seven decades of scientific careers and four decades of patent inventors. We find a marked increase in the average age of innovators who receive recognition, measured by incoming citations. We tested three commonly proposed explanations and found them insufficient. Instead, we identify preferential attachment and network densification as the causal drivers of ageing, and introduce a simple mechanistic model that not only reproduces the observed patterns but also reveals how structural feedback shapes the dynamics of career ageing. Analysis of the model demonstrates a direct link between ageing and network densification, providing a basis for forecasting future recognition patterns once the magnitude of densification is known. These findings contribute to a new empirical and theoretical framework for understanding career dynamics and inform policy design to support early career innovators.

posters.title: Uneven Exposure to Generative AI Across the Scientific Research Pipeline
posters.authors: Yulin Yu and Yizhou Li
posters.keywords: Scientific Innovation Impact of GenAI Task Exposure to GenAI
posters.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT—widely accessible and rapidly adopted—represent a new mode of technological intervention in science. Unlike earlier AI systems embedded in specialized infrastructure or domain-specific pipelines, generative models directly integrate into researchers’ everyday cognitive workflows, assisting with literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, coding, analysis, and writing. Understanding how GenAI fits into the scientific innovation pipeline is therefore central to designing effective human–AI collaboration and autonomous laboratories. While recent large-scale studies document the growing role of AI in science—and even suggest that it may narrow the space of creativity—they largely conceptualize AI as domain-embedded machine-learning techniques rather than interactive generative tools(~\cite{hao2026artificial, gao2024quantifying}). Consequently, we still lack a process-level account of how GenAI reshapes the internal structure of scientific work and produces heterogeneous effects on scientific advancement.

In this paper, we examine this question from the perspective of scientific task composition and their exposure to GenAI tools. We argue that GenAI operates across the \textit{process} of science rather than at a single output stage. Scientific research consists of heterogeneous tasks—literature review, hypothesis generation, experimental execution, coding and analysis, interpretation, and scholarly communication—each requiring distinct cognitive, technical, and social skills. Evidence further shows strong asymmetries in how GenAI performs across these tasks: large language models excel at language-intensive and information-processing activities (\cite{bommasani2021foundation, noy2023experimental}) but exhibit reliability limitations in high-precision reasoning contexts (\cite{zhang2023hallucinations}). This task-level heterogeneity raises a central question: \textbf{how does uneven GenAI exposure in scientific tasks reshape the dynamics of the scientific process across disciplines? Which stages of research are likely to be accelerated, and which remain constrained by physical, cognitive, or coordination limits? }

We construct our analysis corpus by randomly sampling research articles from top-tier scientific journals across 8 disciplines in the recent 5 years(2020--2024). For each paper, we retrieve the abstract and metadata from OpenAlex as the unit of analysis, resulting in 1{,}322{,}326 papers. We prompt GPT-4o-mini along with human validation to identify which of the 332 detailed work activities (IWAs) are reflected in each paper using the IWA taxonomy, which has been used in prior studies to represent general units of work behavior performed across occupations (Examples of IWA include collecting data on consumer needs or opinions and interviewing people to obtain information) \footnote{In the O*NET content model, Intermediate Work Activities (IWAs) are standardized, mid-level task descriptors that represent general units of work behavior performed across occupations. IWAs bridge detailed tasks and broader work-activity categories and are commonly used to quantify the frequency and importance of task performance within occupations. \cite{onet_iwa_reference} , (ii) the abstract text, and (iii) structured instructions to identify relevant IWAs reflected in the described methods and research activities. The resulting set $T(p)$ represents the skill composition of paper $p$}. We classified the IWAs into eight research processes, as shown in Figure 2B based on ~\citep{munafo2017manifesto,creswell2019educational}. We also classified the IWAs into a higher-level taxonomy based on O*NET and~\citep{hosseinioun2025skill} shown in Fig1B. We then compute the following variables for the analysis.

\textbf{AI Applicability Scores by Task:} To quantify AI exposure at the task level, we use the IWA applicability metrics provided by Microsoft Research, which measure generative AI feasibility using Microsoft 365 user–Copilot chat log data. Each chat log is first classified into a specific IWA and then evaluated based on how effectively Copilot completes the associated user-generated task, using both user ratings and AI-based evaluation. These evaluations are then aggregated so that each detailed work activity $t$ is assigned an applicability score $A_t \in [0,1]$.

\textbf{Computing Paper-Level AI Exposure Score:} To calculate the Paper-Level AI Exposure Score, we aggregate IWA coverage within each scientific paper and combine it with task-level AI applicability scores. Specifically, for each paper, we compute the average AI applicability of the IWAs it contains, weighting each task by its frequency in the full corpus. This log-scaled TF-IDF–style weighting scheme down-weights tasks that are common across many papers and assigns greater influence to tasks that are relatively distinctive, thereby capturing how strongly a paper relies on AI-applicable yet less ubiquitous tasks.

We first investigate the extent to which general scientific innovation–related tasks are impacted by GenAI tools by plotting the distribution of AI impact scores. As shown in Figure 1A, we observe that scientific innovation–related tasks are more exposed to AI compared to tasks that are not applicable to scientific innovation. The strongest exposure appears in communication and information-processing cognitive tasks (e.g. Assist technical specialists with projects or research, Advise others on financial matters, Sell products or services, etc.), whereas the weakest exposure remains in physical operations and people-coordination tasks. On average, the scientific innovation–related score is 0.380, compared to 0.309 for non–innovation-related tasks ($p < 0.05$). (Scientific innovation tasks are defined as IWAs identified from all abstracts).

We then find that GenAI exposure varies heterogeneously across research processes and fields. Across the research pipeline, we find that the bottleneck of AI exposure occurs significantly at the data collection stage. As expected, AI exposure is highest in prior knowledge extraction and summarization tasks, such as literature review (Fig. 2B). These patterns help explain disciplinary differences in AI exposure show in Fig. 2A. Fields that do not rely heavily on primary data collection and instead emphasize writing-intensive and cognitively demanding tasks tend to show greater AI exposure. In contrast, disciplines such as medical science often require direct patient data collection, involving human-to-human consent processes and substantial interpersonal interaction, which leads to lower levels of AI exposure.

Lastly, we find that tasks exposure at the individual paper level has heterogeneous effects on citation. Papers in the humanities and social sciences tend to experience neutral to negative citation effects as their AI exposure scores increase. In contrast, papers in hard sciences, such as chemistry and medical science, show more positive citation impacts at higher levels of AI exposure (Fig. 3). While social science and humanities subjects have higher exposure potential to generative AI at the task level, their citation recognition shows the opposite effect.

\subsubsection*{Future Work} Taken together, our findings show that GenAI is not a uniform force in science. Instead, it selectively amplifies communication-intensive and cognitively abstract tasks, reshapes bottlenecks in the research pipeline, and produces heterogeneous returns across fields. By measuring exposure at the levels of skills, processes, and outcomes, we move beyond coarse automation metrics toward a mechanistic understanding of how GenAI reallocates cognitive labor and transforms scientific innovation.

posters.title: Satellite Imagery Embeddings as Pre-Estimation Validity Check for Geographic Causal Inference: Evidence from Indigenous Property Rights in Brazil
posters.authors: Kazuki Sakamoto, Connor Jerzak and Luke Sanford
posters.keywords: geographic regression discontinuity vision transformers causal forests selection bias public policy
posters.abstract: Geographic regression discontinuity design (Geo-RDD) estimates causal effects by comparing units just inside and outside a territorial boundary, but this approach requires that the landscape is continuous across the boundary. We introduce a diagnostic-first workflow that uses satellite vision-transformer embeddings to test this continuity assumption territory-by-territory before any causal estimation. For each territory we train an elastic net classifier on pre-treatment CLIP embeddings and compute two diagnostics: a territory-level AUC and a Wilcoxon rank-sum p-value that jointly identify whether the landscape is separable across the boundary. We additionally restrict to a design-eligible sample of observations with a local cross-border comparison partner within 18 km. Applied to 216 indigenous territories in Brazil, we find that 76% of the conservation effect estimated in the design-eligible primary sample disappears once territories with landscape discontinuities are removed. RATE statistics that suggest genuine treatment effect heterogeneity in the unscreened sample reverse sign entirely in the validity-screened sample, confirming that the apparent heterogeneity was an artifact of pre-existing landscape gradients, not genuine variation in homologation’s causal impact.

posters.title: Do Journal Data Sharing Requirements Promote Humility in Scientific Articles?
posters.authors: Sarah Bratt, Erin Leahey, Charles Gomez, Jina Lee, Sarah Stueve, Charles Lassiter and Yeaeun Kwon
posters.keywords: data sharing open science humility in inquiry text classification PLOS One
posters.abstract:
Despite the rise of data sharing policies, current studies of the impacts of data sharing policies tend to focus on the outcomes of science, like research reproducibility, data quality, integrity, and access to data for further analysis by the scientific community. In this study, we systematically analyzed 15,433 PLOS One research articles to compare the humility expressed before and after PLOS One strengthened its data sharing requirements (DSR) policy, making them mandatory as of March 1, 2014. We hypothesized that the 2014 DSR would generate more humility in scientific writing, especially in PLOS One, which evaluates papers based on scientific validity, not only positive or significant results. We reasoned that the “opening up” of the scientific process, namely, to require scientists to share their research data, would prompt scientists to show greater humility.

To quantify the influence of the 2014 data sharing policy at PLOS One, we performed regression discontinuity in time (RDiT) analysis on the humility expressed in articles before and after the 2014 policy change. Humility was classifier at the sentence level, using a transformer that classifies humility in inquiry (HI), an emerging concept developed in psychology and philosophy to refer to a set of practices reflecting authors’ recognition that they may be wrong.

Findings indicate that the overall humility (HI) in PLOS One articles increases over time. The local linear regression discontinuity in time analysis revealed a statistically significant increase in humility expressions (proportion of any of the four humility types – A,F,I, or T – around the time of the implementation of PLOS One’s 2014 data availability mandate (τ = 0.009, z = 2.75, p = 0.006). Substantively, this suggests the 2014 data sharing mandate had a modest but positive increase (0.9 percentage-point) relative to humility expressions in articles before the introduction of the data sharing policy. surprisingly, a sub-analysis of fallibility (F) reveals a negative trend in F, where fallibility statements decrease after the March 1, 2014 policy. The latter analysis led us to conjecture that when scientists review their data with greater care, it might generate more confidence, less fallibility, but also more tempering. These findings suggest that the 2014 data mandate at PLOS One was associated with an immediate increase in epistemic humility.

posters.title: Collective Causal Learning Under Partial Observability
posters.authors: Russ Yoon, Vicky Chuqiao Yang and Rahul Bhui
posters.keywords: Bayesian learning causal inference partial observability social communication agent-based simulation
posters.abstract: Understanding how groups learn causal structure from fragmented information is central to collective intelligence and organizational decision-making, yet in most real settings no individual observes the full system. We develop an agent-based Bayesian model that extends Bayesian causal induction to populations of partially observing agents who update from private data and from social exchange, and we compare three communication protocols—Evidence Sharing (raw observations), Belief and Confidence Sharing (beliefs with explicit confidence), and Belief Sharing (informal belief samples). Across systematic sweeps of population size, population composition, and communication probability, we evaluate learning speed via time to reach accuracy. Results show that evidence sharing spreads the correct structure fastest until a majority is reached but is slowest to achieve full consensus and degrades with larger, type-imbalanced, or sparsely communicating populations, whereas belief-based protocols are more robust and more consistently reach correct consensus. Notably, Belief Sharing performs comparably to Belief and Confidence Sharing despite transmitting less precise information, suggesting that low-cost, informal exchanges can be sufficient for accurate collective causal learning under partial observability, with implications for communication design in organizations.

posters.title: Reinforcement Learning with People Helps Overcome Conflicts of Interest in Social Dynamics
posters.authors: Edgar Andrade, Ofer Tchernichovski, Nori Jacobi, Dalton Conley and Seth Frey
posters.keywords: social dilemmas collective intelligence large-scale experiments machine learning with humans-in-the-loop
posters.abstract: Most human communities rely on a division of labor in which roles are interdependent yet only partially aligned in their interests. Beyond these interdependencies, social dynamics are also shaped by power, understood as control over the rules of the game. We investigate how assigning such power to one or another role affects collective outcomes in a foraging task involving managers and foragers. In this setting, managers invest in information that can improve collective harvests, while foragers prefer lower commissions and managers prefer higher ones. Using data from 223 asynchronously recruited online participants, we show that power does not drive actors toward extreme self-interested positions, although divergent incentives generate distinct adjustment dynamics across roles. We then combine these behavioral data with a data-efficient reinforcement-learning approach to optimize collective performance. Results suggest that reinforcement learning with people can increase total wealth while reducing between-role inequality, offering a promising framework for improving social systems.

posters.title: Systematic preferences among causal explanations of spurious correlations
posters.authors: Sam Zhang, Amirhossein Nakhaei and Mark Whiting
posters.keywords: explanation experimentation causality misinformation mediation
posters.abstract:
\textit{``The narrative fallacy addresses our limited ability to look at sequences of facts without weaving an explanation into them.''} --- {\small Nassim Nicholas Taleb}~\cite{taleb2007black}. Humans rarely encounter patterns as neutral observers. When presented with a statistical association, we instinctively search for causal explanations, even when the association is completely spurious. This tendency, related to ``belief-bias'' in narrative processing~\cite{sharedbelief2025}, raises the natural question of whether some types of causal explanation are systematically more convincing than others. If so, what determines this preference? Understanding the structure of explanatory persuasiveness has practical implications: unfounded causal beliefs underpin threats to public health, social cohesion, and environmental sustainability~\cite{vanProoijen2025}, and identifying why certain explanations succeed can inform efforts to counter them.

We present a two-part study. First, we report results from a completed pilot experiment ($n = 255$) that reveals structured preferences among causal explanation types for spurious correlations---including a reversal in preference that depends on participants' degree of conviction. Second, building on these findings, we propose a set of pre-registered hypotheses and a fixed analysis plan to be tested on a new sample ($n = 300$) whose data will be collected after acceptance and presented at the conference.

\textbf{Explanation types.} We consolidated an extensive survey of explanatory taxonomies---spanning scientific, biological, psychological, social, and contextual categories (29 types in total)---into three causal structures grounded in the language of causal inference: (1)~a \emph{confounder} explanation, positing a common cause $C$ such that $A \leftarrow C \rightarrow B$; (2)~a \emph{parallel mediation} explanation, with two independent mediators relaying the effect from $A$ to $B$ ($A \rightarrow M_1 \rightarrow B$ and $A \rightarrow M_2 \rightarrow B$); and (3)~a \emph{chained mediation} explanation, in which the effect propagates through three sequential mediators ($A \rightarrow M_1 \rightarrow M_2 \rightarrow M_3 \rightarrow B$).

\textbf{Stimuli.} From the 9,211 spurious correlations compiled by Tyler Vigen~\cite{vigen2015}, we filtered manually and with language-model assistance to 100 correlations that were statistically spurious yet plausibly amenable to causal explanation. The use of spurious correlations is the key design decision: because all associations are artifacts of the sampling period, any conviction a participant reports is attributable entirely to the explanatory structure, not to the underlying truth of the claim. For each correlation, we considered both causal directions ($A \rightarrow B$ and $B \rightarrow A$) and generated three explanations per direction using a large language model (one per causal structure), yielding 600 explanations in total.

\textbf{Pilot study.} We recruited 255 participants from Prolific (54.4\% female, 44.5\% male, 1.2\% other; US and UK residents; ages 20--80) and showed each participant 10 randomly assigned correlations (2,550 total ratings). For each correlation, participants saw two explanations---one per causal direction, representing different causal structures---and indicated which they found more convincing, rating their conviction for each on a four-point scale (not convinced to very convinced). Participants also completed a three-item Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) and a demographic questionnaire covering employment sector, gender, and age. We analyzed pairwise preferences using a Bradley--Terry model~\cite{bradleyterry1952}, which estimates the latent ``strength'' of each explanation type from head-to-head comparisons.

\textbf{Key pilot findings.} The pilot revealed four results that motivate the registered hypotheses below and, taken together, suggest that explanatory preferences are not idiosyncratic but structured by causal architecture. \emph{(i)~Explanatory seduction is pervasive but bounded.} Across all 2,550 matchups, the modal conviction rating for the preferred explanation was ``moderately convinced'', yet not ``very convinced'' (Figure~2). Participants broadly believed in these explanations, but reserved skepticism in the majority of the cases. This suggests that people evaluate \emph{whether a causal story hangs together} rather than \emph{whether it is true}, defaulting to moderate credence when presented with a structurally coherent narrative for a spurious correlation.

\emph{(ii)~Confounders win by default.} The confounder explanation was the most preferred type overall, winning approximately 50\% of matchups against a 33\% chance baseline (Figure~1). This is consistent with a preference for parsimony, since a single hidden common cause is the simplest story that accounts for two co-occurring variables. Note that even confounding explanations are false though, since the correlations end after the time period by design.

\emph{(iii)~The ranking reverses under high conviction.} Among matchups in which both explanations received high conviction ratings, parallel mediators emerged as the preferred type, overtaking confounders (Figure~3). This reversal suggests that at least two evaluation modes are operating: at default engagement, people reward simplicity; under deeper engagement, they reward explanatory robustness. Parallel mediators provide two independent causal pathways, so even if one mechanism is questionable, the other still supports the link. The shift from parsimony to overdetermination as a function of engagement depth is, to our knowledge, a novel empirical finding.

\emph{(iv)~Serial complexity is penalized, not rewarded.} Contrary to our initial expectation that longer, more elaborate causal chains would be more persuasive---a prediction motivated by the common intuition that detailed narratives are compelling---chained mediators were the least preferred type across nearly every subgroup (Figures~5--7). A three-step chain requires believing in three sequential links, any one of which could break. Rather than reading as elaborate and therefore convincing, chains appear to read as contrived. In other words, \emph{parallel} complexity (multiple independent pathways) is rewarded, while \emph{serial} complexity (a single long pathway) is penalized.

\emph{(v)~Preferences are stable across cognitive reflection.} The preference ordering---confounders over parallel mediators over chains---was broadly consistent across CRT scores (Figure~6). If this holds in the confirmatory sample, it implies that explanation-type preference is not primarily a product of analytical engagement: high-CRT individuals still favor simpler causal architectures by default, suggesting a structural feature of explanatory evaluation rather than a heuristic that more reflective thinkers overcome.

\textbf{Registered report.} Based on the pilot, we will pre-register the five main findings from the pilot study, and recruit 400 additional participants from Prolific to test those findings. This sample size is determined by the most demanding hypothesis (H3): each Bradley-Terry comparison reduces to a one-sample proportion test against 50\%, and the bottleneck pairwise win rate of ${\sim}59\%$ requires ${\sim}240$ matchups of the relevant pair, which---given that only ${\sim}20\%$ of matchups are high-conviction---implies $N \approx 360$ before attrition. The analysis plan, including the Bradley-Terry model specification and subgroup definitions, is fixed prior to data collection. If confirmed, these results would establish that preferences for causal explanations of spurious correlations are shaped by the type of causal architecture invoked, with parsimony dominating under low engagement and robustness dominating under high engagement, reframing the challenge of combating unfounded beliefs around causal geometry.

posters.title: Language, Not Novelty: LLM-Assisted Writing and Scientific Impact for ESL Scholars
posters.authors: Haohan Shi and Yulin Yu
posters.keywords: large language models AI-assisted writing scientific publishing knowledge inequality science of science
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming scientific writing, yet whether they reduce or merely mask longstanding inequalities remains unclear. We investigate how LLM-assisted writing affects scientific impact for English-as-a-second-language (ESL) scholars, disentangling linguistic benefits from potential novelty confounds. Using 3.9 million papers in prestigious journals (OpenAlex, 2020–2024) and 4.1 million author-portfolio papers, we estimate paper-level LLM usage via distributional methods and measure research novelty through atypical journal combinations. Within prestigious journals, LLM usage is associated with higher citations, with ESL authors benefiting disproportionately — the LLM×ESL interaction offsets roughly two-thirds of the baseline ESL citation penalty. This premium persists across both conventional and novel papers. At the gatekeeping stage, LLMs modestly increase ESL scholars' access to elite venues without altering research novelty profiles. Triple-interaction models confirm these benefits operate through language rather than research substance. Our findings suggest LLMs selectively reduce linguistic barriers in science rather than functioning as universal equalizers.

posters.title: Mitigating Confounder Bias in Observational Studies of Visual Media Effects
posters.authors: Xinyi Liu, Yilang Peng and Yingdan Lu
posters.keywords: Visual media effects Confounder bias Large language models Double LASSO Causal inference
posters.abstract: The rise of visual-centric social media platforms has made studying visual media effects increasingly important, yet isolating causal relationships between visual features and communication outcomes remains challenging due to confounder bias — visual content is complex, many confounders are difficult to identify or measure, and covariate selection requires careful balancing of overfitting against omitted variable bias. To address these challenges, we propose an LLM-informed, machine learning-based inference framework that integrates large language models, Double LASSO selection, and hierarchical OLS regression across three steps: discovery, measurement, and selection. In the discovery step, LLMs evaluate content and articulate reasoning to surface potential confounders. In the measurement step, LLMs annotate these variables at scale using zero-shot evaluation. In the selection step, Double LASSO identifies a parsimonious set of controls, which are then entered into hierarchical OLS models for causal estimation. We applied this framework to replicate a study of 59,020 Instagram posts from 172 U.S. politician accounts, using GPT-4o to discover and annotate 30 potential confounders validated against human coders. Our results confirmed that personalized images significantly increase engagement even after extensive confounding adjustment, though coefficient fluctuations suggest much of the effect is mediated by informal captioning style, while the effect of a politician's own face on engagement proved highly robust across specifications. This study contributes to observational visual media research by introducing an LLM-informed inference framework that bridges computational methods and causal inference to move the field beyond descriptive analysis toward more rigorous causal estimation in the visual domain.

posters.title: Predictors of Online Visibility and Citations in Science
posters.authors: Jose Cordova, Haohan Shi, Toma Hirose, Daniel Romero and Agnes Horvat
posters.keywords: Science Communication Multiplatform Diffusion Social Media News Online Attention
posters.abstract: The dissemination of scientific articles across digital platforms has become a cornerstone of modern science communication. This study examines the dynamics of online attention to scientific content, analyzing over 530,000 research articles mentioned across platforms such as social media, blogs, and news outlets. We investigate the predictive power of temporal, platform, and paper features, in predicting both online visibility and citation count. Our findings reveal that early temporal features—such as the pace and timing of initial mentions—are the dominant predictors of an article’s eventual online mentions, pointing to the importance of collective dynamics around the online reception of research articles. Notably, the importance of predictive features differ across platforms, with temporal features dominating overall online visibility predictions, while news coverage prediction improves with a more balanced combination of paper and temporal features. Additionally, we show that online mentions of research articles, including their temporal distribution, can serve as early indicators of future citation counts. Overall, we demonstrate how early online signals can be leveraged to identify potentially influential articles. These insights highlight the value of considering how online mentions evolve over time, rather than focusing solely on their volume.

posters.title: Quantifying Spatiotemporal Gaps in Accessibility with Fine-Grained, National, Open-Source Amenity Datasets
posters.authors: Gabriel Agostini, Zhixuan Qi, Katelyn Liu, Shreya Sriram, Esther Li, Emma Pierson and Nikhil Garg
posters.keywords: Accessibility Spatial inequality Urban planning Geography Urban Data Science
posters.abstract: Researchers and policymakers have sought to identify access gaps: areas where access to vital amenities is lacking. Disparities in access reflect and generate new forms of spatial inequality, and quantifying access gaps at scale could facilitate urban planning and assess disproportionate vulnerabilities of many populations. Yet, large, accurate spatiotemporal datasets are not widely available, and existing point of interest (POI) data is often mislabeled or lacks a temporal dimension. We discuss a machine-learning pipeline to produce trustworthy accessibility estimates at the Census Block Group level leveraging Foursquare's global open-source POI data–which details, among other attributes, opening and closing dates of different amenities. We show how we can use this dataset to reveal spatiotemporal insights into national access gaps across fine-grained POI categories. We plan to release our dataset to foster future research.

posters.title: How Big, Open Data Shape Scientific Collaboration: A Comparative Study of Sky Surveys
posters.authors: Erin Leahey, Sarah Stueve and Anissa Tanweer
posters.keywords: Open Science Big Data Astronomy Research Collaboration Team Dynamics
posters.abstract:
Data are “the life blood of scientific research” (Nagaraj et al., 2020) and two prominent characteristics of data motivate our research. Data vary in their size: some datasets are small, containing few observations and/or variables, whereas other datasets are quite big, containing many variables and/or requiring terabytes of space to store them. Data also vary in their openness: some datasets are proprietary and restricted to a small and/or specific set of users, whereas other datasets are public and open to all interested users. Trends toward big data and open data typify modern science. The goal of our research is to understand how the ‘bigness’ and openness of data affect participation and collaboration in science.

These two characteristics are particularly prominent in sky surveys, an important source of data used in Astronomy. Sky surveys reside at the intersection of the two trends under discussion—big data and open data—and provide an unprecedented opportunity to study the relationship between them. Sky surveys are a “systematic, controlled, and repeatable” method for studying astronomical phenomena (Borne, 2013, p. 413). Sky surveys tend to be big, and the increasingly vast amount of data produced by modern sky surveys has propelled an overhaul in data management and analytic methods used in the field and beyond (Zhang & Zhao, 2015). Sky surveys also tend to be open, or archival and available to the entire astronomy community, at least eventually. And yet: some sky surveys are bigger than others, and some are more open.

We capitalize on variation in the bigness and openness of sky surveys in our research design. We study three sky surveys: the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System (Pan-STARRs); the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS); and Gaia. As shown in Figure 1, one of these surveys is quite big, and panoptic in nature (Pan-STARRS), compared to the other two. We compare the biggest sky survey to the others to understand how bigness affects collaboration and team composition in Astronomy. Do big data draw in more junior collaborators, with the new and requisite computational skill sets? Does the breadth of big data allow research teams to migrate to adjacent topics? We also see from Figure 1 that one of these surveys (Gaia) is quite open: it does not have exclusive periods of privileged data access like the other two. We compare the most open sky survey to the others to understand how openness affects collaboration and team composition in Astronomy.
