When data are more openly available, are research teams more likely to include scientists from more, and more diverse developing countries and institutions?

To investigate how bigness and openness affects research collaborations, we use computational methods to extract and analyze bibliometric data. We identified all articles that use one of these three sky surveys from NASA’s Astrophysics Data System (ADS) (Accomazzi, 2024; Accomazzi et al., 1995, 2010), a digital library portal for astronomy and astrophysics. From ADS we select articles that meet at least one of three criteria: mention the sky survey in the abstract or title; cite one of the sky survey’s data/technical papers; formally acknowledge the sky survey using the requested language. We merged the ADS metadata with OpenAlex, a large-scale scholarly database containing approximately 240 million works (Priem et al., 2022) that includes unique author IDs. With author data from OpenAlex, and tools like Genderize and Nationalize, we constructed variables that characterize each research collaboration (i.e., set of coauthors on a paper). These key outcomes of interest capture team diversity in terms of gender, nationality, country of affiliation, sector, institution, and topic. We also collect each author’s past publications to gauge the topics they have studied previously.

We find that the size of data is patterned with the demographic and topical diversity of teams. When we compare the largest sky survey (Pan-STARRS) to the other two, we find that bigness is positively associated with larger teams, greater representation of early-career scholars and scholars from a broader array of countries (though mostly developed countries). Teams that use bigger sky surveys also tend to branch out to new topics, relative to what they have studied in the past, but these new topics tend to be narrow.

The openness of data matters too. When we compare the most open sky survey (Gaia) to the other two, we find that openness is positively associated with inclusion of women, junior scientists, and scholars outside academia and the U.S. (particularly developing countries), and greater diversity in terms of career age. Openness does not lead to greater topical diversity or branching out of authors to new topics; instead, users of more open sky surveys tend to converge around mutually shared interests they have studied in the past.

In sum, we find that big data are associated with large and homogenous teams whose members tend to branch out from their prior work and explore new topics. Open data are associated with demographically, institutionally, and geographically diverse teams that focus on mutually shared interests. These results suggest that big data are associated with diverse topics, whereas open data are associated with diverse scientific teams.

We are currently extending our research in a few ways. First, we are moving from these descriptive analyses to multivariate models, in order to control for possible confounders and get a better handle on causal direction. Do big data prompt topical diversity, or attract team members with diverse interests? Do open data foster demographically diverse teams, or attract them? Second, we are examining not only the composition of collaborative research teams, but also research outcomes. We suspect that bigger and more open data may provide the conditions that are conducive to novel insights that span disciplines or at least subdisciplines and help reroute knowledge streams. So, we are investigating outcomes like novelty, interdisciplinarity, and disruption. Third, we will incorporate a fourth sky survey, LSST, when data and thus journal articles become available. LSST stands out from other sky surveys because it is both big and open. LSST is a deep-field panoptic sky survey, meaning that it is designed to image both nearby objects and distant faint objects and covers 20,000 square degrees of the night sky. LSST will not have a period of exclusive data access, and will be governed by a partially open data access policy: all researchers in the U.S. and Chile, along with international institutions that made contributions to the project’s development, will get simultaneous access to the data. The survey is slated to begin in early 2026 and last 10 years. At the July 2026 IC2S2 conference, we expect to be able to report results from the first and second extensions.

posters.title: Why the Nobel Prize Finds Its Winner Late
posters.authors: Lulin Yang, Jiaxin Pei, Donna Ginther and Lingfei Wu
posters.keywords: Delayed Recognition Credit Allocation Scientific Contribution Scientific Careers Team Collaboration
posters.abstract: In modern science, discoveries now live longer than their discoverers’ careers. Analyzing more than a century of Nobel-winning discoveries, we find that the average team size of prize-winning papers has grown from about one to five authors, while the number of laureates per award remains capped at three. Over the same period, the lag between discovery and recognition has lengthened from under ten to over twenty-five years. As science’s collective memory deepens—reference age has doubled from about six to over twelve years since the 1960s—and research careers shorten—their half-life has fallen from roughly thirty-five to five years—the Nobel Prize increasingly honors a few survivors from the large teams that make discovery possible. Using a large-scale dataset of contribution and credit covering two million scientists over three decades, we show that this widening gap between contribution and recognition is not unique to the Nobel system but symptomatic of contemporary science.

posters.title: BioToolKB: A Knowledge Graph for Quantifying the Hidden Impact of Biomedical Tools and Methods
posters.authors: Rodrigo Dorantes-Gilardi and Albert-Laszlo Barabasi
posters.keywords: Scientific Tools Hidden Citations Named Entity Recognition Knowledge Graph Science of Science
posters.abstract:
Scientific progress in biomedicine depends critically on specialized tools and methods---laboratory techniques such as PCR and CRISPR-Cas9, software applications like DESeq2 and Cytoscape, and modeling methods including Kaplan-Meier estimation and machine learning classifiers. Despite their foundational role, the true impact of these ``BioTools'' remains largely invisible to conventional evaluation frameworks. Traditional citation metrics capture only a fraction of their influence: PCR, for example, is explicitly mentioned in over 3.4 million publications, yet its foundational paper records just 25,000 citations---a hundred-fold discrepancy~\cite{meng_hidden_2024}. This gap reflects a systemic failure in how science measures and rewards methodological contributions~\cite{schindler_role_2022}.

Recent work has demonstrated the severity of this problem for biobanks and cohort studies~\cite{dorantes-gilardi_quantifying_2025}. By computationally identifying 2,663 biobanks and tracking their textual mentions across 228,761 scientific articles, 16,210 grants, 15,469 patents, 1,769 clinical trials, and 9,468 policy documents, that study revealed that 41.2\% of articles mentioning a biobank fail to cite its reference papers (Figure~\ref{fig_biobank}). It further uncovered a ``coauthorship-for-access'' mechanism, where 59.6\% of papers include a biobank team member as co-author, and introduced a multidimensional biobank impact factor integrating visibility across research, innovation, policy, and disease dimensions. Critically, the scientific reach of biobanks---measured through downstream citations of mentioning papers---was found to be 13 times greater than direct citation counts, demonstrating that traditional metrics vastly underestimate the true influence of scientific resources.

This study extends that framework from biobanks to the full landscape of biomedical tools and methods through BioToolKB, a comprehensive knowledge graph (Figure~\ref{fig_biotoolkb}). BioToolKB catalogs three classes of BioTools: laboratory techniques (3,834 tools sourced from SciCrunch and Wikidata), software applications (22,134 entities from the CZI Software Mentions dataset), and modeling methods (4,662 unique tools, including scientific models, algorithms, and statistical tests). These are linked to their mentions across 7.5 million full-text publications from the PubMed Central Open Access subset, as well as grants, patents, clinical trials, and policy documents from the Dimensions database.

A key methodological contribution is a two-stage NLP pipeline for extracting BioTool mentions at scale. In the first stage, regular expression matching against tool names and known aliases identifies candidate text contexts from full-text publications. In the second stage, a fine-tuned SciBERT-based Named Entity Recognition (NER) model~\cite{beltagy_scibert_2019} certifies that candidate matches represent genuine tool mentions rather than spurious string overlaps. SciBERT, a transformer model pre-trained on scientific literature, was fine-tuned on manually annotated contexts---350 samples from laboratory techniques and modeling methods, and 100 from software applications---labeled with the assistance of the Prodigy annotation platform. The model achieves 90\% accuracy in recognizing tool mentions across all three BioTool categories and serves as the backbone of the extraction pipeline applied to the full PMC Open Access corpus.

Preliminary results confirm that the patterns observed for biobanks generalize across other BioTools. Hidden citations are pervasive: a substantial fraction of papers mentioning a tool omit formal citations to its foundational paper, and the magnitude of this gap varies systematically across tool types---software applications and modeling methods tend to exhibit higher rates of hidden citations than laboratory techniques. Beyond hidden citations, a multidimensional impact framework captures BioTool contributions along additional dimensions (Figure~\ref{fig_impact}): policy reach (mentions in public policy documents referencing BioTool-impacted studies), disease impact (the depth and scope of disease research enabled by each tool), and innovation impact (usage across patents and clinical trials). Together, these indicators close the metrics gap between what citation counts reveal and the true value BioTools deliver to science and society. BioToolKB provides a data-driven foundation for evaluating methodological contributions, offering actionable insights for funding agencies, tool developers, and the broader scientific community seeking to understand and promote the creation of transformative research tools.

posters.title: Topic Modeling and Classification of Palm Oil Grievances
posters.authors: Nicole Page, Uriel Fuentes Figueroa, Owakamare Princewill, Helena Card, Theron White, Yuliia Ihnatesku, Satadisha Saha Bhowmick and Meghan Hutch
posters.keywords: topic modeling natural language processing text classification machine learning palm oil
posters.abstract: The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) promotes ethical and sustainable practices in the palm oil industry. To assess the effectiveness of its Conflict Resolution Mechanism (CRM), this study introduces a two-stage pipeline that combines unsupervised topic modeling with transformer-based text classification. This is done to help identify major grievances filed against the palm oil industry and to investigate the efficacy of the CRM. Our unsupervised approach grouped grievances into the following topics: 1) Failed community compensation or land conflicts, 2) Environmental impact, 3) Administrative violations, 4) Deforestation, 5) Labor and human rights violations, and 6) Illegally sourced or contaminated fruit bunches. Our classification model achieved a micro-F1 score of 0.76 for classifying unseen grievances into the previously identified topics. Although the initial classification performance remains modest, by integrating both unsupervised and supervised modeling this project could provide a structured framework for understanding the types of conflicts brought before the RSPO and offers a foundation for evaluating how effectively the CRM addresses them.

posters.title: SpeechSpectrum: A Linguistic Fidelity Spectrum for Accountable Speech-to-Text
posters.authors: Anna Seo Gyeong Choi, Maria Teleki, Miguel Angel del Rio Fernandez, James Caverlee, Corey Miller and Allison Koenecke
posters.keywords: Speech AI speech-to-text LLM verbatimicity linguistic fidelity
posters.abstract: Speech-to-text (STT) systems typically treat transcription as a technical accuracy problem with a single ``correct'' output, obscuring the reality that diverse users and tasks require different balances of linguistic fidelity, concision, and emphasis. To address this accountability gap, we introduce SpeechSpectrum , a framework that reconceptualizes STT conversion as cross-modal translation along a continuous spectrum of representational fidelity, or verbatimicity. To support this framework, we release an open-source Python package allowing users to dynamically navigate this continuum. We validate SpeechSpectrum through two empirical studies. First, a human-subjects study (N=52) demonstrates that user preferences across legal, medical, and business tasks are highly context-dependent and pluralistic, directly challenging the assumption that a single transcription standard suffices. Second, an audit using LLM personas reveals that large language models fail to reliably proxy these human choices, consistently producing rigidly homogenized preference distributions that amplify professional stereotypes. Ultimately, SpeechSpectrum provides both a conceptual reorientation and practical tools to reposition fidelity control as a core site of algorithmic accountability, empowering users to dictate how their speech is rendered.

posters.title: The Emergence of Causal Curiosity from Existing Causal Belief Networks
posters.authors: Zhuoyu Shi, Xintong Jiang, Bohan Jiang and Fred Morstatter
posters.keywords: Causal Curiosity Causal Reasoning Causal language Social Media Reddit
posters.abstract: Causal curiosity is foundational to human cognition. It is the desire to understand why events happen, what mechanisms underlie them, and how outcomes can be explained or anticipated. It motivates exploration, sustains attention, and fuels the search for new knowledge. However, despite consensus on the importance of causal curiosity, little is known about how causal curiosity arises from prior causal belief structures. In our work, we examine how causal curiosity emerges from existing causal belief systems. Leveraging language models to extract cause-and-effect relationship pairs and identify causal curiosity-driven questions from 100 million Reddit posts, our findings reveal that causal curiosity is largely rooted in prior causal belief networks. Particularly, \textit{positive} nouns are more likely to be the object of causal curiosity. Moreover, our findings indicate that concepts that serve more as \textit{causes} are more likely to appear in causal curiosity than those that serve more as effects. Lastly, our results suggest that causal curiosity emerges from the \textit{central} of the existing belief networks. These novel insights reveal that causal curiosity is systematically grounded in prior causal belief networks, and suggest their implication to facilitate the human learning process by motivating people to actively explore and construct deeper understandings rather than passively receiving information.

posters.title: Hidden Hierarchies in Partially Observable Illicit Networks: Latent Geometry and Redundant Leadership
posters.authors: Brinda Gokul
posters.keywords: Generative Network Models Latent Structural Roles Organizational Resilience Centrality Measures Clandestine Organizations
posters.abstract: Covert organizations such as terrorist cells and criminal enterprises must balance secrecy with coordination, giving rise to network structures that differ systematically from observable social or economic networks. This paper introduces a formal model of network formation tailored to clandestine settings, in which attachment is governed by loyalty rather than visibility or popularity. Building on empirical patterns observed in ISIS fighter networks, the model combines proximity to a protected core with betweenness-based attachment to generate hierarchically layered structures. Simulated networks consistently produce structurally embedded intermediaries who are operationally critical yet insulated from direct exposure, forming second-tier leadership buffers that obscure top command while preserving operational efficiency. The results illuminate the design principles underlying resilient clandestine organizations and provide a general framework for analyzing hidden coordination structures in adversarial and illicit networks.

posters.title: Beyond Single Ground Truth: Reference Monism as Epistemic Injustice in ASR Evaluation
posters.authors: Anna Seo Gyeong Choi, Maria Teleki, James Caverlee, Miguel Angel del Rio Fernandez, Corey Miller and Hoon Choi
posters.keywords: ASR epistemic injustice evaluation ground truth AI bias
posters.abstract: Standard evaluation metrics for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), such as Word Error Rate (WER), rely on "reference monism"—the assumption that there is a single correct ground-truth transcription for any speech event. This paper argues that enforcing a single transcription convention commits epistemic injustice by structurally penalizing speakers whose natural communicative practices do not align with the dominant evaluative standard. We introduce the ``hermeneutical gap'' to describe this misalignment and formalize it into a quantifiable metric: Epistemic Injustice Distance ($\text{EID}$). Using the AphasiaBank corpus and multiple commercial ASR systems, we evaluate outputs against verbatim, non-verbatim, and legal ground truths simultaneously. We demonstrate that for identical system outputs, the choice of transcription convention alters WER by up to 1.8x, and that enforcing non-verbatim conventions imposes a massive, avoidable evaluation penalty specifically on speakers with non-fluent aphasia. To mitigate this, we propose replacing single-number WER reporting with ``WER-Range,'' a metric that evaluates system performance across multiple legitimate transcription conventions, thereby repositioning ground truth from a fixed technical parameter to a site of algorithmic accountability.

posters.title: Advisor career stage and PhD advisee development
posters.authors: Xi Hong, Jialin Liu and Chaoqun Ni
posters.keywords: Scientific workforce doctoral education PhD training academic career science of science
posters.abstract: Doctoral education plays a pivotal role in advancing science and innovation through training future scholars and generating scientific outputs, where PhD advisors lies in the centrality of this training system to support student development and success. While factors such as student background and institutional environment also matters, prior studies have widely recognized the role of advisors in shaping PhD advisee development and achievements. Advisors in different career stages can differ substantially in both advising styles and academic profiles. This brings up a key question: how is PhD advisor career stage associated with PhD student development and achievements, such as publication productivity, research impact and career pathways? Integrating multiple large-scale datasets and a sample of 254,499 unique advisor-advisee pairs with student entry years from 2006 to 2019 in the United States, this study provides implications to scientific workforce training by unraveling the relationship between advisor career stage and PhD advisee development. Our study indicates that 1. PhD advisees supervised by early-career advisors exhibit higher publication productivity and greater citation impact in their research. Conversely, those with mid and late career advisors overall show higher research disruption, and such positive association is more pronounced at higher quantiles of the student disruption distribution. 2. PhD advisees who have early-career advisors are more likely to land a faculty job in the United States in Engineering, Medicine and Health, Natural Sciences and Social Sciences. However, in Mathematics and Computing and Applied Science, such difference is not significant after controlling advisor publication metrics. Moreover, in these two fields, students supervised by mid- and late-career advisors present a higher probability to secure an academic job in top 10 and 20 percent institutions. The findings of this study can provide insights that inform institutional policymaking related to PhD training, faculty evaluation and support, as well as doctoral applicants’ decision-making.

posters.title: Persistent, Proximal Remote Sensing of Residential Cooling Dynamics: Quantifying the Dependence of Energy End-use Behavior on Environmental Factors
posters.authors: Gregory Dobler, Kyungmin Lee, Mohit Sharma and Andreas Karpf
posters.keywords: Urban Science Proximal Remote Sensing Energy Use Behavior Computer Vision Machine Learning
posters.abstract: This study presents a novel framework for measuring residential cooling behavior at the unit level using persistent, proximal infrared remote sensing. By analyzing ~110,000 thermal images of a Brooklyn building facade at 10-second intervals, we deployed a 2D-CNN classifier (97% accuracy) to detect the on/off states of 58 HVAC units. This methodology addresses the scarcity of granular energy data by generating high-temporal resolution behavioral metrics. Our analysis reveals a strong linear correlation between aggregate cooling demand and ambient temperature showing a 1.86 percent increase in AC use per degree Celsius, while finding no significant dependence on humidity. This work demonstrates the utility of "Urban Observatory" facilities for quantifying the dynamical interplay between human behavior, the built environment, and the environmental conditions.

posters.title: Estimating latent structure in perceptions of social networks with multilayer Aggregated Relational Data
posters.authors: Izabel Aguiar, Justin Weltz and Tyler McCormick
posters.keywords: Aggregated Relational Data Cognitive Social Structures multilayer networks network sampling survey methods
posters.abstract: Perceptual social networks capture individuals' perceptions of the relationships between other people in their community. However, collecting such perceptual networks necessitates the arduous task of conducting a complete survey. In this work, we discuss an approach for circumventing a complete survey by extending the method of collecting aggregated relational data (ARD)--which consists of asking respondents to estimate the number of connections they have to people with a particular trait--to the setting where we aim to collect multiple perceptions of relationships across given traits. Considering perceptual network data collection in this way not only allows for less survey fatigue (and thus, for much larger perceptual networks to be collected), but also for the flexibility to collect perceptual networks of acquaintances, hard-to-reach populations, or of a general (perceived) population. Furthermore, if the purpose of collecting a perceptual network is not to identify particular discrepancies across perceptions, but rather to identify latent structure in how people are assuming and perceiving connections within their social network, collecting data in this way has potential to invoke these assumptions and schema much more concretely.

posters.title: LEGO Data Model, Catalog, and Loader: An Open-Source Ecosystem for Linking Multi-Source Tabular Sparse Spatio-Temporal Data
posters.authors: Michelle Audirac, Mahima Kaur, Shreya Nalluri and Danielle Braun
posters.keywords: reproducibility data standards spatio-temporal integration multi-source data linkage
posters.abstract:
Motivation. The growing data landscape creates major opportunities for computational social science, but linking multi-source data assets remains a core unresolved challenge. Datasets from different agencies often use incompatible naming conventions, update frequencies, and spatial identifiers. This is especially difficult for **tabular sparse spatio-temporal data**, where observations are uneven across space and time and geographic boundaries change. In practice, integration is handled through ad-hoc scripts and implicit assumptions, creating hidden dependencies that contribute to a quiet reproducibility crisis.

Limitations. FAIR principles and community initiatives have improved metadata discoverability, but a critical “last mile” gap remains between FAIR-compliant data and operationally reproducible, analysis-ready inputs. Domain-specific common data models typically focus within a single domain and do not support cross-domain, multi-resolution spatio-temporal integration—leaving key alignment and assembly decisions to bespoke pipelines.

Contributions. We present the LEGO Ecosystem, an open-source, three-component infrastructure that provides a concrete path from fragmented multi-domain sources to AI-ready spatio-temporal inputs. The ecosystem follows the same principle as toy building blocks: standardized data pieces that fit together. (1) **LEGO Data Standards and Model** define canonical datasets through standardized schemas and deterministic naming/partitioning conventions that encode domain, source, and spatio-temporal resolution. (2) LEGO Catalog is a self-serve registry backed by JSON Schema that validates structured dataset records and supports both discovery and programmatic access. (3) LegoLoaderX is a PyTorch Dataset/DataLoader that consumes canonical assets via a declarative YAML configuration, enforces fail-fast integrity checks (schema, types, alignment, tensor shapes), and outputs standardized tensor batches for modeling.

Researchers specify what datasets and spatio-temporal windows they need, and LEGO handles how to locate, assemble, validate, and deliver consistent inputs. By combining standards, validated metadata, and load-time integrity contracts, LEGO closes the gap between FAIR discoverability and operational reproducibility and lowers the barrier to applying deep learning to linked spatio-temporal data.

posters.title: How Philanthropic Missions Shape Scientific Agendas and Policy Influence
posters.authors: Jin Ai, Jacob A. Dalsgaard and Filipi N. Silva
posters.keywords: Science philanthropy Agenda setting Policy influence Innovation systems
posters.abstract: Philanthropy constitutes one of the largest and most diverse sectors in research funding, yet its agenda-setting effects remain understudied at scale. We examine whether philanthropic missions systematically structure the research they fund and whether mission-driven funding translates into policy influence. We construct a large-scale linked dataset of over 3 million philanthropically funded publications and more than 32,000 philanthropic organizations by disambiguating Web of Science funding acknowledgments and integrating organizational mission statements. Using embedding-based semantic similarity models and large language model–assisted topic modeling, we quantify mission–research correspondence at the funder–article level. We then link funded publications to policy documents using the Overton database to measure policy citation incidence and intensity. This design enables us to test whether higher mission–research correspondence predicts greater policy uptake, particularly in policy-salient domains. The study provides population-level evidence on how philanthropic intent shapes research trajectories and downstream policy engagement within contemporary innovation systems.

posters.title: Reinforcement Learning for Respondent-Driven Sampling
posters.authors: Justin Weltz, Angela Yoon, Yichi Zhang, Alexander Volfovsky and Eric Laber
posters.keywords: network sampling reinforcement learning sample design social networks public health
posters.abstract: Respondent-driven sampling (RDS) is widely used to study hidden or hard-to-reach populations by incentivizing study participants to recruit their social connections. The success and efficiency of RDS can depend critically on the nature of the incentives, including their number, value, call to action, etc. Standard RDS uses an incentive structure that is set a priori and held fixed throughout the study. Thus, it does not make use of accumulating information on which incentives are effective and for whom. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) based adaptive RDS study design in which the incentives are tailored over time to maximize cumulative utility during the study. We show that these designs are more efficient, cost-effective, and can generate new insights into the social structure of hidden populations. In addition, we develop methods for valid post-study inference which are non-trivial due to the adaptive sampling induced by RL as well as the complex dependencies among subjects due to latent (unobserved) social network structure.

posters.title: Modeling Varying Aggregations of Social Networks with Applications to Wealth Dynamics
posters.authors: Justin Weltz, Izabel Aguiar and Daniel Redhead
posters.keywords: network sampling missing data discrete choice households multi-level networks
posters.abstract: Relationships often influence how people accumulate and maintain wealth. Consequently, social and economic networks capture aggregated notions of interconnected welfare. Data on these networks are primarily collected by querying individuals on their ties to other individuals. However, relationships that affect wealth often involve aggregates of individuals because resources are commonly shared among household members. We offer new statistical methodology that bridges the gap between individual level network data and the reality of wealth dynamics.

posters.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders to Measure Social Biases in Podcast Data
posters.authors: Sidhika Balachandar, Andre Shportko, Serina Chang and Emma Pierson
posters.keywords: manosphere podcasts gender bias sparse autoencoders LLM coding
posters.abstract: Understanding how social biases emerge and evolve in large text corpora is a central challenge in computational social science. Existing approaches for measuring bias in text often rely on predefined word lists and embedding-based associations, which struggle to detect higher-level, contextual forms of bias. In this paper, we introduce a sparse autoencoder (SAE) based framework for measuring social biases in text that identifies interpretable latent dimensions of discourse and enables fine-grained longitudinal analysis. We apply this method to study gender-related discourse in the manosphere, a network of online communities and media figures that center discussions of masculinity, gender roles, and critiques of feminism and gender equality. Using a dataset of podcast transcripts from 17 popular manosphere shows released between 2015 and 2025, we find that manosphere discourse on gender includes political and gender conservative topics such as debates over gender identity, discussions of dating dynamics and masculinity, and narratives about women’s roles in family and work. We further analyze temporal trends in the dataset using LLM weak supervision to classify political content and find that political discussion has increased over time, particularly within podcasts that are nominally apolitical. These results could suggest that gender-conservative and culture-war narratives are increasingly diffusing into broader manosphere media ecosystems. Overall, our work demonstrates how sparse autoencoders can provide interpretable, scalable tools for characterizing complex social biases and how they can enable analyses to track how biases evolve over time in large corpora.

posters.title: Spontaneous Divergence in Technological Progress
posters.authors: Siddharth Patwardhan, Chaoming Song and Dashun Wang
posters.keywords: Innovation dynamics Technological progress Pareto frontier dynamics Dynamical phase transition Multi-objective optimization
posters.abstract: Technological progress is rarely about improving a single feature. From efficiency and performance to cost and stability, advances unfold across multiple, often competing objectives, giving rise to trade-offs that define a moving Pareto frontier of what is jointly attainable. While Pareto frontiers capture these trade-offs in static form, little is known about how these frontiers evolve as innovation progresses. Tracing the state-of-the-art trajectories in three domains of rapid innovation—large-language models, perovskite solar cells, and computer hardware—we find that progress follows a universal two-phase pattern. Early progress follows a coordinated phase, in which advances simultaneously improve all objectives and the frontier converges to a single point. Beyond a critical threshold, coordination collapses, giving rise to a fragmented phase with intensified trade-offs and objective-specific leaders. We explain this pattern with a minimal stochastic model of innovation. Two forces compete: (i) a steady pressure toward specialization from moves that help one objective while hurting the other, and (ii) a finite reservoir of “win–win” moves that advance all objectives but become exhausted as the system improves. As universally beneficial moves diminish, the system tips from coordination to fragmentation in a sharp dynamical phase transition whose timing scales with problem complexity —roughly the number of design dimensions times its logarithm— and location shifts with the number of inherent conflicts between objectives. Spontaneous divergence thus emerges as a general organizing principle of technological progress, offering testable forecasts for when frontiers will bifurcate, cautioning against over-extrapolating from early unified leaders, and informing the design of R\&D portfolios, standards, and policy in domains where multiple goals must advance together.

posters.title: Predicting Researcher Entry into Emerging Scientific Subfields
posters.authors: Nandini Banerjee and Diego Gomez-Zara
posters.keywords: Researcher entry Collaboration networks Temporal exposure Network roles Longitudinal network analysis
posters.abstract:
Understanding how researchers enter emerging scientific subfields is central to explaining the evolution of knowledge domains. New research areas often grow through collaboration networks that expose researchers to ideas, methods, and opportunities. Prior diffusion models often assume that a researcher's likelihood of entering a subfield increases with cumulative exposure to researchers entering new areas [1]. However, collaboration networks expose researchers to emerging areas through interactions that vary in timing and connections [2]. As a result, it remains unclear whether entry into new research fields is primarily driven by the amount of exposure researchers accumulate, by when exposure occurs, or by which collaborators provide it.

In this study, we examine how different dimensions of collaboration exposure predict researchers' entry into emerging scientific subfields. Specifically, we evaluate whether entry is better explained by cumulative exposure to collaborators already active in a field, by the timing of initial exposure to recent entrants, or by the composition of collaborators who are part of a researcher's local network environment. By comparing these mechanisms systematically, we aim to clarify which aspects of collaboration networks provide the strongest signal for predicting entry into growing scientific areas.

We analyze longitudinal co-authorship networks derived from the \textit{SciSciNet} dataset [3]. We focus on five subfields that experienced substantial growth between 2015 and 2019: Computer Engineering, Physical Geography, Demographic Economics, Evolutionary Biology, and Combinatorial Chemistry. Across these fields, we analyze the publication histories of over 9 million researchers. We classify researchers according to their entry timing into three groups: \textit{Recent Entrants}, who first published in the subfield during the growth period of 2015-2019; \textit{Potential Entrants}, who collaborated with Recent Entrants but had not yet published in the subfield; and \textit{Established Entrants}, who began publishing in the subfield before 2015.

We construct yearly observations for each potential entrant and predict whether that researcher publishes in the focal subfield in that year. For each researcher–year observation, we derive theory-informed features that capture distinct forms of collaborative exposure within the local co-authorship network. These include (1) timing of first exposure, defined as the number of years since the researcher first collaborated with a Recent Entrant, (2) cumulative exposure, capturing the total accumulated collaboration exposure to Recent Entrants over time, (3) new exposure, representing collaborations formed with Recent Entrants within the current year, and (4) exposure to Established Entrants, reflecting collaboration with researchers who entered the subfield prior to the growth period and are embedded in the mature collaboration structure of the field. These features distinguish between exposure from early contact with frontier researchers, gradual accumulation of collaborative influence, and embedding within research environments.

We train gradient-boosted decision tree models using the LightGBM implementation [4] to predict yearly entry into each subfield. To ensure robust evaluation and prevent information leakage, we use expanding-window temporal cross-validation, training on all observations prior to a given test year and evaluating on that year. Model performance is evaluated using AUC-ROC across temporal folds, and results are reported as mean and standard deviation across folds and across scientific fields. To interpret the contributions of different exposure mechanisms, we combine SHAP-based interpretability analyses [5] with grouped ablation experiments that measure changes in predictive performance when theoretically related feature sets are removed.

Across all five subfields, we observe consistent patterns. First, early exposure to Recent Entrants is strongly associated with subsequent entry into the field. The timing of the first collaboration with a Recent Entrant provides a substantial predictive signal, as removing this feature group produces a notable decline in the model performance (mean $\Delta AUC \approx -0.06$) (Fig. \ref{fig:image1}). Second, the marginal contribution of cumulative exposure diminishes as exposure increases. SHAP dependence plots reveal steep marginal gains at low levels of exposure followed by rapid flattening, indicating diminishing returns from additional collaborations with entrants (Fig. \ref{fig:image2}). Correspondingly, removing cumulative exposure features produces only minimal decreases in predictive accuracy once timing and collaborator composition are considered.

Third, and most interestingly, exposure to Established Entrants is associated with a lower entry probability of entering the emerging subfield. This feature group produces the largest decline in predictive performance when removed (mean $\Delta AUC \approx -0.08$ to $-0.10$), suggesting that researchers embedded in mature collaboration environments may be less likely to transition into newly expanding domains. This pattern replicates across all five subfields and remains stable across temporal cross-validation folds.

Taken together, these findings suggest that entry into emerging scientific fields depends less on \textit{how} much exposure researchers accumulate and more on \textit{when} exposure occurs and \textit{which} researchers are part of their collaboration networks. In particular, early connections to researchers who are themselves entering a field appear to provide an important pathway into emerging domains, whereas strong ties to established collaborators in a subfield may reinforce existing research trajectories.

Empirically, the results reveal robust cross-field patterns in how collaboration exposure relates to researcher entry into growing subfields. Conceptually, the findings challenge diffusion accounts that emphasize the simple accumulation of exposure and instead highlight the importance of temporal dynamics and collaborator roles in shaping opportunities for scientific exploration. Future work can extend this analysis by incorporating additional structural network metrics such as betweenness centrality, brokerage, and structural hole measures, which may capture positional advantages that interact with exposure dynamics. Such extensions would further clarify how collaboration networks shape pathways through which researchers move into emerging scientific domains.

posters.title: Detecting and Linking Science Mentions in Podcasts: A Framework for Off‑Channel Diffusion
posters.authors: Hong Chen, Misha Teplitskiy and David Jurgens
posters.keywords: science communication podcasts off‑channel diffusion large language models information retrieval
posters.abstract: Podcasts are widely consumed; more than 42 % of Americans listen monthly. However, the medium’s informal format allows unverified claims to circulate. Standard altmetric tools capture diffusion through identifiers like DOIs, leaving blind spots for generic statements such as “a study showed.” We define a “science mention” as any podcast utterance that invokes scientific authority, conveys a claim, and may include cues but need not cite a paper. We process over one million podcast episodes from the SPoRC corpus using a hybrid LLM classifier to identify candidate mentions and then employ GPT‑4.1 to search bibliographic databases for potential source papers. Early results indicate that science talk is rare but frequent enough to yield thousands of mentions, concentrated in health and technology. We are able to locate the sources of these mentions with around 70 % accuracy, demonstrating the feasibility of mapping off‑channel diffusion in practice.

posters.title: POIFormer: Improving Behavioral Inference from Mobility Data through Transformer-Based Point-of-Interest Attribution
posters.authors: Nripsuta Ani Saxena, Shang-Ling Hsu, Mehul Shetty, Omar Alkhadra, Cyrus Shahabi and Abigail Horn
posters.keywords: point-of-interest attribution observational data human mobility transformer models behavioral inference
posters.abstract: Mobility data are increasingly used to study social behavior, yet mapping noisy GPS traces to specific points of interest (POIs), a prerequisite for venue-level behavioral analysis, remains error-prone, especially in dense urban settings where dozens of POIs fall within GPS error bounds. We introduce POIFormer, a transformer-based framework that jointly models spatial proximity, temporal context, individual mobility patterns, and crowd-level visitation trends to disambiguate POI visits without requiring detailed spatial metadata. Evaluated on two real-world-derived datasets spanning Los Angeles and a mid-sized Swiss city, POIFormer substantially outperforms existing baselines, including the current state-of-the-art, with top-3 accuracy gains exceeding 11 percentage points. By reducing measurement error before raw coordinates become behavioral observations, POIFormer improves the reliability of downstream behavioral analyses, from food-environment exposure studies to segregation research, which depend on accurate venue-level attribution of observational mobility data.

posters.title: Epistemic Appeals in Scientific Claims on Reddit
posters.authors: Daniel Hickey, Jevin West and David Bamman
posters.keywords: Science communication Reddit Social media
posters.abstract: Social media is increasingly used to learn about, disseminate, and debate scientific issues. However, research shows that many scientific issues are not just accepted truths. They are hotly contested on social media, often in ways that misrepresent the scientific consensus. While prior work indicates that anti-consensus communities often defer to expert authority, communities on either side of a scientific debate may still differ in which experts, institutions, and sources they deem as trustworthy. In this work, we build a model to detect scientific claims on Reddit and introduce a taxonomy for categorizing epistemic appeals -- the ways claims are anchored in external knowledge, authority, or expertise -- in those claims. To understand the shifting landscape of science communication on social media, we apply our scientific claim detection model on a sample of 7 billion Reddit comments from 2005-2022, finding that the rate of scientific claims on the platform has gone down, as well as the rate of URLs that accompanying scientific claims. At the source level, we find that links to Wikipedia have decreased over time in scientific claims, while links to scientific journals have become more frequent. Manual annotation of a sample of scientific claims reveals that while most claims are presented without evidence (66%), claims also frequently appeal to the authority of scientific studies and methods.

posters.title: AI-Assisted Writing Is Growing Fastest Among Non-English-Speaking and Less Established Scientists
posters.authors: Jialin Liu, Yi Bu and Chaoqun Ni
posters.keywords: AI-assisted writing academic writing scientific publishing large language models
posters.abstract: The dominance of English in global science has long created significant barriers for scientists from non-English-speaking environment. The recent emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has the potential to mitigate the constraints, yet it raises a critical question: how is the technology being adopted by the global scientific community, and is it mitigating existing inequities? This study provides large-scale empirical evidence by analyzing over two million full-text biomedical publications from PubMed Central from 2021 to 2024, estimating the fraction of AI-generated content using a distribution-based framework. We observe a significant post-ChatGPT surge in AI-assisted writing, with adoption growing fastest in contexts where language barriers are most pronounced. Notably, this trend is particularly pronounced among less-established scientists, including those with fewer publications and citations, as well as those in early career stages at lower-ranked institutions. Prior AI research experience also predicts greater increase in AI adoption. Finally, increased AI usage is associated with a modest increase in productivity, narrowing the publication gap between scientists from English-speaking and non-English-speaking countries with higher levels of AI adoption. These findings show that AI-assisted writing is growing fastest among individuals who have historically faced barriers in academia. By reducing the burden of academic writing, generative AI has the potential to mitigate inequalities in science, though it raises new questions about disclosure and evaluation.

posters.title: Peer Review and the Exposure and Adoption of New Ideas
posters.authors: Binglu Wang, Zhengnan Ma, Dashun Wang and Brian Uzzi
posters.keywords: Peer review Knowledge diffusion Innovation Adoption Citation dynamics Science of science
posters.abstract: In science, practices that spread ideas sharpen future thinking and foster innovation. Yet, research examining practices beyond journal publications, conferences, or networks remains limited. Here, we investigate the rarely studied link between peer review and knowledge diffusion. Our data cover 37,000 submitting authors and hundreds of thousands of reviewers. To measure exposure and adoption dynamics, we do not study reviewers who accepted the review invitation. Instead, our data permits us to compare reviewers who manually declined the review and reviewers who were auto-declined. These groups receive identical invitation emails containing manuscript summary information but differ in that manual-decliners likely viewed the summary information before declining, while auto-decliners did not. This distinction enables us to compare the adoption patterns of reviewers who were, and were not, exposed to new ideas. We find that peer review predicts substantive changes in idea adoption. First, it increases in the expected frequency of citations to an author’s work. Second, substantial changes are also manifested in new citation patterns. After exposure, peer reviewer invitees increase the range, diversity, and prominence of citations to the submitting author’s broader work. Third, these changes are persistent. After five years, declining reviewer invitees cite an author’s work 29% more than expected. The massive scale of peer review, entailing millions of reviews annually, often drives policy debates about its efficacy. Precisely because of this scale and potential AI-driven changes to the peer review system that increase efficiency but can reduce learning opportunities, our findings raise potentially far-reaching implications for science policy.

posters.title: Hierarchy of urban local centers from mobility divergence
posters.authors: Oh-Hyun Kwon, Damin Lee, Woo-Sung Jung, Hyejin Youn, Jaehyuk Park and Inho Hong
posters.keywords: Human mobility Mobility divergence Urban structure Hierarchy Polycentricity
posters.abstract: We introduce mobility divergence, a vector-field–based measure derived from human mobility flows, to uncover the geographical hierarchy of urban structure beyond dominant downtown cores. Using monthly SafeGraph mobility data for the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas, we construct a discrete mobility vector field on a 2 km × 2 km grid and compute local divergence to identify areas where flows converge (attractive centers) or diverge (repulsive boundaries). Unlike mobility potential, which primarily reflects monocentric structure, mobility divergence captures local distortions in flow, enabling the detection of peripheral and functionally independent centers. By identifying local minima within varying spatial thresholds, we reveal hierarchical relationships among centers and quantify their local coverage. We find that intra-traffic rates increase with population, but also independently with local coverage, indicating that broader-coverage centers function as more self-sustained units. Cross-city comparisons further show that smaller cities tend to exhibit star-like hierarchies, whereas larger cities develop more complex, nested substructures. Overall, mobility divergence provides a new framework for identifying hidden local centers and characterizing the polycentric and hierarchical organization of contemporary cities.

posters.title: The selective use of physics knowledge in policy: how interdisciplinary physics bridges subfields and shapes policy influence
posters.authors: Jeongmin Lee and Jisung Yoon
posters.keywords: Science Policy Use of Science Policy Impact Science of Science Interdisciplinary research
posters.abstract: Scientific knowledge has become central to policymaking as societies face challenges related to technological change, climate risk, and public health. Despite the growing emphasis on evidence-based policy, a systematic understanding of how science is selectively used in policy, specifically which forms of knowledge are preferred and which scientific citations translate into influence, remains limited. We address these questions by constructing a novel dataset that links policy documents from the Overton database with publications from the American Physical Society, enabling an analysis of how physics knowledge enters and circulates in policy discourse. Using subfield classifications, we provide quantitative evidence for a gap between scientific communities and policymakers. First, we find that policy documents draw on broad and interdisciplinary areas of physics, such as General Physics and Interdisciplinary Physics, rather than mirroring the structure of physics research production. Second, we identify substantial institutional heterogeneity with systematic differences in subfield preferences across policy producing organizations and topics. Third, network analysis reveals that interdisciplinary areas of physics act as a central bridge connecting specialized subfields. Finally, regression analysis reveals a clear separation between policy visibility and policy influence. While interdisciplinary areas facilitate entry into policy discourse, it does not necessarily increase downstream policy influence. Conversely, documents citing geophysics are associated with approximately 24 percent higher policy influence, likely driven by the political salience of climate change policy. Our findings underscore the distinction between scientific visibility and policy influence, contributing to a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between scientific communities and policy system.

posters.title: Formalizing Schemata: The Schematicity Corollary
posters.authors: Charles Torres
posters.keywords: simplicity minimum description length learning language change language contact cognitive science
posters.abstract: In extension of the "simplicity principle" in human concept learning we provide a formalization for schemata, or facilitative learning according to past events (Bartlett, 1932). We demonstrate how this formalization is a corollary of the broader simplicity principle. We then consider how this formalization may be used in practice to address large-scale phenomena like contact-induced language change.

posters.title: Suspense and Surprise: How Expectations Shape Technological Innovation
posters.authors: Oh-Hyun Kwon, Seungwoong Ha, Jisung Yoon, Lav R. Varshney, Woo-Sung Jung and Hyejin Youn
posters.keywords: Technological Innovation Recombination Prediction Patent Data Machine Learning
posters.abstract: Innovation is not only a combinatorial search process but also a narrative one, structured by expectations about how technologies ought to evolve. We conceptualize these expectations as generating two distinct inventive dynamics: suspense, when new recombinations fulfill prior expectations, and surprise, when they depart from them. Using 8.9 million USPTO patents (1840–2015), we classify technological recombinations according to whether they align with or deviate from historically grounded expectations about technological trajectories. We find that the vast majority of inventions are suspenseful in two cognitive prediction models: inventors tend to reinforce established patterns, producing combinations that are both visible and technologically coherent. Yet the most impactful breakthroughs do not simply resolve suspense. Instead, they exhibit an asymmetry—introducing surprise in terms of popularity while preserving underlying contextual coherence. Such combinations, which are novel but still “make sense,” have the highest probability of entering the top 5% of citation and market value distributions. Exceptional inventors also adopt this strategy, deviating from prevailing trends without violating technological logic. We argue that high-impact innovation emerges not from surprise alone, but from the strategic balance between fulfilling and betraying expectations. By formalizing suspense and surprise in technological recombination, our framework highlights how the alignment between expectation and realization shapes inventive behavior, risk-taking, and breakthrough impact.

posters.title: Expanding the Remote Associates Task: Capturing h-creativity through random, abstract associations
posters.authors: Hope Schroeder and Ziv Epstein
posters.keywords: creativity LLMs remote associates test convergent creativity
posters.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become embedded in research and problem-solving workflows, debate has emerged over whether they augment creativity or risk homogenizing it. This discussion has centered on the Remote Associates Test (RAT), a canonical benchmark of convergent creativity in which participants identify a single word linking three cues. We first report the most comprehensive benchmark to date of LLM performance on 312 classic RAT items, comparing models of different sizes and difficulty levels alongside human performance on a controlled subset. While larger models outperform smaller ones, classic RAT items largely rely on entrenched lexical associations, potentially favoring statistical fluency over deeper conceptual integration and disadvantaging non-native speakers. To address this limitation, we introduce an expanded RAT that requires models to generate coherent relational principles linking randomly sampled noun triples without predefined solutions. Evaluating 600 generated principles across models and temperature settings, we classify associative strategies into functional, abstract, metaphorical, and structural categories. Results suggest systematic differences in associative style across model size and stochasticity. Together, our benchmarking and expanded task contribute to computational social science efforts to more meaningfully measure convergent creativity in humans, LLMs, and human–AI teams.

posters.title: Towards a Computational Framework for Narrative Causal Structure Analysis
posters.authors: Qiusi Sun, Sarah Hoover, Corinthian Ewesuedo and Joshua Introne
posters.keywords: Narrative Causal Structure Large Language Models Human-AI Annotation News Media
posters.abstract: Narratives structure information through interconnected events, actors, and causal relationships, shaping how people interpret and integrate complex information. However, existing computational text analysis methods often overlook these causal structures. This project develops a computational infrastructure for extracting narrative causal structures from long-form text. We build a large-language-model-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that identifies actors, events, states, and their causal relationships in news articles and converts them into machine-readable narrative graphs. Preliminary results from a human-annotated corpus of news articles suggest that LLM-based tools show promise for scalable extraction of narrative structures for social science research.

posters.title: Meat-Free Day Reduces Carbon Emissions and Support Positive Eating Habits, but Customer Retention Poses a Risk
posters.authors: Giuseppe Russp, Kristina Gligoric, Vincent Moreau and Robert West
posters.keywords: Field Experiments Simulation Nutrition GHG Emissions Meat Free Day
posters.abstract:
Motivation and Research Questions. Current consumption of animal-derived food is in- compatible with the sustainability and nutritional targets set by the UN Sustainability and Nu- trition Strategy 2022-2030 (4). Achieving these goals requires wealthy countries to reduce their meat consumption by 80%, a weekly decrease of 2.4 kg/person of meat eaten (7; 5). Shift- ing behavior towards plant-based diets is difficult due to misconceptions about the nutritional value of plant-based meals (6). In response to these barriers, governments and institutions have funded various initiatives aimed at reducing meat consumption. The most prominent of these initiatives is “Meat-Free Day” (MFD). Proposed more than 20 years ago, MFD has become a global movement implemented in over 40 countries affecting more than 10,000 cafeterias and millions of people. Despite the wide interest in the MFD initiative, existing studies (2; 3) have mainly used qualitative evidence to assess MFD targets: (i) increasing plant-based meal consumption to reduce GHG emissions, (ii) promoting behavioral change to limit reliance on animal-based meals, and (iii) improving nutritional quality. For each of these targets, we formulate a research question: (RQ1) Does restricting the availability of animal-based meals during MFD lead to a measurable reduction in the GHG emissions of food purchases? (RQ2) Does the restriction of choice on MFD trigger behavioral responses that counteract its intended effects? (RQ3) What are the nutritional implications of MFD, and does the removal of meat-based meals lead to compensatory habits? Experimental Setup. To answer these RQs, we implemented 67 MFDs across twelve col- lege cafeterias at the Ecole Polytechnique Fe ́de ́rale de Lausanne (EPFL). The intervention was conducted once a week over 18 months, with a single day each week randomly selected to serve as a MFD. This random selection was made by the administration without prior notice to the campus community, ensuring an unbiased assessment of the intervention’s effects. In total, to study the impact of these 67 MFDs we analyzed 402,536 food purchases. To evaluate the effects of MFD, we adopt two complementary setups (see Figure 1). The first, On MFD Analy- sis, examines the immediate impact of MFD on the day of intervention, assessing its effects on three outcomes: (i) GHG emissions (RQ1), (ii) purchasing behavior (RQ2), and (iii) calories and macronutrients intake (RQ3). To measure this changes, we compared each MFD to a cor- responding non-MFD occured on the preceding week of MFD but on the same weekday (see Figure 1(a)). The second setup, Beyond MFD Analysis, extends the investigation to the days following MFD, evaluating whether the intervention produces beneficial changes in customers’ eating habits or triggers unintended compensatory behaviors that could mitigate its intended benefits. To assess this, we analyze variations in the three outcomes on two non-MFDs from consecutive weeks: one occurring the day after an MFD and another occurring at least two days after the MFD of its respective week (see Figure 1(b)).

Results Our findings demonstrate that MFDs achieve a remarkable 52.9% reduction in food- system GHG emissions compared to non-MFD (RQ1-Same Day Analysis; see Figure 2(a)). Al- though this reduction underscores the significant environmental benefits of MFD, we also iden- tify unintended consequences: meal sales drop by 16.8%, which translates to 520 fewer meals sold compared to the daily baseline of 3,092 meals on non-MFD (RQ2-Same Day Analysissee Figure 2(b)). Opting-out customers are likely to consume animal-based meals off-campus, either from a nearby fast-food restaurant offering burgers or from other off-campus options offering animal-based meals with comparatively lower emissions than the burgers. Due to the lack of direct data on off-campus dining sales, we employed Monte Carlo simulations to esti- mate the impact of off-campus dining on MFD’s overall GHG savings. This analysis revealed that, even when assuming all opting-out customers choose lower-emission off-campus meals, 58.6% of MFD’s GHG savings could be offset (see Figure 3). Our simulation indicates that if 50.1% of opting-out customers—-equivalent to 8.7% of the campus community that dines in cafeterias on a typical day—-choose to eat burgers at the fast-food restaurant, the GHG sav- ings achieved by MFD would be fully counterbalanced by the emissions associated with these off-campus meal choices. Further, we found no evidence that exposure to vegetarian meals during MFD fosters plant- based eating habits beyond the intervention day (RQ2-Beyond-Day Analysis). Instead, we ob- serve a statistically significant 3.5% increase in animal-based meal consumption on the day following an MFD. This rebound contributes an additional increase of 414.2 kgCO2e in GHG emissions compared to non-MFD that occur at least two days after an MFD (RQ2-Beyond- Day Analysis). When considering the rebound effect and off-campus dining, the proportion of customers needed to offset GHG emission savings from Meat-Free Days (MFDs) decreases to 40.1%—equivalent to 6.7% of the campus community that dines in cafeterias on a regular day. If this fraction of customers opts for fast-food restaurants near campus instead of MFDs, the GHG savings from MFDs would be entirely nullified. Regarding the impact of MFD on nutrition (RQ3-Same Day Analysis; see Figure 4), we find no measurable change in total caloric intake, suggesting that implementing MFD does not inherently reduce overall energy consumption (1). However, the impact on macronutrients intake is mixed. Increases in fibers (+27.2%) and reduction in cholesterol (-4.5%) suggest potential health benefits. At the same time, the rise in sugar intake (+39.9%) and decrease in protein consumption (+27.1%) may warrant attention if sustained over time. We find no statistically significant change in neither caloric nor macronutrients in days subsequent to MFD (RQ3-Beyond Day Analysis) Implications. Our studies show that the Meat-Free Day initiative is not a silver bullet. From a nutritional perspective, while MFD can introduce positive dietary shifts such as increased fiber consumption, the concurrent increase in sugar intake and reduction in protein highlight the necessity of carefully designing vegetarian meal options to minimize potential adverse ef- fects. Moreover, MFD yield substantial reductions in GHG emissions associated with campus food consumption. Despite this climate benefit, our findings identify customer retention as a potential threat to the overall success of the intervention. The identification of retention as a pivotal factor highlights two potential strategies for en- hancing the environmental impact of MFDs. The first involves integrating MFD with comple- mentary interventions designed to improve customer participation in MFD on campus. The second approach suggests moving beyond rigid frameworks like MFD by intervening more deeply in the environmental setup of cafeterias. This could involve strategies such as reducing the prominence of high-emission ingredients while promoting a balanced selection of animal- and plant-based meal options.

posters.title: How Do Academic Gatekeepers Evaluate Figures? An Empirical Study of Peer Review Reports Using Large Language Models
posters.authors: Jialin Liu, Xiang Zheng, Weiye Gu, Xi Hong and Chaoqun Ni
posters.keywords: peer review visualization figure quality large language models
posters.abstract: Figures are pivotal components of research presentation, yet how academic gatekeepers evaluate figure quality during peer review remains underexplored. This study compiled over 30,000 multidisciplinary peer review reports from Publons and OpenReview. We manually developed a coding schema to categorize figure critiques into three dimensions: effectiveness, understandability, and readability. Then, we utilized a large language model (GPT-5-mini) for large-scale automated extraction and labeling. Findings reveal that nearly half of the submitted manuscripts received figure-related comments, with biomedical papers attracting the highest volumns. Critiques concerning effectiveness (e.g., missing components) were the most prevalent, followed by understandability and readability. Furthermore, figure quality is significantly correlated with peer review outcomes: manuscripts receiving high ratings or minor revisions accrued noticeably fewer visual critiques, and reviewers reporting higher confidence levels are more likely to identify visual flaws. This study empirically highlights the crucial role of figure quality in academic gatekeeping, validates the efficacy of AI as a data annotator in the science of science, and provides insights for establishing standardized figure evaluation guidelines.

posters.title: Stop Automating Peer Review Without Rigorous Evaluation
posters.authors: Joachim Baumann, Jiaxin Pei, Sanmi Koyejo and Dirk Hovy
posters.keywords: peer review large language models paper laundering artificial hivemind effect
posters.abstract: Large language models offer a tempting solution to address the peer review crisis. This paper argues that today's AI systems should not be used to produce paper reviews. We ground this position in an empirical comparison of human- versus AI-generated ICLR 2026 reviews and an evaluation of the effect of automated paper rewriting on different AI reviewers. We identify two critical issues: 1) AI reviewers exhibit a hivemind effect of excessive agreement within and across papers that reduces perspective diversity. 2) AI review scores are trivially gameable through paper laundering: prompting an LLM to rewrite a paper could significantly increase the scores from AI reviewers, demonstrating that LLM reviewers are easy to game through stylistic changes rather than scientific results. However, non-gameability and review diversity are necessary but not sufficient conditions for automation. We argue that addressing the peer review crisis requires a science of peer review automation--not general-purpose LLMs deployed without rigorous evaluation.

posters.title: Overfitted Inferior Equilibria \\from Two-Sided Learning on the Wisdom of Crowds
posters.authors: Kazuya Inagaki and Yusuke Hara
posters.keywords: wisdom of crowds preferential attachment exploration exploitation demand and supply decision-making
posters.abstract: Rankings and reviews aggregate people’s evaluations and choices and are widely treated as the wisdom of crowds that improves decision-making. We challenge this premise by asking whether decision-making based on the wisdom of crowds, while generally desirable for the social system as a whole, might nevertheless induce systematically biased collective decisions that hinder a better social state. We call this systemic failure an \emph{overfitted inferior equilibrium}: despite diverse options, agents over-trust a crowd-based signal as if it were accurate, complete demand information (overfitting), which can lock the system into an inefficient social state (inferiority). To reveal the mechanism, we build a two-sided agent-based model with individuals (demand-side agents), stores (supply-side agents), and an exogenous online platform provider that can publish store rankings. Individuals and stores repeatedly balance exploration and exploitation under incomplete information, while rankings summarize aggregate choices and feed back into both populations’ decisions, generating a double feedback structure and multiple equilibria. We evaluate equilibrium efficiency using cumulative social welfare and compare equilibria with and without published rankings. Numerical simulations show that rankings typically improve efficiency when only individuals adapt (learned superior equilibrium). However, when stores also adapt, rankings can reduce efficiency, especially under heterogeneous preferences: stores follow the majority signal, minority-preferred options disappear, and welfare-improving matches are prevented. Even under a neutral, transparent platform, endogenous two-sided responses can degrade system performance, highlighting a systemic risk in ranking-mediated markets.

posters.title: Large Language Model Hacking: Using LLMs for Text Annotation Allows Presenting Anything as Significant
posters.authors: Joachim Baumann, Paul Röttger, Aleksandra Urman, Albert Wendsjö, Flor Miriam Plaza-del-Arco, Johannes B. Gruber and Dirk Hovy
posters.keywords: large language models p-hacking research integrity llms for social research reproducibility
posters.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming social science research by enabling the automation of labor-intensive tasks like data annotation and text analysis. However, LLM outputs vary significantly depending on the configuration choices made by researchers (e.g., model selection or prompting strategy). Such variation can introduce systematic biases and random errors, which propagate to downstream analyses and cause Type I, Type II, or Type S errors. We call this phenomenon, where configuration choices lead to incorrect conclusions, LLM hacking. We find that intentional LLM hacking is strikingly simple. By replicating 37 data annotation tasks from 21 published social science studies, we show that, with just a handful of prompt paraphrases, virtually anything can be presented as statistically significant. Beyond intentional manipulation, our analysis of 13 million labels from 18 different LLMs across 2,361 realistic hypotheses reveals a 31-50% risk of accidental LLM hacking, even when following standard research practices.

posters.title: Measuring community and hierarchy in social systems
posters.authors: Maximilian Jerdee, Elizabeth Bruch and Mark Newman
posters.keywords: Network analysis Stratification Hierarchy Community Bayesian inference
posters.abstract:
Social life is organized along two fundamental dimensions: people are ranked relative to one another (vertical stratification), and people cluster into distinct groups and communities (horizontal stratification). Classical stratification theory focused primarily on the vertical dimension—a single ranked order where individuals or groups differ in overall level of esteem and resources (Lenski 1954; Parsons 1940). Later theorists recognized that modern societies involve multiple, partially independent hierarchies producing complex patterns rather than a single ladder (Lenski 1954; Weber 1946). More recently, scholars have distinguished status (vertical inequality in respect and prestige) from patterns of affiliation and power-sharing (horizontal arrangements of who cooperates with whom, who is “in” or “out”) (Ridgeway 2014). Horizontal relations—the boundaries that define communities, cliques, and factions—are conceptually distinct from, though potentially related to, vertical rank.

Yet despite extensive theorizing about how these dimensions might intersect, empirical work has largely examined vertical and horizontal stratification separately. Studies of status hierarchies measure popularity, prestige, or centrality without attending to community structure. Studies of social networks identify clusters, cliques, and communities without examining how these map onto status orderings. This separation obscures a fundamental question: How tightly coupled are vertical and horizontal stratification, and to what extent does this coupling vary across societies?

This question matters because the degree of coupling has implications for social mobility, inequality, and the reproduction of advantage. When vertical and horizontal stratification are tightly coupled—when community membership strongly predicts status position—social organization resembles a caste system: each group occupies a distinct rung on the status ladder, and crossing group boundaries means crossing status boundaries as in Figure~\ref{fig:depth-comparison}B. When coupling is loose—when each community contains its own range of status positions—social organization resembles ``parallel hierarchies": groups are differentiated horizontally but not necessarily ranked vertically, and individuals can achieve high or low status within their own community regardless of that community's position relative to others as typified in Figure~\ref{fig:depth-comparison}E.

There are compelling theoretical reasons to expect these dimensions to interact: to deviate from a pure parallel hierarchy. The ``entourage effect" in adolescent peer networks illustrates how associating with high-status peers elevates an individual's own prestige, independent of their personal traits (Dijkstra et al. 2010; Marks et al. 2012; Milner 2016). Social closure provides another mechanism by which group boundaries become consequential for stratification. Insiders block outsiders from resources and networks, while actively preventing subordinate groups from constructing parallel status systems (Mackert 2021).

As Milner (2016) points out, the coupling between community membership and status is strongly influenced by the size and homogeneity of the broader social setting. In smaller and more homogeneous contexts, it is easier for consensus to form around a single status system and for high-status groups to maintain clear boundaries. This produces a tighter alignment between group membership and social rank, so belonging to a particular community strongly signals an individual's status. In contrast, larger and more diverse environments tend to foster multiple, overlapping hierarchies and greater boundary permeability. Here, group affiliation and status are less tightly linked, resulting in a more pluralistic social structure where individuals can attain high status within their own group regardless of its position in the broader hierarchy.

Despite these expectations, empirical studies have seldom examined vertical and horizontal stratification together. Network science tools to detect hierarchies and communities are typically applied in isolation, leaving the intersection of rank and group boundaries empirically underexplored. This paper remedies the gap by proposing a unified Bayesian statistical model that infers both latent community structure and hierarchical status from social interactions. By integrating the strengths of stochastic block modeling for communities and Bradley-Terry-Luce models for status ranking, our framework quantifies the coupling between group membership and rank, directly corresponding to theoretical mechanisms (Peixoto 2019, Ball 2013, Zermelo 1929). We particularly build upon recent work that infers not only positions within a hierarchy but also the overall ``depth"~$\sigma$ -- the spread in status that captures the extent of behavioral inequality (Jerdee 2024). Our new approach decomposes this overall stratification into within-group ($\sigma_I$) and between-group ($\sigma_C$) components, allowing rigorous testing of whether and how community boundaries predict status, and how this varies across contexts. Bayesian model selection further enables us to directly empirically adjudicate between the ``caste-like" and ``parallel hierarchy" archetypes and possible structures between them.

Applying this joint modeling framework to the AddHealth dataset of U.S. high school peer networks, we uncover significant contextual variation in the relationship between group membership and status. In several schools, community and status are largely independent; individuals achieve status within their community without group boundaries strongly predicting rank. In others, “cool groups” emerge whose members interact primarily among themselves and occupy systematically higher status positions, exemplifying tight coupling between hierarchy and community. This rich variety of structures is summarized in Figure~\ref{fig:depth-comparison}, which shows our inferences and uncertainties for each high school within the data set. Across these examples the model rejects both pure parallel hierarchy ($\sigma_C = 0$) and rigid caste-like archetypes ($\sigma_I = 0$), demonstrating that actual social organization span a rich set of interactions and potentially mechanisms.

Crucially, our findings show that as school size increases, overall depth of stratification diminishes, mainly due to reduced ranking between communities as in Figure~\ref{fig:depth-vs-size}. Within-group hierarchy remains stable regardless of school size—supporting Milner’s hypothesis that in smaller settings greater visibility facilitates a stronger alignment between rank and boundary, while larger schools encourage looser coupling and pluralistic arrangements.

This work advances research in stratification by forging a methodological and conceptual bridge between social theory and empirical technique. By unifying community and hierarchy models within a single Bayesian framework, we bring empirical study closer to nuanced theoretical expectations and enable direct measurement of mechanisms such as social closure and status borrowing. The findings illustrate that neither complete independence nor rigid alignment of group boundaries and status fully capture adolescent networks; instead, stratification is shaped by institutional context, group mechanisms, and broader social architecture. Our approach opens new avenues for investigating how inequality is structured and reproduced, providing tools to rigorously address questions about boundary maintenance, mobility, and the contingent nature of advantage. By aligning theory and measurement, this work lays a foundation for future studies of social organization across a range of contexts and populations.
